docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
Route.get('/blogs', BlogController.index); // (1)!

enum Status { active, draft }

@Dto() // (2)!
class BlogFilter {
  final Status status; // ?status=active, else 422
  const BlogFilter({required this.status});
  static const DtoSchema<BlogFilter> schema =
      $BlogFilterDto; // (3)!
}

class BlogController {
  static Future<List<Blog>> index(
    BlogFilter query, // (4)!
  ) async {
    return Blog()
        .where('status', query.status.name)
        .get(); // (5)!
  }
}
  1. A route points at a static method. No reflection, no controller registry.
  2. @Dto() marks an input class. build_runner generates the checks from the fields and their types.
  3. The generated schema. The same schema feeds the OpenAPI docs.
  4. Ask for the DTO as a parameter. Dox reads the query (or the body), checks it, and gives you a typed object. Bad input gets a 422 before your code runs.
  5. The ORM. The same code runs on Postgres, MySQL and SQLite. Postgres and MySQL use native drivers.

docs.title: Fast backendsin Dart
docs.text:
Everything your Dart backend needs.

Dox is a web backend framework for Dart. Routing, an ORM, migrations, validation, auth and a CLI come in one place. It runs one isolate per CPU core and builds to a small native binary.

Build your first API GitHub Blog

docs.title: How fast
docs.text:
Ahead of Rust hyper. 1.3× Bun. 2.2× Node. 4.9× plain Dart.

A full Dox app answers GET /, with the rules of the-benchmarker. Requests per second on two CPU cores, higher is better.

req/s p99 RAM Doxnative server 638,067fastest 0.7 ms 19 MB Rusthyper 585,6581.09× slower 0.7 ms 13 MB BunBun.serve 501,5291.27× slower 1.0 ms 40 MB Nodenode:http 286,8472.2× slower 1.7 ms 200 MB Gonet/http 242,0432.6× slower 3.3 ms 36 MB dart:ioHttpServer 129,7964.9× slower 3.8 ms 75 MB

Dox · Rust 1.99 · Bun 1.4 · Node 26 · Go 1.26 · Dart 3.13 · 2 cores · 256 connections · wrkAll results

Your code is plain Dart. The speed comes from the native server: it runs on the isolate's own thread, so a request never waits for another thread. See Performance for every route and how it was run.

docs.title: Run it in two minutes
docs.text:
You need Dart 3.13 or newer. Nothing else: the starter project uses SQLite, so there is no database to install.

dart pub global activate dox             # install the CLI
dox create my_app                            # download the starter project
cd my_app
dart pub get
dox s                                        # start the server

Open a second terminal and call the first route:

curl localhost:3000/ping

pong

That is a Dox app. Keep going with the tutorial: it adds a model, a database table, validation, login and a Docker image, one short step at a time.

The CLI is not found?

dart pub global activate puts dox in $HOME/.pub-cache/bin. Add that folder to your PATH. See Installation.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Fast by default

    A native HTTP server, one isolate per CPU core and streamed bodies. dox build makes one native binary. See Performance.

  • ORM and query builder

    Models, relations, migrations and transactions for Postgres, MySQL/MariaDB and SQLite. Postgres and MySQL use native drivers. See Database.

  • Typed validation

    Write a @Dto class. Dox checks the input and gives your controller a typed object. See Validation.

  • OpenAPI

    OpenAPI 3.1 docs and a Scalar docs page, made from your routes and DTOs. See dox_openapi.

  • File storage

    Local disk and S3 behind one API, with signed URLs. See dox_storage.

  • Cache

    Memory, file and Redis cache with tags and locks. See dox_cache.

  • Real time

    Socket.IO, with Redis for many servers.

  • Security

    JWT authentication, CORS, encryption and hashing.

  • CLI

    Create projects, controllers, models and migrations. Run, build and migrate. See CLI reference.

docs.title: Get help
docs.text:
• Found a bug or have a question? Open an issue on GitHub.
  • Using an AI assistant? Give it llms-full.txt: all of these docs as one plain text file. llms.txt is the page list.
  • Want to help? Read Contribute.

docs.title: Contribute
docs.text:
This page shows how to work on Dox: set up the repo, run the tests, release packages and update the docs.

To send a change, fork the repo and open a pull request.

docs.title: 1. Clone the repo
docs.text: git clone git@github.com:dartondox/dox.git

docs.title: 2. Install melos
docs.text:
The repo is a Dart pub workspace. The melos config is in the root pubspec.yaml (under melos:). Use Dart 3.13 or newer.

dart pub global activate melos

docs.title: 3. Run melos bootstrap
docs.text:
It runs one dart pub get at the root. All local packages are linked. There is one pubspec.lock for the whole repo.

melos bs

docs.title: 4. Useful commands
docs.text:
# Run all tests.
# Use `melos run test`. `melos test` is a built-in melos command.
melos run test

# Analyze and check format (same as CI)
melos run analyze
melos run format_check

docs.title: If the project does not run
docs.text:
1. Remove pubspec.lock and .dart_tool at the root.
  2. Remove any old pubspec_overrides.yaml and pubspec.lock in packages/* (left from melos 3).
  3. Run melos bs again.

docs.title: Release (maintainers)
docs.text: The Release GitHub workflow (.github/workflows/publish.yaml) publishes one package to pub.dev. Each package has its own version and its own tag, like dox_builder-v3.1.4 (<package>-v<version>). It uses pub.dev automated publishing, so it needs no token or secret.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
The full guide is RELEASING.md in the repo. In short, for each package that changed:

  1. Run bin/bump.sh <package> <version>. It sets the version of that package only. If the package needs a newer sibling, raise that constraint by hand. Close the ## Unreleased section of its CHANGELOG.md.
  2. Merge the release PR, then push the tag <package>-v<version>. This publishes that package to pub.dev. Release in dependency order: dox_annotation, dox_cache, dox_builder, dox_core.
  3. Release the matching dox-sample template.

A builder-only fix needs a dox_builder release only. It does not need a dox_core release.

The native packages (dox_http_native, dox_postgres_native, dox_mysql_native) are not in this repo. See Native packages below. dox_orm, dox_migration, dox_socketio, dox_storage, dox_queue, dox_queue_database, dox_scheduler, dox_inertia, dox_view and dox_mailer are not in this repo either. See Packages in other repos.

New package only: turn on pub.dev automated publishing for it first. See One-time setup. A new package must first exist on pub.dev, so publish its first version by hand with dart pub publish.

docs.title: What the workflow does
docs.text:
1. It reads the package name and the version from the tag. It stops with an error for an unknown package or a bad version.
  2. It checks that the version in packages/<folder>/pubspec.yaml is the tag version. If not, it stops. Run bin/bump.sh <package> <version> and try again.
  3. It runs the tests. They must pass. Then it checks that the sibling packages it needs are on pub.dev. If not, it stops: "release first".
  4. It checks that one package with a dry run, then publishes it.

    5. A tag for a version that is already on pub.dev is skipped. So if a run fails, fix the problem and click "Re-run jobs".

    To see the packages in publish order on your machine:

    python3 bin/publish_order.py

docs.title: Dry run
docs.text: Open Actions > Release > "Run workflow". Pick one package, or all. It runs dart pub publish --dry-run and publishes nothing. Warnings (for example a missing CHANGELOG entry) show as yellow warnings. They do not fail the run.

docs.title: One-time setup
docs.text:
Do this once for each published package, and for every new package before its first tag. The list of packages is the output of python3 bin/publish_order.py.

On pub.dev:

  1. Open https://pub.dev/packages/<name>/admin.
  2. Under "Automated publishing", click "Enable publishing from GitHub Actions".
  3. Repository: dartondox/dox.
  4. Tag pattern: <package>-v{{version}}, like dox_core-v{{version}}. Each package has its own pattern.
  5. Tick "Require GitHub Actions environment" and set the environment to pub.dev.
  6. Save.

On GitHub, in dartondox/dox > Settings > Environments, there must be an environment named pub.dev. The publish job runs in it. Optional: add yourself as a required reviewer, and allow only the tags dox_annotation-v*, dox_builder-v*, dox_cache-v* and dox_core-v*.

docs.title: Packages in other repos
docs.text:
Package Repo dox (the CLI) dartondox/dox-cli dox_orm, dox_migration, dox_cache_database dartondox/dox-orm dox_auth dartondox/dox-auth dox_openapi dartondox/dox-openapi dox_validation dartondox/dox-validation dox_socketio dartondox/dox-socketio dox_storage dartondox/dox-storage dox_queue, dox_queue_database dartondox/dox-queue dox_scheduler dartondox/dox-scheduler dox_inertia dartondox/dox-inertia dox_view dartondox/dox-view dox_mailer dartondox/dox-mailer

The packages here use them from pub.dev. The database tests (Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, SQLite) run in dox-orm. dox_core uses dox_openapi and dox_validation. CI in this repo uses their newest code: ci/clone-siblings.sh, then ci/use-siblings.sh.

To work on one of them and Dox together:

  1. Clone the repos next to the Dox repo, like ../dox-orm. ci/clone-siblings.sh clones dox-orm, dox-auth, dox-openapi, dox-validation, dox-socketio, dox-storage, dox-queue, dox-scheduler and dox-cli. Clone dox-mailer, dox-view and dox-inertia by hand when you need them.

  2. Add them to the root pubspec_overrides.yaml of the Dox repo. Git ignores this file. For dox_openapi and dox_validation, ci/use-siblings.sh writes this file for you.

    dependency_overrides:
  dox_openapi:
    path: ../dox-openapi
  dox_validation:
    path: ../dox-validation

  3. Run dart pub get.

The apps in examples/ already use these clones (their pubspec_overrides.yaml), so clone them before you run an example. In the other repo, a pubspec_overrides.yaml that points to ../dox/packages/... uses your local Dox packages.

Each repo has its own version. Push a v<version> tag in that repo to release it.

docs.title: Native packages
docs.text:
The three native packages live in their own repos:

Package Repo dox_http_native dartondox/dox-http-native dox_postgres_native dartondox/dox-postgres-native dox_mysql_native dartondox/dox-mysql-native

Dox uses them from pub.dev. Their build hooks download ready-built libraries, so you do not need Rust to work on Dox.

To work on a native package and Dox together:

  1. Clone the package next to the Dox repo, like ../dox-http-native.

  2. Add it to the root pubspec_overrides.yaml of the Dox repo. Git ignores this file.

    dependency_overrides:
  dox_http_native:
    path: ../dox-http-native

  3. Run dart pub get.

Each native package is released from its own repo, with its own version. Push a v<version> tag in that repo. Its CI builds the libraries, uploads them, fills the hashes and publishes the package to pub.dev. Then raise the version constraint in the Dox packages that use it.

docs.title: Docs
docs.text:
The docs site is https://dartondox.dev. It is built with MkDocs Material and mike. mike keeps one folder per version on the gh-pages branch.

URL What it is /3.x/... 3.x docs, built from main /latest/... a copy of the newest version (now 3.x) / redirects to /latest/ old links like /the-basic/routing/ redirect to /latest/the-basic/routing/

docs.title: Write and preview
docs.text:
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
.venv/bin/mkdocs serve           # live preview of this branch
.venv/bin/mkdocs build --strict  # the same build as CI. Broken links fail.

hooks/docs_hooks.py runs during the build. It makes the changelog page from packages/*/CHANGELOG.md, and writes llms.txt and llms-full.txt.

The Docs check workflow (.github/workflows/docs-check.yaml) runs on every pull request that changes the docs. It runs three checks:

  • mkdocs build --strict
  • a spell check: codespell docs --skip "*.svg,*.png,*.ico,*.css,*.js" --ignore-words .codespell-ignore
  • ci/check-no-tabs.sh: the docs must not use content tabs

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
• 3.x deploys with each release. The Docs workflow (.github/workflows/docs.yaml) runs on a dox_core-v<version> tag, the same tag that publishes dox_core. So docs for a feature that is not released yet stay off the site. It runs mike deploy --update-aliases 3.x latest.
  • To deploy the docs only (a typo fix, or the docs of a package from another repo that was just released), push a docs-v<version> tag on main, like git tag docs-v3.0.1-1 && git push origin docs-v3.0.1-1. It publishes no package and runs no tests.
  • After each deploy, the workflow writes small redirect pages for the old root links, the root index.html, a 404.html and the CNAME file. So dartondox.dev and old links keep working.
  • The workflow pushes with the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN. This works because gh-pages is not a protected branch.

docs.title: New major version
docs.text: When 4.x starts, deploy 4.x with mike deploy --update-aliases 4.x latest. Keep a v3.x branch, and add 3.x to the workflow input, so 3.x can still be fixed.

docs.title: Meet Doxie
docs.text: Doxie is the official mascot of Dox. Doxie is a blue dachshund.

docs.title: Why a dachshund
docs.text:
"Doxie" is a common nickname for a dachshund. It sounds like Dox, so the name came first.

A dachshund is small, fast and full of energy. Dox tries to be the same: a small native binary that serves a lot of requests.

docs.title: Logo and mascot
docs.text:
Dox has a logo and a mascot. They have different jobs.

Logo Mascot What A hexagon with a "D" cut out Doxie, the blue dachshund Where The docs header, the favicon, the README, pub.dev The home page, social cards, talks, stickers Files logo.svg (white, for dark backgrounds) mascot.png (transparent background)

Use the logo when the space is small, like an icon or an avatar. Doxie has too much detail to read well at 16 or 32 pixels.

docs.title: Colors
docs.text: Name Hex Used for Sky blue #5CC6FF Doxie's body, links in dark mode Dart blue #0A5FC2 Doxie's ears and collar, links in light mode Navy #0B1B36 The docs header, outlines

docs.title: Use Doxie
docs.text: You are welcome to use Doxie when you write or talk about Dox: blog posts, slides, videos and stickers. Please do not change Doxie's colors, and do not use Doxie to brand another product.

docs.title: Showcase
docs.text: This page lists real open source apps built with Dox that you can read, run and copy from.

docs.title: Monthly Expense
docs.text:
Monthly Expense is an expense tracker for you and the people you share money with. You log expenses, track wallets in many currencies and keep a shopping list. An AI assistant like Claude can add expenses and read summaries for you over MCP.

Part What it uses API Dox, with SQLite or Postgres Web app React, Vite, Tailwind and shadcn/ui Sign-in Firebase (Google), checked on every API request AI An MCP server with OAuth sign-in, 44 tools Deploy One Docker image with the web app and a native API binary

What you can learn from it:

  • ORM and migrations. Groups, members, categories, expenses, wallets and budgets as models. The app runs the migrations when it starts. See Model and Migration.
  • Token auth from another service. The API checks a Firebase ID token in middleware. It makes the user on the first sign-in. See Middleware.
  • MCP for AI clients. Each HTTP route has a matching MCP tool with the same input. See MCP.
  • Scheduled jobs. See Scheduler.
  • One container in production. The API serves the built web app and compiles to a native binary. CI runs the tests on SQLite and Postgres, then pushes the image. See Docker.

Run it on your machine:

git clone https://github.com/necessarylion/monthly-expense.git
cd monthly-expense
./dev.sh

The README lists the Firebase settings and env vars you need first.

docs.title: Add your app
docs.text: Built something with Dox? Open a pull request that adds it to this page. Your app must be open source, so readers can see the code.

docs.title: Coming from Laravel
docs.text:
This page is for Laravel developers: it shows the Laravel way and the Dox way side by side.

The Laravel code is Laravel 11. The biggest changes are in What is different.

docs.title: Routing
Controllers
docs.text:
Laravel Dox php artisan make:controller BlogController dox make:controller Blog php artisan make:controller BlogController --resource dox make:controller Blog -r (or --resource) php artisan make:controller BlogController --api dox make:controller Blog --api php artisan make:controller BlogController --model=Blog dox make:controller Blog --model=Blog public function show(Request $request, int $id) Future<Blog?> show(DoxRequest req, int id) public function store(StoreBlogRequest $request) Future<Blog> store(CreateBlog body) constructor injection by the service container constructor injection by the container: @Inject() above the class method injection filled by type: DoxRequest, one @Dto class, path params, models, container classes implicit route model binding the same: a User user parameter loads {user} by its key

Dox fills a parameter by its type, not by its name. Path params go by position. The container is generated code, not reflection. See Dependency injection. A controller can be a class method, a static method or a plain function.

Requests and validation
Responses

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
With dox_view, templates end in .dox.html. Most Blade tags have the same name. A block ends with @end.

A Blade name that is not a Dox tag, like @foreach or @endif, is printed as text. Dox writes a warning to stderr that names the template, the line and the Dox way. See Coming from Blade.

Laravel Blade Dox {{ $user->name }}, {!! $html !!} {{ user.name }}, {{{ html }}} @if ... @endif, @foreach ($users as $user) @if ... @end, @each(user in users) ... @end @isset, @empty, @auth, @guest, @env, @production, @once, @verbatim the same names, closed with @end @class, @checked, @selected, @disabled the same @include('nav'), @include('card', ['title' => 'Hi']) @include('nav'), @include('card', { title: 'Hi' }) @includeWhen($user, 'account') @includeWhen(user, 'account') $loop->iteration, $loop->remaining, $loop->even, $loop->parent $loop.iteration, $loop.remaining, $loop.even, $loop.parent @json($data), Js::from($data) @json(data), {{ json(data) }} @error('email') {{ $message }} @enderror @error('email') {{ message }} @end <x-button>, $attributes->merge([...]), $slot @button(...) ... @end, $attributes.merge({...}), $slot @extends('layouts.app'), @section ... @endsection, @yield('content') @extends('layouts/app'), @section ... @end, @yield('content') @stack('scripts'), @push ... @endpush, @prepend ... @endprepend @stack('scripts'), @push ... @end, @prepend ... @end @csrf, @method('PUT'), old('email') @csrf, @method('PUT'), old('email') Blade::directive('datetime', ...) View.directive('datetime', DateTimeDirective())

Three things are not the same as in Blade:

  • @includeIf(condition, 'name') in Dox takes a condition first. It does not check if the template exists.
  • {{ true }} prints true, a variable that does not exist prints nothing, and the text '0' is true. Turn on the bladeOutput, strictVariables and stringZeroIsFalse options to work like Blade. See Strict options.
  • @json is safe in a <script> block and in an attribute in single quotes, not in an attribute in double quotes.

docs.title: Migrations and schema
Artisan vs the dox CLI
docs.text:
Laravel Dox laravel new blog dox create blog php artisan serve dox serve (or dox s), with hot restart and build_runner watch php artisan make:resource dox make:serializer php artisan key:generate dox key:generate php artisan route:list dox route:list (also --json) php artisan tinker not there php artisan optimize dox build (one native binary in build/bundle) php artisan queue:work dox queue:work php artisan schedule:work dox schedule:work php artisan schedule:clear-cache dox schedule:clear-cache

The make:* and migrate commands are in the tables above. Two commands have no Laravel twin: dox build_runner:build makes the generated code, and dox env:generate makes the typed env class. See Dox CLI.

docs.title: Auth
docs.text:
Laravel Dox config/auth.php guards and providers Auth.initialize(AuthConfig(guards: ...)) in a provider Auth::attempt(['email' => $e, 'password' => $p]) await Auth().attempt(<String, dynamic>{'email': e, 'password': p}) gives a token (an access token or a JWT, by the guard), or null Auth::login($user) Auth().login(user) gives a JWT. With access tokens, use Auth().createAccessToken(user) Auth::user() req.auth?.user<User>() Auth::id() req.auth?.id() Auth::guest() req.auth == null Auth::check() Auth().check() (the same as isLoggedIn()) Auth::once($credentials) await Auth().once(credentials) gives true or false, with no token and no session Auth::attempt(...) for a web page (session) await Auth().attemptSession(req, <String, dynamic>{...}) gives true or false Auth::logout() Auth().logout(req) for a session. For a token: await Auth().revokeToken(req) ->middleware('auth:sanctum') AuthMiddleware() from dox_auth ->middleware('auth:web,api') AuthMiddleware(guards: <String>['web', 'api']) ->middleware('guest') GuestMiddleware(redirectTo: '/dashboard') Crypt::encryptString($v), Crypt::decryptString($v) Crypt.encryptString(v), Crypt.decryptString(v) Hash::make($p), Hash::check($p, $hash) Hash.make(p), Hash.check(p, hash) (or Hash.verify)

For an API, use access tokens (AccessTokenAuthDriver), like Sanctum. JWT is also available. dox auth:tokens-table makes the auth_access_tokens table. $user->createToken('cli', ['posts:read']) is Auth().createAccessToken(user, name: 'cli', abilities: <String>['posts:read']), and $request->user()->tokenCan('posts:read') is (req.auth as Auth).tokenCan('posts:read'). To renew a token, use rotateAccessToken. For web pages, a guard with SessionAuthDriver keeps the login in the session cookie. See Authentication.

docs.title: Cache
docs.text:
Laravel Dox config/cache.php lib/config/cache.dart, CacheConfig(defaultStore:, stores:) Cache::put('k', $v, 600) await Cache().put('k', v, duration: Duration(minutes: 10)). The time is a named duration:, not the third value. Cache::many(['a', 'b']), Cache::putMany([...], 600) await Cache().many(<String>['a', 'b']), await Cache().putMany(<String, Object?>{...}, duration: ...) Cache::get('k', 'default') await Cache().get('k', 'default') Cache::remember('k', 600, fn) await Cache().remember('k', Duration(minutes: 10), fn) Cache::forget('k') await Cache().forget('k') Cache::store('redis') Cache().store('redis') Cache::tags(['a']) Cache().tags(<String>['a']) Cache::lock('k', 10) Cache().lock('k', Duration(seconds: 10)) drivers: file, redis, memcached, database, array drivers: file, redis, memory, null

A value must be a JSON type. The memory store is per isolate. See Cache.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Laravel Dox config/filesystems.php disks lib/config/storage.dart, StorageConfig(defaultDisk:, disks:), passed to a StorageProvider (dox_storage) Storage::put('a.txt', $bytes) await Storage().put('a.txt', bytes, exact: true) Storage::putFile('avatars', $file) await Storage().putFile('avatars', file) Storage::putFileAs('avatars', $file, 'u1.png') await Storage().putFileAs('avatars', file, 'u1.png') $request->file('f')->store('avatars') await file.store('avatars') $request->file('f')->storeAs('avatars', 'u1.png') await file.storeAs('avatars', 'u1.png') Storage::get($path) await Storage().get(path) Storage::exists($path) / missing($path) await Storage().exists(path) / missing(path) Storage::delete($path) await Storage().delete(path) Storage::copy($from, $to) / move($from, $to) await Storage().copy(from, to) / move(from, to) Storage::files($dir) / allFiles($dir) await Storage().files(dir) / allFiles(dir) Storage::directories($dir) / deleteDirectory($dir) await Storage().directories(dir) / deleteDirectory(dir) Storage::setVisibility($path, 'private') await Storage().setVisibility(path, Visibility.private) Storage::url($path) await Storage().url(path) Storage::temporaryUrl($path, now()->addMinutes(10)) await Storage().signedUrl(path, expiresIn: Duration(minutes: 10)) Storage::disk('s3') Storage().disk('s3') Storage::download($path, $name) return Storage().download(path, name: name); drivers: local, s3, ftp, sftp drivers: local, s3 (also R2, MinIO, Spaces), memory

Three things are different from Laravel:

  • setVisibility() and getVisibility() on a local disk change and read the file mode only when the disk has 'permissions': true. Without it, setVisibility() does nothing on a local disk, and getVisibility() gives the disk visibility (public by default). Laravel always runs chmod. So a file you made private is not private on disk until you turn this on.
  • Paths that Dox gives you start with /. This is true for putFile, store, files, allFiles and directories.
  • put() returns nothing. download() takes name: but no headers. For headers, use response(await Storage().download(path)).header('Cache-Control', 'no-store').

See File Storage.

docs.title: Config and .env
docs.text:
Laravel Dox config/*.php files lib/config/*.dart files, put together in AppConfig env('APP_KEY') env.appKey (a getter in lib/config/env.dart) env('APP_PORT', 3000) env.appPort (the default is in the getter: int get appPort => 3000;) config('app.name') env.appName from the typed env class (@DoxEnv()) php artisan config:cache not needed. The typed env is read once, at start.

The typed env class gives you an int for APP_PORT and a build error for a bad type. A missing key stops the app at start, with a list of every missing key. See Environment Variables.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Laravel Dox php artisan test dart test $this->get('/api/ping')->assertStatus(200) (await client.get('/api/ping')).expectStatus(200) with DoxTestClient RefreshDatabase run the migrations in setUpAll, then setUp(refreshDatabase) from package:dox_orm/testing.dart Storage::fake('s3') Storage.manager.fake('s3') Mail::fake() Mail.fake(), then mail.assertSent() and mail.assertQueued() Queue::fake() Queue.fake(), then queue.assertPushed<T>() Cache::fake() Dox().cache = CacheManager(CacheConfig(...)) with a memory store $this->actingAs($user) client.withToken(token) with a token from Auth().createAccessToken(user) (access tokens) or Auth().login(user) (JWT)

Dox has no fake HTTP kernel. DoxTestClient.start(appConfig) starts the real server inside the test, on a free port, and sends real requests. See Testing.

docs.title: What is different
docs.text:
• A generated container. Like Laravel, Dox makes your controllers and injects what the constructor asks for. You add @Inject() to the class. build_runner writes lib/generated/container.g.dart with every registration. You do not register classes by hand in a provider. A singleton is one instance per isolate, not one per request.
  • Isolates, not PHP-FPM workers. One process runs one isolate per CPU core. Each isolate runs your whole app and has its own memory. A static value or a singleton lives once per isolate. A PHP worker starts from zero on each request. A Dox isolate keeps its state between requests, so a memory leak stays. Anything that must be shared goes to the database, Redis or files. See How Dox works.
  • Code generation, not reflection. Laravel reads your classes at run time. Dart has no usable reflection in a compiled app. So build_runner with dox_builder writes the model code, the DTO checks, the env class and the OpenAPI docs into .g.dart files. Run dox build_runner:build after a change, or let dox serve watch for you.
  • One native binary. dox build makes an AOT binary in build/bundle. There is no interpreter, no vendor/ folder and no composer install on the server. The Docker image is about 11 MB.
  • A native HTTP server and native database drivers. Rust parses HTTP and talks to Postgres and MySQL. Your code stays in Dart. They come ready-built, so you do not need Rust.
  • Types everywhere. A DTO is a class with typed fields. A path param is an int. A model field is a String?. The compiler finds many mistakes before you run the app.
  • Async is explicit. Database calls return a Future. You write await. One isolate serves many requests at the same time while it waits for the database.
  • JSON API first. Dox returns text, JSON, files and streams. For HTML pages, add views (dox_view) or Inertia (dox_inertia).

docs.title: What is missing today
docs.text:
Dox does not have these Laravel features yet:

  • events and listeners (model events are there)
  • password reset

See What Dox does not have yet for what to use today.

What is there, as separate packages: validation, OpenAPI docs, storage, cache, Socket.IO, auth, queues, the scheduler, mail, views and Inertia. Sessions are in dox_core.

docs.title: Dox and the other Dart backends
docs.text:
This page compares Dox with four other ways to build a backend in Dart: Dart Frog, Serverpod, Shelf (with shelf_router) and Alfred.

It lists facts only. Each project is good at different things.

Facts can change

The facts about the other projects come from their own docs, READMEs and pub.dev pages, read on 2026-10-22. Projects change. Check their docs before you decide. Where this page is not sure, the table says "see their docs".

docs.title: What each one is for
docs.text:
• Dox is a full backend framework, in the style of Laravel. It has routes, controllers, typed DTOs, an ORM, migrations, auth, cache, storage and a CLI.
  • Dart Frog is a small backend framework. It is built on Shelf. Routes come from the files in the routes/ folder. It describes itself as "a fast, minimalistic backend framework for Dart".
  • Serverpod is a full-stack framework for Flutter. You write endpoint methods on the server. Serverpod generates a typed Dart client for the Flutter app. It has an ORM, auth, streaming and a hosted service (Serverpod Cloud).
  • Shelf is the request and middleware model from the Dart team. It is a library, not a framework. shelf_router adds a router. You pick every other part yourself.
  • Alfred is a small server in the style of Express.js. Routes, middleware, WebSocket and static files are built in.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text: This page does not compare speed. Dox's own numbers (hello world and a /db read) are on Performance. To compare, run the same test on your own machine, with each server on the same number of cores.

docs.title: When to pick Dox
docs.text:
• You want a full framework in one place: routes, typed input, ORM, migrations, auth, cache, storage and OpenAPI docs.
  • You know Laravel. See Coming from Laravel.
  • You need MySQL or MariaDB, not only Postgres.
  • You want typed DTOs with the same rules on the server and in a Dart or Flutter client. See Share code with Flutter.
  • You want an OpenAPI document made from your code, for clients that are not written in Dart.

docs.title: When to pick something else
docs.text:
• You want a framework with many years of use. Dart Frog, Serverpod and Shelf have been out for years. Dox is new.
  • You want a hosted service. Serverpod has Serverpod Cloud. Dox has no hosted service. You deploy it yourself (a binary or Docker).
  • Your app is Flutter only, and you want the client made for you. Serverpod generates a typed client for every endpoint. Dox does not generate a Dart client. It generates an OpenAPI document.
  • You want a small tool with few parts. Dart Frog is simpler. You add only what you need.
  • You want to build your own stack. Shelf gives you the base parts, and the Dart team publishes it.
  • You need features Dox does not have yet, like events and listeners. See What Dox does not have yet.

docs.title: How Dox works
docs.text: This page explains what happens inside Dox when a request comes in, how isolates work and what each folder of an app is for.

docs.title: The life of a request
docs.text:
Dox has two parts:

  • A native server, written in Rust (dox_http_native). It owns the sockets and parses HTTP.
  • Your app, written in Dart. Routes, middleware, DTOs, controllers and the ORM all run here.

A request goes through these steps:

  1. Rust accepts the connection and reads the request. It parses the HTTP request line, the headers and the body. A bad request gets 400. Headers over 16 KB get 431. A body over the size limit gets 413. Dart never sees these requests.
  2. Rust hands the requests to Dart in a batch. One message holds many requests.
  3. Dart finds the route. It matches the method, the Host (for domain routes) and the path. A plain path is a map lookup. A path with {params} is a pattern match. No match gives 404. A CORS preflight (OPTIONS) gets 204.
  4. Dart adds the CORS headers of the route.
  5. Dart reads the body, only when the request has a Content-Type. A request without a body skips this step.
  6. Dart runs the middleware list of the route, in this order: global middleware, router middleware, group middleware, route middleware. A middleware returns the request to go on. Anything else is sent as the response, and the controller does not run.
  7. Dart fills the controller parameters. Path params are converted first. A value that does not fit its type (abc for int id) gets 404. Then the DTO is read and checked. Bad input gets 422. A body that is not JSON gets 400. A content type Dox can not read gets 415.
  8. The controller runs and returns a value.
  9. The responseHandler from AppConfig runs, when you set one. It can change every response.
  10. Dox turns the value into the response: a String is text, a Map or model is JSON, a File is streamed.
  11. Dart sends the answers of the batch back to Rust in one call. Rust writes the bytes to the socket.

When a step throws, Dox catches the error. An IHttpException (like NotFoundHttpException) gives its own status. Any other error gives 500 and goes to the report method of the ExceptionHandler in AppConfig.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant R as Rust (dox_http_native)
    participant D as Dart isolate
    participant M as Middleware
    participant K as Controller

    C->>R: TCP connection, HTTP request
    R->>R: parse request, check size limits
    R->>D: batch of requests (one message)
    D->>D: router: method, host, path
    D->>D: CORS headers, read body
    D->>M: global, router, group, route middleware
    M-->>D: request (go on) or a response
    D->>D: path params, DTO check
    D->>K: call with typed parameters
    K-->>D: return value
    D->>D: responseHandler, build the response
    D->>R: batch of answers (one call)
    R->>C: bytes

No reflection

Dox reads the parameter types of every controller once, at start. It does not use dart:mirrors. DTOs come from a generated list (lib/generated/dtos.g.dart). This is why dox build can make a native (AOT) binary.

docs.title: Where things are decided
docs.text:
Step Code What it decides Route match lib/routes/*.dart, Route.get(...) which controller runs Middleware AppConfig(globalMiddleware:), Router.middleware, Route.middleware(...), the route list go on, or answer early Input a @Dto class in lib/app/dtos/<name>/ what the controller gets, or 422 Output the return value, response(...), responseHandler status, headers, body Errors IHttpException, AppConfig(exceptionHandler:) the error response, logging

See Routing, Middleware, Validation and Response.

docs.title: Isolates
docs.text: Dart runs code on isolates. An isolate is like a thread, but it has its own memory. Dox starts one isolate per CPU core (Platform.numberOfProcessors). Every isolate runs the full app.

docs.title: One port, many isolates
docs.text:
Every isolate runs its own HTTP server on the same port. The operating system spreads the connections.

System Native server Linux one socket per isolate (SO_REUSEPORT) macOS the isolates share one socket Windows only one isolate serves HTTP

Each isolate does its own socket work on its own thread. See Native server.

docs.title: What each isolate gets
docs.text:
Before it starts an isolate, Dox copies three things to it:

  • the AppConfig,
  • the list of providers,
  • the routes and route binders (Route.bind) you added before startServer().

Then each isolate does this, once:

  1. It runs setup() of every provider, in list order. This is where a database pool is opened.
  2. It registers the routes of your routers.
  3. It reads the parameter types of every controller.
  4. It starts its HTTP server.

Nothing in this list runs per request.

Because the config and the providers are copied, they must not hold open sockets or pools. Open these in setup(). See Providers.

docs.title: Each isolate has its own memory
docs.text:
• A static value or a singleton exists once per isolate. A change in one isolate is not seen in the others.
  • The memory cache store is per isolate. Use the redis store to share cache data.
  • To share data between isolates, use the database, Redis or files.
  • Dox().isolateId tells you which isolate runs the code. The first one is 1.

docs.title: When an isolate crashes
docs.text:
• An error in a request is caught. Dox answers 500 and keeps going.
  • An async error outside a request is caught and passed to the ExceptionHandler. The isolate keeps running.
  • When a worker isolate still dies, Dox prints [dox] isolate N exited, restarting and starts a new one after 1 second.
  • When the first (main) isolate dies, the process exits with a non-zero code. A supervisor (Docker restart:, systemd Restart=always) must start it again.

docs.title: How many isolates
docs.text: Set totalIsolate in AppConfig, or APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE in .env. In code, Dox().totalIsolate(2) before startServer() wins over the config. Use 1 in tests. See Isolate.

docs.title: Where the database pools live
docs.text:
The ORM is started in a provider (ORMProvider). Every isolate runs setup(), so every isolate opens a pool. The native drivers live in Rust. There, isolates that open the same settings get the same pool.

Driver Per isolate Per process Postgres native (dox_postgres_native) nothing one pool of maxConnectionCount connections per settings, and one Rust runtime (extra['threads'], default 1) MySQL native (dox_mysql_native) nothing one pool of maxConnectionCount connections per settings, and one Rust runtime SQLite one connection nothing shared

So for Postgres and MySQL, the app opens at most maxConnectionCount connections, for any number of isolates. The pool size is always your choice. Set it below the max_connections of the database.

The pool closes when the last isolate that uses it closes it. See Native Postgres driver.

Postgres and MySQL have only the native drivers. When the native library does not load, the app stops with an error that says why and how to fix it. See Database.

docs.title: The layout of a Dox app
docs.text:
dox create my_app copies the dox-sample template. It looks like this:

my_app/
├── bin/
│   ├── server.dart          # starts the app
│   ├── migrate.dart         # runs the migrations (dox migration:*)
│   ├── seed.dart            # runs the seeders (dox db:seed)
│   ├── queue.dart           # the queue worker (dox queue:*)
│   └── schedule.dart        # the scheduler (dox schedule:*)
├── db/
│   ├── factories/           # model factories, *.factory.dart
│   ├── migration/           # migrations (.dart with a registry, or .sql)
│   └── seeders/             # seeders, *.seeder.dart
├── lib/
│   ├── app/
│   │   ├── http/
│   │   │   └── controllers/     # *.controller.dart
│   │   ├── jobs/                # queue jobs, *.job.dart
│   │   └── models/              # one folder per model, *.model.dart
│   ├── config/
│   │   ├── app.dart             # AppConfig: port, isolates, middleware
│   │   ├── cache.dart           # cache stores
│   │   ├── cors.dart
│   │   ├── database.dart        # DatabaseConfig: connections
│   │   ├── env.dart             # typed env class (@DoxEnv)
│   │   ├── logger.dart
│   │   ├── queue.dart           # QueueConfig
│   │   ├── schedule.dart        # ScheduleConfig and your tasks
│   │   └── storage.dart         # storage disks
│   ├── routes/
│   │   ├── api.dart             # ApiRouter, prefix `api`
│   │   └── web.dart             # WebRouter
│   ├── providers/               # one DoxProvider per file, runs in every isolate
│   │   ├── orm_provider.dart        # opens the database
│   │   ├── queue_provider.dart
│   │   ├── schedule_provider.dart
│   │   └── storage_provider.dart
│   └── generated/               # made by build_runner, do not edit
│       ├── container.g.dart     # @Inject classes, routers, providers
│       ├── jobs.g.dart          # the list of queue jobs
│       └── openapi.g.dart       # the OpenAPI docs
├── test/
├── .env                         # local settings, not in git. `dox create` makes it
├── .env.example
├── Dockerfile
├── docker-compose.yml
└── pubspec.yaml

The dox make:* commands add more folders when you need them:

  • dox make:dto adds lib/app/dtos/<name>/<name>.dto.dart. Then build_runner writes lib/generated/dtos.g.dart, the list of DTOs.
  • dox make:middleware adds lib/app/http/middleware/.
  • dox make:serializer adds lib/app/serializers/.

The app makes storage/ when it writes files (the local disk, the file cache, uploads).

Folder What goes there bin/ server.dart calls Dox().initialize(appConfig), runs the migrations, then Dox().startServer(). The other files are the entry points that the dox migration:*, db:seed, queue:* and schedule:* commands run. db/ Your migrations, factories and seeders. Dart migrations are listed in db/migration/migrations.dart, which the CLI writes. lib/app/http/ Everything about HTTP: controllers and middleware. lib/app/serializers/ Serializers. They are not only for HTTP: MCP and websocket use them too. lib/app/dtos/ One folder per DTO: typed and checked input. lib/app/jobs/ Queue jobs. lib/app/models/ One folder per model. build_runner writes the .g.dart file next to it. lib/config/ One file per config object. app.dart puts them together in AppConfig. lib/routes/ One Router class per file. Dox finds each router by itself. lib/providers/ Classes that extend DoxProvider. Their setup() runs in every isolate. Dox finds each provider by itself. lib/generated/ Generated files. Do not edit them. Run dox build_runner:build to make them again. storage/ Files the app writes: uploads, the file cache, SQLite files.

build_runner with dox_builder makes the model classes, the DTO checks, the typed env class, the OpenAPI docs and the list of queue jobs.

docs.title: Status and roadmap
docs.text: This page shows what works in Dox today, what is missing and what is planned.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
What the states mean:

  • Stable: works, has tests and has had real use.
  • New: works and has tests, but it is newer and has had less real use.

All packages follow semantic versioning: a breaking change only comes in a new major version.

Each package has its own version number. Some packages live in their own repos. See Contribute.

Mostly tested through dox_builder. dox (CLI) dox create, dox serve, dox build, make:*, migration:*, db:seed, queue:*, schedule:*, package commands Stable 132 tests in 12 files dox_migration Migrations for Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite Stable 36 tests in 5 files. CI runs them on each database. dox_auth JWT and session auth guards and middleware, access tokens you can revoke, gates and policies Stable 201 tests in 8 files dox_cache Memory, file and Redis cache, tags, locks, encryption Stable 126 tests in 7 files, with Redis in CI dox_cache_database The database cache store, for dox_cache New 78 tests in 4 files, with SQLite, Postgres, MariaDB and MySQL in CI dox_storage Local disk and S3 (and S3-compatible) storage Stable 153 tests in 10 files, with MinIO in CI dox_openapi OpenAPI 3.1 document and a docs page Stable 63 tests in 4 files dox_socketio Socket.IO v4 server with a Redis adapter Stable 119 tests in 11 files, with Redis and the real socket.io-client in CI dox_queue Queues and jobs, the Redis and sync drivers, chains, batches, workers New 46 tests in 7 files. Most queue tests run in dox_queue_database, on every store. dox_queue_database The database queue driver, the batch store and afterCommit for dox_queue New 234 tests in 16 files, with SQLite, Postgres, MariaDB and Redis in CI dox_scheduler Run tasks on a schedule New 106 tests in 6 files, with Redis in CI dox_mcp MCP server: tools for AI clients over Streamable HTTP, signed sessions New 15 tests in 1 file dox_view Views: .dox.html templates with layouts and components New 40 tests in 2 files dox_inertia Inertia.js server side: single page apps with React, Vue or Svelte and Dox controllers New 34 tests in 2 files dox_mailer Email with SMTP, Amazon SES, Azure, Resend, Mailgun, Postmark and sendmail, mailables, Markdown mail, notifications New 168 tests in 16 files, with a fake SMTP server dox_http_native Native HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket server in Rust, on the isolate's own thread. Dox has no other server. New 65 Dart tests in 4 files, and 32 Rust tests dox_postgres_native Native Postgres client (Rust tokio-postgres), the Postgres driver. Has TLS (sslmode, sslRootCert). New 41 tests in 7 files, plus the dox_orm tests dox_mysql_native Native MySQL and MariaDB client (Rust mysql_async), the MySQL driver. Has TLS. New 30 tests in 2 files, plus the dox_orm tests

Hash (bcrypt password hashing) is in dox_core.

About test coverage

The repos do not measure line coverage. Counts are test( calls in each package's test/ folder. A test inside a loop counts once, so dart test can report more tests. The CI setup of the main repo is in .github/workflows/test.yaml. The packages in their own repos have their own CI.

docs.title: What Dox does not have yet
docs.text: Feature Status What to do today Events and listeners Not there Model events are there. See Model events. Password reset Not there Make a signed, short-lived token, send it with Mail and check it in a controller. Localization Partly Validation messages can follow the request locale (req.locale). There is no general translation helper. Keep your own message maps.

docs.text:
• Localization

The package CHANGELOGs have an Unreleased section when changes wait for the next version.

docs.title: How to help
docs.text:
• Try Dox and open an issue when something breaks or is missing.
  • Pick an item above and open an issue first, so the design can be discussed.
  • See Contribute to set up the repo and run the tests.

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
Connect Dox to Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB or SQLite with the dox_orm package.

  • Query builder: build SQL with methods.
  • Models: one class per table.
  • Transactions: many queries that succeed or fail together.
  • Migration and Schema: create and change tables.

This is how a query travels from your code to the database:

flowchart LR
    M["Model or QueryBuilder"] --> S["SQL text<br>quoted names, @values"]
    S --> D{"Driver"}
    D --> N["Native Rust pool<br>dox_postgres_native, dox_mysql_native"]
    D --> T["sqlite3"]
    N --> DB[("Database")]
    T --> DB

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The query builder and the models are in the dox_orm package. A new app already has it.

dox add orm --driver=sqlite

--driver is sqlite (the default), postgres or mysql. It adds dox_orm and dox_migration, writes lib/config/database.dart, the ORM provider, bin/migrate.dart and db/migration/, and adds the DB_* keys to .env. It also skips the build of the drivers you do not use, see Skip unused drivers. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice. See Add a package.

docs.title: Set it up by hand
docs.text:
To add only the package, run dart pub add dox_orm.

import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

docs.title: Supported databases
docs.text:
Database Driver Driver Pool Good for Postgres Driver.postgres dox_postgres_native Yes Production MySQL 8+ and MariaDB Driver.mysql dox_mysql_native Yes Production SQLite Driver.sqlite sqlite3 No, one connection per isolate Development, tests, small apps

Native drivers

Postgres and MySQL use a native (Rust) driver. There is no other driver. When the native library can not load, the app stops with an error. See the Postgres and MySQL pages.

docs.title: Skip unused drivers
docs.text:
dox_orm brings all three drivers. The build downloads a native library for each one. An app needs only the driver of its database. To skip the others, add a hooks: user_defines: block to pubspec.yaml.

  • Put it in the pubspec.yaml of your app.
  • In a pub workspace, put it in the root pubspec.yaml of the workspace. Dart reads user_defines only from the root package.

skip: true turns off the download of a driver. Only the bool true skips. Any other value does nothing.

docs.title: SQLite app
docs.text:
A new app uses SQLite. Its pubspec.yaml already has this block.

pubspec.yaml
hooks:
  user_defines:
    dox_postgres_native:
      skip: true
    dox_mysql_native:
      skip: true

docs.title: Postgres app
docs.text:
pubspec.yaml
hooks:
  user_defines:
    dox_mysql_native:
      skip: true
    sqlite3:
      source: system

docs.title: MySQL app
docs.text:
pubspec.yaml
hooks:
  user_defines:
    dox_postgres_native:
      skip: true
    sqlite3:
      source: system

sqlite3: source: system comes from the sqlite3 package. The build does not download SQLite. The app loads the libsqlite3 library of the system when it opens SQLite.

SQLite on a system without libsqlite3

With source: system, the app fails when it opens SQLite on a system without libsqlite3. The FROM scratch Docker image has no libsqlite3. When your app opens SQLite, remove the sqlite3 lines.

docs.title: Switch the database
docs.text:
When you switch the database, remove the skip line of the driver you now use. Then run dart pub get.

A driver that is still skipped stops the app when it opens a pool. The error says that the native library is not in the build, and to remove skip.

docs.title: Config
docs.text:
Put the connections in lib/config/database.dart. connection is the name of the default connection.

lib/config/database.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: env.dbConnection,
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.postgres,
      host: env.dbHost,
      port: env.dbPort ?? 5432,
      user: env.dbUsername,
      password: env.dbPassword,
      database: env.dbName,
      extra: <String, dynamic>{'maxConnectionCount': 10},
      debug: env.isDevelopment,
    ),
    'mysql': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.mysql, // also for MariaDB
      host: env.dbHost,
      port: env.dbPort ?? 3306,
      user: env.dbUsername,
      password: env.dbPassword,
      database: env.dbName,
      extra: <String, dynamic>{'maxConnectionCount': 10},
      debug: env.isDevelopment,
    ),
    'sqlite': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.sqlite,
      database: env.dbName, // file path, like db/dox.sqlite, or ':memory:'
      debug: env.isDevelopment,
    ),
  },
);

env is the typed env of the app, in lib/config/env.dart. Change my_app to the name of your app in pubspec.yaml.

  • debug: true prints each SQL query and its values. The app template turns it on only in development. The default printer, PrettyQueryPrinter, prints one line per query with the values put into the SQL. You can copy the SQL and run it in psql, mysql or the sqlite CLI:

▌ [db:default] SELECT * FROM "users" WHERE "email" = 'a@b.com' LIMIT 1;
- user, password, host and port are not used by SQLite.

Start the ORM in a provider. The app template already has this file. Each isolate runs the provider. Isolates with the same settings share one pool, so maxConnectionCount is for the whole process.

lib/providers/orm_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';

class ORMProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig);
  }

  /// Close the database connections when the server stops.
  @override
  Future<void> shutdown() async {
    await SqlQueryBuilder.close();
  }
}

Dox finds every DoxProvider class on its own. After you add a provider, run dart run build_runner build.

docs.title: ORM flags
docs.text:
OrmFlags turns on opt-in ORM behaviors. Each flag is off by default. With all flags off, the ORM works as this page and the other database pages say. Pass the flags as flags: in DatabaseConfig:

lib/config/database.dart
DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: env.dbConnection,
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{ /* ... */ },
  flags: OrmFlags.all(), // every flag on
);

Turn on only some flags by name:

flags: const OrmFlags(pluralTableNames: true, sumReturnsZero: true),
Flag Off (default) On skipCleanUpdateEvents save() with no changes fires saving, updating, updated and saved. It fires only saving and saved. A model with a Map or List field always counts as changed. A save with changes runs beforeSave two times, and a save with no changes runs it one time. belongsToKeyFromRelation The default belongsTo foreign key comes from the class name: @BelongsTo(User) User? author uses user_id. It comes from the relation name: author_id. pluralTableNames The default table name is singular: User uses user. It is plural, with English plural rules: users, blog_posts, categories. createWritesNull create() does not send a null key, so the column default is used. It writes NULL for a key that is null in the map. sumReturnsZero sum() gives null when no row matches. It gives 0. selectRawAdds selectRaw() replaces the select list. It adds to it, so select('a').selectRaw('count(*) as c') selects both. groupByAdds A second groupBy() replaces the first. It adds to the first. groupByRaw() too. lastPageAtLeastOne paginate() gives lastPage 0 when there are no rows. It gives 1. updateSetsUpdatedAt A model query update(), like Blog().where('id', 1).update({...}), does not touch updated_at. It sets updated_at, unless the data already has it. incrementFiresEvents increment() and decrement() on a model do not fire events or set updated_at. They fire saving, updating, updated and saved, and set updated_at. A hook that cancels stops the write. preloadUnknownThrows preload('typo') loads nothing, with no error. It throws an ArgumentError. With a dot path, each level is checked. toJsonLoadedRelations toJson() has only the relations named in preload(). It also has the relations loaded with $getRelation(). laravelPostgresTypes On Postgres, timestamps() and softDeletes() make TIMESTAMPTZ, and json() makes JSONB. A new table gets TIMESTAMP and JSON.
  • OrmFlags.all() turns on every flag. New apps can start with it.
  • The ORM keeps the flags in SqlQueryBuilder().flags. Each isolate runs the ORM provider, so each isolate gets the same flags. All connections use them.
  • SqlQueryBuilder.initialize(..., flags: ...) takes the flags too.
  • pluralTableNames does not change a name set with @DoxModel(table: ...). The default foreign key stays singular (user_id).
  • belongsToKeyFromRelation needs the relation name. The model generator does not pass it yet, so a generated model still uses the class name. Set foreignKey on the relation to be sure.
  • laravelPostgresTypes changes only tables made with Schema.create. It never changes a table that is already there, and Schema.table keeps the old types. MySQL and SQLite do not change.
  • Migrations get the flags from SqlQueryBuilder().flags. bin/migrate.dart does not start the ORM, so give the flags to the migrator: Migrator(migrations: migrations, flags: databaseConfig.flags). See Migration.

docs.title: .env
docs.text:
The app config and the migration commands read these values.

.env
DB_CONNECTION=postgres # postgres, mysql or sqlite
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432           # 3306 for mysql
DB_NAME=dox            # for sqlite: the file path, like db/dox.sqlite
DB_USERNAME=postgres
DB_PASSWORD=postgres

docs.title: DATABASE_URL
docs.text:
Many hosts (Fly, Render, Heroku and others) give you one database url. Dox reads it from the DATABASE_URL environment variable.

The rule: when DATABASE_URL is set, it wins. It replaces the config of the default connection (DatabaseConfig.connection). That config still gives debug, printer, slowQueryMs and extra. Other named connections do not change.

DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:s%40cret@db.example.com:5432/blog?sslmode=require
Form Database postgres://user:pass@host:5432/db or postgresql://... Postgres mysql://user:pass@host:3306/db or mariadb://... MySQL, MariaDB sqlite:///abs/path.db, sqlite://db/dox.sqlite, sqlite::memory:, file:db/dox.sqlite SQLite
  • The user, password and database name are url-decoded. Write @ in a password as %40.
  • No port: 5432 for Postgres, 3306 for MySQL.
  • For Postgres, sslmode works like libpq (disable, prefer, require, verify-ca, verify-full). require does not check the certificate. Use verify-full when your host supports it. See Postgres TLS.
  • For MySQL, ssl=true (or sslmode=require) turns TLS on, and it checks the certificate. Add verifyCertificate=false to skip the check, only for a self-signed certificate in development.
  • host=/path (or socket=/path) connects to a Unix socket, like host=/cloudsql/project:region:instance. See Unix socket.
  • Any other option goes to extra, like ?maxConnectionCount=20. A number becomes an int, true and false a bool. This works for SQLite too, like sqlite://db/dox.sqlite?background=true.

The ORM reads DATABASE_URL from the real environment, not from .env. To use a url from .env, or any other url, give it yourself:

DatabaseConfig(
  connection: 'postgres',
  connections: {...},
  url: Env.get<String?>('DATABASE_URL'),
);

An empty url (url: '') turns DATABASE_URL off. To make one ConnectionConfig from a url, use ConnectionConfig.fromUrl(url). Migrations read DATABASE_URL too, also from .env.

docs.title: Unix socket
docs.text:
A host that starts with / is a Unix socket. Google Cloud SQL on Cloud Run uses /cloudsql/PROJECT:REGION:INSTANCE.

DB_HOST=/cloudsql/my-project:europe-west1:blog
# or
DATABASE_URL=postgres://blog:secret@/blog?host=/cloudsql/my-project:europe-west1:blog

Postgres: the host is the socket folder, like in libpq. The driver uses the socket file <folder>/.s.PGSQL.<port>. A host that already ends with /.s.PGSQL.5432 works too.

MySQL and MariaDB: the host is the socket file itself. The port is not used. On Cloud SQL, the socket file is /cloudsql/PROJECT:REGION:INSTANCE. A local server often uses /var/run/mysqld/mysqld.sock or /tmp/mysql.sock.

DB_CONNECTION=mysql
DB_HOST=/var/run/mysqld/mysqld.sock
# or
DATABASE_URL=mysql://app:secret@/app?socket=/var/run/mysqld/mysqld.sock

?socket= and ?host= do the same thing.

docs.title: extra options
docs.text:
extra is a map in ConnectionConfig for driver options.

Key Database Default What it does maxConnectionCount Postgres, MySQL 10 Most connections in the pool. threads Postgres, MySQL 1 Rust threads of the native driver. requestTimeout Postgres, MySQL 300 s The longest wait for one request. maxConnectionAge Postgres, MySQL none on Postgres, 12 hours on MySQL A connection older than this is closed once it has no query. idleTimeout Postgres, MySQL no limit on Postgres, 12 hours on MySQL A connection not used for this long is closed. serverKill MySQL true Stop a cancelled or timed out query on the server with KILL. preparedStatementCacheSize MySQL, SQLite 100 Prepared statements kept per connection. sslMode Postgres disable TLS mode: disable, prefer, require, verify-ca or verify-full. sslRootCert Postgres none Path of a PEM file with the CA certificates to trust for verify-ca and verify-full. verifyCertificate MySQL true false skips the TLS certificate check. Only for development. timeZone Postgres UTC Time zone of the session. applicationName Postgres none Name of the app in pg_stat_activity. busyTimeout SQLite 5000 Milliseconds a query waits for a lock. background SQLite false true (or 1, 'true', '1') runs the queries in a helper isolate. See Run queries in a helper isolate.

docs.title: Pool settings
docs.text:
requestTimeout, maxConnectionAge, idleTimeout and serverKill set how the pool treats its connections. A time is a Duration, or a number of seconds. So ?requestTimeout=30 in DATABASE_URL works.

extra: <String, dynamic>{
  'maxConnectionCount': 10,
  'requestTimeout': const Duration(seconds: 30),
  'maxConnectionAge': const Duration(minutes: 30),
  'idleTimeout': const Duration(minutes: 5),
  'serverKill': false, // MySQL only
},
  • requestTimeout: a request is a free connection, the connect and the query. Over this time it fails, and its connection is closed. A transaction with no request for this long is rolled back.
  • maxConnectionAge: a connection older than this is closed and opened again. It is never closed while it runs a query or a transaction. This helps behind a load balancer, or after a database failover.
  • idleTimeout: a free connection that is not used for this long is closed.
  • serverKill (MySQL): the server stops a cancelled or timed out query with KILL QUERY. Set it to false behind a proxy like ProxySQL, because the KILL may reach another server. Then a cancelled query stops in Dart at once, but it runs to its end on the server.

To stop one query by hand, see Cancel a query.

docs.title: Table and column names are quoted
docs.text:
Table and column names you pass to select, where, join, groupBy, orderBy, insert and update are quoted. Postgres and SQLite use "name". MySQL uses `name`. So names like order or key work.

  • table.column, table.*, * and column as alias are quoted in the right way.
  • Anything else (for example count(*) as total) throws an ArgumentError. So user input can not add SQL.
  • For expressions, use the raw methods (selectRaw, whereRaw, orderByRaw, groupByRaw, joinRaw).
  • On Postgres, a quoted name is case sensitive. userId is not the same column as userid.

docs.title: Raw queries
docs.text:
QueryBuilder.query() runs SQL on the default connection. Use @name for values. The values are sent as bound parameters.

List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.query(
  'select * from blog where id = @id',
  substitutionValues: <String, dynamic>{'id': 1},
);

Pass connection to run it on another connection.

await QueryBuilder.query('select 1', connection: 'mysql');

docs.title: Other connections
docs.text:
Use withConnection() with a connection name from the config.

List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.table('blog')
    .withConnection('mysql')
    .get();

A model keeps its connection. save() and delete() use it. Models that a query returns use the connection of the query.

Blog blog = Blog()..withConnection('mysql');
blog.title = 'Hello';
await blog.save(); // saved on 'mysql'

docs.title: Listen to queries
docs.text:
SqlQueryBuilder().listen() runs your function after each query. It works on every connection and inside a transaction. Use it for metrics or your own query log.

void onQuery(QueryEvent e) {
  print('${e.connection} ${e.time.inMilliseconds} ms: ${e.sql}');
}

SqlQueryBuilder().listen(onQuery);

A QueryEvent has:

  • sql: the SQL text, with @name for each value.
  • bindings: the values. A value named in logRedact shows as ***.
  • time: how long the query took, a Duration.
  • connection: the name of the connection.

The function runs only after a query that worked. A failed query is not sent: its error goes to your code. It also gets the queries of Schema, truncate() and the migrator, when they run on a connection of the ORM. A migrator that opens its own database from .env does not use a connection of the ORM, so its queries are not sent. If the function throws, Dox logs the error and the query still returns its rows. SqlQueryBuilder().removeListener(onQuery) stops it.

docs.title: Slow query log
docs.text:
Set slowQueryMs on a connection to log each query that takes longer than that many milliseconds. It is off by default. It works with debug off, so you can use it in production.

'postgres': ConnectionConfig(
  driver: Driver.postgres,
  // ...
  debug: env.isDevelopment,
  slowQueryMs: 500,
),

The log line goes to the query printer. It has the connection name, the time and the SQL. PrettyQueryPrinter (the default) prints it like this:

▌ [db:postgres SLOW 812ms] SELECT * FROM "orders" WHERE "user_id" = 42;

Other printers, like ConsoleQueryPrinter and FileQueryPrinter, get Slow query (812 ms, postgres): select .... A value named in logRedact shows as *** ('***' in the PrettyQueryPrinter line). Set slowQueryMs to 0 to log every query. A failed query is not logged here. With debug on, a slow query of the query builder shows twice: the debug line before it runs, and the slow line with its time after it.

docs.title: MySQL and MariaDB
docs.text:
• The driver is dox_mysql_native. Its page lists how values are converted.
  • CREATE, ALTER and DROP are saved right away. A transaction can not undo them.

docs.title: SQLite
docs.text:
SQLite is good for development, tests and small apps. For a busy production app, use Postgres or MySQL.

How it runs

The sqlite3 package calls SQLite directly (FFI). A query blocks the isolate while it runs. Each isolate has one connection. The file uses WAL mode, so readers do not wait for the writer. busyTimeout makes a query wait for a lock from another isolate, instead of failing. Foreign keys are on. Before each SELECT, the driver checks PRAGMA schema_version to see if a table changed.

Types

SQLite has no bool, JSON or date type. Dox converts them for you:

  • boolean() is saved as 0/1 and read back as bool.
  • json() is saved as text and read back as Map or List.
  • Dates are saved as ISO text in UTC and read back as DateTime.

The driver uses the column type in CREATE TABLE. It finds the table by the table names in the query. So it works on tables made by Schema, or by SQL with the same type names (BOOLEAN, JSON, TIMESTAMP, DATE, DATETIME). A column with an alias (active as is_active) is not converted.

Limits

  • Schema limits (change(), dropColumn, NOT NULL columns) are in SQLite notes.
  • dropColumn does not work on a primary key column.
  • insertMultiple with rows that have different keys inserts the rows one by one, because SQLite has no DEFAULT in VALUES.
  • SQLite before 3.39 has no RIGHT JOIN.

Native library

The sqlite3 package (v3) bundles SQLite with a build hook. You do not install a system library. For the AOT binary, use dox build. It puts the library in build/bundle/lib/, next to build/bundle/bin/server. Keep the two folders together. dart compile exe does not work with build hooks. See Deployment.

docs.title: Run queries in a helper isolate
docs.text:
A SQLite query blocks the isolate while it runs. So one slow query stops every other request on that isolate.

Set background to true to run the queries in a helper isolate. The helper isolate opens the database and runs every query. Your isolate only waits for the answer, so it keeps serving other requests.

'sqlite': ConnectionConfig(
  driver: Driver.sqlite,
  database: 'db/dox.sqlite',
  debug: false,
  extra: {'background': true},
),

It is off by default. Queries, transactions, :memory: databases, the query listener and the slow query log work the same. A SQL error is the same SqliteException. A database that does not open (for example a wrong folder) does not throw at startup. The error comes on the first query, and on every query after it. To turn it on with DATABASE_URL, add ?background=true, like sqlite://db/dox.sqlite?background=true.

Each query costs one message to the helper isolate and one back.

  • Turn it on when some queries are slow, like a big report or a search with no index.
  • Leave it off when the app runs many tiny queries. They get a little slower.

docs.title: Factories
docs.text:
A factory makes models with sample data.

Use it in tests and in seeders.

docs.title: Create a factory
docs.text:
dox make:factory User

This makes db/factories/user.factory.dart. Set the default values in definition(). For example:

db/factories/user.factory.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/factory.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

class UserFactory extends Factory<User> {
  @override
  User definition() {
    User user = User();
    user.name = 'Jane';
    user.email = 'jane@example.com';
    return user;
  }
}

definition() gives one new model with the default values. It runs once for each model, so random values are new each time.

docs.title: Make and create
State
docs.text:
state() changes each model after definition(). The examples below use a bool? isAdmin and a String? role field on User.

User admin = await UserFactory()
    .state((User u) => u..isAdmin = true)
    .createOne();

You can add more than one state. They run in the order you add them.

A factory method makes a state easy to use again:

class UserFactory extends Factory<User> {
  @override
  User definition() => User()..name = 'Jane';

  UserFactory admin() {
    state((User u) => u..isAdmin = true);
    return this;
  }
}

List<User> admins = await UserFactory().admin().count(3).create();

Call your own methods first. count() and state() return a Factory<User>, not a UserFactory.

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
sequence() is a state that also gets the index of the model: 0, 1, 2 and so on.

List<User> users = await UserFactory()
    .count(3)
    .sequence((User u, int i) => u..email = 'user$i@example.com')
    .create();
// user0@example.com, user1@example.com, user2@example.com

To switch between a few values, use the index:

List<String> roles = <String>['admin', 'editor'];
await UserFactory()
    .count(4)
    .sequence((User u, int i) => u..role = roles[i % roles.length])
    .create();

docs.title: Belongs to
docs.text:
Set the parent key with a state:

User user = await UserFactory().createOne();

await PostFactory()
    .count(3)
    .state((Post p) => p..userId = user.id)
    .create();

docs.title: Has many
docs.text:
has() creates child models for each saved model. The second argument sets the parent on each child.

List<User> users = await UserFactory()
    .count(2)
    .has(PostFactory().count(3), (Post p, User u) => p..userId = u.id)
    .create();
// 2 users, each with 3 posts

has() only works with create() and createOne(). make() saves nothing, so it makes no children.

docs.title: Fake data
docs.text:
Dox has no fake data generator. The faker package works well with factories:

dart pub add faker
db/factories/user.factory.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/factory.dart';
import 'package:faker/faker.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

class UserFactory extends Factory<User> {
  @override
  User definition() {
    return User()
      ..name = faker.person.name()
      ..email = faker.internet.email();
  }
}

docs.title: Use in tests
docs.text:
A factory needs the ORM. Set it up first, the same as in your app.

import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/factories/user.factory.dart';

void main() {
  test('lists users', () async {
    await UserFactory().count(3).create();
    // call your route and check the result
  });
}

See Testing with a database.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Each call like count() or state() changes the factory and returns it. Make a new factory for each set of models.
  • Import factories from package:dox_orm/factory.dart. The main dox_orm import does not include them.

docs.title: Migration
docs.text:
A migration changes your database schema step by step, with an up method that makes the change and a down method that undoes it.

Write migrations in Dart with the schema builder. The same migration then works on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite. Plain .sql migrations work too.

docs.title: Create a migration
docs.text:
dox make:migration create_users_table

This makes db/migration/2026_10_21_120000_create_users_table.dart. The numbers are the date and time when you run the command.

db/migration/2026_10_21_120000_create_users_table.dart
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

class CreateUsersTable extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.create('users', (Table table) {
      table.id();
      table.timestamps();
    });
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.dropIfExists('users');
  }
}

Add your columns in up, for example table.string('email').unique();. See Schema for all column types.

The name of the migration decides what the new file contains:

Name The file has create_users_table schema.create('users', ...) in up, and dropIfExists('users') in down add_avatar_to_users_table (also _from_, _in_, _on_) schema.table('users', ...) in up and down any other name empty up and down
  • create:migration does the same.
  • dox make:model Blog -m makes the model and a create_blogs_table migration.

Raw SQL and data in a Dart migration

schema.driver runs raw SQL on the same connection and transaction: await schema.driver.execute("UPDATE users SET role = 'admin' WHERE id = 1"); Do not use models or QueryBuilder in a migration. They use another connection.

docs.title: The registry
docs.text:
An AOT build can not load a file at run time. So Dox keeps a list of your Dart migrations in db/migration/migrations.dart:

// Made by `dox make:migration` and the `dox migration:*` commands.
// Do not edit, it is made again from the files in this folder.
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import '2026_10_21_120000_create_users_table.dart' as m1;

final List<MigrationEntry> migrations = <MigrationEntry>[
  MigrationEntry(
    '2026_10_21_120000_create_users_table',
    m1.CreateUsersTable(),
  ),
];
  • dox make:migration and every dox migration:* command write this file again. You do not edit it.
  • It lists each file named YYYY_MM_DD_HHMMSS_name.dart and its class ... extends Migration.
  • The name of a migration is its file name without .dart. The order is by name.

The first dox make:migration also makes bin/migrate.dart in your app:

import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await Migrator(migrations: migrations).run(args);
}

The dox migration:* commands run dart run bin/migrate.dart <command>. So your migrations run as part of your app code.

docs.title: Run migrations
docs.text:
Command What it does dox migration:run Run the migrations that did not run yet. Short name: dox migrate. dox migration:rollback Undo the last batch. dox migration:rollback --step=2 Undo the last 2 migrations, even across batches. dox migration:rollback --batch=3 Undo only the migrations of batch 3. dox migration:reset Undo all migrations. dox migration:refresh Undo all migrations, then run them again. dox migration:fresh Drop all tables, then run all migrations. It also drops tables that no migration made. dox migration:status Show each migration, its batch, and if it ran.

migrate:rollback, migrate:reset, migrate:refresh, migrate:fresh and migrate:status are short names.

Add --seed to migration:run, migration:refresh or migration:fresh to run the seeders after it.

When APP_ENV=production, migration:rollback, migration:reset, migration:refresh and migration:fresh ask before they drop the tables. Type y to go on. Add --force to skip the question. With no terminal (CI or a deploy script), they print a warning and run.

A batch is the group of migrations that ran in one migration:run. Migrations are undone newest first. When the file of a migration that ran is gone, rollback prints Migration not found: <name>. It keeps the row of that migration and rolls back the others. The ran migrations are saved in the dox_db_migration table.

When a migration fails, the error shows its name, and the command exits with code 1. The failed migration is not saved, and the later ones do not run.

You can also run dart run bin/migrate.dart run (or rollback --step=2, reset, refresh, status) yourself.

docs.title: Run on server start
docs.text:
The AOT server binary can run the migrations, because the registry is compiled in. The new app template already does this:

bin/server.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() async {
  Dox().initialize(appConfig);
  await Migrator(
    migrations: migrations,
    config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig(),
  ).migrate();
  await Dox().startServer();
}

It uses the config from lib/config/database.dart, so it also works without a .env file.

Keep the db/migration folder next to the binary if you also have .sql migrations.

docs.title: Database settings
docs.text:
The migrations read the .env file and the environment variables. A real environment variable wins over .env, the same as Env.get().

When DATABASE_URL is set, it wins over all DB_* keys. See DATABASE_URL.

.env
DB_CONNECTION=postgres # or mysql (also MariaDB), or sqlite
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432
DB_NAME=postgres
DB_USERNAME=admin
DB_PASSWORD=password

For SQLite, only two variables are needed:

.env
DB_CONNECTION=sqlite
DB_NAME=db/dox.sqlite # file path, made if missing
  • DB_DATABASE works too, in place of DB_NAME.
  • Without DB_CONNECTION, the migrations use Postgres. So always set it in .env.
  • The default port is 5432 for Postgres and 3306 for MySQL.
  • One run opens one driver and closes it at the end. Each migration runs on one connection.
  • A DB_HOST that starts with / is a Unix socket.
  • Migrations use TLS only with a DATABASE_URL that has sslmode (Postgres) or ssl (MySQL), like ?sslmode=require. The url options are on the Database page.

You can also give the database yourself:

  • Migrator(migrations: migrations, config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig()) opens this config, and closes it at the end.
  • Migrator(migrations: migrations, connection: SqlQueryBuilder().dbDriver) runs on a driver that is already open. The migrator does not close it.
  • Migrator(migrations: migrations, flags: databaseConfig.flags) gives the ORM flags to the Schema of each migration. Without it, the migrator uses SqlQueryBuilder().flags.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
Each migration runs in one transaction. On Postgres and SQLite, a failed migration undoes all its changes.

MySQL

On MySQL and MariaDB, CREATE, ALTER and DROP save right away. So if a migration fails half way, these changes stay. Only data changes are undone. Keep each MySQL migration small: one table change per migration.

To run a migration without a transaction (for example CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on Postgres):

class AddSearchIndex extends Migration {
  @override
  bool get withinTransaction => false;

  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.driver.execute(
      'CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY posts_title_index ON posts (title)',
    );
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.driver.execute('DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY posts_title_index');
  }
}

SQLite foreign keys

On SQLite, foreign key checks are off while a migration runs. This lets Dox make a table again (see SQLite notes). Before the end, Dox checks all foreign keys. The migration fails if one is broken.

docs.title: SQL migrations
docs.text:
Use a .sql migration for SQL that only one database understands.
