dox make:migration create_blog_table --sql

-- up
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS blog (
    id serial PRIMARY KEY,
    title VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL
);

-- down
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS blog
  • Put the up SQL under a line -- up, and the down SQL under a line -- down. Each of these lines must be on its own line. Other -- lines are normal SQL comments.
  • Statements are split on ;. A ; inside quotes, comments or a postgres $$ ... $$ body does not split.

SQLite ids

In SQLite, id serial PRIMARY KEY does not make an auto increment id. The id stays NULL. Use id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT for SQLite. table.id() in Dart does this for you.

docs.title: Dart and SQL in one folder
docs.text:
Both kinds can live in db/migration. They run in file name order (the timestamp).

  • With bin/migrate.dart: the Migrator runs the Dart migrations from the registry and reads the .sql files from the folder, merged by name.
  • Without bin/migrate.dart (a project with only .sql files): dox runs the .sql files itself.
  • A Dart and a .sql migration with the same name is an error.

docs.title: Native MySQL driver
docs.text:
dox_mysql_native is the MySQL and MariaDB driver of the Dox ORM, written in Rust.

You use it through your models and queries. It needs no extra config. Rust (mysql_async) owns the connections and the pool. Each connection keeps its prepared statements. It works with MySQL 8.4 (the default caching_sha2_password login) and MariaDB 11.

New driver

This driver is new. If you see a problem, please open an issue.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text: A find-by-id query takes about 65 µs alone, and about 10 µs each with 32 queries in flight (AOT build, local MySQL 8.4 or MariaDB 11, Apple M-series). See Performance: database drivers.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
dox_orm depends on dox_mysql_native. You do not add it yourself. Add it only to use MysqlNativePool without the ORM:

dart pub add dox_mysql_native

You do not need Rust. The build hook downloads a ready-built library for your system.

The package lives in its own repo: dartondox/dox-mysql-native.

docs.title: When the library does not load
docs.text:
MySQL has no other driver in Dox. When the native library does not load, SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig (and every other place that opens a MySQL connection) throws an UnsupportedError like this:

dox_mysql_native did not load: <reason>.
Dox needs it to talk to MySQL. Fix: run the app with `dart run` or `dart build cli`. ...

To fix it:

  • Run the app with dart run, dart test or dart build cli. They run the build hook. dart compile exe does not.
  • Or install Rust. The build hook then builds the library from source.
  • When you set lib_path in pubspec.yaml, check that the file is there and is built for your system.

A driverFactory on the connection wins over all of this: the ORM uses your driver.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
The driver reads the normal fields of the ConnectionConfig (host, port, user, password, database, useSSL) and these keys from extra:

Key Default What it does maxConnectionCount 10 Most connections in the pool. requestTimeout 300 s The longest wait for one request. maxConnectionAge 12 hours A connection older than this is closed once it has no query. idleTimeout 12 hours A connection with no traffic for this long is closed. serverKill true Stop a cancelled or timed out query on the server with KILL. preparedStatementCacheSize 100 Prepared statements kept per connection. threads 1 Rust threads for all pools of the process. Only the first pool sets it. One thread is the fastest for most apps. verifyCertificate true With useSSL, TLS checks the server certificate. Set it to false only for a self-signed certificate in development.

Isolates that open a pool with the same settings share one pool in Rust. So maxConnectionCount is for the whole process, not per isolate. You can also give driver.pool.handle (an int) to another isolate and use MysqlNativeDriver(MysqlNativePool.fromHandle(handle)) there. MysqlNativeDriver comes from package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart.

A CREATE, ALTER, RENAME or DROP makes every connection prepare its statements again. If your app runs CREATE TEMP TABLE or DROP on every request, this happens each time. Do it once at start up, not per request.

docs.title: Use it without the ORM
docs.text:
MysqlNativePool pool = MysqlNativePool.open(
  host: 'localhost',
  user: 'root',
  password: 'password',
  database: 'app',
);

MysqlNativeResult result = await pool.query(
  'SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE id = ?',
  parameters: <Object?>[1],
);
print(result.rows); // [{id: 1, name: Ada}]

MysqlNativeResult insert = await pool.query(
  'INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES (@name)',
  parameters: <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Bob'},
);
print(insert.insertId); // the new AUTO_INCREMENT id
print(insert.affectedRows); // 1

int tx = await pool.begin();
await pool.execute('UPDATE users SET name = ?', parameters: <Object?>['Cy'], transaction: tx);
await pool.commit(tx); // or pool.rollback(tx)
  • parameters is a list for ?, or a map for @name.
  • execute is like query, but the rows are not sent back to Dart.
  • A transaction runs on one connection. Its queries run in the order you send them.

docs.title: Pool settings
docs.text:
All are optional. In the ORM, put them in extra (see Pool settings). Without the ORM, pass them to MysqlNativePool.open. A time is a Duration.

MysqlNativePool pool = MysqlNativePool.open(
  host: 'localhost',
  user: 'root',
  password: 'password',
  database: 'app',
  requestTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 30),
  maxConnectionAge: const Duration(minutes: 30),
  idleTimeout: const Duration(minutes: 5),
  serverKill: true,
);
  • requestTimeout (default 300 s): the longest wait for one request. A request is a free connection, the connect and the query. Over it, the request fails, and its connection is closed. A transaction with no request for this long is rolled back.
  • maxConnectionAge (default: 12 hours in the ORM config, no limit in MysqlNativePool.open): a connection older than this is closed once it has no query. It is a real age, also for a busy connection.
  • idleTimeout (default 12 hours): a connection with no traffic for this long is closed once it has no query.
  • serverKill (default true): the driver stops a cancelled or timed out query on the server with KILL QUERY, sent on a new connection. In the url of MysqlNativePool.fromUrl, the option is server_kill. In DATABASE_URL of the ORM, use ?serverKill=false.

A connection that runs a query is never closed by these.

The KILL connection goes to the same address as the connection of the query. With serverKill on, each connection reads the server name once after login (@@server_uuid, on MariaDB the hostname, port and server_id). The KILL is sent only when both connections name the same server. Else no KILL is sent, and a warning is printed. This small query shows in the general log and the audit log of the server.

Behind a proxy

The KILL goes on a new connection. Behind a proxy or a load balancer (like ProxySQL, or a cloud endpoint over many servers), that connection may reach another server. The server name check stops a KILL that reaches another server. Two servers with the same server_uuid (eg. a copied data folder) still look like one server. Behind a proxy with its own connection ids, like ProxySQL, set serverKill: false. A cancelled query then fails in Dart at once, but it runs to its end on the server. A timed out query only has its socket closed.

The KILL connection also counts for max_user_connections. A KILL that fails prints a warning on stderr.

docs.title: Cancel a query
docs.text:
MysqlCancelToken token = MysqlCancelToken();
Future<MysqlNativeResult> slow = pool.query('SELECT SLEEP(10)', cancelToken: token);
token.cancel(); // slow fails with MysqlQueryCancelledException
  • query, execute and stream take cancelToken.
  • Not started yet: it does not run. Running: the driver sends KILL QUERY, so the server stops it (see serverKill). Ended already: nothing changes.
  • In a transaction, the next queries wait until the KILL has its answer, so it can only stop the cancelled query.
  • When more queries wait on the same connection, the cancelled one runs to its end instead, and its rows are dropped.
  • A connection that got a KILL QUERY closes once it has no query. Inside a transaction it stays, and the transaction goes on.

In the ORM, use cancelWith().

docs.title: Stream rows
docs.text:
await for (MysqlNativeResult chunk in pool.stream('SELECT * FROM logs', chunkSize: 1000)) {
  print(chunk.rows.length); // up to 1000
}
  • Each event is a chunk of up to chunkSize rows, with the same columns and rows as query.
  • Rows are read from the server as they come. Rust reads at most 2 chunks ahead of your listener. A paused listener stops the reading, so a big result does not fill the memory.
  • Stop listening (break in await for) to stop the query. It is stopped with KILL QUERY, and the connection is closed.
  • Outside a transaction, a stream gets a connection of its own. Pass transaction: to stream inside a transaction.
  • The server stops a connection whose client does not read for net_write_timeout (60 s by default). Do not pause a stream for longer.

In the ORM, use cursor().

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
MySQL / MariaDB Dart TINYINT(1) (boolean()) bool TINYINT, SMALLINT, INT, BIGINT, YEAR int FLOAT, DOUBLE, DECIMAL double CHAR, VARCHAR, TEXT, ENUM String DATE, DATETIME, TIMESTAMP DateTime in UTC TIME String, like 12:34:56 JSON the decoded JSON value BLOB, BINARY, VARBINARY Uint8List NULL null

MariaDB keeps JSON columns as LONGTEXT. So on MariaDB, TEXT that is a JSON object or array comes back decoded.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Every error throws MysqlException. For an error from the server, code is the MySQL error number (eg. 1062 for a duplicate key) and sqlState is the 5 letter SQLSTATE. For other errors (eg. the server is down) both are null. MysqlException comes from package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart.

try {
  await QueryBuilder.table('users').insert(<String, dynamic>{'email': email});
} on MysqlException catch (error) {
  if (error.code == 1062) print('taken');
}

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text:
• The timeZone, collation, serverPublicKey and timeoutMs keys are not read. The connection uses utf8mb4.
  • A login with sha256_password (not the default) does not work. The default caching_sha2_password and mysql_native_password work.

docs.title: Native Postgres driver
docs.text:
dox_postgres_native is the Postgres driver of the Dox ORM, written in Rust.

You use it through your models and queries. It needs no extra config. Rust (tokio-postgres) owns the connections and the pool. Each connection keeps its prepared statements.

New driver

This driver is new. If you see a problem, please open an issue.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text: A find-by-id query takes about 60 µs alone, and about 12.5 µs each with 64 queries in flight (AOT build, local Postgres 14, Apple M-series). See Performance: database drivers.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
dox_orm depends on dox_postgres_native. You do not add it yourself. Add it only to use PgNativePool without the ORM:

dart pub add dox_postgres_native

You do not need Rust. The build hook downloads a ready-built library for your system.

The package lives in its own repo: dartondox/dox-postgres-native.

docs.title: When the library does not load
docs.text:
Postgres has no other driver in Dox. When the native library does not load, SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig (and every other place that opens a Postgres connection) throws an UnsupportedError like this:

dox_postgres_native did not load: <reason>.
Dox needs it to talk to Postgres. Fix: run the app with `dart run` or `dart build cli`. ...

The reason tells what went wrong, for example no library for your system. To fix it:

  • Run the app with dart run, dart test or dart build cli. They run the build hook. dart compile exe does not.
  • Or install Rust. The build hook then builds the library from source.
  • When you set lib_path in pubspec.yaml, check that the file is there and is built for your system.

A driverFactory on the connection wins over all of this: the ORM uses your driver.

docs.title: TLS
docs.text:
Set the TLS mode with useSSL or extra['sslMode'], or with sslmode in the DATABASE_URL:

Mode What it does disable No TLS. The default. prefer TLS when the server has it. No certificate check. require TLS. No certificate check, like libpq. useSSL: true gives this mode. verify-ca TLS. The certificate is checked, the host name is not. verify-full TLS. The certificate and the host name are checked.

Without sslRootCert, verify-ca and verify-full use the Mozilla roots and the roots of the system.

In mode require, Dox prints a warning (once per isolate), because the server certificate is not checked. To hide it, set extra['sslWarning'] to false, or add sslWarning=false to DATABASE_URL.

ConnectionConfig(
  driver: Driver.postgres,
  // ... host, user, password, database as before
  extra: <String, dynamic>{'sslMode': 'verify-full'},
  debug: false,
),

To trust your own CA (for example the CA bundle of your cloud database, or a self-signed CA in development), give the path of a PEM file in extra['sslRootCert'], or with sslrootcert in the url. Then verify-ca and verify-full trust only the certificates in that file. prefer and require do not use it.

extra: <String, dynamic>{
  'sslMode': 'verify-full',
  'sslRootCert': '/etc/ssl/certs/db-ca.pem',
},

DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:secret@db.example.com/blog?sslmode=verify-full&sslrootcert=/etc/ssl/certs/db-ca.pem

A missing file, or a file with no valid certificate, throws PgException when the pool opens.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
The driver reads these keys from extra of the ConnectionConfig:

Key Default What it does maxConnectionCount 10 Most connections in the pool, for the whole process. requestTimeout 300 s The longest wait for one request. maxConnectionAge no limit A connection older than this is closed once it has no query. idleTimeout no limit A free connection not used for this long is closed. sslMode disable TLS mode, see TLS. sslRootCert none Path of a PEM file with the CA certificates to trust for verify-ca and verify-full, see TLS. timeZone UTC Time zone of the session. applicationName none Name of the app in pg_stat_activity. threads 1 Rust threads for all pools of the process. 0 is one thread with a single-thread runtime. Only the first pool sets it.

Isolates that open a pool with the same settings share one pool in Rust. So maxConnectionCount is for the whole process, not per isolate. The pool closes when the last isolate closes it. You can also give driver.pool.handle (an int) to another isolate and use PostgresNativeDriver(PgNativePool.fromHandle(handle)) there. PostgresNativeDriver comes from package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart.

Each connection keeps up to 512 prepared statements. When it is full, it drops the one used longest ago.

A CREATE, ALTER or DROP makes every connection prepare its statements again. If your app runs CREATE TEMP TABLE or DROP on every request, this happens each time. Do this once at start up, not per request.

docs.title: Use it without the ORM
docs.text:
PgNativePool pool = PgNativePool.open(
  host: 'localhost',
  user: 'postgres',
  password: 'postgres',
  database: 'postgres',
);

PgNativeResult result = await pool.query(
  'SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE id = @id',
  parameters: <String, dynamic>{'id': 1},
);
print(result.rows); // [{id: 1, name: Ada}]

int tx = await pool.begin();
await pool.query('UPDATE users SET name = @n', parameters: <String, dynamic>{'n': 'Bob'}, transaction: tx);
await pool.commit(tx); // or pool.rollback(tx)
  • parameters is a map for @name, or a list for $1, $2.
  • A transaction runs on one connection. Its queries run in the order you send them.
  • PgNativePool.fromUrl('postgres://user:pass@host:5432/db?sslmode=require') makes a pool from a url.

docs.title: Pool settings
docs.text:
All are optional. In the ORM, put them in extra (see Pool settings). Without the ORM, pass them to PgNativePool.open:

PgNativePool pool = PgNativePool.open(
  host: 'localhost',
  user: 'postgres',
  password: 'postgres',
  database: 'postgres',
  requestTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 30),
  maxConnectionAge: const Duration(minutes: 30),
  idleTimeout: const Duration(minutes: 5),
);
  • requestTimeout (default 300 s): the longest wait for one request. A request is a free connection, the connect and the query. Over it, the request fails with a PgException that says timeout. A CancelRequest stops the query on the server, and its connection is closed. A transaction with no request for this long is rolled back.
  • maxConnectionAge (default: no limit): a connection older than this is closed when it is next free. It is never closed while a query or a transaction uses it. This helps behind a load balancer, or to follow a DNS change after a failover.
  • idleTimeout (default: no limit): a free connection that is not used for this long is closed. A new one opens when it is needed.

fromUrl takes the same three. Isolates share one pool only when all settings are the same.

docs.title: Cancel a query
docs.text:
PgCancelToken token = PgCancelToken();
Future<PgNativeResult> slow = pool.query('SELECT pg_sleep(60)', cancelToken: token);
token.cancel();
try {
  await slow;
} on PgQueryCancelledException {
  print('stopped');
}
  • Cancel before the query starts: it does not run.
  • Cancel while it runs: the driver sends a Postgres CancelRequest, and the future fails with PgQueryCancelledException.
  • Cancel after it ended: nothing happens. You keep the result.
  • A query with a token gets a connection for itself, so the cancel can not stop another query.
  • In a transaction, a cancelled query is an error, so Postgres aborts the transaction. Roll it back.
  • One token can stop many queries. Use it in the isolate that made it.
  • The CancelRequest goes in plain text on a new connection, like libpq before Postgres 17.

In the ORM, use cancelWith().

docs.title: Stream rows
docs.text:
For a big result, stream gives the rows in chunks. Each chunk is a PgNativeResult with up to chunkSize rows (default 1000).

await for (PgNativeResult chunk in pool.stream(
  'SELECT * FROM events WHERE day = @day',
  parameters: <String, dynamic>{'day': '2026-01-01'},
  chunkSize: 500,
)) {
  for (Map<String, dynamic> row in chunk.rows) {
    // ...
  }
}
  • The query runs on a server-side portal. The driver asks for the next chunk only when your listener is ready. So only about two chunks are in memory, also for millions of rows.
  • The query starts when you listen. Stop listening (break in await for) to stop it. Its connection is free again.
  • cancelToken stops it too. Then the stream fails with PgQueryCancelledException.
  • An error comes as a stream error, then the stream ends.
  • It holds one connection until it ends. A paused listener that waits longer than requestTimeout fails with a timeout.
  • It works in a transaction (transaction: tx). Other queries of that transaction wait until the stream ends.

In the ORM, use cursor().

docs.title: Values
docs.text:
You send plain Dart values: null, bool, int, double, String, DateTime, Duration (an interval), Uint8List (bytea), Map (json) and List (an array, eg. for int4[]).

  • The server picks the type. When it can not, add a cast in the SQL, eg. @id::int8.
  • A List is an array, not json. On insert and update the ORM sends a List as json text, so a List in a json column works. With the pool alone, send jsonEncode(list) for a json column.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
Postgres Dart int2, int4, int8 int float4, float8 double numeric String text, varchar, char String bool bool timestamp, timestamptz, date DateTime in UTC infinity dates the text 'infinity' or '-infinity' time String, eg. '13:45:01.5' interval Duration (a month is 30 days) json, jsonb the decoded JSON value uuid String bytea Uint8List arrays of most types above List NULL null

Other types come back as Uint8List.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A server error throws PgServerException. It has code (the SQLSTATE, eg. 23505 for a unique violation), severity, message, and detail, hint, schema, table, column and constraint when the server sends them. Other errors (eg. the server is down, a TLS error, a timeout) throw PgException. A query stopped with a cancel token throws PgQueryCancelledException, which is a PgException. They come from package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart.

try {
  await QueryBuilder.table('users').insert(<String, dynamic>{'email': email});
} on PgServerException catch (error) {
  if (error.code == '23505') print('taken: ${error.constraint}');
}

docs.title: Query Builder
docs.text:
The query builder makes SQL from chained methods and runs it with bound values on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite.

Set up the database first. See Database.

docs.title: Start a query
docs.text:
There are two ways to start a query.

// with a model: the result is a list of Actor models
List<Actor> actors = await Actor().where('age', '>=', 23).get();

// with a table name: the result is a list of maps, one map per row
List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.table('actor')
    .where('age', '>=', 23)
    .get();

The examples on this page use an Actor model on the table actor. The SQL in the examples is for Postgres. MySQL quotes names with ` instead of ".

Start each query with a new object

A query object keeps its where, orderBy and other parts. Use Actor() (or QueryBuilder.table(...)) again for each new query.

docs.title: get
docs.text:
Runs the query and returns all rows that match.

List<Actor> actors = await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').get();
// SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "name" = @name_p0

docs.title: all
docs.text:
Returns all rows that match the where part. all() ignores join, orderBy and limit. Use get() for those.

List<Actor> actors = await Actor().all();
// SELECT * FROM "actor"

docs.title: find
docs.text:
Returns one row, or null when there is no match.

// by primary key
Actor? actor = await Actor().find(1);
// SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "id" = @id_p0 LIMIT 1

// by another column
Actor? byName = await Actor().find('name', 'John Wick');
// SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "name" = @name_p0 LIMIT 1

docs.title: getFirst and first
docs.text:
Returns the first row of the query, or null. first() does the same.

Actor? actor = await Actor().where('age', '>', 60).orderBy('age').getFirst();
// SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "age" > @age_p0 ORDER BY "age" LIMIT 1

Actor? same = await Actor().where('age', '>', 60).orderBy('age').first();

docs.title: firstOrFail and findOrFail
docs.text:
They work like getFirst() and find(). When no row matches, they throw a ModelNotFoundException. So the result is never null.

Actor actor = await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').firstOrFail();

Actor byId = await Actor().findOrFail(1);
Actor byName = await Actor().findOrFail('name', 'John Wick');

The exception has the table, and for findOrFail() also the column and the id it looked for. When a route does not catch it, the client gets 404 with {"code": "not_found", "message": "Not Found"}.

try {
  Actor actor = await Actor().findOrFail(id);
} on ModelNotFoundException catch (e) {
  print(e.table); // actor
  print(e.id);    // the id
}

docs.title: sole
docs.text:
sole() returns the only row of the query. It throws a ModelNotFoundException when no row matches. It throws a MultipleRecordsFoundException when more than one row matches.

Actor actor = await Actor().where('email', 'john@example.com').sole();

It reads 2 rows at most.

docs.title: count
docs.text:
Returns the number of rows as an int.

int total = await Actor().count();
int adults = await Actor().where('age', '>=', 18).count();
// SELECT count(*) as total FROM "actor" WHERE "age" >= @age_p0
  • count() ignores limit, offset and orderBy.
  • With groupBy, count() returns the number of groups.
  • With distinct(), count() returns the number of distinct rows. See distinct.

docs.title: hasRows and hasNoRows
docs.text:
hasRows() returns true when at least one row matches. hasNoRows() returns the opposite. doesntExist() is the same as hasNoRows(). They read one row at most, so they are faster than count() > 0.

bool taken = await User().where('email', email).hasRows();

if (await User().where('email', email).hasNoRows()) {
  await User().create(<String, dynamic>{'email': email});
}

A model also has the exists getter. It tells if that one model is saved in the table. hasRows() checks a query.

There is no exists() method on a query, because a model already has the getter exists. Use hasRows(). There is no value() either, because value is a common column name. Use valueOf.

docs.title: pluck and pluckMap
docs.text:
pluck() returns the values of one column, as a list.

List<dynamic> names = await Actor().orderBy('name').pluck('name');
// ['John Doe', 'John Wick']

pluckMap() returns a map. The second column gives the keys. When two rows have the same key, the last row wins.

Map<dynamic, dynamic> names = await Actor().pluckMap('name', 'id');
// {1: 'John Wick', 2: 'John Doe'}

Both use where, join, orderBy, limit and distinct. A date comes back as an ISO string.

docs.title: valueOf
docs.text:
Returns the value of one column of the first row. It returns null when no row matches.

dynamic age = await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').valueOf('age');

docs.title: paginate
docs.text:
Returns one page of rows and the page info. It runs a count() query and a get() query.

Pagination<Actor> page = await Actor()
    .where('age', '>=', 18)
    .paginate(currentPage: 2, perPage: 10);

List<Actor> actors = page.data;
print(page.total);    // rows that match
print(page.lastPage); // number of pages

page.toJson() gives total, per_page, last_page, current_page and data. So you can return a Pagination from a controller.

  • perPage must be 1 or more. A smaller value throws an ArgumentError.
  • With no rows, lastPage is 0. The lastPageAtLeastOne flag makes it 1.
  • A currentPage below 1 is read as page 1.

docs.title: simplePaginate
docs.text:
Like paginate(), but without the total count. So it runs one query, not two. It reads one row more to know if there is a next page.

SimplePagination<Actor> page = await Actor()
    .orderBy('id')
    .simplePaginate(currentPage: 2, perPage: 10);

List<Actor> actors = page.data;
print(page.hasMorePages); // true when there is a next page

page.toJson() gives per_page, current_page, from, to, has_more_pages and data. from and to are the numbers of the first and last row of the page. They are null on an empty page.

docs.title: cursorPaginate
docs.text:
Returns one page of rows after a cursor. It uses a WHERE on the order columns, not OFFSET, so it stays fast on a big table. Use it for an endless list or an API.

CursorPagination<Actor> page = await Actor()
    .where('age', '>=', 18)
    .orderBy('age', 'desc')
    .cursorPaginate(perPage: 10, cursor: req.input('cursor'));

List<Actor> actors = page.data;
print(page.nextCursor); // send it back as `cursor` to read the next page
print(page.prevCursor); // send it back as `cursor` to read the page before

page.toJson() gives per_page, next_cursor, prev_cursor and data. next_cursor is null on the last page. prev_cursor is null on the first page.

  • The rows are ordered by all the orderBy() columns. You can mix asc and desc.
  • With no orderBy(), they are ordered by the primary key. Or use column and direction: cursorPaginate(perPage: 10, column: 'created_at', direction: 'desc').
  • The primary key is added as the last order column, so rows with the same value are never skipped.
  • orderBy() together with column, orderByRaw() and inRandomOrder() throw a StateError.
  • It does not work on a union or a fromSub query. It throws a StateError there. Use paginate() or simplePaginate().
  • The order columns must be in the select, and they must have no null values.
  • The cursor is safe to take from a user. The columns and the order come from your code. The values of the cursor are only sent as query values, never as SQL.
  • A cursor that is not valid gives the first page. This is also true for a changed cursor with a value of the wrong kind, like a text for a number column.

docs.title: chunk and chunkById
docs.text:
Use them to work on a big table. They read a few rows at a time, so the rows do not fill the memory.

await Actor().where('age', '>=', 18).chunk(100, (List<Actor> actors) {
  for (Actor actor in actors) {
    print(actor.name);
  }
  return true; // go on to the next page
});
  • The function gets one page of rows.
  • Return true to go on, or false to stop. After a stop, chunk() returns false. Otherwise it returns true.
  • Without orderBy(), chunk() orders by the primary key. So each page has other rows.

chunk() pages with OFFSET. When the function changes or deletes rows, some rows can be skipped or read twice. Use chunkById() then.

await Actor().where('age', '>', 100).chunkById(100, (List<Actor> actors) async {
  for (Actor actor in actors) {
    await actor.delete();
  }
  return true;
});
  • chunkById() reads the rows after the last id: WHERE "id" > @last.
  • It orders by the id itself. A query with orderBy() throws a StateError.
  • chunkById() does not work on a union or a fromSub query. It throws a StateError there. Use chunk().
  • To use another column, add column: 'uuid'. The column must be unique.

docs.title: lazy, lazyById and cursor
docs.text:
These give the rows as a Stream, one row at a time. You do not write a function. Use await for.

await for (Actor actor in Actor().where('age', '>=', 18).lazy()) {
  print(actor.name);
}

await for (Actor actor in Actor().orderBy('id').cursor(chunkSize: 500)) {
  print(actor.name);
}

lazy() and lazyById() read the rows in chunks, with many queries. cursor() runs one query, and the driver streams the rows.

Method Queries How it pages lazy({chunkSize}) many By id when there is no orderBy(). With OFFSET when there is an orderBy(), a limit() or an offset(). lazyById({chunkSize, column}) many By id (or the unique column) like chunkById(). It throws a StateError with an orderBy(). cursor({chunkSize}) one The database sends the rows when you are ready for more.

The default chunkSize is 1000.

  • Stop reading (break, or .take(10)) to stop the queries.
  • lazy() starts at the offset() of the query and stops after its limit().
  • lazy() works on every database. It also works on a union or a fromSub query.
  • cursor() does not fill the memory with a big result. Postgres uses a server-side portal. MySQL sends the rows as they come. SQLite uses a statement cursor.
  • Relations of preload() load for each chunk.
  • In a transaction on Postgres or MySQL, cursor() with preload() throws a StateError. The one connection of the transaction is busy. Use lazy() there.
  • In a transaction on Postgres or MySQL, do not run another query of the same transaction inside a cursor() loop. It waits forever, because the stream holds the one connection. Use lazy() there.
  • Query listeners and the slow query log see a cursor() query once, when its first chunk comes. The time is the time to the first chunk.

docs.title: Cancel a query
docs.text:
Give a QueryCancelToken to a query with cancelWith(). token.cancel() stops the query on Postgres and MySQL.

QueryCancelToken token = QueryCancelToken();
Future<List<Actor>> actors = Actor().where('age', '>', 18).cancelWith(token).get();

token.cancel();
try {
  await actors;
} on PgQueryCancelledException {
  // Postgres: the query was stopped
} on MysqlQueryCancelledException {
  // MySQL: the query was stopped
}
  • A token that is cancelled already fails a new query at once.
  • The relation queries of preload() use the token too.
  • cursor() takes a token too.
  • SQLite does not support cancel. The query runs to its end.

docs.title: Aggregates
docs.text:
sum, avg, min and max return one value for all rows that match. They return null when no row matches.

num? total = await Actor().where('age', '>=', 18).sum('age');
double? average = await Actor().avg('age');
dynamic youngest = await Actor().min('age');
dynamic newest = await Actor().max('created_at');
  • sum() returns a num. It is an int or a double, by driver. Use toInt() or toDouble(). When no row matches, it is null. The sumReturnsZero flag makes it 0.
  • avg() returns a double.
  • min() and max() return the value as the driver gives it. A date is an ISO string. A Postgres numeric is a String. A MySQL DECIMAL is a double.
  • Like count(), they use where, join and soft deletes. They ignore limit, offset and orderBy.
  • After distinct(), sum() and avg() use only the distinct values.
  • With groupBy() they throw a StateError. Use selectRaw() and get() for groups.

docs.title: where
docs.text:
// equal
await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').get();
// WHERE "name" = @name_p0

// other operator
await Actor().where('age', '>=', 23).get();
await Actor().where('name', '!=', 'John Wick').get();
await Actor().where('name', 'like', 'John%').get();

Many where calls are joined with AND.

Info

The operator must be one of =, !=, <>, <, >, <=, >=, like, not like or ilike (any case). Any other value throws an ArgumentError. The column must be a plain name. Use whereRaw for expressions.

docs.title: null values
docs.text:
A null value makes an IS NULL or IS NOT NULL check.

await Actor().where('deleted_at', null).get();
// WHERE "deleted_at" IS NULL

await Actor().where('deleted_at', '=', null).get();
// WHERE "deleted_at" IS NULL

await Actor().where('deleted_at', '!=', null).get();
// WHERE "deleted_at" IS NOT NULL
  • = with null is IS NULL.
  • != or <> with null is IS NOT NULL.
  • Any other operator with null throws an ArgumentError.
  • where('name') with no value throws an ArgumentError.

whereNull and whereNotNull do the same. See whereNull.

docs.title: orWhere
docs.text:
await Actor().where('name', 'John Doe').orWhere('name', 'John Wick').get();
// WHERE "name" = @name_p0 OR "name" = @name_p1

await Actor().where('age', '<', 18).orWhere('age', '>', 60).get();

orWhere takes the same arguments as where, also null.

docs.title: whereGroup and orWhereGroup
docs.text:
Use them to put conditions in brackets. The function gets the query. Add the conditions to it.

await Actor()
    .where('status', 'active')
    .whereGroup((QueryBuilder<Actor> q) {
      q.where('age', '<', 18).orWhere('age', '>', 60);
    })
    .get();
// WHERE "status" = @status_p0 AND ("age" < @age_p1 OR "age" > @age_p2)

await Actor()
    .where('id', 1)
    .orWhereGroup((QueryBuilder<Actor> q) {
      q.where('status', 'active').where('age', '>', 60);
    })
    .get();
// WHERE "id" = @id_p0 OR ("status" = @status_p1 AND "age" > @age_p2)
  • A group can have another group in it.
  • An empty group adds nothing.
  • Add only where conditions in the function. The function gets the same query, so an orderBy() there is for the whole query.

docs.title: whereNot and orWhereNot
docs.text:
whereNot keeps the rows where the conditions in the brackets are not true.

await Actor()
    .whereNot((QueryBuilder<Actor> q) {
      q.where('status', 'draft').orWhere('age', '<', 18);
    })
    .get();
// WHERE NOT ("status" = @status_p0 OR "age" < @age_p1)

await Actor()
    .where('id', 1)
    .orWhereNot((QueryBuilder<Actor> q) => q.where('status', 'draft'))
    .get();

They also take a column and a value, like where:

await Actor().whereNot('status', 'draft').get();
await Actor().whereNot('age', '<', 18).get();
await Actor().where('id', 1).orWhereNot('status', 'draft').get();

Give the function its type, like (QueryBuilder<Actor> q) {...}. Without it, q is dynamic.

Note

A row with NULL in a column of the brackets matches neither the brackets nor NOT of them. This is how SQL works with NULL.

docs.title: whereAny and whereAll
docs.text:
whereAny keeps the rows where at least one of the columns matches. whereAll keeps the rows where all of the columns match. They take the same values as where, after the list of columns.

await Actor().whereAny(<String>['name', 'email'], 'like', '%john%').get();
// WHERE ("name" like @name_p0 OR "email" like @email_p1)

await Actor().whereAll(<String>['first_name', 'last_name'], 'like', 'J%').get();
// WHERE ("first_name" like @first_name_p0 AND "last_name" like @last_name_p1)
  • The conditions go in one bracket.
  • Each one has an or form: orWhereAny and orWhereAll.
  • An empty list adds nothing.

docs.title: whereIn and whereNotIn
docs.text:
await Actor().whereIn('id', <int>[1, 2]).get();
// WHERE "id" IN (@id_p0,@id_p1)

await Actor().whereNotIn('id', <int>[1, 2]).get();
await Actor().where('age', 60).orWhereIn('id', <int>[1, 2]).get();
await Actor().where('age', 60).orWhereNotIn('id', <int>[1, 2]).get();
  • On Postgres, a list of only int or only String values is sent as one array parameter: "id" = ANY(@id_p0) (<> ALL for whereNotIn).
  • An empty list matches no rows for whereIn, and all rows for whereNotIn.

The list can also be another Iterable, like a Set. The value can also be a query that selects one column. Its values are bound too.

await Actor()
    .whereIn('id', QueryBuilder.table('award').select('actor_id').where('year', 2024))
    .get();
// WHERE "id" IN (SELECT "actor_id" FROM "award" WHERE "year" = @dox_sub0_year_p0)
  • The sub query is built when it is added. A change to it after whereIn is not used. This is the same for joinSub, fromSub and union.
  • MySQL and MariaDB do not allow LIMIT in an IN (sub query).

docs.title: whereNull and whereNotNull
docs.text:
await Actor().whereNull('deleted_at').get();
await Actor().whereNotNull('deleted_at').get();
await Actor().where('age', 60).orWhereNull('deleted_at').get();
await Actor().where('age', 60).orWhereNotNull('deleted_at').get();

docs.title: whereBetween and whereNotBetween
docs.text:
The list has two values: from and to. Both are in the range.

await Actor().whereBetween('age', <int>[18, 60]).get();
// WHERE "age" BETWEEN @age_p0 AND @age_p1

await Actor().whereNotBetween('age', <int>[18, 60]).get();
await Actor().where('id', 1).orWhereBetween('age', <int>[18, 60]).get();
await Actor().where('id', 1).orWhereNotBetween('age', <int>[18, 60]).get();

The list must have two values that are not null. Otherwise it throws an ArgumentError.

docs.title: whereColumn
docs.text:
Compares two columns. Both names are columns, not values.

await Actor().whereColumn('created_at', 'updated_at').get();
// WHERE "created_at" = "updated_at"

await Actor().whereColumn('updated_at', '>', 'created_at').get();
// WHERE "updated_at" > "created_at"

await Actor().where('id', 1).orWhereColumn('updated_at', '>', 'created_at').get();

docs.title: whereLike and whereNotLike
docs.text:
Matches a column with a pattern. % is any text. _ is one character.

await Actor().whereLike('name', '%wick%').get();
await Actor().whereNotLike('name', '%doe%').get();
await Actor().where('id', 1).orWhereLike('name', 'John%').get();
await Actor().where('id', 1).orWhereNotLike('name', 'John%').get();

By default, the match does not care about upper or lower case. Add caseSensitive: true to care about case.

await Actor().whereLike('name', 'John%', caseSensitive: true).get();
Database Default caseSensitive: true Postgres ILIKE LIKE MySQL, MariaDB LIKE. The column collation decides. The default collations do not care about case. LIKE BINARY SQLite LIKE. It does not care about case for ASCII letters only. GLOB. Dox changes the pattern for you.

docs.title: whereExists and whereNotExists
docs.text:
whereExists keeps the rows where a subquery finds a row. The function gets a new query on the other table.

List<User> users = await User()
    .whereExists('post', (QueryBuilder<Map<String, dynamic>> q) {
      q.whereColumn('post.user_id', 'user.id');
    })
    .get();
// WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM "post" WHERE "post"."user_id" = "user"."id")

await User()
    .whereNotExists('post', (QueryBuilder<Map<String, dynamic>> q) {
      q.whereColumn('post.user_id', 'user.id');
    })
    .get();

orWhereExists and orWhereNotExists join the condition with OR.

Info

The subquery does not use global scopes or soft deletes. Add those conditions in the function, for example q.whereNull('deleted_at'). For a relation of a model, whereHas is shorter.

docs.title: whereDate, whereTime, whereYear, whereMonth and whereDay
docs.text:
They compare one part of a date or datetime column. Like where, they take an optional operator.

await Actor().whereDate('created_at', '2024-05-01').get();
await Actor().whereDate('created_at', '>=', DateTime(2024, 5, 1)).get();
await Actor().whereTime('created_at', '>', '18:00:00').get();
await Actor().whereYear('created_at', 2024).get();
await Actor().whereMonth('created_at', 5).get();
await Actor().whereDay('created_at', 15).get();
  • whereDate takes a DateTime or a yyyy-mm-dd string.
  • whereTime takes a DateTime or a hh:mm:ss string.
  • On SQLite, a whereDate or whereTime string must be zero padded, like 2024-05-01 or 09:00:00. A value like 2024-5-1 matches no row.
  • whereYear, whereMonth and whereDay take an int, a number string or a DateTime.
  • Each one has an or form, like orWhereDate.
  • The column is read as it is stored. On SQLite and Postgres, Dox stores a DateTime in UTC.
  • A DateTime value is compared the same way where binds it: in UTC on SQLite and Postgres, and as the wall clock on MySQL and MariaDB.
  • On Postgres, a timestamptz is read in the session time zone (UTC by default). If the connection sets another timeZone, a DateTime value does not match.
  • On Postgres, a column with fractions of a second does not equal a time without them. For example, 10:00:00.5 is not 10:00:00.
Database whereDate whereYear Postgres CAST(col AS date) EXTRACT(year FROM col) MySQL, MariaDB DATE(col) YEAR(col) SQLite date(col) strftime('%Y', col)

docs.title: whereJsonContains and whereJsonDoesntContain
docs.text:
whereJsonContains keeps the rows where a JSON column has the value. For a JSON array, the value is one item. A list value needs all its items.

await Actor().whereJsonContains('tags', 'action').get();
await Actor().whereJsonContains('tags', <String>['action', 'drama']).get();

// a key inside the JSON
await Actor().whereJsonContains('options->languages', 'en').get();

await Actor().whereJsonDoesntContain('tags', 'horror').get();
  • column->key reads a key inside the JSON. Keys can have letters, digits and _. Any other key throws an ArgumentError.
  • Each one has an or form, like orWhereJsonContains.
  • On SQLite, it also matches a value inside a JSON object, one level down. For example, {"a": "x"} matches 'x'.
Database SQL Postgres CAST(col AS jsonb) @> CAST(@value AS jsonb) MySQL, MariaDB JSON_CONTAINS(col, @value) SQLite EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM json_each(col) WHERE value = @value)

Note

On SQLite, the value must be a string, a number, a bool or a list of them. A map throws an ArgumentError. SQLite stores true as 1, so true, 1 and 1.0 match each other there.

Note

whereJsonDoesntContain on a row that does not have the key is not the same on every database. SQLite and MariaDB keep the row. Postgres and MySQL drop it.

docs.title: JSON columns
docs.text:
Use -> in a column name to read a key inside a JSON column. Use -> again for a nested key.

await Actor().where('options->lang', 'en').get();
await Actor().where('options->address->city', 'Paris').get();
await Actor().where('options->rating', '>', 4).get();
await Actor().where('options->active', true).get();

await Actor().whereIn('options->lang', <String>['en', 'de']).get();
await Actor().whereNull('options->lang').get();

List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.table('actor')
    .select(<String>['name', 'options->lang as lang'])
    .orderBy('options->lang')
    .get();
  • It works in where, the other where* methods, select, orderBy, groupBy and joins.
  • Keys can have letters, digits and _. Any other key throws an ArgumentError.
  • In select, give the value a name with as.
Database options->address->city SQLite json_extract("options", '$."address"."city"') MySQL, MariaDB json_unquote(json_extract(`options`, '$."address"."city"')) Postgres CAST("options" AS jsonb)->'address'->>'city'

Note

In where, a number or a bool value works the same on every database. On Postgres, the other methods compare the value as text. For example, whereBetween('options->rating', [1, 5]) and whereIn('options->rating', [4, 5]) compare text there. sum('options->rating') and avg(...) fail on Postgres, because the value is text. Use selectRaw with a cast for them.

Note

where('options->lang', null) and whereNull('options->lang') match a missing key. On SQLite and Postgres they also match a JSON null. On MySQL and MariaDB they do not.

Note

On SQLite, and in where on Postgres, the number 5 does not match the string "5". MySQL and MariaDB compare text with a number as numbers, so 5 matches "5" there.

docs.title: whereRaw and orWhereRaw
docs.text:
Write the condition yourself. Put values in a map, and use @key in the SQL. The column names are not quoted.

await Actor().whereRaw('name = @name', <String, dynamic>{'name': 'John Wick'}).get();

await Actor()
    .where('age', 60)
    .orWhereRaw('lower(name) = @name', <String, dynamic>{'name': 'john wick'})
    .get();

Warning

Never put user input into the SQL text. Always send it in the map.

docs.title: Filter by a relation
docs.text:
whereHas, whereDoesntHave and has keep the rows that have (or do not have) related rows. See Query by relations.

List<User> users = await User().whereHas('posts').get();

docs.title: when
docs.text:
Runs the function only when the condition is true. So you can keep the query in one chain.

List<Actor> actors = await Actor()
    .when(status != null, (QueryBuilder<Actor> q) {
      q.where('status', status);
    })
    .get();

A third function runs when the condition is false.

await Actor()
    .when(
      sort == 'name',
      (QueryBuilder<Actor> q) => q.orderBy('name'),
      (QueryBuilder<Actor> q) => q.latest(),
    )
    .get();

docs.title: unless and whenValue
docs.text:
unless is the opposite of when. It runs the function only when the condition is false.

await Actor()
    .unless(showDrafts, (QueryBuilder<Actor> q) {
      q.where('status', 'published');
    })
    .get();

whenValue runs the function when the value is not null. The function gets the value, and it is not null there.

await Actor()
    .whenValue(req.query['status'], (QueryBuilder<Actor> q, status) {
      q.where('status', status);
    })
    .get();

Both take a third function too. It runs in the other case.

docs.title: Select
docs.text:
select sets the columns. Each call replaces the columns of the call before.

// a list
await Actor().select(<String>['id', 'name']).get();
// SELECT "id","name" FROM "actor"

// comma separated
await Actor().select('id, name, age').get();

// with an alias
await Actor().select('name as actor_name').get();

// raw: nothing is quoted
await QueryBuilder.table('actor').selectRaw('count(*) as total, name').groupBy('name').get();

Each part must be a plain name: name, table.name, table.*, * or name as alias. Anything else, like count(*), throws an ArgumentError. Use selectRaw for it.

selectRaw() replaces the select list. The selectRawAdds flag makes it add to the list.

selectRaw() takes values, like whereRaw. Write @name in the SQL and put the value in the map. Use unique names. A name that the query uses in another place, like in whereRaw or in another selectRaw, throws an ArgumentError. A name may not start with dox_. The ORM uses these names for its own values.

await QueryBuilder.table('actor')
    .selectRaw('age * @rate as score', <String, dynamic>{'rate': 2})
    .get();

Info

A model loaded with select() only has the selected fields. save() on it only updates the fields it has.

docs.title: distinct
docs.text:
distinct() returns each row only once (SELECT DISTINCT).

List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.table('actor')
    .select('age')
    .distinct()
    .get();
// SELECT DISTINCT "age" FROM "actor"

int ages = await QueryBuilder.table('actor').select('age').distinct().count();

docs.title: orderBy
docs.text:
await Actor().orderBy('name').get();
await Actor().orderBy('name', 'desc').get();
await Actor().orderBy('name', 'asc').orderBy('id', 'desc').get();
// ORDER BY "name" asc,"id" desc
  • The direction must be asc or desc. Any other value throws an ArgumentError.
  • The column must be a plain name. Anything else throws an ArgumentError.
  • For an expression, use orderByRaw('count(*) desc'). Nothing is quoted there, so never put user input in it.

docs.title: orderByDesc and reorder
docs.text:
await Actor().orderByDesc('age').get();
// ORDER BY "age" desc

// remove the order
await Actor().latest().reorder().get();

// remove the order, then order by name
await Actor().latest().reorder('name').get();
await Actor().latest().reorder('name', 'desc').get();

docs.title: latest, oldest and inRandomOrder
docs.text:
Actor? newest = await Actor().latest().getFirst();
// ORDER BY "created_at" desc

await Actor().latest('updated_at').get();
await Actor().oldest().get();
// ORDER BY "created_at" asc

Actor? random = await Actor().inRandomOrder().getFirst();
  • latest() and oldest() use created_at when you give no column.
  • inRandomOrder() is RANDOM() on Postgres and SQLite, and RAND() on MySQL. It sorts the whole table, so it is slow on a big table.

docs.title: limit, take and offset
docs.text:
limit and take do the same thing.

await Actor().limit(10).get();
await Actor().take(10).get();
await Actor().limit(10).offset(20).get();
// LIMIT @dox_limit OFFSET @dox_offset

The numbers are sent as bound parameters.

docs.title: skip and forPage
docs.text:
skip is the same as offset. forPage gets one page of rows. The first page is 1. The page size is 15 when you give none.

await Actor().skip(20).take(10).get();

// rows 31 to 45
await Actor().forPage(3).get();

// rows 51 to 100
await Actor().forPage(2, 50).get();

docs.title: groupBy
docs.text:
Takes one column, or a list of columns.

List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.table('actor')
    .selectRaw('count(*) as total, age')
    .groupBy('age')
    .get();

For an expression, use groupByRaw('date(created_at)'). Nothing is quoted there.

A second groupBy() replaces the first. The groupByAdds flag makes it add to the first.

Info

Use QueryBuilder.table() for groupBy. A group row is a map, not a model. On a model, get() gives models (List<Actor>), so a groupBy there throws a StateError. count() with groupBy works on a model too.

docs.title: having
docs.text:
having filters the groups. It goes after GROUP BY. It takes the same arguments as where.

await QueryBuilder.table('actor')
    .selectRaw('status, count(*) as total')
    .groupBy('status')
    .having('status', '!=', 'draft')
    .orHaving('status', 'retired')
    .get();
// GROUP BY "status" HAVING "status" != @status_p0 OR "status" = @status_p1

Use havingRaw and orHavingRaw for an aggregate, like count(*). Put values in the map, like in whereRaw.

await QueryBuilder.table('actor')
    .selectRaw('status, count(*) as total')
    .groupBy('status')
    .havingRaw('count(*) > @min', <String, dynamic>{'min': 5})
    .get();

Note

Postgres does not allow a select alias (like total) in HAVING. Write the aggregate again: havingRaw('count(*) > @min', ...).

docs.title: Join
docs.text:
await Actor().join('actor_info', 'actor_info.actor_id', 'actor.id').get();
// JOIN "actor_info" on "actor_info"."actor_id" = "actor"."id"

await Actor().leftJoin('actor_info', 'actor_info.actor_id', 'actor.id').get();
await Actor().rightJoin('actor_info', 'actor_info.actor_id', 'actor.id').get();

// with an operator
await Actor().join('actor_info', 'actor_info.actor_id', '=', 'actor.id').get();

For a join with more conditions, pass a function in place of the columns. It works with join, leftJoin and rightJoin.

await Actor()
    .join('contact', (JoinClause j) {
      j
          .on('contact.actor_id', 'actor.id')
          .orOn('contact.agent_id', 'actor.id')
          .where('contact.active', true);
    })
    .get();
// JOIN "contact" on "contact"."actor_id" = "actor"."id"
//   OR "contact"."agent_id" = "actor"."id"
//   AND "contact"."active" = @contactactive_p0
  • on and orOn compare two columns. They take an operator too, like on('a.x', '>=', 'b.x').
  • where and orWhere compare a column with a value. The value is bound.
  • Give the function its type, like (JoinClause j) {...}.
  • The function must add at least one condition, or it throws an ArgumentError.

Note

SQL reads a OR b AND c as a OR (b AND c).

crossJoin joins each row with each row of the other table.

await QueryBuilder.table('size').crossJoin('color').get();
// SELECT * FROM "size" CROSS JOIN "color"

For other join conditions, use the raw methods. Nothing is quoted. Values go in the map, like in whereRaw.

await Actor().joinRaw('actor_info on actor_info.actor_id = actor.id').get();
await Actor().leftJoinRaw('actor_info on actor_info.actor_id = actor.id').get();
await Actor().rightJoinRaw(
  'actor_info on actor_info.actor_id = actor.id and actor_info.type = @type',
  <String, dynamic>{'type': 'main'},
).get();

Note

SQLite before 3.39 has no RIGHT JOIN.

docs.title: joinSub and leftJoinSub
docs.text:
They join the rows of another query. The second argument is the name of those rows.

QueryBuilder<Map<String, dynamic>> latest = QueryBuilder.table('post')
    .selectRaw('actor_id, MAX(created_at) as last_post')
    .groupBy('actor_id');

await Actor()
    .joinSub(latest, 'latest', 'latest.actor_id', 'actor.id')
    .get();
// JOIN (SELECT actor_id, MAX(created_at) as last_post FROM "post"
//   GROUP BY "actor_id") AS "latest" on "latest"."actor_id" = "actor"."id"

await Actor()
    .leftJoinSub(latest, 'latest', 'latest.actor_id', '=', 'actor.id')
    .get();

docs.title: fromSub
docs.text:
fromSub reads from the rows of another query, not from a table.

QueryBuilder<Map<String, dynamic>> totals = QueryBuilder.table('order')
    .selectRaw('actor_id, SUM(amount) as total')
    .groupBy('actor_id');

List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.table('totals')
    .fromSub(totals, 'totals')
    .where('total', '>', 100)
    .get();
// SELECT * FROM (SELECT ... GROUP BY "actor_id") AS "totals"
// WHERE "total" > @total_p0

The name is also the table name of the query, so totals.total works in where and orderBy.

docs.title: Union
docs.text:
union adds the rows of another query. It drops rows that are the same. unionAll keeps them, and it is faster.

List<Actor> actors = await Actor()
    .where('age', '<', 18)
    .union(Actor().where('age', '>', 60))
    .orderBy('name')
    .get();
// SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "age" < @age_p0
// UNION SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "age" > @dox_sub0_age_p0) AS "dox_union0"
// ORDER BY "name"

await QueryBuilder.table('actor')
    .select('name')
    .unionAll(QueryBuilder.table('director').select('name'))
    .get();
  • Both queries must select the same number of columns.
  • orderBy, limit and offset of the first query sort and cut the whole result. Use a plain column name in orderBy, not table.column.
  • The added query can have its own orderBy and limit.
  • count(), paginate(), sum(), avg(), min() and max() use the whole result: SELECT SUM("age") as dox_aggregate FROM (...) as dox_union_aggregate.
  • sum(), avg(), min() and max() keep orderBy, limit and offset. count() does not.
  • cursorPaginate() and chunkById() do not work on a union. They throw a StateError. Use paginate(), simplePaginate() or chunk().
  • update, delete, forceDelete, increment, decrement, touch and all() throw a StateError on a union, because they would use only the first query. Use get() to read it.

docs.title: Row locks
docs.text:
lockForUpdate() and sharedLock() lock the rows that a select reads. Use them inside a transaction. See Row locks.

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  Actor actor = await Actor().lockForUpdate().findOrFail(1);
  actor.age = actor.age! + 1;
  await actor.save();
});

docs.title: create and insert
docs.text:
create and insert do the same thing. They insert one row, then return it as it is in the table.

Actor actor = await Actor().create(<String, dynamic>{
  'name': 'John Wick',
  'age': 60,
});
print(actor.id);

Map<String, dynamic> row = await QueryBuilder.table('actor').insert(<String, dynamic>{
  'name': 'John Doe',
});
print(row['id']);
  • On a model, the result is the model. On QueryBuilder.table(...), the result is a map.
  • The result has the column defaults of the table too. Postgres and SQLite read the row with RETURNING *. MySQL reads it again by its id.
  • It works with any primary key type, for example a uuid string.
  • On a model with events, create calls save(), so the hooks run.
  • On a model without events, create does not set created_at and updated_at. Put them in the map, or use save().

MySQL and a table without an auto increment id

MySQL can not read the new row when the table has no auto increment id, and the map has no id (for example a pivot table). Then the result is made from the map you gave.

docs.title: insertMultiple
docs.text:
Inserts many rows in one query. It does not return models. It returns the new ids:

  • Postgres and SQLite: one map per row, like [{id: 4}, {id: 5}].
  • MySQL and MariaDB: one map with the first id, like [{id: 4}]. It is an empty list when the table has no auto increment id.
await Actor().insertMultiple(<Map<String, dynamic>>[
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'John Wick', 'age': 60},
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'John Doe', 'age': 25},
]);

The columns are the keys from all rows. When a row does not have a key, that column gets its default value.

docs.title: insertGetId and insertMany
docs.text:
insertGetId inserts one row and returns its new id. The id is the auto increment id, or the id in the map when the table has no auto increment.

dynamic id = await QueryBuilder.table('actor').insertGetId(<String, dynamic>{
  'name': 'John Wick',
});

insertMany inserts many rows, reads nothing back and returns true. It works on a table with no id column, like a pivot table. An empty list runs no query.

await QueryBuilder.table('actor_movie').insertMany(<Map<String, dynamic>>[
  <String, dynamic>{'actor_id': 1, 'movie_id': 2},
  <String, dynamic>{'actor_id': 1, 'movie_id': 3},
]);
  • Both fire no model events and set no timestamps.
  • On a model, the keys that fillable and guarded do not allow are dropped.

docs.title: upsert
docs.text:
upsert inserts rows, or updates the row that is already there. It runs one query and returns the number of changed rows.

int count = await Flight().upsert(
  <Map<String, dynamic>>[
    <String, dynamic>{'from': 'Oakland', 'to': 'San Diego', 'price': 99},
    <String, dynamic>{'from': 'Chicago', 'to': 'New York', 'price': 150},
  ],
  <String>['from', 'to'], // the unique columns
  <String>['price'], // the columns to update
);
  • The second list is the columns that find the old row. They must be the primary key or a unique index.
  • The third list is the columns to update. Leave it out to update every other column. An empty list keeps the old row as it is.
  • Every row must have the same keys. Otherwise it throws an ArgumentError.
  • On a model, keys that fillable and guarded do not allow are dropped. A model with no fillable throws, see mass assignment. created_at and updated_at are set. An update does not change created_at.
  • It fires no model events.
Database SQL Count Postgres, SQLite ON CONFLICT (...) DO UPDATE 1 for each new or updated row MySQL, MariaDB ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE 1 for each new row, 2 for each updated row, 0 for a row that did not change

Note

MySQL and MariaDB do not use the unique columns you give. Any unique index of the table can find the old row. Postgres throws when two rows of one call have the same unique values.

docs.title: insertOrIgnore
docs.text:
insertOrIgnore inserts rows and skips the rows that clash with a unique key. It returns the number of inserted rows.

int added = await QueryBuilder.table('tag').insertOrIgnore(<Map<String, dynamic>>[
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'action'},
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'drama'},
]);
  • Every row must have the same keys. Otherwise it throws an ArgumentError.
  • On a model, keys that fillable and guarded do not allow are dropped. A model with no fillable throws, see mass assignment.
  • It fires no model events.
Database SQL Also skips Postgres ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING nothing else SQLite INSERT OR IGNORE rows that break a NOT NULL or CHECK rule MySQL, MariaDB INSERT IGNORE some bad values become a warning, for example text that is too long is cut

docs.title: firstOrCreate, firstOrNew and updateOrCreate
docs.text:
The first map finds the row. The second map has the other values.

// find the user, or create it
User user = await User().firstOrCreate(
  <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com'},
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann'},
);

// find the user, or make a new model that is not saved yet
User other = await User().firstOrNew(<String, dynamic>{'email': 'bob@example.com'});
if (!other.exists) {
  await other.save();
}

// update the user, or create it
User updated = await User().updateOrCreate(
  <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com'},
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann Lee'},
);
Method Row found No row found firstOrCreate returns it creates a row from both maps firstOrNew returns it returns a new model from both maps, not saved updateOrCreate updates it with the second map creates a row from both maps
  • They return the row as it is in the table: a model, or a map for QueryBuilder.table().
  • On a model, firstOrCreate and updateOrCreate use create() and save(), so the model events run.
  • On a model, keys that fillable and guarded do not allow are dropped. A model with no fillable throws, see mass assignment.

Warning

Two requests at the same time can both create a row. Add a unique index, and use upsert when this matters.

docs.title: updateOrInsert
docs.text:
updateOrInsert updates the rows that match the first map with the second map. When no row matches, it inserts one row from both maps.

await QueryBuilder.table('setting').updateOrInsert(
  <String, dynamic>{'key': 'theme'},
  <String, dynamic>{'value': 'dark'},
);
  • It updates every row that matches the first map, not only one.
  • It does not read the row back. Use updateOrCreate when you need the row.
  • It returns true when it inserted a row, or when the update changed a row. MySQL and MariaDB count only the rows that really changed.
  • An empty first map throws an ArgumentError, so it can never update every row by mistake.
  • On a model, it uses the model's insert() and update():
    • fillable and guarded apply.
    • The insert is a create(), so the create model events run and the timestamps are set.
    • The update fires no model events and does not set updated_at.
    • Soft deleted rows do not match. So a match that is soft deleted gives a new row.

Warning

Two calls at the same time can both insert a row. Add a unique index, and use upsert when this matters.

docs.title: update
docs.text:
Updates all rows that match the where part. It returns the number of changed rows.

int count = await Actor()
    .where('id', 3)
    .where('status', 'active')
    .update(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'Updated AJ', 'age': 120});
// UPDATE "actor" SET "name" = @name_p2,"age" = @age_p3
//   WHERE "id" = @id_p0 AND "status" = @status_p1
  • An empty map runs no query and returns 0.
  • On a model, keys that fillable and guarded do not allow are dropped. A model with no fillable throws, see mass assignment. When no key is left, it runs no query and returns 0. To set every key of the map, use forceUpdate(), see skip the fillable check.
  • Postgres and SQLite count every row that the where part matched.
  • MySQL and MariaDB count only the rows that really changed. A row that already has the new values counts 0.

Warning

On a model, update needs a where (or a global scope). Actor().update({...}) with no where throws a StateError and runs no query. To change every row on purpose, see write every row. A query update does not set updated_at and fires no model events. To do that, load the model, change it and call save().

docs.title: increment and decrement
docs.text:
They add to (or take from) a number column in one query. They return the number of changed rows.

await Actor().where('id', 1).increment('views');
// UPDATE "actor" SET "views" = "views" + @views_p1 WHERE "id" = @id_p0

await Actor().where('id', 1).increment('views', 5);
await Actor().where('id', 1).decrement('views', 2);

// set other columns in the same query
await Actor().where('id', 1).increment('views', 1, <String, dynamic>{'status': 'hot'});
  • The amount is 1 when you give none.
  • A NULL column stays NULL, like in SQL.
  • They do not set updated_at and fire no model events.
  • On a model, they need a where, a global scope or a model from the table. Actor().increment('views') with no where throws a StateError and runs no query.

On a model from the table, they change only the row of that model. update on a model from the table does the same: await actor!.update({'name': 'AJ'}). It runs one query and fires no model events. Use save() for the events and updated_at. The field of the model gets the new value too. This example has an int? views column field on Actor.

Actor? actor = await Actor().find(1);
await actor!.increment('views');
print(actor.views); // the new value

docs.title: delete
docs.text:
Deletes all rows that match the where part. It returns the number of deleted rows.

int count = await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').delete();
// DELETE FROM "actor" WHERE "name" = @name_p0

On a model with softDelete: true, delete sets deleted_at and keeps the row. Rows that are already soft deleted are not counted.

Warning

On a model, delete needs a where, a global scope, or a model from the table with its primary key. Actor().delete() with no where throws a StateError and runs no query. A model read without its primary key (like after select('name')) throws too. So it can not delete every row by mistake. forceDelete does the same. To delete every row on purpose, see write every row.

docs.title: forceDelete
docs.text:
On a model with softDelete: true, forceDelete really deletes the rows. It also deletes rows that are already soft deleted, so you do not need withTrash(). It returns the number of deleted rows.

int count = await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').forceDelete();

docs.title: withTrash
docs.text:
A model with softDelete: true hides soft deleted rows. withTrash() shows them too. On a model without soft deletes it does nothing.

List<Actor> actors = await Actor().withTrash().where('name', 'John Wick').get();

docs.title: onlyTrashed
docs.text:
onlyTrashed() gives only the soft deleted rows. On a model without soft deletes it throws a StateError.

List<Actor> trashed = await Actor().onlyTrashed().get();

// delete the soft deleted rows for good
await Actor().onlyTrashed().forceDelete();

docs.title: restore
docs.text:
restore() on a query sets deleted_at back to NULL for every soft deleted row of the query. It sets updated_at too, when the model has timestamps. It returns true when it changed a row, else false. It fires no model events. With no where(), it throws a StateError, so it can not restore every row by mistake.

bool restored = await Blog().withTrash().where('status', 'old').restore();

docs.title: touch
docs.text:
Sets updated_at of the rows to now. Give a column name to set another column. It returns the number of changed rows.

await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').touch();
await Actor().where('id', 1).touch('seen_at');

On a query, touch() fires no model events. On a model query with no where() (and no global scope), touch() throws a StateError. On MySQL and MariaDB, it can return 0 when the new time is the same as the stored one (the same second), because they count only changed rows. On a model from the table, touch() changes only the row of that model. See Models.

docs.title: Write every row
docs.text:
On a model, delete, forceDelete, update, increment, decrement and touch with no where throw a StateError. To write every row on purpose, use whereRaw('1 = 1'):

await Actor().whereRaw('1 = 1').update(<String, dynamic>{'status': 'old'});
await Actor().whereRaw('1 = 1').delete();

It keeps soft deletes (a soft delete model sets deleted_at) and global scopes.

Warning

QueryBuilder.table('actor').delete() and truncate are not the same. They skip soft deletes, so they really delete the rows. They also skip global scopes and fillable. On Postgres, truncate runs CASCADE: it also empties every table with a foreign key to this table.

docs.title: truncate
docs.text:
Deletes all rows of the table and resets the id counter.

await Actor().truncate();
await Actor().truncate(resetId: false); // keep the id counter on Postgres and SQLite

On Postgres it runs TRUNCATE TABLE ... RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE. On MySQL it runs TRUNCATE TABLE, and MySQL always resets the id counter. On SQLite it runs DELETE FROM.

docs.title: toSql
docs.text:
Returns the SQL of the query with the values filled in. The values are not quoted or escaped, so use it only to read the query.

String sql = Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').toSql();
print(sql); // SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "name" = John Wick

docs.title: toRawSql
docs.text:
Returns the SQL with each value quoted for the database. Use it for logs and debugging. Run queries with bound values, not with this text.

String sql = Actor().where('name', "it's").toRawSql();
print(sql); // SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "name" = 'it''s'

docs.title: debug
docs.text:
Prints the SQL and the values of the query when it runs.

await Actor().debug(true).where('age', 60).get();

With the default PrettyQueryPrinter, it prints one line:

▌ [db:default] SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "age" = 60;

To print all queries, set debug: true in the ConnectionConfig. See Database.

docs.title: Custom drivers
docs.text: A custom DBDriver must override affectingStatement(). It runs an UPDATE, DELETE or INSERT and returns the number of changed rows. update(), delete(), increment() and upsert() use it. The default throws an UnsupportedError.

docs.title: Read replicas
docs.text:
A read replica is a copy of your database that only answers reads. Dox can send reads to replicas and writes to the main database. This spreads the load over more servers.

Postgres and MySQL support it. SQLite does not.

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text:
Add read to the ConnectionConfig. The host of the config is the write host.

lib/config/database.dart
'postgres': ConnectionConfig(
  driver: Driver.postgres,
  host: env.dbHost, // the write host
  user: env.dbUsername,
  password: env.dbPassword,
  database: env.dbName,
  debug: _debug,
  read: <Map<String, dynamic>>[
    <String, dynamic>{'host': 'replica-1.db'},
    <String, dynamic>{'host': 'replica-2.db', 'user': 'reader'},
  ],
  sticky: true,
),

Each map in read can change host, port, user, password, database and extra. The other settings are shared with the config.

To change the write host, add write. It has the same keys as one read map. Without write, the config itself is the write host.

write: <String, dynamic>{'host': 'primary.db', 'port': 6432},

Without read, nothing changes.

docs.title: What goes where
docs.text:
The read hosts take turns, in the order of the list (round robin).

Goes to a read host Goes to the write host A plain SELECT INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE A raw query that is not a SELECT Schema changes and migrations A SELECT with a lock (lockForUpdate(), sharedLock()) or with INTO Every query in a transaction

Use onWriteConnection() to read from the write host. Use it when a replica may be behind, or when a SELECT changes data.

User? user = await User().onWriteConnection().find(id);

It also sends the queries of preload() to the write host. insert(), create() and updateOrCreate() read the new row back from the write host, so you always get it.

docs.title: Sticky reads
docs.text:
A replica can be a little behind the main database. A user saves a post, then the page loads, and the post is not there yet.

sticky: true fixes this. After a write, the reads of the same request go to the write host. So a request reads what it just wrote. Other requests still read from the replicas.

In a Dox app this works by itself. dox_orm adds the stickyReads middleware as a global middleware when a connection uses sticky. You change nothing.

Outside a request, like in a job or a script, wrap the work in stickyScope():

await ReplicaDriver.stickyScope(() async {
  await Post().create(<String, dynamic>{'title': 'Hello'});
  List<Post> posts = await Post().get(); // read from the write host
});

dox_orm prints a warning on stderr, once, when sticky cannot work: a read from a replica that follows a write, outside stickyScope(). In a Dox app every request runs inside a scope, so the warning only shows for scripts, jobs or startup code.

docs.title: With DATABASE_URL
docs.text: When DATABASE_URL is set, the url is the write host. The read hosts and sticky stay. write is not used then.

docs.title: Schema builder
docs.text:
The schema builder creates, changes and drops tables with Dart code that works on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite.

You mostly use it inside a migration.

await schema.create('posts', (Table table) {
  table.id();
  table.foreignId('user_id').constrained().cascadeOnDelete();
  table.string('title');
  table.text('body').nullable();
  table.enumeration('status', <String>['draft', 'published']).defaultTo('draft');
  table.timestamps();
});

docs.title: Get a schema
docs.text:
In a migration, up and down get a Schema. It runs on the migration connection.

Outside a migration, Schema() uses the query builder connection. You can also give a driver: Schema(driver).

Schema schema = Schema();
await schema.dropIfExists('posts');

docs.title: Tables
docs.text: Method What it does create('t', (Table table) {...}) Create table t. It fails when the table exists. table('t', (Table table) {...}) Change table t: add columns, change columns, keys. drop('t') Drop table t. It fails when the table is missing. dropIfExists('t') Drop table t when it exists. rename('from', 'to') Rename a table. hasTable('t') true when the table exists. hasColumn('t', 'c') true when the column exists. hasColumns('t', ['a', 'b']) true when every column exists. hasIndex('t', index) true when the index exists. See Check an index. getColumnListing('t') The column names, in order.

docs.title: Column types
docs.text:
Method Postgres MySQL / MariaDB SQLite id() / bigIncrements('id') BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT increments('id') SERIAL PRIMARY KEY INT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT string('c', [255]) VARCHAR(n) VARCHAR(n) VARCHAR(n) char('c', [255]) CHAR(n) CHAR(n) CHAR(n) text('c') TEXT TEXT TEXT mediumText('c') TEXT MEDIUMTEXT TEXT longText('c') TEXT LONGTEXT TEXT integer('c') INTEGER INT INTEGER bigInteger('c') BIGINT BIGINT INTEGER smallInteger('c') SMALLINT SMALLINT INTEGER tinyInteger('c') SMALLINT TINYINT INTEGER unsignedInteger('c') (and unsignedBigInteger, unsignedSmallInteger, unsignedTinyInteger) signed type ... UNSIGNED INTEGER float('c') REAL FLOAT FLOAT double('c') DOUBLE PRECISION DOUBLE DOUBLE decimal('c', [8], [2]) DECIMAL(p, s) DECIMAL(p, s) DECIMAL(p, s) boolean('c') BOOLEAN TINYINT(1) BOOLEAN date('c') DATE DATE DATE dateTime('c') TIMESTAMP DATETIME DATETIME dateTimeTz('c') TIMESTAMPTZ DATETIME DATETIME time('c') TIME TIME TIME timestamp('c') TIMESTAMP TIMESTAMP TIMESTAMP timestampTz('c') TIMESTAMPTZ TIMESTAMP TIMESTAMP json('c') / jsonb('c') JSONB JSON JSON uuid(['uuid']) UUID CHAR(36) TEXT binary('c') BYTEA BLOB BLOB enumeration('c', ['a', 'b']) VARCHAR(255) + CHECK ENUM('a', 'b') VARCHAR(255) + CHECK foreignId('user_id') BIGINT BIGINT UNSIGNED INTEGER foreignUuid('user_id') UUID CHAR(36) TEXT foreignIdFor(User()) BIGINT BIGINT UNSIGNED INTEGER ulid(['ulid']) / foreignUlid('user_id') CHAR(26) CHAR(26) CHAR(26) year('c') INTEGER YEAR INTEGER ipAddress(['ip_address']) VARCHAR(45) VARCHAR(45) VARCHAR(45)

Helpers:

  • timestamps(): nullable created_at and updated_at (timestampTz).
  • softDeletes(['deleted_at']): nullable deleted_at (timestampTz), for models with softDelete: true.
  • With the laravelPostgresTypes flag, a new Postgres table gets TIMESTAMP for timestamps() and softDeletes(), and JSON for json().
  • rememberToken(): nullable remember_token VARCHAR(100).
  • softDeletesTz(['deleted_at']): the same as softDeletes. It is already a time with a zone.
  • morphs('owner'): owner_id (unsigned big integer), owner_type (string) and one index on both columns.
  • nullableMorphs('owner'): the same as morphs, but both columns can be NULL.
  • uuidMorphs('owner'): the same as morphs, with a uuid owner_id.

foreignIdFor(User()) makes the foreign key column of the model, like user_id. Give a name as the second argument to change it. .constrained() then points to the table and primary key of the model:

table.foreignIdFor(User()).constrained().cascadeOnDelete();

It is always a big integer. For a model with a text key, use foreignUuid or foreignUlid.

JSON on SQLite

SQLite has no JSON type. The column is declared as JSON, so the SQLite driver knows to decode it when you read it.

docs.title: Modifiers
docs.text:
Modifiers come after the column type. They can be chained: table.string('email').nullable().unique().

Modifier What it does Notes nullable() Allow NULL. Columns are NOT NULL by default. nullable(false) makes it NOT NULL again. defaultTo(value) Default value. Strings are escaped, so any text is safe. bool, numbers, null, Map/List (saved as JSON) and DateTime work too. withDefault does the same. defaultRaw('sql') Default as raw SQL. It is not escaped. Put expressions in ( ): defaultRaw('(1 + 1)'). MySQL and SQLite need it. useCurrent() Default to the current time. Same as defaultRaw('CURRENT_TIMESTAMP'). useCurrentOnUpdate() Set the current time on each update. MySQL only. Postgres and SQLite ignore it. Set the time in your code there. unique() Add a unique index {table}_{column}_unique. index() Add an index {table}_{column}_index. primary() Make the column the primary key. unsigned() UNSIGNED. MySQL only. Others ignore it. comment('text') Column comment. Postgres and MySQL. SQLite ignores it. collation('utf8mb4_bin') Column collation, eg. so A and a are two keys. MySQL and MariaDB only. Postgres and SQLite ignore it. Text columns only, others throw an ArgumentError. Give it again in .change(). after('column') Put the new column after another one. MySQL only, only in schema.table. Others add it at the end. change() Change an existing column (in schema.table). See Change columns.

MySQL defaults on TEXT and JSON

MySQL only allows a default on TEXT, BLOB and JSON as an expression. The schema builder writes it as DEFAULT ('value') for you.

docs.title: Change a table
docs.text:
await schema.table('users', (Table table) {
  table.string('avatar').nullable().after('email'); // add
  table.string('name', 100).nullable().change();    // change
  table.renameColumn('bio', 'about');
  table.dropColumn('age');
  table.dropColumns(<String>['a', 'b']);
});

Drop helpers:

  • dropTimestamps(): drops created_at and updated_at.
  • dropSoftDeletes(['deleted_at']): drops deleted_at.
  • dropConstrainedForeignId('user_id'): drops the foreign key of the column, then the column.
