A column in schema.table is added. Add .change() to change a column that exists.

docs.title: Change columns
docs.text:
change() sets the full new column: type, null, default and comment. Give every modifier you want to keep.

// before: string('title') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'x'
table.string('title', 500).nullable().defaultTo('x').change();

How it runs:

Driver SQL Postgres One ALTER TABLE: ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE ... USING col::type, SET/DROP NOT NULL, SET/DROP DEFAULT, and the enum CHECK again. MySQL ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN <full column>. SQLite SQLite can not change a column. Dox makes the table again (see below).

change() with unique() or index() adds the index. It fails when the index already exists.

docs.title: Indexes and keys
docs.text:
columns is a column name or a list of names.

table.index(<String>['state', 'created_at']);  // posts_state_created_at_index
table.unique('slug');                          // posts_slug_unique
table.primary(<String>['post_id', 'tag_id']);  // composite primary key

table.dropIndex(<String>['state', 'created_at']); // by columns
table.dropUnique('posts_slug_unique');            // or by name

table.fullText('body');                           // posts_body_fulltext
table.renameIndex('posts_slug_unique', 'posts_url_unique');
table.dropPrimary();                              // posts_pkey on Postgres
  • fullText makes a FULLTEXT index on MySQL. On Postgres it makes a gin index on to_tsvector('english', ...).
  • dropPrimary([name]) takes the name for Postgres. The default is {table}_pkey. MySQL needs no name.

Index names are {table}_{columns}_{index|unique|foreign}. You can give your own name as the last argument: table.unique('slug', 'my_name').

docs.title: Check an index
docs.text:
hasIndex takes an index name, or a list of its columns:

await schema.hasIndex('posts', 'posts_slug_unique');                   // by name
await schema.hasIndex('posts', <String>['state', 'created_at']);       // by columns
  • The list must have all the columns of the index, in the same order.
  • The primary key is named primary on MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite. On Postgres it has its real name, like posts_pkey.
  • The name is compared like the database does. MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite ignore the case. Postgres needs the exact case.

docs.title: Foreign keys
docs.text:
table.foreignId('user_id').constrained().cascadeOnDelete();
// same as:
table.foreignId('user_id');
table.foreign('user_id').references('id').on('users').onDelete('cascade');
  • constrained([table], [column = 'id']) guesses the table from the column: user_id becomes users, category_id becomes categories. Dox models use singular table names by default (User is user). If your table is singular, give it: constrained('user').
  • Actions: onDelete('cascade' | 'set null' | 'restrict' | 'no action'), onUpdate(...), and the short ones cascadeOnDelete(), nullOnDelete(), restrictOnDelete(), cascadeOnUpdate(), nullOnUpdate() and restrictOnUpdate().
  • Put nullable() before constrained(): table.foreignId('editor_id').nullable().constrained('users').
  • Drop it: table.dropForeign(<String>['user_id']) or table.dropForeign('posts_user_id_foreign').

Same type on both sides

id() is a big integer. foreignId() is a big integer too, so they match. If the parent uses increments() (a normal integer), use unsignedInteger() for the child on MySQL.

docs.title: Turn the foreign key checks off
docs.text:
Sometimes you must write rows before their parent rows, for example when you copy data. Turn the foreign key checks off for that work:

await schema.withoutForeignKeyConstraints(() async {
  // the post first, its user later
  await QueryBuilder.table('posts').insert(<String, dynamic>{'user_id': 1, 'title': 'Hi'});
  await QueryBuilder.table('users').insert(<String, dynamic>{'id': 1, 'name': 'Ann'});
});

withoutForeignKeyConstraints turns the checks on again after the function, also when it throws. Use it when you can.

disableForeignKeyConstraints() and enableForeignKeyConstraints() do the same in two steps:

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  await schema.disableForeignKeyConstraints();
  // ...
  await schema.enableForeignKeyConstraints();
});

Each database works in its own way:

Database SQL Limits SQLite PRAGMA foreign_keys = OFF It is for the one connection of the isolate. So other code of that isolate is not checked either while it is off. Inside a transaction it does nothing. MySQL, MariaDB SET FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS = 0 It is a setting of one pool connection. So disable and enable must run inside a transaction, else they throw a StateError. Turn the checks on again before the transaction ends. Postgres SET CONSTRAINTS ALL DEFERRED Only keys made DEFERRABLE wait, and only until the checks are on again. Dox keys are not DEFERRABLE, so they are still checked. It must run inside a transaction too.
  • On MySQL, MariaDB and Postgres, withoutForeignKeyConstraints runs in a transaction. So all its queries use the same connection. Inside another transaction it uses a savepoint.
  • On SQLite, run withoutForeignKeyConstraints outside a transaction.
  • A migration runs in a transaction, so disable and enable work there on every database. On SQLite, a migration already runs with the checks off.

docs.title: SQLite notes
docs.text:
SQLite ALTER TABLE can only add, rename and drop columns. For these changes, Dox makes the table again:

  • change() of a column,
  • foreign(...) on an existing table,
  • dropForeign(...).

It makes a new table with the change, copies the rows, drops the old table and renames the new one. It keeps the columns, primary key, AUTOINCREMENT, foreign keys, indexes and enum checks. All of it runs in one transaction. It fails on tables with other CHECK constraints or with generated columns.

Other SQLite limits:

  • primary(...) on an existing table is not supported.
  • fullText and dropPrimary throw an UnsupportedError. SQLite has no full text index, and it can not drop a primary key.
  • renameIndex drops the index and makes it again with the new name. So it only runs on a database, not in See the SQL.
  • A new column that is NOT NULL needs a default. A new column can not default to CURRENT_TIMESTAMP.
  • dropColumn fails when the column is in an index or a foreign key. Drop those first.

docs.title: Per driver notes
docs.text: Feature Postgres MySQL / MariaDB SQLite comment COMMENT ON COLUMN inline COMMENT ignored add/drop foreign key on a table ALTER TABLE ALTER TABLE table rebuild schema changes in a transaction yes no, saved right away yes index name length 63 64 no limit

docs.title: See the SQL
docs.text:
Every change is a Table blueprint. A grammar turns it into SQL, without a database:

Table table = Table('users', creating: true)
  ..id()
  ..string('email').unique();
print(table.toSql(PostgresGrammar()));
// [CREATE TABLE "users" ("id" BIGSERIAL NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY, "email" VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL),
//  CREATE UNIQUE INDEX "users_email_unique" ON "users" ("email")]

Grammars: PostgresGrammar, MysqlGrammar and SqliteGrammar. On SQLite, the changes that need a table rebuild only run on a database.

docs.title: Seeders
docs.text:
A seeder puts data in your database.

Use it for sample data in development, or for data your app needs, like a list of countries.

docs.title: Create a seeder
docs.text:
dox make:seeder UserSeeder

This makes three files:

File What it is db/seeders/user.seeder.dart the new seeder db/seeders/seeders.dart the list of all seeders. Dox writes it again on each make:seeder and db:seed. Do not edit it. bin/seed.dart the script that runs a seeder. It is made only when it is missing.

Write your code in run(). For example:

db/seeders/user.seeder.dart
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import '../factories/user.factory.dart';

class UserSeeder extends Seeder {
  @override
  Future<void> run() async {
    await UserFactory().count(10).create();
  }
}

Use factories, models or the query builder in run().

docs.title: DatabaseSeeder
docs.text:
dox db:seed runs DatabaseSeeder by default. Use it to call your other seeders.

dox make:seeder DatabaseSeeder
db/seeders/database.seeder.dart
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import 'post.seeder.dart';
import 'user.seeder.dart';

class DatabaseSeeder extends Seeder {
  @override
  Future<void> run() async {
    await call(<Seeder>[UserSeeder(), PostSeeder()]);
  }
}

call() runs the seeders one after another, in the list order.

docs.title: Run seeders
docs.text:
Command What it does dox db:seed Run DatabaseSeeder. dox db:seed --class=UserSeeder Run one seeder. dox migration:fresh --seed Drop all tables, run all migrations, then run DatabaseSeeder. dox migration:refresh --seed Undo all migrations, run them again, then run DatabaseSeeder. dox migration:run --seed Run new migrations, then run DatabaseSeeder.

migrate:fresh and migrate:refresh are short names, so dox migrate:fresh --seed works too.

The database comes from .env, the same as the migrations: DATABASE_URL, or DB_CONNECTION, DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD and DB_NAME.

Warning

migration:fresh drops every table of the database, also tables that no migration made. Do not run it on a production database.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
A seed runs in one transaction. When a seeder throws an error, nothing is saved, and the command exits with code 1.

On MySQL and MariaDB, CREATE, ALTER and DROP TABLE save right away. A rollback can not undo them. Keep schema changes in migrations.

A very large seed can turn the transaction off:

class BigSeeder extends Seeder {
  @override
  bool get withinTransaction => false;

  @override
  Future<void> run() async {
    // ...
  }
}

Only the seeder you run says if there is a transaction. For dox db:seed it is DatabaseSeeder.

docs.title: bin/seed.dart
docs.text:
dox db:seed runs dart run bin/seed.dart. You can run it yourself too, for example in a deploy script:

dart run bin/seed.dart
dart run bin/seed.dart --class=UserSeeder
bin/seed.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import '../db/seeders/seeders.dart';

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await SeederRunner(seeders: seeders).run(args);
}

SeederRunner sets up the ORM, runs the seeder and closes the ORM. Pass config: to use your app's database config instead of .env:

import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await SeederRunner(
    seeders: seeders,
    config: databaseConfig,
  ).run(args);
}

docs.title: Use in tests
docs.text:
A seeder is a normal class. Call run() after you set up the ORM:

await DatabaseSeeder().run();

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
A transaction runs many queries as one unit, so either all of them are saved or none of them.

QueryBuilder.transaction() takes a function:

  • It commits when the function ends.
  • It rolls back when the function throws. Then the error is thrown again.

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
// a transaction
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  Actor actor = Actor();
  actor.name = 'John Wick';
  await actor.save();
  await QueryBuilder.table('actor_info').insert(<String, dynamic>{
    'actor_id': actor.id,
  });
});

// return a value
int? id = await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  Actor actor = Actor();
  actor.name = 'John Wick';
  await actor.save();
  return actor.id;
});

// on another connection
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  // ...
}, connection: 'mysql');
  • All queries and models inside the function use the transaction. You do not pass a transaction object around.
  • A transaction inside another transaction uses a savepoint. See Nested transactions.

MySQL

On MySQL and MariaDB, CREATE, ALTER and DROP TABLE are saved right away. A rollback can not undo them.

docs.title: Nested transactions
docs.text:
A transaction inside another transaction uses a savepoint. It runs on the same connection as the outer one.

  • When the inner function ends, its work stays in the outer transaction. It is saved when the outer one commits.
  • When the inner function throws, only its work is undone. Then the error is thrown again.
  • If you catch that error, the outer transaction goes on and can still commit.
  • If you do not catch it, the outer transaction rolls back too.
  • When the outer transaction rolls back, the inner work is undone too.
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  await Actor().create(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'John Wick'});
  try {
    await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
      await Actor().create(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'Bad row'});
      throw StateError('stop');
    });
  } on StateError {
    // only 'Bad row' is undone
  }
});
// 'John Wick' is saved

This works on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite. You can nest many levels.

  • Run nested transactions one after another, not at the same time (for example in Future.wait). They share one connection.
  • On MySQL and MariaDB, a CREATE, ALTER or DROP TABLE inside a nested transaction saves the outer work and ends the savepoint. Do not change the schema there.

docs.title: Run again after a deadlock
docs.text:
Two transactions can wait for each other's rows. The database then stops one of them with a deadlock error. Often one more run works. attempts runs the whole function again, up to that many runs in all:

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  // ...
}, attempts: 3);
  • It runs again only on a deadlock or a lock / serialization failure. Other errors are thrown at once.
  • When the last run fails too, its error is thrown.
  • There is no wait between the runs.
  • The default is 1: one run, no retry. 0 and below also run once.
  • Only the outermost transaction runs again. A nested transaction gives the error to the outer one.
  • afterCommit() functions of a failed run are dropped. Only the functions of the run that commits run.
  • An error after the commit (for example in an afterCommit() function) never runs it again.
  • The function runs again from the start. So keep work that is not in the database (a mail, a call to another service) out of it, or put it in afterCommit().

The errors that count:

Database Errors Postgres SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization failure), 40P01 (deadlock) MySQL, MariaDB error 1213 (deadlock), 1205 (lock wait timeout), 1020 (record changed), SQLSTATE 40001 SQLite SQLITE_BUSY and SQLITE_LOCKED ("database is locked")

DatabaseTransaction.isConcurrencyError(error) gives the same answer for your own error checks.

docs.title: Begin and commit by hand
docs.text:
QueryBuilder.transaction() is the simple way. Use it when you can. When the work can not fit in one function, begin the transaction by hand:

DatabaseTransaction tx = await QueryBuilder.beginTransaction();
try {
  await tx.run(() async {
    User user = await User().create(<String, dynamic>{'email': email});
    await QueryBuilder.afterCommit(() => sendWelcomeMail(user));
  });
  await tx.run(() => QueryBuilder.table('audit').insert(<String, dynamic>{'event': 'signup'}));
  await tx.commit();
} finally {
  await tx.rollBack(); // does nothing after commit
}
  • Only code inside tx.run() uses the transaction. Queries outside it, and queries of other requests, never join it.
  • Nested QueryBuilder.transaction() calls (savepoints) and afterCommit() work inside run().
  • Await each run() before commit().
  • commit() saves the work, then runs the afterCommit() functions. It throws a StateError when the transaction is closed already.
  • rollBack() undoes the work and drops the afterCommit() functions. It does nothing when the transaction is closed already, so it is safe in a finally.
  • tx.isOpen is true until commit(), rollBack() or the timeout.
  • connection: picks a named connection, like transaction().

Limits:

  • The transaction holds one connection until you close it. When it is still open after timeout (default 1 minute), it is rolled back, so its connection is free again. Set your own: QueryBuilder.beginTransaction(timeout: const Duration(seconds: 10)).
  • After the timeout, run() and commit() throw a StateError. The work is lost.
  • On SQLite, other queries of the isolate wait until the transaction is closed. This is true for a plain query and for QueryBuilder.transaction() outside run(). They wait until the transaction ends or times out. So do not await them while it is open.
  • beginTransaction() throws a StateError inside a transaction of the same connection. Use QueryBuilder.transaction() for nested work.
  • Use the transaction only in the code that began it: the same request, job or test.

Postgres: roll back after a database error

On Postgres, a database error inside run() breaks the whole transaction. Call rollBack() then. A commit() saves nothing and gives no error, because the server answers COMMIT with ROLLBACK. A plain QueryBuilder.transaction() works the same way when you catch a database error inside it.

docs.title: Run code after the commit
docs.text:
Some work must only happen when the data is saved. A mail or a queue job, for example. QueryBuilder.afterCommit() runs a function after the transaction commits:

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  User user = await User().create(<String, dynamic>{'email': email});
  await QueryBuilder.afterCommit(() => sendWelcomeMail(user));
});
  • Inside a transaction, the function runs after the outermost transaction commits. The data is saved, and other connections can see it.
  • When the transaction rolls back, the function does not run.
  • Outside a transaction, the function runs at once.
  • A function added in a nested transaction waits for the outermost commit. When that nested transaction rolls back, its functions are dropped, even when the outer one commits.
  • The functions run one by one, in the order you added them.
  • The function can be async. The QueryBuilder.transaction() call waits for it.
  • A function can open a new transaction, or call afterCommit() again. Outside a transaction, that call runs at once.
  • connection: picks a named connection, like transaction(). The function waits only for a transaction of that connection. With no connection, it uses the default connection.

When a function throws, the data stays saved. The commit is not undone. The other functions still run. Then the QueryBuilder.transaction() call throws the first error.

await QueryBuilder.afterCommit(() => notify(order), connection: 'mysql');

A driver has it too: driver.afterCommit(() => ...).

Limits:

  • Code can outlive its transaction, like a Timer or a future that you did not await. When it calls afterCommit() after the transaction ended, the function runs at once if the transaction committed. It is dropped if the transaction rolled back. It never waits for a later transaction. When such a late function throws, the error goes to the Future that afterCommit() returns. Await it or catch it. Else it is an uncaught async error.
  • A transaction opened with the default connection's own name (like connection: 'main') uses another driver than no name. So afterCommit() with no name runs at once there. Pass the same connection: to both, or no name to both.
  • A custom DBDriver that does not use the afterCommitZone() and runAfterCommit() helpers runs the functions at once.

Queue jobs use it with dispatch(afterCommit: true).

docs.title: Row locks
docs.text:
A row lock stops two requests from changing the same row at the same time.

Think of a stock count. Two requests read stock = 5 at the same time. Each one takes 1 and saves 4. The right value is 3. A lock makes the second request wait until the first one is done. This example has an int? stock column field on a Product model.

Future<void> buy(int productId, int quantity) async {
  await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
    // read the row and lock it
    Product product = await Product().lockForUpdate().findOrFail(productId);

    if (product.stock! < quantity) {
      throw BadRequestException(message: 'Not enough stock');
    }

    // change it and save it while the lock is held
    product.stock = product.stock! - quantity;
    await product.save();
  });
  // the lock ends here, when the transaction commits
}
  • lockForUpdate() adds FOR UPDATE to the select. Other transactions that lock or change these rows wait.
  • sharedLock() adds a shared lock. Other transactions can still read the rows, but they wait to change them.
  • Use them with find(), findOrFail(), getFirst(), firstOrFail(), get(), all() and pluck().
  • count(), sum() and the other aggregates do not lock.
Database lockForUpdate() sharedLock() Postgres FOR UPDATE FOR SHARE MySQL, MariaDB FOR UPDATE LOCK IN SHARE MODE SQLite nothing nothing

Use a lock only inside a transaction

A lock lasts until the transaction ends. Outside a transaction, each query commits right away, so the lock ends at once.

SQLite has no row locks, so the lock does nothing there. But a Dox transaction on SQLite starts with BEGIN IMMEDIATE. It takes the write lock of the whole database. So the same code is safe on SQLite too.

Note

Postgres does not allow a lock with groupBy(), distinct(), or on the nullable side of a left join. The database throws an error then.

For one number column, increment() is simpler. It changes the value in one query, so it needs no lock.

docs.title: Connections
docs.text:
• Postgres and MySQL use a connection pool. Set the size with maxConnectionCount in the extra map of the connection.
  • A transaction uses one connection of the pool. Other queries use the other connections.
  • SQLite has one connection per isolate. While a transaction is open, the other queries of that isolate wait.
  • When a model has more than one relation to load (preload or eager), the relation queries run at the same time outside a transaction. Inside a transaction, they run one after another on its connection.
  • A query runs in a transaction only when you use QueryBuilder.transaction(), or tx.run() of a transaction you began by hand.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
A model is a Dart class for one database table, used to read, create, change and delete its rows.

A model has all the query builder methods too.

docs.title: Create a model
docs.text:
dox make:model Blog      # only the model
dox make:model Blog -m   # the model and a migration for the table `blogs`
dox make:model Blog -a   # the model, a migration, a factory, a seeder and a resource controller

This makes lib/app/models/blog/blog.model.dart. create:model is another name for the same command.

Other options: -c controller, -r resource controller, --api resource controller without create and edit, -f factory, -s seeder. You can join them, like -mfs. See CLI reference.

The model code uses a generated class (BlogGenerator). Run the generator after you make or change a model:

dart run build_runner build

dart run build_runner watch runs the generator again each time you save a file.

docs.title: A model
Model options
docs.text:
All options go in @DoxModel(...).

Option Default What it does table class name in snake_case The table name. primaryKey 'id' The primary key column. primaryKeyType int The Dart type of the primary key, like String for a UUID. createdAt 'created_at' The column that keeps the create time. updatedAt 'updated_at' The column that keeps the last update time. timestamps true false turns off createdAt and updatedAt. softDelete false delete() sets deleted_at and keeps the row.

docs.title: table
docs.text:
The default table name is the class name in snake_case, and singular. Blog uses blog, and BlogPost uses blog_post. With the pluralTableNames flag it is plural: blogs and blog_posts.

@DoxModel(table: 'blogs')
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {}

Info

dox make:model Blog always sets table: 'blogs' for you, with or without -m. The migration that -m makes uses the same plural table blogs.

docs.title: primaryKey
docs.text:
@DoxModel(primaryKey: 'uid')
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {}

The field name is the key in camelCase. With primaryKey: 'blog_id', the field is blogId.

docs.title: primaryKeyType
docs.text:
The primary key field is int? by default. Use primaryKeyType for another type, like a UUID string.

@DoxModel(primaryKey: 'uuid', primaryKeyType: String)
class Device extends DeviceGenerator {}

Device device = Device();
device.uuid = '0b6f2c1e-1a2b-4c3d-8e9f-001122334455';
await device.save(); // insert

save() inserts a new model, also when you set the key yourself. It updates a model that was read from the table or saved before. model.exists tells which one it is.

docs.title: createdAt and updatedAt
docs.text:
save() sets these columns to the current UTC time. Use the options when your columns have other names.

@DoxModel(createdAt: 'created', updatedAt: 'modified')
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {}

Read the values with blog.createdAt and blog.updatedAt.

docs.title: timestamps
docs.text:
Set timestamps: false when the table has no created_at and updated_at columns.

@DoxModel(timestamps: false)
class Setting extends SettingGenerator {}

To turn off only one of them, set it to null, like @DoxModel(updatedAt: null).

docs.title: softDelete
docs.text:
@DoxModel(softDelete: true)
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {}

The table needs a nullable deleted_at column. In a migration, add table.softDeletes();.

  • delete() sets deleted_at to the current time. The row stays in the table. When the model has timestamps, it sets updated_at too.
  • Queries do not return soft deleted rows. Use withTrash() to get them too, or onlyTrashed() to get only them.
  • forceDelete() really deletes the row.
  • restore() sets deleted_at back to NULL. When the model has timestamps, it sets updated_at too.

docs.title: Field types
docs.text:
The field type tells Dox how to read the value.

Field type Column String? text, varchar int? integer types double? float, double. MySQL also gives DECIMAL as double. Postgres gives numeric as String. bool? boolean, or a number like tinyint (0 is false) DateTime? date, datetime, timestamp Map<String, dynamic>? or List<dynamic>? JSON an enum, like Status? text with the enum name

For other conversions, use a cast, or beforeSave and beforeGet.

docs.title: beforeSave and beforeGet
docs.text:
These options take a static function of the model class. The function gets a map and returns the value.

  • beforeSave runs before a save. It gets the model values (column name => value). It returns the value to save in this column.
  • beforeGet runs when a row is read. It gets the row from the database. It returns the value for this field.
@DoxModel()
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  // beforeSave: make the slug from the title
  @Column(beforeSave: makeSlug)
  String? slug;

  // beforeGet: old rows have no status, show them as draft
  @Column(beforeGet: readStatus)
  String? status;

  static String? makeSlug(Map<String, dynamic> map) {
    return map['title']?.toString().toLowerCase().replaceAll(' ', '-');
  }

  static String? readStatus(Map<String, dynamic> map) {
    return map['status'] as String? ?? 'draft';
  }
}

docs.title: Save
docs.text:
save() inserts a new model, or updates a model that has an id.

// insert
Blog blog = Blog();
blog.title = 'My first blog';
await blog.save();
print(blog.id); // the new id

// update
Blog? found = await Blog().find(1);
found?.title = 'New title';
await found?.save();

// set a field to null
found?.status = null;
await found?.save(); // status is now NULL in the database

// create from a map: returns the new model as it is in the table.
// Blog needs `fillable`, see mass assignment below.
Blog created = await Blog().create(<String, dynamic>{
  'title': 'My first blog',
  'status': 'draft',
});
  • On insert, null fields are not sent, so the database default is used. With the createWritesNull flag, create() writes NULL for a key that is null in the map.
  • On update, only the fields that changed are sent. A field is compared to its value from the last load or save. A Map or List field is always sent, because it can change in place.
  • When nothing changed, save() runs no query, and updated_at stays as it is. It still fires updating and updated, unless the skipCleanUpdateEvents flag is on.
  • When you set updatedAt yourself, save() keeps your value. Else it sets updated_at to now.
  • On update, a field is set to NULL only when it had a value before (loaded from the database, or saved). Fields that were not loaded, for example with select(), are not changed.
  • save() returns true when it saved, and false when a model event cancels it.
  • blog.update(<String, dynamic>{...}) on a loaded model changes only that row and sets updated_at too. It fires no model events.

create() works like save() on a new model

create() fills a new model from the map, so only the @Column fields are saved. It runs beforeSave and sets created_at and updated_at when the map has no value for them. On a model with events, it calls save(), so the hooks run too.

docs.title: Mass assignment
docs.text:
create(), insert(), update(), upsert() and the find or create methods take keys from a map. If they took every key, User().create(req.body) with {"is_admin": 1} would make an admin. So a model is guarded by default. Set fillable to the keys that may be taken from a map.

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  // only these keys are taken from a map
  @override
  List<String> get fillable => <String>['name', 'email'];

  // or: every key but these is taken from a map
  @override
  List<String> get guarded => <String>['is_admin'];
}
  • A model with no fillable (and the default guarded) throws a MassAssignmentException when it gets a map with keys. It does not save an empty row.
  • With fillable, keys that are not in it are dropped. They do not throw.

  • To take every key (not safe with user input), set guarded to an empty list:

    @override
List<String> get guarded => const <String>[];

  • save() is not changed. Fields you set in code are always saved.

docs.title: Skip the fillable check
docs.text:
Sometimes your own code must set a guarded column, like is_admin. These methods ignore fillable and guarded. Never pass user input, like req.body, to them.

// create a row with every key of the map
User admin = await User().forceCreate(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann', 'is_admin': true});

// update the rows of a query with every key of the map
await User().where('id', 1).forceUpdate(<String, dynamic>{'is_admin': true});

// set fields on a model, then save it
User? user = await User().find(1);
await user!.forceFill(<String, dynamic>{'is_admin': true}).save();

// turn the check off for everything inside the callback
await Model.unguarded(() async {
  await User().create(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'Bob', 'is_admin': true});
  await User().where('id', 2).update(<String, dynamic>{'is_admin': true});
});
  • forceFill() does not save. Call save() after it. It skips a key that is not a column. A value of the wrong type throws an ArgumentError.
  • Model.unguarded() covers every await inside the callback. Other requests that run at the same time still use fillable.
  • Work that starts inside the callback and finishes later also runs with the check off. This means timers, futures that are not awaited, and stream listeners. So await everything inside the callback.
  • A query update() keeps the check, so update(req.body) stays safe. Use forceUpdate() when you need to skip the check.
  • Model events that fire inside forceCreate() and forceUpdate() (like created) also run with the check off. A create() or update() inside such a hook skips fillable too.

docs.title: Find or create
docs.text:
These methods find a row by the first map. When there is no row, they use both maps.

// find the user, or create it
User user = await User().firstOrCreate(
  <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com'},
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann'},
);

// find the user, or make a new model that is not saved yet
User other = await User().firstOrNew(<String, dynamic>{'email': 'bob@example.com'});
if (!other.exists) {
  await other.save();
}

// update the user, or create it
User updated = await User().updateOrCreate(
  <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com'},
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann Lee'},
);

firstOrCreate() and updateOrCreate() use create() and save(), so the model events run. firstOrNew() does not save, so no event runs. See Query builder.

docs.title: Increment
docs.text:
increment() and decrement() change a number column in one query. On a model from the table, they change only the row of that model. The field of the model gets the new value too. This example has an int? views column field on Blog.

Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);
await blog!.increment('views');      // views + 1
await blog.increment('views', 5);    // views + 5
await blog.decrement('views');       // views - 1
print(blog.views);
  • They return the number of changed rows: 1, or 0 when the row is not there.
  • They fire no model events and do not set updated_at.
  • A third argument sets other columns in the same query: increment('views', 1, <String, dynamic>{'status': 'hot'}). Keys that fillable and guarded do not allow are dropped.

docs.title: Touch and replicate
docs.text:
touch() sets updated_at to now. Give a column name to set another column. On a model from the table it changes only that row, and the field gets the new time too.

Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);
await blog!.touch();               // updated_at = now
await blog.touch('published_at');  // published_at = now
  • It returns the number of changed rows: 1, or 0 when the row is not there. It also returns 0 when the model has no updated_at column and you give no column.
  • It fires the save events: saving, updating, updated and saved, like save(). A hook that throws CancelModelEvent stops it, and it returns 0.
  • touchQuietly() does the same with no events.
  • A model with no primary key value (never saved, or read without the key) throws a StateError. So touch() can not change every row by mistake.

replicate() makes a new model with the same column values. It is not saved yet. It has no primary key, created_at or updated_at, so save() inserts a new row.

Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);
Blog copy = blog!.replicate()..title = 'Copy of ${blog.title}';
await copy.save();

// leave out some columns, they are set to null
Blog other = blog.replicate(<String>['slug']);
  • Relations are not copied.
  • It copies deleted_at. A copy of a soft deleted model is soft deleted too.
  • A column in the list that can not be null, or that is not a column, throws an ArgumentError.

docs.title: Changed columns
docs.text:
A model knows which columns changed since it was read or saved. The names are column names, like user_id, not the Dart field names.

Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);
blog!.title = 'New title';

blog.isDirty();                     // true
blog.isDirty('title');              // true
blog.isDirty(<String>['body']);     // false
blog.isClean('body');               // true
blog.getDirty();                    // {title: New title}
blog.getOriginal('title');          // the old title

await blog.save();
blog.wasChanged('title');           // true
blog.getChanges();                  // {title: New title, updated_at: ...}
  • getChanges() and wasChanged() tell what the last save() changed. update(), increment(), decrement(), touch(), restore() and a soft delete on the model count as a save too.

docs.title: Read the row again
docs.text:
refresh() reads the row again and sets the fields of this model. It also loads the relations again, like reload(). fresh() gives a new model of the row. This model does not change.

Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);
await blog!.refresh();          // this model now has the values of the table
Blog? now = await blog.fresh(); // a new model, or null when the row is gone
  • Both read by primary key from the write database. They find a soft deleted row too, and skip global scopes.
  • refresh() throws a StateError on a model that is not in the table, and a ModelNotFoundException when the row is gone.

docs.title: Delete
docs.text:
// delete a record
Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);
int count = await blog!.delete(); // deletes only this record

// force delete
Blog? trashed = await Blog().withTrash().find(1);
await trashed?.forceDelete(); // deletes the row, also with softDelete

// restore
Blog? deleted = await Blog().withTrash().find(1);
await deleted?.restore(); // sets deleted_at back to NULL, and updated_at
  • delete() and forceDelete() return the number of deleted rows.
  • They return 1 when the row was deleted.
  • They return 0 when the row was not there, or when a model event cancels.
  • A model with no primary key value (never saved, or read without the key) throws a StateError and runs no query. So Blog().delete() can not delete every row by mistake. Blog().where('status', 'draft').delete() is a query delete, and it works. update(), increment(), decrement() and touch() on a model with no key and no where throw too. A global scope counts as a where, see global scopes. To delete every row on purpose, use Blog().whereRaw('1 = 1').delete(). See write every row.

On a model with soft deletes, trashed() is true when its deleted_at is set:

Blog? blog = await Blog().withTrash().find(1);
if (blog!.trashed()) await blog.restore();

save(), touch(), delete(), forceDelete() and restore() fire model events.

docs.title: Convert to a map or JSON
docs.text:
Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);

Map<String, dynamic>? map = blog?.toMap();  // all columns and computed values
Map<String, dynamic>? json = blog?.toJson(); // the same, without hidden fields
Map<String, dynamic>? row = blog?.toMap(original: true); // the raw database row

jsonEncode(blog) uses toJson(). So you can return a model, or a list of models, from a controller.

docs.title: Hide fields
docs.text:
Fields in hidden are left out of toJson(). Use the column names.

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @override
  List<String> get hidden => <String>['password', 'remember_token'];
}

visibleFields is the opposite: toJson() keeps only these fields. Empty (the default) keeps every field.

@override
List<String> get visibleFields => const <String>['id', 'name'];

makeHidden() and makeVisible() change the fields of one model, or of a list of models. makeVisible() also shows a field that is in hidden.

return user.makeVisible(<String>['email']).toJson();
return users.makeHidden(<String>['phone']);

docs.title: Computed values
docs.text:
A computed value is a getter that is added to toJson() and toMap(). Add @Computed() to the getter, then run dart run build_runner build.

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column(name: 'first_name')
  String? firstName;

  @Column(name: 'last_name')
  String? lastName;

  @Computed() // json key: full_name
  String get fullName => '$firstName $lastName';

  @Computed(name: 'initials') // custom json key
  String get shortName => '${firstName?[0]}${lastName?[0]}';
}

User? user = await User().find(1);
print(user?.toJson());
// {id: 1, first_name: John, last_name: Wick, ..., full_name: John Wick, initials: JW}
  • The default key is the getter name in snake_case (fullName becomes full_name). A name: is used exactly as written.
  • A computed value is never a column. It is not read from the database, and it is not sent in INSERT or UPDATE.
  • hidden also hides computed values. Use the json key, for example ['full_name'].
  • Computed values of loaded relations are in the nested JSON too.
  • toMap(original: true) returns the raw database row, so it has no computed values.
  • A getter runs each time toJson() or toMap() is called, so keep it fast.

docs.title: New query
docs.text:
A model object keeps the parts of its query (where, orderBy, ...). query() gives a new, empty model, so you can start another query.

Blog blog = Blog();
List<Blog> active = await blog.where('status', 'active').get();

// a new query, without the where above
List<Blog> deleted = await blog.query().where('status', 'deleted').get();

docs.title: Debug
docs.text:
debug(true) prints the SQL of this model in the terminal.

Blog blog = Blog();
blog.debug(true);
blog.title = 'John Wick';
await blog.save();

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: A model can load related models. See HasOne, HasMany, BelongsTo, ManyToMany, HasManyThrough and Polymorphic.

docs.title: Nested and filtered preload
docs.text:
A dot path loads the relations of the loaded rows too. It runs one query for each level.

List<User> users = await User().preload('posts.comments').get();

A callback adds conditions to the query of the relation. With a dot path, it is for the last relation.

await User().preload('posts', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('published', true);
}).get();

// all posts, and only the approved comments of each post
await User().preload('posts.comments', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('approved', true);
}).get();

docs.title: Save through a relation
docs.text:
These methods set the foreign key for you. They work with @HasMany, @HasOne, @MorphMany and @MorphOne.

Blog blog = (await Blog().find(1))!;
Comment c = await blog.createRelated<Comment>('comments', <String, dynamic>{'body': 'hi'});
await blog.saveRelated('comments', Comment()..body = 'hi');
await blog.saveManyRelated('comments', <Comment>[c1, c2]);
  • createRelated() uses create(), so fillable, events and timestamps work. The foreign key does not need to be in fillable.
  • For a @BelongsTo, comment.associate('blog', blog) sets the key and comment.dissociate('blog') sets it to null. Call save() after them.

After reload() or a preload

await user.reload() and a preload set the relation fields again, also when there is no related row. A to-one field that can be null becomes null. A to-many field becomes []. A to-one field that can not be null keeps its old value.

The relationship pages use these tables:

erDiagram
    user ||--o| user_info : "HasOne"
    user ||--o{ post : "HasMany"
    user ||--o{ comment : "BelongsTo, from comment"
    artist ||--o{ artist_song : "ManyToMany"
    song ||--o{ artist_song : "ManyToMany"
    user {
        int id PK
        string name
    }
    user_info {
        int id PK
        int user_id FK
        string address
    }
    post {
        int id PK
        int user_id FK
        string title
    }
    comment {
        int id PK
        int user_id FK
        string content
    }
    artist_song {
        int id PK
        int artist_id FK
        int song_id FK
    }

docs.title: Attribute casts
docs.text:
A cast changes a column value between the database and Dart.

For example, it reads JSON text as a map, or saves an enum by its name. Casts work the same on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite.

Set a cast with cast on @Column(). Then run dart run build_runner build.

enum Status { draft, live }

enum Level { low, mid, high }

@DoxModel()
class Item extends ItemGenerator {
  @Column(cast: JsonCast())
  Map<String, dynamic>? meta;

  @Column(cast: ListCast<String>())
  List<String>? tags;

  @Column()
  bool? active; // gets BoolCast()

  @Column()
  Status? status; // gets EnumCast(Status.values)

  @Column(cast: EnumCast<Level>(Level.values, byIndex: true))
  Level? level;
}

The cast runs when a row is read (get(), find() and others), when the model is saved, and in toJson().

docs.title: Built-in casts
docs.text:
Cast Dart value Database value JsonCast() a map or a list JSON, or JSON in a text column ListCast<E>() a typed list, like List<String> JSON, or JSON in a text column BoolCast() bool boolean, or a number like tinyint (0 is false), or the text 1, 0, true, false, t, f EnumCast<E>(E.values) an enum text with the enum name EnumCast<E>(E.values, byIndex: true) an enum a number, the enum index

You do not need cast for two field types:

  • A bool field gets BoolCast().
  • An enum field gets EnumCast(values), so it is saved by its name.

DateTime fields need no cast either. Dox reads them on every database.

Info

A cast changes the values of a model. It does not change a where() value. Use the database value there, like where('status', Status.live.name).

docs.title: Your own cast
docs.text:
Extend Cast<T>. get() gets the database value and returns the Dart value. set() gets the Dart value and returns the value to save. The class needs a const constructor.

class Money {
  final int cents;
  const Money(this.cents);
}

class MoneyCast extends Cast<Money> {
  const MoneyCast();

  @override
  Money? get(dynamic value) => value == null ? null : Money(value as int);

  @override
  dynamic set(Money? value) => value?.cents;
}

@DoxModel()
class Product extends ProductGenerator {
  @Column(cast: MoneyCast())
  Money? price;
}

A cast can take const arguments, like EnumCast does. The generator copies the cast code into the generated file, so the names in it must be imported in the model file.

A column with beforeGet does not use its cast.

docs.title: Counting relations
docs.text:
withCount() adds the number of related rows to each model.

It does not load the rows. It adds a subquery to the select, so you get the counts with the same query.

It works with hasOne, hasMany, hasOneThrough, hasManyThrough, manyToMany, morphOne and morphMany relations.

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @HasMany(Post)
  List<Post> posts = <Post>[];
}

List<User> users = await User().withCount('posts').get();

users.first.countOf('posts'); // 3
users.first.toJson();         // {..., "posts_count": 3}

The key is the relation name in snake_case and _count, like posts_count. Use the relation name (the field name) in withCount() and countOf().

docs.title: Count only some rows
docs.text:
Give a function to add conditions to the related rows. Use as to give the count its own key.

List<User> users = await User()
    .withCount('posts')
    .withCount('posts as published_count', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
      q.where('published', true);
    })
    .get();

users.first.countOf('posts');               // all posts
users.first.aggregate('published_count');   // published posts

The global scopes and soft deletes of the related model are used in the count.

docs.title: With other query methods
docs.text:
withCount() works with where(), orderBy(), find(), getFirst(), paginate() and with preload() or eager relations:

User? user = await User().preload('posts').withCount('posts').find(1);
user?.posts;              // the posts
user?.countOf('posts');   // the number of posts

docs.title: Sum, average, min and max
docs.text:
withSum(), withAvg(), withMin() and withMax() work the same way, on one column of the related rows. The value is null when there is no related row.

User? user = await User()
    .withSum('posts', 'views')
    .withAvg('posts', 'views')
    .withMin('posts', 'views')
    .withMax('posts', 'views')
    .find(1);

user?.aggregate('posts_sum_views');
user?.aggregate('posts_avg_views');
user?.aggregate('posts_min_views');
user?.aggregate('posts_max_views');

docs.title: Exists
docs.text:
withExists() adds <relation>_exists. It is true when there is at least one related row. It takes a function and as, like withCount().

User? user = await User()
    .withExists('posts')
    .withExists('posts as has_published', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
      q.where('published', true);
    })
    .find(1);

user?.aggregate('posts_exists');   // true or false
user?.aggregate('has_published');  // true or false

Info

withCount() is not for belongsTo relations. It throws an UnsupportedError. It works for a relation to the same table, like the children of a category.

To keep only the rows that have related rows, use whereHas() or has(). See Query by relations.

docs.title: Model events
docs.text:
A model fires events when you save, delete or restore it, and you can run your own code on them.

There are two ways to listen:

  • Hooks: methods in the model class. Use them for code that belongs to the model, like filling a value.
  • Observers: separate classes. Use them for code that needs other services, like a mailer.

docs.title: Hooks in the model
docs.text:
Override an on... method in the model. Then run dart run build_runner build.

lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart
@DoxModel()
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  @Column()
  String? slug;

  @override
  Future<void> onSaving() async {
    slug = title?.trim().toLowerCase().replaceAll(' ', '-');
  }
}

Post post = Post()..title = 'Hello World';
await post.save(); // onSaving runs first, so slug is 'hello-world'

All hooks come in pairs: one runs before the query, one after it.

Before hook After hook Run on onSaving onSaved every save(): a new or a loaded model onCreating onCreated save() or create() on a new model (INSERT) onUpdating onUpdated save() on a loaded model (UPDATE) onDeleting onDeleted delete() onForceDeleting onForceDeleted forceDelete(): really removes a soft-deleted row onRestoring onRestored restore(): brings back a soft-deleted row

onTrashed runs after onDeleted, when a soft delete changed the row. It has no before hook.

  • A before hook runs before the query. The row is not written yet. You can change values, or cancel the operation.
  • An after hook runs after the query. The row is written, and a new model has its id. Use it for side effects.
  • Declare the hooks in the model class itself. The generator looks there.

docs.title: Order of events
docs.text:
Call Events, in order save() on a new model saving → creating → INSERT → created → saved save() on a loaded model saving → updating → UPDATE → updated → saved create({...}) the same as save() on a new model firstOrCreate(), updateOrCreate() the same as save() when they create or update a row delete() deleting → DELETE or soft delete → deleted (→ trashed after a soft delete) forceDelete() forceDeleting → deleting → DELETE → deleted → forceDeleted restore() restoring → UPDATE deleted_at = NULL and updated_at → restored touch() saving → updating → UPDATE updated_at → updated → saved (touchQuietly() fires none)
  • The model hook runs first. Then the observers run, in the order you added them.
  • save() on a loaded model with no changes fires the same events, but runs no UPDATE. A model with a Map or List field is always sent, because the field can be changed in place. With the skipCleanUpdateEvents flag, it fires only saving and saved. With this flag on, a save with changes runs beforeSave two times, and a save with no changes runs it one time.
  • When a model has events, create({...}) saves only the @Column fields.

Query updates and deletes fire no events

Events fire only on one model instance. Post().where('draft', true).update({...}), Post().where(...).delete(), insertMultiple(), upsert(), increment(), decrement() and Post().where(...).touch() run one query and fire no events.

docs.title: Set a value only on create
docs.text:
onCreating runs only for a new row. Updates do not change the value again.

@override
Future<void> onCreating() async {
  status ??= 'draft';
  publicId = Uuid().v4(); // from package:uuid
}

docs.title: Stop an operation
docs.text:
Throw CancelModelEvent in a before hook. The query does not run. save() and restore() return false. delete() and forceDelete() return 0.

lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart
@override
Future<void> onDeleting() async {
  if (status == 'published') {
    throw CancelModelEvent('unpublish the post first');
  }
}
lib/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart
Future<Map<String, String>> destroy(DoxRequest req, int id) async {
  Post? post = await Post().find(id);
  if (post == null) throw NotFoundHttpException();

  int deleted = await post.delete();
  if (deleted == 0) {
    throw BadRequestException(message: 'Unpublish the post first');
  }
  return <String, String>{'message': 'deleted'};
}
  • save() and restore() return false when a hook cancels.
  • delete() and forceDelete() return the number of deleted rows. It is 0 when a hook cancels.
  • create({...}) returns the unsaved model. Its id is null.
  • Any other error from a hook is thrown to the caller.

docs.title: Do something after a change
docs.text:
After hooks are for side effects. The row is already in the database.

@override
Future<void> onSaved() async {
  await Cache().forget('post:$id'); // the next read gets the new data
}

@override
Future<void> onDeleted() async {
  if (coverPath != null) {
    await Storage().delete(coverPath!); // remove the file of the post
  }
}

docs.title: Observers
docs.text:
An observer is a class that listens to one model. Use it when the code needs other objects, like a mailer, or when you do not want it in the model.

The methods have the same names as the hooks. Each one gets the model. Override only the ones you need.

Before method After method Run on onSaving(T model) onSaved(T model) every save(): a new or a loaded model onCreating(T model) onCreated(T model) save() or create() on a new model (INSERT) onUpdating(T model) onUpdated(T model) save() on a loaded model (UPDATE) onDeleting(T model) onDeleted(T model) delete() onForceDeleting(T model) onForceDeleted(T model) forceDelete() onRestoring(T model) onRestored(T model) restore()

A before method can stop the operation with CancelModelEvent, like a before hook.

lib/app/observers/user.observer.dart
class UserObserver extends ModelObserver<User> {
  final Mailer mailer;

  UserObserver(this.mailer);

  @override
  Future<void> onCreated(User model) async {
    await mailer.sendWelcome(model.email!);
  }
}

Add it in the setup() of a provider. Observers live in memory, and each isolate has its own memory, so every isolate must add them.

lib/providers/observer_provider.dart
class ObserverProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Model.observe<User>(UserObserver(Mailer()));
  }
}

Dox finds ObserverProvider by itself, like every DoxProvider. Run dart run build_runner build after you add it.

To hear about soft deletes, add the TrashedObserver mixin and override onTrashed(T model):

class PostObserver extends ModelObserver<Post> with TrashedObserver<Post> {
  @override
  void onTrashed(Post post) => print('trashed ${post.id}');
}
  • You can add more than one observer to a model.
  • Model.forgetObservers<User>() removes the observers of User. Model.forgetObservers() removes all.

docs.title: Skip events
docs.text:
Use this for imports, seed data or tests.

await user.saveQuietly(); // save without events

await Model.withoutEvents(() async {
  await user.save();
  await post.delete();
});

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
save() does not start a transaction. If an after hook throws, the row stays written. To undo the row when a hook fails, wrap the call in QueryBuilder.transaction():

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  await user.save(); // if onCreated() throws, the INSERT is rolled back
});

A model with no hooks and no observers does no event work.

docs.title: Query by relations
docs.text:
whereHas(), whereDoesntHave() and has() keep the rows of a query by their related rows.

For example: get the users that have a post. These methods do not load the related rows. They add a subquery to the where part, so it is still one query. To load the related rows, use preload(). See HasMany.

The examples on this page use these models:

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @HasMany(Post)
  List<Post> posts = <Post>[];
}

@DoxModel()
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Column()
  bool? published;

  @BelongsTo(User)
  User? user;

  @HasMany(Comment)
  List<Comment> comments = <Comment>[];
}

docs.title: whereHas
docs.text:
Keeps the rows that have at least one related row. Use the relation name (the field name).

List<User> users = await User().whereHas('posts').get();
// WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM "post" WHERE ...)

Give a function to add conditions to the related rows.

List<User> users = await User().whereHas('posts', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('published', true);
}).get();

This keeps the users that have at least one published post.

docs.title: whereDoesntHave
docs.text:
Keeps the rows that have no related row.

List<User> users = await User().whereDoesntHave('posts').get();
// WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM "post" WHERE ...)

List<User> noDrafts = await User().whereDoesntHave('posts', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('published', false);
}).get();

docs.title: orWhereHas and orWhereDoesntHave
docs.text:
They are the same, but they join the condition with OR.

List<User> users = await User()
    .where('name', 'Ann')
    .orWhereHas('posts')
    .get();
// WHERE "name" = @name_p0 OR EXISTS (...)

await User().where('name', 'Ann').orWhereDoesntHave('posts').get();

docs.title: has
docs.text:
has() counts the related rows. Give an operator and a number.

// at least one post
await User().has('posts').get();

// three posts or more
await User().has('posts', '>=', 3).get();

// no post
await User().has('posts', '=', 0).get();

// more than one published post
await User().has('posts', '>', 1, (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('published', true);
}).get();
  • The default is '>=' and 1: at least one related row.
  • The operator must be one of =, !=, <>, <, >, <= or >=. Any other operator throws an ArgumentError.

docs.title: Relations of relations
docs.text:
Use a dot to check a relation of a relation.

// users that have a post with a comment
await User().whereHas('posts.comments').get();

// users that have a post with a comment by user 1
await User().whereHas('posts.comments', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('user_id', 1);
}).get();

// users that have no post with a comment
await User().whereDoesntHave('posts.comments').get();

The function is for the last relation (comments).

With has(), the count is for the last relation of one row. has('posts.comments', '>=', 2) keeps the users that have a post with two comments or more.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• It works with hasOne, hasMany, hasOneThrough, hasManyThrough, belongsTo, manyToMany, morphOne and morphMany relations. A morphTo relation throws an UnsupportedError.
  • Soft deleted related rows do not count. To count them, set q.withTrashed = true in the function.
  • The global scopes and the onQuery function of the relation are used.
  • It works with where(), count(), paginate(), withCount() and the other query methods.
  • Start the query with a model, like User(). On QueryBuilder.table() it throws a StateError.
  • A name that is not a relation of the model throws an ArgumentError.
  • It works for a relation to the same table, like a Category with a parent Category.

docs.title: A relation to the same table
docs.text:
The subquery gives the table its own name, so each row is not compared with itself.

// categories that have at least one child category
List<Category> parents = await Category().whereHas('children').get();

// categories whose parent is named 'Books'
List<Category> books = await Category()
    .whereHas('parent', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
      q.where('name', 'Books');
    })
    .get();

Warning

In the function, write the column without the table name: name, not categories.name. With the table name, the column points to the parent row, not to the related row.

docs.title: Query scopes
docs.text:
A scope is a query part that you use again and again, like "only active users".

You write it once in the model. Then you call it like a query method.

docs.title: Local scopes
docs.text:
Add a static method with @Scope() to the model. It takes the query first and returns the query. Then run dart run build_runner build.

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column()
  bool? active;

  @Column()
  int? age;

  @Scope()
  static QueryBuilder<User> isActive(QueryBuilder<User> q) {
    return q.where('active', true);
  }

  @Scope()
  static QueryBuilder<User> olderThan(QueryBuilder<User> q, int age) {
    return q.where('age', '>', age);
  }
}

The generator adds each scope as a method on the query of the model:

List<User> users = await User().isActive().get();

List<User> adults = await User()
    .where('name', 'like', 'a%')
    .isActive()
    .olderThan(18)
    .get();

A scope can take more arguments: required, optional ([...]) and named ({...}). The generated method takes the same arguments, without the query.

Pick a free name

The scope name must not be a field or a method of the model. For example, a scope active next to a field active does not work. Use isActive. A scope named like a query method (count, get) is never called.

docs.title: Global scopes
docs.text:
@Scope(global: true) adds the scope to every query of the model. This includes get(), find(), all(), count(), paginate(), query updates and deletes, and relation queries. A global scope counts as a where: Post().delete() deletes only the rows in the scope. With withoutGlobalScopes() and no where, the write throws a StateError.

@DoxModel()
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Column()
  bool? archived;

  /// every query leaves out archived posts
  @Scope(global: true)
  static QueryBuilder<Post> notArchived(QueryBuilder<Post> q) {
    return q.where('archived', false);
  }
}

await Post().get(); // ... WHERE ("archived" = false)

The global scope goes in brackets, and your own conditions too. So an orWhere() in your query can not skip the scope.

Remove a global scope for one query with withoutGlobalScope(), or remove all of them with withoutGlobalScopes():

await Post().withoutGlobalScope('notArchived').get();
await Post().withoutGlobalScopes().find(1);

The name of a global scope is the method name.

Info

save(), delete() and restore() on a model instance work on that one row. They do not use the global scopes. Soft deletes are not a global scope. Use withTrash() for them.

docs.title: BelongsTo
docs.text:
Use BelongsTo when this table keeps the foreign key to another table.

For example, a comment belongs to a user. The comment table has the column user_id.

BelongsTo is the other side of HasOne and HasMany.

docs.title: Define it
docs.text:
Add a field with @BelongsTo(...) to the model. The field type is the related model, nullable.

lib/app/models/comment/comment.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../user/user.model.dart';

part 'comment.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Comment extends CommentGenerator {
  @Column()
  int? userId; // column user_id

  @Column()
  String? content;

  @BelongsTo(User)
  User? user;
}
lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @Column()
  String? status;
}

Run dart run build_runner build after you add a relationship.

docs.title: Load it
docs.text: The relation is not loaded by default. Load it in one of these ways. Use the field name ('user') as the relation name.

docs.title: preload
docs.text:
Use it when you load the models with a query.

List<Comment> comments = await Comment().preload('user').all();
for (Comment comment in comments) {
  print(comment.user?.name);
}

preload works with find, get, all and getFirst. It runs one query for all comments, not one query per comment.

docs.title: $getRelation
docs.text:
Use it when you already have the model.

Comment? comment = await Comment().find(1);
await comment?.$getRelation('user');
print(comment?.user?.name);

Do not call it in a loop over many models. Use preload for a list.

docs.title: related
docs.text:
Use it when you need more conditions on the related row.

Comment? comment = await Comment().find(1);
User? activeUser = await comment
    ?.related<User>('user')
    ?.where('status', 'active')
    .getFirst();

It does not set comment.user.

docs.title: eager
docs.text:
Use it when every query of Comment should load the relation.

@BelongsTo(User, eager: true)
User? user;

You do not call preload.

The load runs this SQL:

SELECT * FROM "user"
  WHERE "user"."id" IN (@userid_p0, ...)

Each user is read once, also when it has many comments. Comments of the same user get the same User object.

reload() and a preload set the relation fields again, also when there is no related row. See Relationships.

docs.title: Filter by it
docs.text:
whereHas() keeps the comments by a user that matches. It does not load the users.

List<Comment> comments = await Comment().whereHas('user', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('name', 'Ann');
}).get();

See Query by relations.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default What it is foreignKey {related model}_id, like user_id The column in this table that points to the related model. localKey the primary key of the related model The column in the related table that foreignKey points to. onQuery none A static function that changes the query. eager false Load the relation on every query.

The default foreignKey uses the class name of the related model in snake_case. User gives user_id, also when the table is users. The belongsToKeyFromRelation flag takes it from the relation name (author_id). The model generator does not pass the relation name yet, so set foreignKey when it is not the class name.

docs.title: foreignKey and localKey
docs.text:
@BelongsTo(User, foreignKey: 'author_id', localKey: 'id')
User? author;

docs.title: onQuery
docs.text:
onQuery is a static function in the same model class. It gets the query of the related model and returns it.

@DoxModel()
class Comment extends CommentGenerator {
  @Column()
  int? userId;

  @BelongsTo(User, onQuery: onlyActive)
  User? activeUser;

  static QueryBuilder<User> onlyActive(User q) {
    return q.where('status', 'active');
  }
}

docs.title: In JSON
docs.text:
• A relation with eager: true is always in toJson().
  • A relation loaded with preload is in toJson() of that query.
  • The JSON key is the field name in snake_case: user.

docs.title: HasMany
docs.text:
Use HasMany when one row of this table has many rows in another table.

For example, a user has many posts. The other table keeps the foreign key (post.user_id).

docs.title: Define it
docs.text:
Add a field with @HasMany(...) to the model. The field type is a list of the related model. Start it as an empty list.

lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../post/post.model.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @HasMany(Post)
  List<Post> posts = <Post>[];
}
lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'post.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Column()
  int? userId; // column user_id

  @Column()
  String? title;

  @Column()
  String? status;
}

Run dart run build_runner build after you add a relationship.

docs.title: Load it
docs.text: The relation is not loaded by default. Load it in one of these ways. Use the field name ('posts') as the relation name.

docs.title: preload
docs.text:
Use it when you load the models with a query.

User? user = await User().preload('posts').find(1);
print(user?.posts.length);

List<User> users = await User().preload('posts').get();

preload works with find, get, all and getFirst. For a list of users, it runs one query for all of them. A user without posts gets an empty list.

docs.title: $getRelation
docs.text:
Use it when you already have the model.

User? user = await User().find(1);
await user?.$getRelation('posts');
print(user?.posts.length);

docs.title: related
docs.text:
Use it when you need more conditions on the related rows.

User? user = await User().find(1);
List<Post> activePosts = await user
        ?.related<Post>('posts')
        ?.where('status', 'active')
        .orderBy('id', 'desc')
        .get() ??
    <Post>[];

It does not set user.posts.

docs.title: eager
docs.text:
Use it when every query of User should load the relation.

@HasMany(Post, eager: true)
List<Post> posts = <Post>[];

You do not call preload.

The load runs this SQL:

SELECT *, "user_id" as "_owner_id" FROM "post" WHERE "user_id" IN (@user_id_p0, ...)

reload() and a preload set the relation fields again, also when there is no related row. See Relationships.

docs.title: Filter by it
docs.text:
whereHas() keeps the users that have a post. whereDoesntHave() keeps the users with no post. It does not load the posts.

List<User> writers = await User().whereHas('posts', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('status', 'active');
}).get();

List<User> noPosts = await User().whereDoesntHave('posts').get();
List<User> busy = await User().has('posts', '>=', 10).get();

See Query by relations.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default What it is foreignKey {this model}_id, like user_id The column in the related table that points to this model. localKey the primary key of this model The column in this table that foreignKey points to. onQuery none A static function that changes the query. eager false Load the relation on every query.

The default foreignKey uses the class name in snake_case. User gives user_id, also when the table is users.

docs.title: foreignKey and localKey
docs.text:
@HasMany(Book, foreignKey: 'author_code', localKey: 'code')
List<Book> books = <Book>[];

docs.title: onQuery
docs.text:
onQuery is a static function in the same model class. It gets the query of the related model and returns it. You can have two fields on the same model with different queries.

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @HasMany(Post)
  List<Post> posts = <Post>[];

  @HasMany(Post, onQuery: onlyActive)
  List<Post> activePosts = <Post>[];

  static QueryBuilder<Post> onlyActive(Post q) {
    return q.where('status', 'active').orderBy('id', 'desc');
  }
}

docs.title: In JSON
docs.text:
• A relation with eager: true is always in toJson().
  • A relation loaded with preload is in toJson() of that query.
  • The JSON key is the field name in snake_case.

docs.title: HasOne
docs.text:
Use HasOne when one row of this table has one row in another table.

For example, a user has one user info row. The other table keeps the foreign key (user_info.user_id).

docs.title: Define it
docs.text:
Add a field with @HasOne(...) to the model. The field type is the related model, nullable.

lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../user_info/user_info.model.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @HasOne(UserInfo)
  UserInfo? userInfo;
}
lib/app/models/user_info/user_info.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'user_info.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class UserInfo extends UserInfoGenerator {
  @Column()
  int? userId; // column user_id

  @Column()
  String? address;
}

Run dart run build_runner build after you add a relationship.

docs.title: Load it
docs.text: The relation is not loaded by default. Load it in one of these ways. Use the field name ('userInfo') as the relation name.

docs.title: preload
docs.text:
Use it when you load the models with a query.

User? user = await User().preload('userInfo').find(1);
print(user?.userInfo?.address);

preload works with find, get, all and getFirst. For a list of users, it runs one query for all of them.

docs.title: $getRelation
docs.text:
Use it when you already have the model.

User? user = await User().find(1);
await user?.$getRelation('userInfo');
print(user?.userInfo?.address);

docs.title: related
docs.text:
Use it when you need more conditions on the related row.

User? user = await User().find(1);
UserInfo? info = await user
    ?.related<UserInfo>('userInfo')
    ?.where('address', '!=', '')
    .getFirst();

It does not set user.userInfo.

docs.title: eager
docs.text:
Use it when every query of User should load the relation.

@HasOne(UserInfo, eager: true)
UserInfo? userInfo;

You do not call preload.

The load runs this SQL:

SELECT *, "user_id" as "_owner_id" FROM "user_info" WHERE "user_id" IN (@user_id_p0)

reload() and a preload set the relation fields again, also when there is no related row. See Relationships.

docs.title: Filter by it
docs.text:
whereHas() keeps the users that have a user_info row. whereDoesntHave() keeps the users without one. It does not load the UserInfo.

List<User> users = await User().whereHas('userInfo').get();

List<User> inParis = await User().whereHas('userInfo', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('address', 'Paris');
}).get();

List<User> noInfo = await User().whereDoesntHave('userInfo').get();

See Query by relations.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default What it is foreignKey {this model}_id, like user_id The column in the related table that points to this model. localKey the primary key of this model The column in this table that foreignKey points to. onQuery none A static function that changes the query. eager false Load the relation on every query.

The default foreignKey uses the class name in snake_case. User gives user_id, also when the table is users.

docs.title: foreignKey and localKey
docs.text:
@HasOne(UserInfo, foreignKey: 'owner_id', localKey: 'id')
UserInfo? userInfo;

docs.title: onQuery
docs.text:
onQuery is a static function in the same model class. It gets the query of the related model and returns it.

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @HasOne(UserInfo, onQuery: onlyActive)
  UserInfo? userInfo;

  static QueryBuilder<UserInfo> onlyActive(UserInfo q) {
    return q.where('status', 'active');
  }
}

docs.title: In JSON
docs.text:
• A relation with eager: true is always in toJson().
  • A relation loaded with preload is in toJson() of that query.
  • The JSON key is the field name in snake_case: user_info.

docs.title: ManyToMany
docs.text:
Use ManyToMany when rows on both sides can have many rows on the other side.

For example, an artist has many songs, and a song has many artists.

The link is kept in a third table, the pivot table. It has one foreign key to each side.

docs.title: Tables
Define it
docs.text:
Add a field with @ManyToMany(...) to each model that needs it. The field type is a list of the related model. Start it as an empty list.

lib/app/models/artist/artist.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../song/song.model.dart';

part 'artist.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Artist extends ArtistGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @ManyToMany(Song)
  List<Song> songs = <Song>[];
}
lib/app/models/song/song.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../artist/artist.model.dart';

part 'song.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Song extends SongGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  @ManyToMany(Artist)
  List<Artist> artists = <Artist>[];
}

Run dart run build_runner build after you add a relationship.

docs.title: Load it
docs.text: The relation is not loaded by default. Load it in one of these ways. Use the field name ('songs') as the relation name.

docs.title: preload
docs.text:
Use it when you load the models with a query.

Artist? artist = await Artist().preload('songs').find(1);
print(artist?.songs.length);

List<Song> songs = await Song().preload('artists').get();

preload works with find, get, all and getFirst. For a list of models, it runs one query for all of them. A model without links gets an empty list.

docs.title: $getRelation
docs.text:
Use it when you already have the model.

Artist? artist = await Artist().find(1);
await artist?.$getRelation('songs');
print(artist?.songs.length);

docs.title: related
docs.text:
Use it when you need more conditions on the related rows.

Artist? artist = await Artist().find(1);
List<Song> songs = await artist
        ?.related<Song>('songs')
        ?.orderBy('song.title')
        .get() ??
    <Song>[];

It does not set artist.songs. The query joins the pivot table, so write table.column for column names.

docs.title: eager
docs.text:
Use it when every query of Artist should load the relation.

@ManyToMany(Song, eager: true)
List<Song> songs = <Song>[];

You do not call preload. Do not set eager: true on both sides. Each side would load the other side again and again.

The load runs this SQL:

SELECT "song".*, "artist_song"."artist_id" as "_owner_id" FROM "song"
  LEFT JOIN "artist_song" on "artist_song"."song_id" = "song"."id"
  WHERE "artist_song"."artist_id" IN (@artist_songartist_id_p0, ...)

With withPivot or withTimestamps, it also selects those pivot columns, like "artist_song"."role" as "_pivot_role".

reload() and a preload set the relation fields again, also when there is no related row. See Relationships.

docs.title: Read pivot columns
docs.text:
The pivot table can have more columns, like a role. List them in withPivot. Read them with pivot on each related model.

@ManyToMany(Song, withPivot: <String>['role'])
List<Song> songs = <Song>[];

Artist? artist = await Artist().preload('songs').find(1);
for (Song song in artist!.songs) {
  print(song.pivot['role']);
}
  • pivot has the two pivot keys, like artist_id and song_id, when the rows are loaded by the relation: with preload, $getRelation, eager or related('songs')!.get(). They are read from the loaded rows, so a relation without withPivot runs no extra SQL.
  • withTimestamps: true adds created_at and updated_at to pivot. attach(), sync() and toggle() then set them. updateExistingPivot() sets updated_at. The pivot table needs both columns (table.timestamps()).
  • A model that was not loaded by a ManyToMany relation has an empty pivot.
  • toJson() of a model loaded by a ManyToMany relation has a pivot key with these values. Dates are ISO text. Put 'pivot' in hidden to leave it out. A model with its own pivot column keeps its column value in that key. Then the pivot values are only in the pivot getter in Dart, not in toJson().

docs.title: Change the links
docs.text:
These methods add and remove rows in the pivot table. The first argument is the relation name, like 'songs'. Save the model first. A model without an id throws a StateError.

The ids can be:

  • one id: 1
  • a model: song
  • a list of ids or models: [1, 2, song]
  • a map of id => pivot values: {1: {'role': 'singer'}, 2: {}}

null means no ids. So attach('songs', null) and detach('songs', null) change nothing, and sync('songs', null) deletes every link, like sync('songs', []). Ids match with one rule:

  • Two texts only match when the text is the same. So on a text key column, '007' and '7' are two ids. The ORM does not know the type of the key column, so attach('songs', ['1', '01']) adds two rows.
  • When one id is a number (int or double), Dart reads the other one as a number. It trims the text, drops a .0 end, and tries int.tryParse (' 1', '+1', '01', '1.0'), then double.tryParse ('1.', '1e0'). They match when the two numbers are the same. Rows of a number key column come back as numbers, so sync('songs', ['01']) keeps the row of song 1.
  • This is only how Dart matches ids. The databases read some texts in other ways. For example, '0x1' is 1 in Dart and on Postgres, 0 on MariaDB, and an error on MySQL. Postgres throws for '1.0', '1.' and '1e0' on an integer column.
  • A given text that only reads as a number at or past ±2^53, like '1e20' or '9007199254740993.', is not exact. It throws an ArgumentError when it is matched to a number. sync checks every id before its first write.
  • A stored value never throws. A value in the table that can not be read exactly does not match a number. So a long digit text in a text key column does not stop sync.
  • A bool id is 1 or 0, like the databases read it. So sync('songs', true) keeps the row of song 1.
  • A BigInt id is an int when it fits, else it throws an ArgumentError. Any other id type that is not an int, a String, a bool, a double or a model throws an ArgumentError.
