Any name is safe in the header. Quotes are escaped, a new line becomes _, and a name like résumé.pdf is also sent as filename*=UTF-8''r%C3%A9sum%C3%A9.pdf.

To add headers, put the download in a response():

Route.get('/invoice', (DoxRequest req) async {
  DownloadableFile file = await Storage().download('invoices/42.pdf');
  return response(file).header('Cache-Control', 'no-store');
});

docs.title: Full disk API
docs.text: Storage().use('s3') returns the dox_storage Disk: listAll with pages, getMetaData, putStream, deleteAll, write options and more. See dox_storage.

docs.title: Serve local signed URLs
docs.text:
// lib/routes/web.dart
Storage.route('files');                    // GET /files/{key*}, signed URLs only
Storage.route('public', signed: false);    // any file of the disk
Storage.route('docs', disk: 'memory', signed: false); // another disk than the default
Storage.route('uploads', download: true);  // every file is a download

An html, svg, xml or javascript file is always sent as a download in a sandbox, so its script does not run on your site. Every file has X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.

String url = await Storage().signedUrl('invoices/1.pdf'); // https://app.test/files/invoices/1.pdf?expires=...&signature=...

A missing, wrong or expired signature answers 403. Signed URLs work only on a local disk. For another disk, use signed: false. A signed URL works only on the route of its own disk. An old signed URL, made before the disk name was part of the signature, still works on any local disk with the same app key. This ends when it expires. Set the disk url option to the full URL of the route (https://app.test/files).

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: To swap a disk with a memory disk in tests, see Testing.

docs.title: Your own driver
docs.text:
Implement DriverContract from package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart. Register it in a provider, so every isolate has it:

Storage.manager.register('dropbox', DropboxDriver());
await Storage().disk('dropbox').put('notes/a.txt', 'hello', exact: true);

docs.title: Health check
docs.text: A health route tells a load balancer, Docker or Kubernetes if the app can serve requests.

docs.title: Add the route
docs.text:
Add it in register() of a router:

lib/routes/web.dart
@override
void register() {
  Route.get('/ping', (WebController c) => c.pong);
  Route.health('/health');
}

GET /health answers 200 with:

{"status": "ok"}

docs.title: Check the database and the cache
docs.text:
Give named checks. Each check is a function. Put the Route.health call in register(), as above:

lib/routes/web.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

Route.health(
  '/health',
  checks: <String, HealthCheckFunction>{
    'database': () => QueryBuilder.query('select 1'),
    'cache': HealthCheck.cache(),
  },
);

When all checks pass, the answer is 200:

{"status": "ok", "checks": {"database": "ok", "cache": "ok"}}

When one check fails, the answer is 503 Service Unavailable:

{"status": "fail", "checks": {"database": "fail", "cache": "ok"}}

A check fails when it:

  • throws an error,
  • returns false,
  • or takes longer than timeout (default 5 seconds).

The checks run at the same time.

  • HealthCheck.cache() writes a key to the default cache store and reads it back. HealthCheck.cache('redis') checks the store with that name.
  • Any other check is your own function, like a call to another API.

docs.title: Error details
docs.text:
The error of a failed check is passed to exceptionHandler.report(), so you see it in your logs.

The answer has the error text (in errors) only when APP_ENV is development or local. In other envs the text is left out, because it can show hosts or user names.

docs.title: Change the timeout
docs.text:
Route.health(
  '/health',
  timeout: Duration(seconds: 2),
  checks: <String, HealthCheckFunction>{
    'database': () => QueryBuilder.query('select 1'),
  },
);

Tip

A route in a router gets the middleware of that router and the global middleware. Put Route.health in a router with no auth middleware, or the health check gets 401.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Docker for a health check in the image
  • Deployment

docs.title: Isolate
docs.text: This page explains how Dox runs your app on many isolates (threads), and what that means for your code.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Dox starts many isolates. Each one runs its own native server on the same port. The operating system spreads the connections between them.

  • Linux: each isolate has its own socket (SO_REUSEPORT).
  • macOS: the isolates share one socket.
  • Windows: only one isolate serves HTTP.

Each isolate has its own Rust acceptor on the port:

flowchart TD
    OS["Port 3000<br>the OS spreads the connections"] --> A1["Rust acceptor"]
    OS --> A2["Rust acceptor"]
    OS --> A3["Rust acceptor"]
    A1 --> I1["Isolate 1, main<br>own memory cache"]
    A2 --> I2["Isolate 2<br>own memory cache"]
    A3 --> I3["Isolate N<br>own memory cache"]
    I2 -. "crash: started again after 1 second" .-> I2
    I1 -. "crash: the process exits" .-> S["Supervisor restarts the process<br>Docker, systemd"]

With the Postgres and MySQL drivers, all isolates share one database pool in Rust. See How Dox works.

docs.title: How many isolates
docs.text:
By default Dox starts one isolate per CPU core (Platform.numberOfProcessors).

To change it, set totalIsolate in lib/config/app.dart. A new app reads it from APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  totalIsolate: env.appTotalIsolate ?? Platform.numberOfProcessors,
);

You can also set it in code, before startServer(). This wins over the config:

bin/server.dart
Dox().initialize(appConfig);
Dox().totalIsolate(2);
await Dox().startServer();

Use fewer isolates when the machine also runs the database or other heavy work.

docs.title: Each isolate has its own memory
docs.text:
Isolates do not share memory:

  • A static value or a singleton exists once per isolate. When you change it in one isolate, the others do not see it.
  • The memory cache store is per isolate. See Cache.
  • To share data between isolates or servers, use a database, Redis or files.

Dox().isolateId tells you which isolate runs the code. The first isolate is 1.

docs.title: Send a message to the other isolates
docs.text:
IsolateBus sends a message from one isolate to all the others in the same process. Use it to tell them that something changed, for example "forget this cache key". Socket.IO uses it to share broadcasts (see Socket.IO).

IsolateBus.instance.on('users').listen(onMessage); // in a provider's setup()
IsolateBus.instance.publish('users', <Object>['changed', 42]);
  • A message goes to one channel. A listener on 'users' never gets the messages of another channel.
  • An isolate never gets its own message.
  • Dox().isolateCount is the number of isolates that run, in every isolate.
  • IsolateBus.instance.size is the number of isolates that listen, this one included.
  • A message must be something a SendPort can send: null, bool, num, String, typed data, and lists and maps of those.
  • A value that a SendPort can not send throws an ArgumentError in publish. Then no isolate gets the message. In the main isolate it throws only when another isolate listens on the bus. With no other isolate there, nobody gets it and nothing throws.
  • It works inside one process only. For many servers, use Redis.
  • There is no backpressure. publish never waits. A slow listener gets the messages in a queue in its memory.
  • A message reaches only the isolates that listen at that moment. An isolate that calls on() later does not get the messages sent before.
  • size changes a little after an isolate joins or leaves. The new number comes in a message, so it can be old for a short time.

docs.title: What each isolate does at start
docs.text:
Dox copies the AppConfig, the providers and the routes you added before startServer() to each new isolate. Then every isolate:

  1. runs setup() of each provider (for example, it opens the database pool),
  2. registers the routes of your routers,
  3. reads the parameter types of each controller once,
  4. runs boot() of each provider,
  5. starts its HTTP server.

Because the config and providers are copied, they must not hold open sockets or database pools. Open these in setup(). See Providers.

docs.title: When an isolate crashes
docs.text:
• An error in a request is caught. Dox sends a 500 and keeps going.
  • An async error outside a request (for example a future that nobody awaits) is caught and passed to the report method of the exception handler. The isolate keeps running.
  • If a worker isolate still dies, Dox prints [dox] isolate N exited, restarting to stderr. It starts a new isolate after 1 second.
  • If the first (main) isolate dies, the process exits with a non-zero code. Let a supervisor start it again, like Docker restart: or systemd Restart=always. See Deployment.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
The dox_mailer package sends email from your app with SMTP, Amazon SES, Azure, Resend, Mailgun, Postmark or sendmail.

You write a Message and call Mail.send(). A transport sends it. You pick the transport in a config file, so you can change providers with no code change.

The package has its own SMTP client, AWS signer and MIME builder. Next to dox_core, it only needs dox_view, markdown, http and crypto.

Send slow emails from the queue with Mail.queue(), so the request does not wait. See Queue an email.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
dox add mailer

Add --transport=smtp (or resend, mailgun, postmark, ses) to pick a transport. log is the default. It adds the package and writes the mail config and the provider. It adds MAIL_MAILER, MAIL_FROM and the keys of the transport to .env. When the app has dox_view, it also makes the resources/views/emails folder. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice.

docs.title: Set it up by hand
docs.text: dart pub add dox_mailer

docs.title: 1. Config
docs.text:
A mailer is a name and a transport. defaultMailer is the one that Mail.send() uses.

lib/config/mail.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';

MailConfig mailConfig = MailConfig(
  /// the mailer of Mail.send()
  defaultMailer: Env.get('MAIL_MAILER', 'log'),

  /// for messages with no from address
  from: Address(Env.get('MAIL_FROM', 'hello@example.com'), 'My app'),

  mailers: <String, Transport>{
    'smtp': SmtpTransport(
      host: Env.get('MAIL_HOST', 'localhost'),
      port: Env.get<int>('MAIL_PORT', 587),
      username: Env.get<String?>('MAIL_USERNAME'),
      password: Env.get<String?>('MAIL_PASSWORD'),
    ),

    /// prints emails, sends nothing
    'log': LogTransport(),
  },
);

Env.get() reads the .env file and the real environment. You can also add the keys to the AppEnv class of your app and use env.mailHost.

.env
MAIL_MAILER=smtp
MAIL_FROM=hello@example.com
MAIL_HOST=smtp.example.com
MAIL_PORT=587
MAIL_USERNAME=me
MAIL_PASSWORD=secret
Option Default What it does defaultMailer log the mailer of Mail.send() mailers a log mailer each mailer name and its transport from none the from address of a message that has none replyTo none the reply-to addresses of a message that has none

docs.title: 2. Provider
docs.text:
The provider sets up the mailers in every isolate. Put it in lib/providers/, so the generated container finds it.

lib/providers/mail_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';

import '../config/mail.dart';

/// Sets up the mailers. Dox finds every DoxProvider class,
/// see lib/generated/container.g.dart.
class AppMailProvider extends MailProvider {
  AppMailProvider() : super(mailConfig);
}

When the server stops, the provider closes open SMTP connections and HTTP clients.

docs.title: Without Dox
docs.text:
dox_mailer also works on its own. Call Mail.configure() once at start, and Mail.close() at the end:

import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  Map<String, String> env = Platform.environment;

  Mail.configure(MailConfig(
    defaultMailer: 'smtp',
    from: Address('hello@example.com', 'My app'),
    mailers: <String, Transport>{
      'smtp': SmtpTransport(
        host: env['MAIL_HOST'] ?? 'localhost',
        username: env['MAIL_USERNAME'],
        password: env['MAIL_PASSWORD'],
      ),
    },
  ));

  await Mail.send(Message(
    to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com')],
    subject: 'Hello',
    text: 'Hello Ann!',
  ));

  // closes open SMTP connections and HTTP clients
  await Mail.close();
}

The rest of this page works the same way.

docs.title: Send an email
docs.text:
import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';

await Mail.send(
  Message(
    to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com', 'Ann Lee')],
    subject: 'Welcome',
    text: 'Hello Ann, welcome!',
    html: '<p>Hello Ann, <b>welcome</b>!</p>',
  ),
);

Send with another mailer:

await Mail.mailer('ses').send(message);

send() gives a SentMessage. Its messageId is the id of the provider (or the Message-ID header for SMTP and sendmail).

When the message can not be sent, send() throws a MailException. It has the statusCode and the body of the answer of the server.

docs.title: Short ways to send
docs.text:
Mail.raw() sends a plain text email. Mail.to() starts an email with chained calls. Both take plain email text:

await Mail.raw('Your code is 1234', to: 'ann@example.com', subject: 'Your code');

await Mail.to('ann@example.com')
    .cc('Bob Lee <bob@example.com>')
    .bcc(<String>['audit@example.com'])
    .send(WelcomeMail(user));
  • to(), cc() and bcc() take an Address, an email text, or a list of these.
  • send() takes a mailable. The recipients are added to the ones of the mailable.
  • queue() and later() work too, like Mail.to(email).queue(WelcomeMail(user)).
  • Address.list() reads addresses the same way: Message(to: Address.list('ann@example.com'), ...).
  • One text is one address. For more addresses, pass a list: Address.list(<String>['ann@example.com', 'bob@example.com']).

docs.title: The message
docs.text:
Field What it is from an Address. Null: MailConfig.from to, cc, bcc lists of Address replyTo a list of Address subject text text the plain text body html the HTML body attachments a list of Attachment headers extra headers, like {'X-Campaign': 'fall'} tags tags for the reports of the provider metadata key and value data for the provider, like {'user_id': '42'}

An Address is an email and an optional name: Address('ann@example.com', 'Ann'). Address.parse('Ann <ann@example.com>') reads one from text.

A message needs a from address, at least one recipient, and a text or HTML body. A subject or header with a line break is an error, so user input can not add headers.

docs.title: Attachments
docs.text:
Message(
  to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com')],
  subject: 'Your invoice',
  text: 'The invoice is attached.',
  attachments: <Attachment>[
    Attachment(pdfBytes, 'invoice.pdf'),
    Attachment.fromFile('storage/terms.pdf'),
  ],
);

The content type comes from the file extension. Pass contentType to set it.

To attach a file from a storage disk, like S3, read its bytes first. This works with every disk:

Uint8List? pdf = await Storage().disk('s3').get('invoices/42.pdf');
Attachment(pdf!, 'invoice.pdf');

docs.title: Inline images
docs.text:
Give the file a cid. Use it in the HTML with cid:.

Message(
  to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com')],
  subject: 'Hello',
  html: '<img src="cid:logo.png"> Hello!',
  attachments: <Attachment>[
    Attachment.fromFile('assets/logo.png', cid: 'logo.png'),
  ],
);

Mailgun uses the file name as the cid. So for Mailgun, use a cid like logo.png, with the file extension.

docs.title: HTML from a view
docs.text:
With views, render a template to HTML:

String html = View.render('emails/welcome', <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann'});
await Mail.send(Message(to: to, subject: 'Welcome', html: html));

docs.title: Mailables
docs.text:
A mailable is one kind of email in its own class, for example the welcome email. It keeps the address, the subject, the template and the data in one place. Override the getters you need:

class WelcomeMail extends Mailable {
  WelcomeMail(this.user);

  final User user;

  @override
  List<Address> get to => <Address>[Address(user.email, user.name)];

  @override
  String get subject => 'Welcome';

  @override
  String? get view => 'emails/welcome';

  @override
  Map<String, Object?> get data => <String, Object?>{'name': user.name};
}

To make a mailable, run dox make:mail Welcome. It writes lib/app/mail/welcome_mail.dart and the view resources/views/emails/welcome.dox.html. Add --no-view for a mail with a plain text body and no view. See dox make:mail.

Then send it, or put it on the queue:

await WelcomeMail(user).send();
await WelcomeMail(user).queue();
await WelcomeMail(user).later(Duration(minutes: 10));

queue() and later() render the templates at once. The worker sends the finished email, so it needs no templates and no data. They take the same queue and encrypt options as Mail.queue().

Getter What it is to, cc, bcc, replyTo the addresses from the sender. Null: the from of the mail config subject the subject html, text the body as text, when there is no template view a dox_view template for the HTML body textView a dox_view template for the plain text body markdown a dox_view template with Markdown, see below data the variables of the templates attachments the files mailer the mailer name, eg. ses. Null: the default mailer

toMessage() gives the email as a Message. To set more, like headers or tags, override it:

@override
Message toMessage() {
  return super.toMessage().copyWith(tags: <String>['welcome']);
}

{{ }} in a template escapes HTML. For the plain text body of textView and markdown, the escape is undone, so Tom & Jerry stays Tom & Jerry.

docs.title: Markdown mail
docs.text:
Write the email in Markdown. You get a simple HTML email with a layout, and a plain text part, from one template. The Markdown is CommonMark with tables.

resources/views/emails/welcome.dox.html:

# Hi {{ name }}

Thanks for joining. Here is what you can do next:

- Fill in your profile
- Invite your team

[Open your profile]({{ profileUrl }})

<a href="https://example.com/dashboard" class="button">Open the app</a>

@override
String? get markdown => 'emails/welcome';
  • The HTML body is the Markdown as HTML, inside a white card on a grey page.
  • The text body is the Markdown itself.
  • <a class="button"> shows as a button. In the text body it stays an <a> tag, so the link is still there.

User data in Markdown

{{ }} escapes HTML and Markdown. A user's name like [click](https://evil.example) shows as that text. It does not become a link. This counts for text values in data, in its maps, lists and sets, and in objects with toJson(). Values from View.global() and from functions are not changed. To put Markdown from a value in the email, pass a SafeString. The kept characters are backslash, backtick, *, [, ], # and |. A _ is not changed, so _word_ can still be italic. In @if, a value with one of these characters is not equal to the same text written in the template. Links and images with an unsafe URL, like javascript:, vbscript: or data:, lose their URL. Only http, https, mailto, tel, cid and relative URLs are kept. The same goes for the lines of MailMessage. MailMessage.action() throws an ArgumentError for an unsafe URL. Raw HTML in the template, like <a href="{{ url }}">, is not checked. In raw HTML, use only full URLs that your app builds. Email apps can not open a relative link like /dashboard. For a URL, write [text]({{ url }}) or <{{ url }}>. They go through the URL check, and the URL stays as it is, with & and %XX. A bare URL does not become a link. Most email apps make it a link anyway. Entity text inside a URL is decoded. So ?q=<b> reaches the browser as ?q=<b>.

Indent

Markdown makes a line that starts with 4 spaces into a code block. So do not indent the Markdown inside @if or @each. Keep it at the start of the line.

To use your own look, override layout(). It gets the HTML of the Markdown and returns the full page. Put it in a base class to use it for all your mailables:

import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';
import 'package:dox_view/dox_view.dart'; // View, SafeString

abstract class AppMail extends Mailable {
  @override
  String layout(String body) {
    return View.render('emails/layout', <String, Object?>{'body': SafeString(body)});
  }
}

docs.title: A simple email with no template
docs.text:
MailMessage is a mailable made of lines and a button. It needs no template. It uses the Markdown layout.

await (MailMessage(subject: 'Invoice paid', to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com')])
      ..line('We got your payment.')
      ..action('View invoice', 'https://example.com/invoices/1')
      ..line('Thank you!'))
    .send();

More options:

  • cc: in the constructor adds cc addresses.
  • attach(Attachment(...)) adds a file.
  • error() makes the buttons red, for a message about a problem.

The email starts with greeting (default Hello!) and ends with salutation (default none). Set them to null to leave them out. Lines can use Markdown, like **bold**. HTML in a line shows as text. See "User data in Markdown" above.

To send one email on more than one channel, see Notifications.

docs.title: Queue an email
docs.text:
Sending an email can take a second or more. With a queue, the request does not wait. A queue worker sends the email later.

This uses dox_queue, which dox_mailer depends on. You only need the dox_queue QueueProvider and a worker. The mail jobs are part of dox_mailer. build_runner adds them to lib/generated/jobs.g.dart, so the worker can read them. The worker (bin/queue.dart) must still run MailProvider: the job sends with your mail config, and MailProvider sets it up. Without it, the job fails with "Mail is not set up". Then:

await Mail.queue(message);

// send it in 10 minutes
await Mail.later(Duration(minutes: 10), message);

// another mailer and another queue
await Mail.mailer('ses').queue(message, queue: 'emails');

queue() and later() return the job id.

  • The message is checked at once. A bad message fails in the request, not in the worker.
  • The default from and reply-to addresses are added at once.
  • The mailer name is saved with the job. The worker sends with the same mailer, so with the same transport.
  • The worker starts the providers of your app, so your MailProvider and mail config are there too.
  • The worker flags --tries and --timeout work for queued emails, like for other jobs.
  • With the sync queue driver, the email is sent at once. later() does not wait.
Option Default What it does queue default the queue name encrypt false save the job data encrypted with the app key. The worker needs the same key

The whole email is saved in the queue

The addresses, the subject, the body and every attachment are saved in Redis or in the jobs table. Attachments are saved as base64, so they take about 4/3 of their size. Keep attachments small, a few MB at most. MySQL and MariaDB refuse a job bigger than max_allowed_packet (by default 64 MB in MySQL 8, 16 MB in MariaDB). Redis keeps every job in memory. For a big file, write your own job. Save the file path or a storage key in the job, and build the email in handle().

Encrypt personal data

An email has personal data. When other people can read Redis or the jobs table, use encrypt: true. With encrypt: true, a send error is encrypted with the app key too. The plain text of the error is only its type and code, for example RedactedMailError: MailException (code 550). Details are encrypted: .... The full error text, with the answer of the server, is inside the encrypted part (at most the first 64K characters, counted in UTF-16 code units). To read it, take a FailedJob from Queue.driver.failed() and call RedactedMailError.decrypt(job.error) (from package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart). It works with the app key or any key in AppConfig.previousKeys.

By default Mail.queue() and Mail.later() use the dox_queue queue. To use another queue, call Mail.useQueue(queue) (null goes back to the dox_queue queue).

In tests, Mail.fake() also catches Mail.queue() and Mail.later(). The email goes to mail.queued, not to the job queue. You need no queue setup. See Testing.

docs.title: SMTP
docs.text:
'smtp': SmtpTransport(
  host: 'smtp.example.com',
  port: 587,
  username: Env.get('MAIL_USERNAME'),
  password: Env.get('MAIL_PASSWORD'),
  encryption: SmtpEncryption.starttls,
),
Option Default What it does host required the server port 465 for tls, 587 for starttls, 25 for none the port username, password none the login. No username: no login encryption starttls none, starttls (switch to TLS after connect) or tls (TLS from the start) allowInsecure false accept a self-signed TLS certificate. Only for test servers auth PLAIN, or LOGIN when the server has no PLAIN SmtpAuth.plain, SmtpAuth.login or SmtpAuth.xoauth2 localDomain localhost the name of this machine, for EHLO timeout 30 seconds the time to connect, and to wait for each reply keepAlive false keep the connection open for the next message

With starttls, the send fails when the server does not offer STARTTLS. Your password is never sent in plain text by mistake.

For Gmail or Outlook with OAuth 2, use auth: SmtpAuth.xoauth2. The username is the email and the password is the access token.

keepAlive: true is good when you send many emails. One connection sends them one by one. When the server closed it, the next send opens a new one.

For local work, Mailpit catches all emails:

'mailpit': SmtpTransport(
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 1025,
  encryption: SmtpEncryption.none,
),

docs.title: Amazon SES
docs.text:
There are two classes. Both send the same MIME message, with attachments and inline images.

  • SesTransport: SES API v1, SendRawEmail.
  • SesV2Transport: SES API v2, SendEmail with raw content.
'ses': SesV2Transport(
  key: Env.get('AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID'),
  secret: Env.get('AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY'),
  region: Env.get('AWS_REGION', 'us-east-1'),
),
Option Default What it does key required the AWS access key id secret required the AWS secret access key sessionToken none for temporary keys, eg. from a role region us-east-1 the AWS region of SES configurationSet none the SES configuration set, to track events endpoint https://email.<region>.amazonaws.com/ another API address

The requests are signed with AWS Signature Version 4. No AWS SDK is needed.

docs.title: Azure Communication Services
docs.text:
'azure': AzureTransport(
  endpoint: 'https://my-app.europe.communication.azure.com',
  accessKey: Env.get('AZURE_EMAIL_KEY'),
),

Or with the connection string of the Azure portal:

'azure': AzureTransport.fromConnectionString(
  Env.get('AZURE_EMAIL_CONNECTION_STRING'),
),
Option Default What it does endpoint required the address of your resource accessKey required the access key of the resource apiVersion 2023-03-31 the API version disableTracking false turn off open and click tracking

Requests are signed with the access key (HMAC-SHA256). Inline images need a newer apiVersion that supports them.

docs.title: Resend
docs.text: 'resend': ResendTransport(apiKey: Env.get('RESEND_API_KEY')),

docs.title: Mailgun
docs.text:
'mailgun': MailgunTransport(
  apiKey: Env.get('MAILGUN_API_KEY'),
  domain: 'mg.example.com',
  region: MailgunRegion.eu,
),

region is MailgunRegion.us (the default) or MailgunRegion.eu. Use the region of your Mailgun domain.

docs.title: Postmark
docs.text:
'postmark': PostmarkTransport(
  serverToken: Env.get('POSTMARK_TOKEN'),
  messageStream: 'outbound',
),

messageStream is optional. Without it, Postmark uses the default stream of the server.

docs.title: sendmail
docs.text:
Sends with the sendmail program of the server (Postfix, Exim, msmtp and others).

'sendmail': SendmailTransport(
  path: '/usr/sbin/sendmail',
  mode: SendmailMode.smtp,
),
Mode Command How it works SendmailMode.smtp (default) sendmail -bs speaks SMTP on stdin and stdout SendmailMode.pipe sendmail -t -i pipes the message in. sendmail reads the recipients from the headers

docs.title: Log
docs.text:
Prints each email and sends nothing. Good for local work.

'log': LogTransport(),

Pass output to print somewhere else, eg. LogTransport(output: stderr.writeln) (from dart:io).

Two options, both off by default:

  • useLogger: true writes each email to the app log with Logger.info, not with print. The logger is off by default: set LoggerConfig(enabled: true), or nothing is written. The logger level must allow info. When the logger throws (eg. Dox is not set up), the email is printed.
  • bothBodies: true shows the text body and the HTML body when the email has both. When it is off, only the text body is shown.
'log': LogTransport(useLogger: true, bothBodies: true),

docs.title: Array
docs.text:
Keeps each email in a list and sends nothing. See Testing.

'array': ArrayTransport(),

docs.title: Failover
docs.text:
Tries each transport in order, until one sends the email. When every transport fails, it throws the error of the last one. To see why the first ones failed, pass onError. It gets the error of each transport that fails. When onError throws, the error is ignored and the next transport is still tried. An async onError is not awaited. A line break in an address, the subject or a header throws a MailException at once, and no transport tries it.

SesV2Transport ses = SesV2Transport(key: '...', secret: '...');
SmtpTransport smtp = SmtpTransport(host: 'smtp.example.com');

MailConfig mailConfig = MailConfig(
  defaultMailer: 'main',
  mailers: <String, Transport>{
    'main': FailoverTransport(<Transport>[ses, smtp]),
  },
);

docs.title: Tags and metadata
docs.text:
Each provider has its own way to group and mark emails. This is what each transport does with tags and metadata:

Transport tags metadata SES not used message tags Resend tags with the value true tags Mailgun o:tag variables (v:name) Postmark the first tag metadata Azure, SMTP, sendmail not used not used

For SMTP and sendmail, use headers instead.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
Run code before or after each email is sent, eg. to log it. Dox has no event system, so hooks are plain functions.

Each isolate has its own hooks: the server isolates and the queue worker. So add them in setup() of your mail provider, after super.setup(). Then every isolate gets them. A hook added in main() does not reach queued emails.

class AppMailProvider extends MailProvider {
  AppMailProvider() : super(mailConfig);

  @override
  void setup() {
    super.setup();
    Mail.clearHooks(); // a second setup() does not add each hook twice
    Mail.onSending((Message message) {
      print('sending "${message.subject}" to ${message.to}');
    });
    Mail.onSent((SentMessage sent) {
      print('sent ${sent.messageId}');
    });
  }
}
  • Hooks run for every mailer. They also run for queued emails, when the worker sends them, and with Mail.fake().
  • When an onSending hook throws, the email is not sent. send() throws that error.
  • When an onSent hook throws, the error is logged and send() does not throw. The email is already sent, so a queue worker does not try the job again and send it twice. The other onSent hooks still run.
  • Mail.clearHooks() removes all hooks. Call it first in setup(), as above, and in tests.

docs.title: Send all email to one address
docs.text:
On a staging server, send every email to your own inbox, so real users get nothing. Like hooks, call it in setup() of your mail provider, after super.setup(), so every isolate gets it:

class AppMailProvider extends MailProvider {
  AppMailProvider() : super(mailConfig);

  @override
  void setup() {
    super.setup();
    if (Env.get<String>('APP_ENV') == 'staging') {
      Mail.alwaysTo('qa@example.com');
    }
  }
}

The to of each email becomes that address, and cc and bcc are cleared. It counts for queued emails too. Mail.alwaysTo(null) turns it off.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Mail.fake() sends every mailer to one ArrayTransport. Nothing goes out. Then check what was sent.

import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  late ArrayTransport mail;

  setUp(() {
    mail = Mail.fake();
  });

  tearDown(() {
    Mail.restore();
  });

  test('sign up sends a welcome email', () async {
    await signUp('ann@example.com');

    expect(mail.messages, hasLength(1));
    Message message = mail.messages.single;
    expect(message.to.single.email, 'ann@example.com');
    expect(message.subject, 'Welcome');
  });
}

Mail.fake() works with or without a config. The fake stays on when MailProvider sets up the config again.

Mail.fake() also catches Mail.queue(), Mail.later(), the queue() and later() of a Mailable, and notifications with shouldQueue. These emails go to mail.queued, not to mail.sent and not to the job queue. Each item is a QueuedMessage with mailer, message, id, delay, queue and encrypt.

await Mail.queue(message);

mail.assertQueued((Message m) => m.subject == 'Welcome');
mail.assertNothingSent();
Method Checks assertSent([test]) an email was sent. With test, one of them passes it assertSentCount(count, [test]) exactly count emails were sent. With test, count emails pass it assertNotSent(test) no sent email passes test assertNothingSent() no email was sent assertQueued([test]) an email was queued. With test, one of them passes it assertNotQueued(test) no queued email passes test assertNothingQueued() no email was queued

test is a bool Function(Message). A failed check throws a StateError.

mail.clear() forgets the sent and the queued emails. Mail.restore() stops the fake.

docs.title: Your own transport
docs.text:
Extend Transport and add it to mailers:

class MyApiTransport extends Transport {
  @override
  Future<SentMessage> send(Message message) async {
    // call your API here
    return SentMessage(message, messageId: 'id from the API');
  }
}

The message is checked, and has a from address, when it gets to send().

For a provider that takes raw MIME, MimeBuilder().build(message) gives the MIME text.

docs.title: Native server
docs.text:
Dox runs on a native HTTP server from the package dox_http_native.

You do not need to set anything. Every app uses it, also an app with WebSocket or Socket.IO routes.

  • Rust owns the sockets and parses HTTP. It runs on the isolate's own thread, so a request never waits for another thread.
  • All your code stays in Dart: routes, controllers, DTOs, middleware, ORM.
  • It is much faster than the dart:io server: about 5 times more requests on one or two cores. See Performance.

You do not need Rust. The package downloads a ready-built library for your system when you build the app.

docs.title: Without Dox
docs.text:
dox_http_native also works on its own, in any Dart app:

dart pub add dox_http_native

import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_http_native/dox_http_native.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  NativeHttpServer server = await NativeHttpServer.bind(3000);
  server.listen((HttpRequest req) async {
    req.response.write('Hello World');
    await req.response.close();
  });
}
  • NativeHttpServer.bind(port, address: '127.0.0.1') listens on one host. With no address, it listens on all interfaces.
  • NativeHttpServer.bind(port, maxConnections: 10000) stops accepting new connections at the limit, until one closes. Default: no limit.
  • close() waits for open requests. close(force: true) closes every connection at once.

The rest of this page is the same with or without Dox.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The server runs on the thread of the isolate, in a loop:

  1. Dart calls Rust (one FFI call).
  2. Rust writes the answers of the last batch, reads the sockets and parses the new requests. It gives them back to Dart as one batch.
  3. Dart runs your handlers and calls Rust again with their answers.

Under load there is no other thread, so a request never waits for a thread to wake up. When the isolate has nothing to do, a small helper thread watches the sockets. When a request comes, it wakes the isolate once. Then the isolate takes over again.

The loop gives the event loop a turn after a few batches, so timers, database answers and other async work of the isolate still run on time. A slow synchronous handler holds the sockets of its isolate, like in Node and Bun. await is fine.

The native server has the same API as the dart:io HttpServer. So req.httpRequest, HttpResponse and code written for dart:io keep working.

Each isolate runs its own server on the same port. See Isolate. The OS spreads connections, not requests. A keep-alive connection stays on one isolate. So a few busy connections (eg. from one proxy or a load test with few connections) can keep some isolates idle. Use more connections than isolates.

docs.title: When the library does not load
docs.text:
Dox stops at start, before any isolate runs. The error says why and how to fix it:

Unsupported operation: dox_http_native did not load: <reason>.
Fix: install Rust (cargo, see https://rustup.rs), then run the app again ...

<reason> is for example native library ABI 8, expected 9: the library on disk is from another version of the package. See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: WebSocket
docs.text:
Rust also does the WebSocket upgrade and the WebSocket protocol.

  1. Rust marks a request that asks for an upgrade.
  2. Dart runs the route, the middleware and the Origin check, like for any request. A normal answer (eg. 403) refuses the upgrade.
  3. When Dart accepts, Rust sends the 101 answer. From then on Rust answers pings, does the close handshake, checks that text is UTF-8 and checks the size of each message.

  4. Dart gets whole messages, in the same batches as requests. It sends messages back the same way as answers.

  5. A message or frame over the size limit closes the socket with code 1009. Dart never reads it. NativeWebSocket.upgrade takes maxMessageSize. Socket.IO uses maxHttpBufferSize.

  6. Compression (permessage-deflate) is never agreed. A small compressed message could grow very big in memory.
  7. On a graceful stop (SIGTERM), every open WebSocket gets close code 1001.
  8. In your own code, use NativeWebSocket.upgrade(request) from dox_http_native. It gives a dart:io WebSocket.

docs.title: Threads
docs.text: Each isolate does its own socket work on its own thread. Each server also has two small helper threads: one watches the sockets while the isolate is idle, one does gzip (only with compress: true). Under load both sleep.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Max size of the request line plus headers: 16 KB. Bigger gets 431.
  • A bad request gets 400.
  • A multipart form over maxMultipartSize, or any other body over maxBodySize, gets 413 from Rust. When Content-Length is too big and the client sent Expect: 100-continue, the 413 comes before the body is sent. Else Rust reads and drops the body first, so the client sees the 413. Dart checks the limits again.
  • A client that sends no body bytes for 120 seconds (idle time) gets 408. A slow but steady upload is fine.
  • A request head must arrive within 30 seconds. A keep-alive connection with no request for 30 seconds is closed.
  • A client that does not read its answer for 30 seconds is cut off.
  • A request with both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding: chunked gets 400. A transfer encoding other than chunked gets 501.
  • At most 64 requests of one connection wait for an answer, and at most 1 MB of answers waits to be sent. Then the server stops reading that connection until the answers go out.
  • A streamed response with a contentLength must send exactly that many bytes. add() throws when the body passes it, and close() fails when it is shorter.
  • A small response is sent in one piece when it is closed. A streamed response (a file, a download, any Stream) over 64 KB goes out in parts: the client gets the first bytes early. At most 1 MB of it waits in memory. Dart reads more of the file only when the client has read what was sent. When the client leaves, Dart stops reading.
  • A request body of 64 KB or more goes to Dart without a copy.
  • compress: true in AppConfig works: Rust gzips the body on a helper thread, so the isolate does not wait. A streamed response is not compressed.
  • WebSocket: one turn reads at most 256 KB of one socket, so one busy client can not hold the isolate. While more than 256 KB waits to be sent to a client (eg. pongs for a client that does not read), the server stops reading its frames.

docs.title: Security notes
docs.text:
• Run it behind a reverse proxy (Caddy, nginx) on the internet. The proxy does HTTPS, buffers slow clients and caps connections.
  • Set maxConnections when the app port is open to the internet.
  • Another process of the same OS user can bind the same port (macOS shared socket, Linux SO_REUSEPORT). Do not run untrusted code as the user of the app.
  • req.uri resolves .. in the path. Never build a file path from the raw path. Use the storage helpers.

docs.title: Where the library comes from
docs.text:
The build hook of dox_http_native (hook/build.dart) picks the first one that works:

  1. A path you give in the root pubspec.yaml of your app:

    hooks:
  user_defines:
    dox_http_native:
      lib_path: /path/to/libdox_http_native.so

  2. A local build in native/target/release of the package (for work on the package itself).

  3. The ready-built library from the GitHub release, checked with sha256. There are builds for macOS (arm64, x64), Linux (x64, arm64) and Windows (x64).
  4. A build from source with cargo, when Rust is installed.

This order is for the package from pub.dev. For a git or path dependency, step 4 comes before step 3, because the source can be newer than the release.

When none works, the app still builds, but it stops at start with the error above. Install Rust and run it again, so step 4 works.

Use dart build cli

dart compile exe does not run build hooks. Use dox build or dart build cli. See Deployment.

docs.title: Work on the native code
docs.text:
dox_http_native lives in its own repo: dartondox/dox-http-native. The Rust code is in its native folder.

cd dox-http-native/native
cargo build --release   # the hook uses this build from now on
cargo test
cd .. && dart test --concurrency=1

To use your local copy in the Dox repo, or to release the package, see Contribute.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
Notifications are in the dox_mailer package.

Set up mail first.

A notification tells a user about something, like "your invoice is paid". It can go out on more than one channel: email, a database table, SMS. Each notification is a class. via() picks the channels.

class InvoicePaid extends Notification {
  InvoicePaid(this.invoiceId);

  final int invoiceId;

  @override
  List<NotificationChannel> via(Object notifiable) {
    return <NotificationChannel>[const MailChannel()];
  }

  @override
  Mailable toMail(Object notifiable) {
    return MailMessage(subject: 'Invoice paid')
      ..line('We got your payment.')
      ..action('View invoice', 'https://example.com/invoices/$invoiceId');
  }
}

toMail() can return any mailable, so a WelcomeMail with a template works too.

docs.title: Who gets it
docs.text:
Add the Notifiable mixin to the class that gets notifications, usually the user model. routeNotificationFor('mail') gives the email address:

class User extends Model<User> with Notifiable {
  @override
  Object? routeNotificationFor(String channel) {
    return channel == 'mail' ? Address(email!, name) : null;
  }
}

The route can be an Address, an email text like Ann <ann@example.com>, or a list of these.

Then send:

await user.notify(InvoicePaid(1));

// many users
await Notification.send(users, InvoicePaid(1));

// an address with no user
await Notification.send(<Object>[Address('ann@example.com')], InvoicePaid(1));

When the mailable has its own to address, that address is used and the route is not.

When a channel throws, the other channels and the other notifiables still get the notification. At the end, Notification.send() throws a NotificationException. Its errors list says which notifiable and channel failed, and why. When via() throws, the channel is null. The error text has one line per failure: the place and the type of the notifiable, the channel, and the error type. It has no email addresses and no error text, so it is safe for logs. For the details, read errors.

With one notifiable and one error, like user.notify(), the error is thrown as it is. So on MailException catch (e) still works there.

docs.title: Queue it
docs.text:
Override shouldQueue. The mail channel then puts the email on the job queue, like Mail.queue(). This needs a queue.

@override
bool get shouldQueue => true;

The email is rendered at once. The worker sends the finished email.

These getters set the queue options. They work like the options of Mail.queue():

Getter Default What it does queue null (default) the queue name delay null the worker sends the email after this wait encrypt false save the job data encrypted with the app key

When shouldQueue is false, the email is sent at once and these options do nothing. shouldQueue and these options only change the mail channel. Your own channels still run at once. To queue them, dispatch a job in the channel.

docs.title: Your own channel
docs.text:
Write a class that implements NotificationChannel. toArray() of the notification gives its data. For example, a channel that saves notifications in a table:

import 'dart:convert';

class DatabaseChannel implements NotificationChannel {
  @override
  Future<void> send(Object notifiable, Notification notification) async {
    // only a user has a row. An Address or an email text has none.
    if (notifiable is! User) return;
    AppNotification row = AppNotification()
      ..userId = notifiable.id
      ..data = jsonEncode(notification.toArray(notifiable));
    await row.save();
  }
}

class InvoicePaid extends Notification {
  @override
  List<NotificationChannel> via(Object notifiable) {
    return <NotificationChannel>[const MailChannel(), DatabaseChannel()];
  }

  @override
  Map<String, Object?> toArray(Object notifiable) {
    return <String, Object?>{'type': 'invoice_paid', 'invoice_id': invoiceId};
  }

  // ...
}

dox_mailer has no database channel of its own, so it does not need the ORM.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
Mail.fake() catches the emails of the mail channel too:

ArrayTransport mail = Mail.fake();
await user.notify(InvoicePaid(1));
expect(mail.messages.single.subject, 'Invoice paid');

With shouldQueue, the email goes to mail.queued, not to mail.messages. It does not reach the job queue. Check it with mail.assertQueued(). See Mail.

docs.title: Package commands
docs.text:
A package can add its own dox commands.

Your app can add its own commands too. You do not write a bin file, and you do not register anything. The dox CLI finds the commands by itself.

For example, dox queue:table comes from the dox_queue_database package, and dox auth:tokens-table comes from the dox_auth package.

docs.title: Use a package command
docs.text:
Add the package and run dart pub get. Then run the command:

dart pub add dox_queue_database
dox queue:table

dox help lists the commands of each package, under the package name.

docs.title: Add a command to your package
1. Write the command
docs.text:
A command extends Command from package:dox_core/command.dart.

A package that does not use dox_core imports package:dox_annotation/command.dart instead.

lib/src/commands/hello_command.dart
import 'package:dox_core/command.dart';

class HelloCommand extends Command {
  @override
  String get name => 'hello:say';

  @override
  String get description => 'Say hello';

  /// optional, shown by `dox help`. The default is the name.
  @override
  String get usage => 'hello:say <name>';

  @override
  Future<void> run(List<String> args) async {
    print('Hello ${args.join(' ')}');
  }
}

dox hello:say Ann calls run(['Ann']). The words after the name are the args.

docs.title: 2. List the commands
docs.text:
Make one library with a top-level commands list:

lib/commands.dart
import 'package:dox_core/command.dart';

import 'src/commands/hello_command.dart';

final List<Command> commands = <Command>[HelloCommand()];

docs.title: 3. Name the library in pubspec.yaml
docs.text:
pubspec.yaml
dox:
  commands: package:my_package/commands.dart

The value must be a library of the package itself, like package:my_package/commands.dart. Use only letters, digits, _, -, . and / in the path, and no ... That is all. An app that depends on your package now has dox hello:say.

docs.title: Add a command to your app
docs.text:
It works the same way. Put the command in lib/ of your app, and add the key to the app's own pubspec.yaml:

pubspec.yaml
dox:
  commands: package:my_app/commands.dart

To make the command file, run dox make:command send_report. It writes lib/app/commands/send_report_command.dart, adds the command to lib/app/commands/commands.dart, and sets the dox: commands: key for you. The command name is app:send-report. See dox make:command.

docs.title: Exit codes and errors
docs.text:
• When run ends, dox exits with code 0.
  • To fail, set exitCode from dart:io (like exitCode = 1), or throw. A thrown error is printed with its stack trace, and the exit code is 1.
  • The exit code of the command is the exit code of dox, so scripts and CI see it.

docs.title: Write a migration
docs.text:
A command can add a migration file with MigrationFile. The file gets the same name as dox make:migration makes, like 2026_10_21_120000_create_queue_tables.dart.

String? path = MigrationFile().create('create_queue_tables', source);
if (path == null) {
  print('A create_queue_tables migration is already in db/migration.');
  exitCode = 1;
}

create returns null and writes nothing when a migration with this name is already there, with any time in its name. dox migrate writes db/migration/migrations.dart again before it runs, and makes bin/migrate.dart when it is missing. So dox migrate runs the new file.

docs.title: Ship an install command
docs.text:
dox add <x> adds the package dox_x, then runs its <x>:install command. So a package that needs setup (config files, .env keys, a provider) ships an <x>:install command. The dox CLI has no code of any package.

Use Installer from package:dox_annotation/install.dart. Each step is safe to run twice: it never overwrites a file and never adds a key twice.

lib/src/commands/hello_install_command.dart
import 'package:dox_annotation/command.dart';
import 'package:dox_annotation/install.dart';

class HelloInstallCommand extends Command {
  @override
  String get name => 'hello:install';

  @override
  String get description => 'Set up dox_hello in this app';

  @override
  Future<void> run(List<String> args) async {
    Installer installer = Installer();
    String app = installer.appName;
    installer.writeFile(
      'lib/config/hello.dart',
      "import 'package:$app/config/env.dart';\n",
    );
    installer.addEnvGetter("String get helloName => 'world';");
    installer.addEnv('HELLO_NAME', 'world');
    await installer.buildRunner();
    installer.printSummary(<String>['Restart the server.']);
  }
}
Method What it does writeFile(path, content) Writes the file only when it is not there. makeFolder(path) Makes the folder when it is not there. addEnv(key, value) Adds KEY=value to .env.example and .env when the key is missing. A key that is there is never changed. addEnvGetter(getter) Adds a getter to AppEnv in lib/config/env.dart when the class has no member with that name. When it can not find the class, it changes nothing and prints a hint. addDependency(package, dev: false) Runs dart pub add when the app does not have the package. buildRunner() Runs dart run build_runner build. note(line) Adds your own line to the summary, like added hooks to pubspec.yaml. printSummary(nextSteps) Prints what was done and the next steps. Sets exit code 1 when a step failed.

Then:

  • Read the options from args, like --driver=postgres. Give a good default, so dox add <x> with no options works.
  • Test it on an app made without your package. Run it twice and check that nothing changes the second time.
  • Add dox add <x> to the skill of your package (skills/<name>/SKILL.md), so AI agents set it up the same way.

dox_orm has an example: orm:install.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• A built-in command always wins. When a package has a command with the same name as a built-in one, dox runs the built-in one. dox help marks the package command as not used.
  • When two packages have a command with the same name, dox <name> prints an error with both package names, and exits with code 1.
  • A bad dox: commands: key (not a library of the package, or a file that is not there) prints a warning with the package name. The commands of the other packages still work.
  • An unknown command prints Could not find a command named "<name>", with a hint about the dox: commands: key.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. dox <name> first looks for a built-in command.
  2. Then it reads .dart_tool/package_config.json, and the dox: commands: key in the pubspec.yaml of each package and of the app.
  3. It writes .dart_tool/dox/commands.dart. This file imports each commands library and runs the command with your args.
  4. It runs that file with dart run.

dox writes the file again only when .dart_tool/package_config.json, your pubspec.yaml, or the pubspec.yaml of a package change. So after dart pub get, or after you change the key in a local package. When a package had a warning (like a commands library that is not there yet), dox looks again on the next run. The code of the commands is always the newest, because dart run compiles it each time.

dox help keeps the list of package commands in .dart_tool/dox/commands.json. It loads the list again when a package or a commands library (the file in the key) changes. When you change only a file that the commands library imports, dox help can show the old description until then. The command itself always runs the new code.

An app inside a pub workspace works too, also when the workspace: list uses a glob like apps/*. dox finds the workspace root from .dart_tool/pub/workspace_ref.json, which dart pub get writes in each member.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
This page shows how fast Dox is, and how to keep your app fast in production.

The short version:

  1. Build with dox build and run the AOT binary. Never dart run in production.
  2. Put Caddy or nginx in front for HTTPS and gzip.
  3. Keep the default isolates (one per CPU core).
  4. Keep the body limits on. Uploads stream to disk.

docs.title: Benchmark
docs.text:
The rules of the-benchmarker/web-frameworks: each server answers GET / (empty body), GET /user/:id (the id) and POST /user (empty body). Dox is a full Dox app with these three routes. "Dox server only" is dox_http_native with no framework, to show what the framework costs.

This only measures the HTTP stack. A real app spends most of its time on the database, JSON and your own code, so the gaps are smaller there. See App benchmark.

docs.title: 2 cores
docs.text:
2 cores: ahead of Rust hyper and Bun

GET /, 256 connections. Every server has one worker per core: Dox one isolate, Bun and Node one process, Go and Rust one thread.

req/s p99 RAM Doxfull app 638,067fastest 0.7 ms 19 MB Rusthyper 585,6581.09× slower 0.7 ms 13 MB BunBun.serve 501,5291.27× slower 1.0 ms 40 MB Nodenode:http 286,8472.2× slower 1.7 ms 200 MB Gonet/http 242,0432.6× slower 3.3 ms 36 MB dart:ioHttpServer 129,7964.9× slower 3.8 ms 75 MB

Dox · Rust 1.99 · Bun 1.4 · Node 26 · Go 1.26 · Dart 3.13 · 2 cores · 256 connections · wrk

Requests per second on GET / at 64, 256 and 512 connections:

Server 64 256 512 p99 at 256 peak MB Dox 494,223 638,067 612,032 0.74 ms 19 Dox server only 589,866 692,705 699,938 0.68 ms 16 Rust (hyper) 499,734 585,658 560,181 0.71 ms 13 Bun (Bun.serve) 508,243 501,529 531,310 1.00 ms 40 Node (node:http) 252,866 286,847 296,257 1.70 ms 200 Go (net/http) 248,951 242,043 232,687 3.27 ms 36 dart:io 125,428 129,796 132,112 3.83 ms 75

The other two routes at 256 connections:

Server GET /user/:id POST /user Dox 572,658 545,986 Dox server only 672,098 683,477 Rust (hyper) 564,411 569,313 Bun 482,328 498,518 Node 274,067 301,084 Go 230,845 231,050 dart:io 93,561 126,027

docs.title: Why it is fast
docs.text:
The server runs on the isolate's own thread. One FFI call writes the answers, reads the sockets and parses the new requests. Dart runs the handlers and calls again. A request never waits for another thread to wake up. A small helper thread only watches the sockets while the isolate has nothing to do. See Native server.

A profile with perf (4 server cores, 64 connections) shows the effect:

Dox Bun CPU time per request 4.85 µs 5.5 µs Context switches per request 0.08 0.035

docs.title: How it was run
docs.text:
• Docker on an Apple M2 (8 CPUs in the Docker VM), linux/arm64.
  • One server at a time. The server and wrk run in two containers on different CPUs: the server on 2 CPUs, wrk on the other 6. Host network, keep-alive.
  • wrk 4.1, 64, 256 and 512 connections, 5 seconds warm-up, then 15 seconds per route.
  • Every server has as many workers as server CPUs.
  • Peak memory is the peak of the container (all workers).
  • Dart 3.13.6, AOT build with dart build cli (this is what dox build does). dox_core and dox_http_native as released when these numbers were measured. Node 26.12, Bun 1.4.4, Go 1.26, Rust 1.99 with hyper 1.

docs.title: App benchmark
docs.text:
A small real app, the same in each language: GET /json returns a map, GET /db reads one row by id from Postgres, GET /queries?n=20 reads 20 rows one after another. The table has 10,000 rows. Each app uses its database driver directly, with no ORM. Dox uses dox_postgres_native.

2 cores: one row from Postgres

GET /db, 256 connections. Requests per second, higher is better.

req/s p99 RAM Doxdox_postgres_native 266,432fastest 1.8 ms 106 MB BunBun.sql 198,2961.34× slower 2.1 ms 64 MB Rusttokio-postgres 128,0652.1× slower 2.6 ms 11 MB Nodepg 75,4473.5× slower 4.1 ms 232 MB Gopgx 55,9034.8× slower 6.3 ms 31 MB dart:iopackage:postgres 28,5989.3× slower 14.2 ms 47 MB

Dox · Bun 1.4 · Rust 1.99 · Node 26 · Go 1.26 · Dart 3.13 · Postgres 18 · 2 cores · 256 connections · wrk

All three routes at 256 connections, requests per second:

Server /json /db /queries?n=20 peak MB Dox (dox_postgres_native) 555,216 266,432 17,772 106 Bun (Bun.sql) 564,362 198,296 18,994 64 Rust (hyper + tokio-postgres) 667,718 128,065 9,312 11 Node (node:http + pg) 205,774 75,447 7,458 232 Go (net/http + pgx) 206,398 55,903 6,635 31 dart:io (+ package:postgres) 89,480 28,598 2,269 47
  • On one query per request, Dox is the fastest: 1.3 times Bun.
  • On 20 queries per request, Dox and Bun are about the same. Postgres is the limit here. Both are about twice as fast as Rust.

The same app on MySQL 8.4 (dox_mysql_native). The dart:io app has no MySQL version.

Server /json /db /queries?n=20 peak MB Dox (dox_mysql_native) 558,886 247,242 12,347 70 Bun (Bun.sql) 561,340 201,923 12,676 65 Rust (hyper + mysql_async) 653,244 46,795 3,158 10 Node (node:http + mysql2) 205,630 74,809 6,001 239 Go (net/http + go-sql-driver) 211,713 55,322 5,520 27

How it was run: the same rig as the benchmark above. The server gets 2 CPUs, the database gets 2 CPUs and wrk gets the other 4. Each server has 4 database connections per core, 8 in total. One run of 15 seconds per route. dox_postgres_native and dox_mysql_native as released when these numbers were measured.

docs.title: Dart VM flags
docs.text: We tried a bigger young generation (DART_VM_OPTIONS=--new_gen_semi_max_size=64 and 128) for a better p99. Over 5 runs the change was inside the noise, and memory did not move. So there is no flag to set. Dox never sets VM flags for you. DART_VM_OPTIONS is read by the AOT binary from dox build, so you can try your own.

docs.title: Database drivers
docs.text:
One find-by-id query, AOT build (dart build cli), database on the same machine (Apple M-series), one isolate:

Database One query at a time Many queries in flight App CPU time per query Postgres 14 (4 connections) 60 µs 12.5 µs each (64 in flight) MySQL 8.4 (10 connections) 67 µs 11 µs each (32 in flight) 13.5 µs MariaDB 11 (10 connections) 63 µs 9.7 µs each (32 in flight) 12.4 µs
  • The CPU time counts the Dart thread and the Rust thread. For MySQL, it is about 75,000 queries per second on one core.
  • Dart sends many queries to Rust in one call. Rust sends many results back in one message.
  • One query alone spends most of its time on the trip to the database. Many requests at the same time, like in a web server, get the most out of the driver.

docs.title: Bodies, uploads and big responses
docs.text:
These are on by default. You only need to keep them:

  • A body over maxBodySize or maxMultipartSize gets 413 from the native server, before Dart reads it. Set the same limit in the proxy. See Size limits.
  • An upload over 1 MB streams to a temp file, so it does not fill the memory. See Request.
  • A File or Stream response is streamed, not loaded into memory. See Files and big responses.

docs.title: gzip
docs.text:
gzip in Dart is off by default.

AppConfig(compress: true);
  • It saves bandwidth, but costs CPU on every response. The native server gzips on a Rust thread. Streamed responses are not compressed.
  • A proxy (Caddy, nginx) does it better. Turn it on in Dart only when there is no proxy.
  • Only a body over 256 bytes is gzipped, and only when the client accepts gzip. The gzipped body still gets a Content-Length.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
LogMiddleware logs one line per request through Logger. Writing to stdout blocks the isolate. So Logger collects log lines and writes them every 20 ms (or every 64 KB) in one write. A warn, warning, danger or error line is written right away, with the waiting lines before it, so the order stays. The buffer is also written when the app stops. If the process is killed hard, the last 20 ms of logs can be lost.

Turn LogMiddleware off when a proxy already writes access logs. The new project does this for you: enabled is false when APP_ENV is production or not set.

Leave responseHandler unset when you do not need it. With no handler, a plain value (text, map, list) is sent without building a DoxResponse.

docs.title: What Dox does for you
docs.text:
• Routes are grouped by method. The regex of each route is built once, not on every request.
  • The argument types of each controller are read once at start, not on every request.
  • JSON and text responses are encoded once, straight to bytes, with Content-Length set.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
A provider is a class that sets up one part of your app when it starts, for example the database, auth or a Redis connection.

A provider has three methods:

  • setup() runs when the app starts. You must write it.
  • boot() runs after setup() of every provider is done. It is optional. See Boot.
  • shutdown() runs when the app stops. It is optional.

docs.title: Why providers
docs.text: Dox runs your app on many isolates, and they do not share memory. Code that you run once in bin/server.dart only sets up the first isolate. The others have, for example, no database connection. A provider fixes this: each isolate runs setup() itself.

docs.title: Create a provider
docs.text:
Extend DoxProvider and put your code in setup(). setup() can be async. Dox waits for it.

A package that does not use dox_core imports DoxProvider from package:dox_annotation/provider.dart.

lib/providers/orm_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';

class ORMProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig);
  }

  /// Close the database connections when the server stops.
  @override
  Future<void> shutdown() async {
    await SqlQueryBuilder.close();
  }
}

To make the file, run dox make:provider Cache. It writes lib/providers/cache_provider.dart with an empty setup(). See dox make:provider.

docs.title: Register it
docs.text:
You do not need to. Dox finds every class that extends DoxProvider. Run dart run build_runner build. The provider is then in lib/generated/container.g.dart. Each isolate makes its own instance from the container. Its constructor can ask for other classes of the container. See Dependency injection.

Providers run in the order of their file path. To run one first, list it in AppConfig:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  container: registerContainer,
  providers: <DoxProvider>[ORMProvider()], // runs before the others
);

A listed provider runs first. Then the others run. No provider runs twice.

You can also add a provider in code, before startServer():

bin/server.dart
Dox().initialize(appConfig);
Dox().addProvider(MyProvider());
await Dox().startServer();

docs.title: Example: auth
When setup() runs
docs.text:
In each isolate, Dox runs setup() of each provider, one after the other: the listed ones first, then the ones of the container. Then it registers the routes and starts the server, so routes can use what a provider set up. See What each isolate does at start.

dox openapi:generate also runs setup() of every provider, because it needs the routes.

docs.title: Boot
docs.text:
boot() runs in each isolate after setup() of every provider is done. So all other providers are ready. Use it for work that needs them, like a background worker. The boots run one by one, in the provider order.

class ReportProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {}

  @override
  Future<void> boot() async {
    // every provider has run setup() here
  }
}

The web server and the queue worker (bin/queue.dart) run boot(). The scheduler (bin/schedule.dart) and dox openapi:generate do not. They run only setup(). The queue inProcess worker starts in boot(), so it does not run in the scheduler process.

docs.title: Clean up on shutdown
docs.text:
On SIGTERM or SIGINT Dox stops the server gracefully (see Deployment). After the open requests are done, it runs shutdown() of every provider. It runs in every isolate. Use it to close connections or flush data. A provider that has nothing to close does not need to write shutdown().

The ORMProvider of a new project already does this: its shutdown() calls SqlQueryBuilder.close(). Dox closes the cache stores (eg. Redis) by itself, after the providers.

lib/providers/redis_provider.dart
class RedisProvider extends DoxProvider {
  late RedisConnection redis;

  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    redis = await RedisConnection.open();
  }

  @override
  Future<void> shutdown() async {
    await redis.close();
  }
}

An error in shutdown() goes to the report method of the exception handler. The other providers still run.

docs.title: Rules for a provider
docs.text:
• Open connections in setup(), not in the constructor. A provider listed in AppConfig is copied to each isolate. An open socket or database pool can not be copied, so the isolate fails to start.
  • Keep setup() short. It runs once per isolate. Data you load in it is kept once per isolate, so 8 isolates keep 8 copies.

docs.title: Queue
docs.text:
A queue runs slow work in the background, so the request can answer at once.

A worker process does the work later.

Use it to send emails, call slow APIs, make reports or resize images. The dox_queue package gives you jobs, two drivers (Redis and sync), retries, delays and a worker. The database driver is in the dox_queue_database package, see Database driver.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
dox add queue

Add --driver=redis or --driver=sync to pick another driver. database is the default. It adds the package and writes the config, the provider, bin/queue.dart and a sample job. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice. database also adds dox_queue_database and the jobs tables migration. It needs dox add orm first. redis adds the REDIS_* keys. A new app already has it.

docs.title: Set it up by hand
docs.text:
dart pub add dox_queue

The job builder is in dox_builder. Your app already runs build_runner with it, so nothing else is needed.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. You write a job class with @Job().
  2. dart run build_runner build writes lib/generated/jobs.g.dart. It knows how to save and load each job.
  3. Your code calls dispatch(). The job is saved in Redis, or in the database with dox_queue_database.
  4. A worker (dart run bin/queue.dart) takes the job and runs its handle() method.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text: A new app from dox create already has the files of steps 1 to 4. Check them, and change the driver if you want.

docs.title: 1. Config
2. Provider
docs.text:
The provider sets up the queue in every isolate. Put it in lib/providers/, so the generated container finds it.

lib/providers/queue_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';

import '../config/queue.dart';

/// Sets up the queue. Dox finds every DoxProvider class,
/// see lib/generated/container.g.dart.
class AppQueueProvider extends QueueProvider {
  AppQueueProvider() : super(queueConfig);
}

docs.title: 3. Worker file
4. Database driver and tables
docs.text:
The database driver, job batches and afterCommit are in the dox_queue_database package. Skip this step when you use only Redis or sync and none of these.

dart pub add dox_queue_database

Make your queue provider extend DatabaseQueueProvider in place of QueueProvider. It turns them on:

lib/providers/queue_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_queue_database/dox_queue_database.dart';

import '../config/queue.dart';

class AppQueueProvider extends DatabaseQueueProvider {
  AppQueueProvider() : super(queueConfig);
}

The jobs and failed_jobs tables are for the database driver. The job_batches table is for job batches. If you use batches, you need it with every driver.

Run dox queue:table. It writes a migration in db/migration that makes all three tables. Then run dox migrate.

dox queue:table
dox migrate

queue:table is a package command of dox_queue_database. It does not overwrite: when a create_queue_tables migration is already there, it prints so and stops.

The migration it writes looks like this. You can also write it by hand. QueueTables.up makes the jobs and failed_jobs tables. QueueTables.upBatches makes the job_batches table.

db/migration/2026_10_25_000000_create_queue_tables.dart
// ignore_for_file: file_names
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue_database/dox_queue_database.dart';

/// The jobs, failed_jobs and job_batches tables of dox_queue_database.
class CreateQueueTables extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await QueueTables.up(schema);
    await QueueTables.upBatches(schema);
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await QueueTables.downBatches(schema);
    await QueueTables.down(schema);
  }
}

docs.title: Write a job
What is saved
docs.text:
The parameters of the unnamed constructor are saved with the job. Each parameter needs a field or getter with the same name.

These types work:

  • int, double, num, String, bool
  • DateTime
  • enums (saved by name)
  • List and Map<String, ...> of these, also nested
  • dynamic and Object (the value must be JSON)
  • nullable versions of all of them

Any other type stops the build with a clear message.

Save an id, not an object

Do not save a User. Save the userId, and load the user in handle(). The user may change between dispatch and run. The id gives you fresh data.

docs.title: Encrypt the saved data
docs.text:
Add the ShouldBeEncrypted mixin to save the job data encrypted. A person who can read Redis or the jobs table then can not read it.

@Job()
class ChargeCard extends DoxJob with ShouldBeEncrypted {
  // ...
}

The data is encrypted with the app key (AppConfig.appKey). The worker needs Dox().initialize() with the same key, or one of AppConfig.previousKeys. The job name, the queue and the id stay plain text.

docs.title: Services in a job
docs.text:
A job is made again from its saved data, so it can not get services in its constructor. Get them in handle() from the Dox container:

UserService users = Dox().ioc.get<UserService>();

The worker runs registerContainer, so every @Inject() class of your app is there.

docs.title: Job names
docs.text: The class name is saved with each job. When you rename a class, queued jobs of the old name can not be found. Keep the old name with @Job(name: 'SendWelcomeEmail').

docs.title: Dispatch a job
docs.text:
await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: user.id).dispatch();

Both ways do the same:

await Queue.dispatch(SendWelcomeEmail(userId: user.id));

A delay, another queue:

await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatch(
  delay: Duration(minutes: 10),
  queue: 'emails',
);

Wait until a time:

await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatch(
  delayUntil: DateTime.utc(2030, 1, 1, 9),
);

Give delay or delayUntil, not both.

dispatch() returns the job id.

Dispatch only when a condition is true, or false:

await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatchIf(user.wantsEmail);
await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatchUnless(user.isBlocked);

They return null when the job was not dispatched.

Run a job now, in this process, with no queue:

await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatchSync();

Run a job in this process after the answer is sent. The client does not wait for it:

SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatchAfterResponse();

Do not await it. It returns nothing. It does not go on the queue. So it has no job id and no retry. Outside a request, the job runs soon. When the job throws, its failed() runs and the error goes to the exception handler, never to the client. QueueProvider turns on AfterResponse for it. When the server stops, a job that did not run yet is lost.

docs.title: Dispatch after the commit
docs.text:
A job that you dispatch inside a database transaction is pushed at once. This option needs dox_queue_database (see step 4). Without it, a dispatch with afterCommit on throws a StateError. A worker can run it before the transaction commits, or after it rolls back. Then the job reads data that is not saved yet, or data that is never saved.

afterCommit: true waits for the commit:

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  User user = await User().create(<String, dynamic>{'email': email});
  await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: user.id).dispatch(afterCommit: true);
});
  • Inside a transaction, the job is pushed after the outermost transaction commits.
  • When the transaction rolls back, the job is not pushed.
  • Outside a transaction, the job is pushed at once.
  • dispatch() returns the job id at once. The id is made before the push.
  • A job that is not in the registry, or data that is not JSON, throws at dispatch(), not at the commit.
  • When the push fails after the commit, the QueryBuilder.transaction() call throws that error. The data stays saved.
  • The sync driver runs the job after the commit.
  • It waits only for a transaction on the default dox_orm connection, opened with no connection: name. A transaction opened by name pushes the job at once, also when the name is the one of the default connection.
  • dispatchIf(), dispatchUnless() and Queue.dispatch() take afterCommit too.
  • Chains and batches take it too: Queue.chain(jobs).dispatch(afterCommit: true) and Queue.batch(jobs).dispatch(afterCommit: true). A batch saves its job_batches row and pushes its jobs after the commit. A rollback drops it all.
  • Before the commit, the returned Batch is not saved yet. It has the id and the counts of a new batch.
  • A sync chain runs as a whole after the commit. It gives a new id before the commit, because its ids are made when it runs.
  • dispatchSync() and dispatchAfterResponse() run the job as before. They do not wait for a commit.

Turn it on for every dispatch with QueueConfig(afterCommit: true). Batches and chains follow it too. Then afterCommit: false on one dispatch pushes that job at once.

Queue.fake() keeps the job when you call dispatch(), also when the transaction later rolls back.

It works through QueryBuilder.afterCommit() of dox_orm, set up by dox_queue_database.

docs.title: Queue an email
docs.text:
You do not need a job class to send an email later. With dox_mailer, call Mail.queue():

await Mail.queue(message);
await Mail.later(Duration(minutes: 10), message, queue: 'emails');

The mail jobs are part of dox_mailer. The queue provider and a worker run them.

docs.title: Run the worker
docs.text:
dart run bin/queue.dart

Commands:

Command What it does work run jobs. This is the default failed list the failed jobs retry <id> put one failed job back on its queue retry all put all failed jobs back forget <id> delete one failed job flush delete all failed jobs clear [queue] delete the jobs of a queue, also the running ones. It frees the locks of unique jobs. Default: default restart stop the running workers after their current jobs prune-failed delete failed jobs older than --hours=N (default 24) prune-batches delete finished batches older than --hours=N (default 24). --unfinished=N also deletes old batches that never finished

Flags of work:

Flag Default What it does --queue=high,default default the queues to work. The first one goes first --concurrency=4 1 jobs at once in this process --once off run one job, then stop --tries=3 1 tries of a job that does not set tries --timeout=60 60 max run time in seconds of a job that does not set timeout --sleep=3 3 seconds to wait when the queues are empty --stop-when-empty off stop when the queues are empty --timeout-grace=10 none after a timeout, wait up to this many seconds for the old run to end before the next try --backoff=1,5,10 none seconds to wait before each retry of a job that does not set backoff --max-jobs=1000 off stop after this many jobs --max-time=3600 off stop after this many seconds --memory=256 off stop when the process uses more than this many MB

With --max-jobs, --max-time and --memory, the worker stops after its running jobs. Let your process manager start it again.

dart run bin/queue.dart work --queue=emails,default --concurrency=4

The dox CLI runs the same file: dox queue:work, dox queue:failed, dox queue:retry <id|all>, dox queue:forget <id>, dox queue:flush, dox queue:clear [queue], dox queue:restart and dox queue:prune-failed. They take the same flags.

--concurrency runs jobs as async tasks on one thread. It helps for jobs that wait (email, HTTP, database). For CPU heavy jobs, run more worker processes.

docs.title: Stop the worker
docs.text:
Press Ctrl+C, or send SIGTERM (docker stop does it). The worker takes no new job. It waits for the running jobs, then it stops. A second signal stops it at once.

Restart the worker after a deploy

The worker keeps your code in memory. Restart it after each deploy, or it runs the old code.

dart run bin/queue.dart restart tells every running worker to stop after its current jobs. Your process manager then starts it with the new code. It writes a time to the app cache. Each worker reads it every 3 seconds. So the workers and the command must use the same cache store, like file on one machine, or redis. The memory store does not work for it.

docs.title: Keep it running
docs.text:
In production, run the binary, not dart run. dox build makes build/bundle/bin/queue, next to the server:

cd build/bundle
./bin/queue work --concurrency=4
