It takes the same commands and flags as dart run bin/queue.dart.

Run the worker as its own process, next to the web server. For example with Docker Compose and the image of the project Dockerfile:

services:
  web:
    build: .
    command: /app/bin/server
  worker:
    build: .
    command: /app/bin/queue work --concurrency=4

Or with systemd, Supervisor or a second Fly.io process. Set it to restart when it stops.

docs.title: Retries and failed jobs
docs.text:
When handle() throws:

  1. The worker waits the backoff time and tries again, up to tries times.
  2. After the last try, the job goes to the failed jobs, and failed() runs.

A timeout counts as a failed try.

A timeout does not stop the code

Dart can not stop a running Future. After a timeout the try counts as failed, but handle() keeps running in the background until it ends. Write jobs that are safe to run twice.

To wait for the old run, start the worker with --timeout-grace=SECONDS. Or set workerTimeoutGrace in QueueConfig for the in-process worker. The worker waits up to that time for the old run to end before it retries or fails the job. It takes no other job while it waits. Keep timeout plus the grace time below retryAfter. If not, another worker can take the job while this one waits.

When a worker crashes, its job stays reserved. After retryAfter another worker takes it. This counts as a try. When there are no tries left, the job fails with a message that the worker did not finish.

Failed jobs are kept until you retry or delete them:

dart run bin/queue.dart failed
dart run bin/queue.dart retry 6f1c0e...
dart run bin/queue.dart retry all
dart run bin/queue.dart forget 6f1c0e...
dart run bin/queue.dart flush

docs.title: Control the job in handle()
docs.text:
Add the opt-in InteractsWithQueue mixin. Then, inside handle(), the job can decide what happens next:

Call What it does attempts() how many times a worker took the job. The first run gives 1 release(delay) put the job back on its queue. It runs again after delay fail(error) fail the job now, with no retry. failed() runs delete() delete the job, with no retry and no failed() 
@Job()
class SendReport extends DoxJob with InteractsWithQueue {
  SendReport({required this.reportId});

  final int reportId;

  @override
  int get tries => 5;

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    ReportApi api = Dox().ioc.get<ReportApi>();
    if (await api.isBusy()) {
      release(Duration(seconds: 30));
      return;
    }
    if (!await api.hasReport(reportId)) {
      delete();
      return;
    }
    await api.send(reportId);
  }
}

The worker does the call when handle() ends. When you call more than one, the last one wins. A call also wins over an error that handle() throws after it. When handle() times out, the call is dropped, and the timeout rules count.

release() counts as a try. The default tries is 1, so the job then fails on its next pickup. Set tries above 1 (or retryUntil) when a job calls release().

With dispatchSync(), dispatchAfterResponse() and the sync driver there is no queue. There attempts() is 1, release() and delete() do nothing, and fail() only runs failed().

In a test file, package:test has its own fail(). Inside a job class with the mixin, a bare fail(...) calls the job method. Write this.fail(...) to make it clear.

docs.title: Job middleware
docs.text:
Middleware wraps handle() of a job. Use it for rules that many jobs share, like a rate limit. Add the opt-in HasMiddleware mixin and list the middleware. The first one runs first.

@Job()
class SendReport extends DoxJob with HasMiddleware {
  SendReport({required this.reportId});

  final int reportId;

  @override
  int get tries => 5;

  @override
  List<JobMiddleware> get middleware => <JobMiddleware>[
    RateLimited('report-api', 10, Duration(minutes: 1)),
    WithoutOverlapping(
      'report-$reportId',
      releaseAfter: Duration(seconds: 30),
      expireAfter: Duration(minutes: 10), // longer than the longest report run
    ),
  ];

  // ...
}

Write your own with JobMiddleware. Call next() to go on. Do not call it to skip the job. The job is then done. Call release(job, delay) to put the job back on the queue.

class SkipAtNight extends JobMiddleware {
  @override
  Future<void> handle(DoxJob job, JobNext next) async {
    if (DateTime.now().hour < 6) {
      release(job, Duration(hours: 1));
      return;
    }
    await next();
  }
}

The middleware runs in the worker, with the sync driver, with dispatchSync() and with dispatchAfterResponse(). A release counts as a try, like release() in Control the job in handle(). Outside a worker there is no queue. A release then logs a warning, and handle() does not run.

docs.title: Rate limits and locks
docs.text:
Middleware What it does RateLimited(key, max, per) runs at most max jobs of key in each per window. The others go back on the queue until the window ends WithoutOverlapping(key, releaseAfter:, expireAfter:) runs one job of key at a time. The others go back after releaseAfter (default: zero, so at once). With releaseAfter: null, they are dropped. expireAfter frees the lock after this time, also while a job still runs. Default: no expiry. Set expireAfter longer than the longest run of the job, so a crash can not hold the lock forever and two runs do not overlap ThrottlesExceptions(key, maxAttempts:, decay:, retryAfter:) after maxAttempts errors, jobs of key wait until decay is over. A job that threw goes back after retryAfter. Defaults: maxAttempts 10, decay 10 minutes, retryAfter zero

Things to know:

  • They keep their counts and locks in the default cache store. All workers must use the same store: file on one machine, or redis for several servers. A memory store is per process, so the limit would not work.
  • A release counts as a try. A job that is released and has tries of 1 fails on its next pickup. Set tries above 1, or a retryUntil.
  • The lock of WithoutOverlapping has no class name in it. Job classes with the same key share one lock. Put the class name in the key if they should not.

docs.title: Unique jobs
docs.text:
Some jobs should wait in the queue only once, like "rebuild the search index of product 5". Add the opt-in ShouldBeUnique mixin. While a job with the same class and uniqueId waits or runs, dispatch() pushes nothing and returns ''.

@Job()
class UpdateSearchIndex extends DoxJob with ShouldBeUnique {
  UpdateSearchIndex({required this.productId});

  final int productId;

  @override
  String get uniqueId => '$productId';

  @override
  Duration? get uniqueFor => Duration(hours: 1);

  // ...
}
  • uniqueId is the key next to the class. The default is empty: only one job of the class at a time.
  • uniqueFor ends the lock after a time, also when the job never ran. null means no end.
  • The worker frees the lock when the job is done, deleted or failed for good. A release or a retry keeps it.
  • ShouldBeUniqueUntilProcessing frees the lock when a worker starts the job. A new job can then be queued while this one runs.
  • The lock is in the default cache store. The web app and the workers must use the same store, like redis.
  • queue:clear frees the locks of the jobs it deletes.
  • queue:retry of a failed job does not take the lock.
  • dispatchSync() ignores uniqueness.
  • With afterCommit inside a transaction, the lock is taken at the commit. dispatch() returns the id at once, also when the job is then skipped.
  • When a worker crashes, its lock stays. With no uniqueFor, the lock never ends, and dispatch() keeps returning ''. So set uniqueFor on unique jobs.
  • Queue.fake() keeps its own locks and needs no cache.

docs.title: Job chains
docs.text:
A chain runs jobs one after the other. The next job is pushed only when the job before it is done.

await Queue.chain(<DoxJob>[
  ResizeImage(imageId: 1),
  UploadImage(imageId: 1),
  TellUser(imageId: 1),
]).catchError(TellAdmin(imageId: 1)).dispatch(queue: 'images');
  • The rest of the chain is saved in the job that runs now. So the chain works across worker processes and restarts.
  • A job that is released or retried keeps the chain. The chain goes on only after the job is done.
  • A job that ends with delete(), or that a middleware skips, counts as done. The chain goes on.
  • When a job fails for good, the rest of the chain is dropped and the catch job runs.
  • queue:retry of the failed job brings the chain back. When the job is then done, the chain goes on.
  • dispatch() returns the id of the first job. queue and connection count for every job. delay counts for the first job only.
  • The sync driver runs the jobs now, one after the other. When one throws, the catch job runs and dispatch() throws the error.

docs.title: The catch job
docs.text:
A function can not be saved in the queue. So the catch handler is a job too, of a class in jobRegistry. Run dart run build_runner build after you add it. It runs once, in the worker where the job failed. It has no queue and no retry, like dispatchSync(). Add the CatchesError mixin to read the error:

@Job()
class TellAdmin extends DoxJob with CatchesError {
  TellAdmin({required this.imageId});

  final int imageId;

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    await alertAdmin('image $imageId failed: $caughtError');
  }
}

An error in the catch job is logged. For slow work, dispatch a new job from it.

docs.title: Chain traps
docs.text:
• Each job carries the data of the jobs after it. Keep chains short. Save ids in the jobs, not big data.
  • A ShouldBeEncrypted job stays encrypted inside the job before it.
  • A unique job in the chain that is skipped stops the chain. The catch job runs with a StateError. When the first job is skipped, dispatch() returns '' and nothing runs.
  • A next job that can not be read, for example when its class was removed, stops the chain. The catch job runs with the error.
  • The worker pushes the next job before it deletes the job that is done. A crash between the two can run the next job twice. Make chain jobs safe to run twice.
  • When the push of the next job fails, the try of the current job counts as failed, even though its handle() worked. The job is tried again. When no try is left, it fails and the catch job runs. With the default tries of 1 the first failed push does this. So give chain jobs more than one try.
  • The unique lock of a job is freed before the next job is pushed. So a next job with the same unique id is not skipped.

docs.title: Job batches
docs.text:
A batch runs many jobs and acts when they are all done:

Batch batch = await Queue.batch(<DoxJob>[
  ImportRows(from: 0),
  ImportRows(from: 1000),
  ImportRows(from: 2000),
])
    .name('import')
    .then(ImportDone())
    .catchError(ImportFailed())
    .whenComplete(CleanUpImport())
    .dispatch(queue: 'imports');

print(batch.id);

docs.title: The table
docs.text:
A batch is saved in the job_batches table. It uses the database connection of QueueConfig.connection, also with the Redis driver and the sync driver. Batches need dox_queue_database: install it, extend DatabaseQueueProvider in your queue provider, and run dox queue:table. See step 4. Without the package, Queue.batch() throws a StateError that says to add dox_queue_database.

An app that does not use batches does not need the table. If you use batches, you need it with every driver.

docs.title: Callbacks
Jobs of a batch
docs.text:
Add the opt-in Batchable mixin to a job to read its batch. batchId is the id. batch() reads the batch as it is now. A job can skip its work when the batch was cancelled:

@Job()
class ImportRows extends DoxJob with Batchable {
  ImportRows({required this.from});

  final int from;

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    Batch? batch = await this.batch();
    if (batch?.cancelled ?? false) return;
    await importRows(from);
  }
}

A Batch has these fields:

Field What it holds id, name the id and the name totalJobs how many jobs the batch has pendingJobs how many jobs are not done. It also counts failed jobs, because they can be retried failedJobs how many jobs failed processedJobs how many jobs are done. Failed jobs are not counted progress the percent of done jobs, from 0 to 100 finished true when every job ran, or the batch was cancelled cancelled true after cancel(), or after a first failure

A Batch is the state at the time it was read. Read it again with Queue.findBatch(id). It gives null when there is no such batch.

  • The first job that fails for good cancels the batch. Add allowFailures() to keep it going.
  • cancel() does not stop the jobs. They still run and count. A Batchable job reads cancelled to skip its work.
  • add(jobs) adds jobs to the batch, for example from a job of the batch. They go on the queue and connection of the batch. It throws a StateError when the batch is finished, cancelled or deleted. Then it pushes nothing.
  • A failed job that you retry with queue:retry is not counted again when it fails again. When it is done, pendingJobs and failedJobs both go down by one. So catchError can run again when a later job fails.
  • An empty batch throws an ArgumentError, because it would never finish.
  • then and whenComplete run once, also with many workers. Each count changes in one atomic step.

docs.title: A chain inside a batch
docs.text:
Add chain(jobs) to put a chain in the batch. Its jobs run one after the other:

await Queue.batch(<DoxJob>[ImportUsers()])
    .chain(<DoxJob>[ImportOrders(), SumOrders()])
    .dispatch();
  • The batch counts the chain as one job. It is done when its last job is done.
  • When a job of the chain fails for good, the rest of the chain is dropped. The batch counts one failed job.
  • The usual failure rules apply. The first failure cancels the batch, unless you call allowFailures().
  • When the first job of the chain is a skipped unique job, the chain is taken out of the counts. A skipped later job fails the chain.
  • add(jobs) takes jobs only, not chains.

docs.title: Batch traps
docs.text:
• A skipped unique job is taken out of totalJobs and pendingJobs. progress does not run for it. When it was the last open job, then and whenComplete run.
  • When a push fails in dispatch() or add(), the jobs that were not pushed are taken out of the counts. The batch is cancelled and the error is thrown. The jobs that were pushed before still run, and the callbacks still fire for them.
  • The counts follow the at-least-once rule of the queue. A job that runs twice, for example when it runs longer than retryAfter, can be counted twice. failedJobs never goes below 0.
  • The batch is marked finished before then and whenComplete run. So add() from a callback throws a StateError.
  • When a worker crashes after a job is done and before it counted the job, the batch keeps that job as pending. Then then and whenComplete never run. Prune such batches with --unfinished, see below.
  • Inside a transaction, use dispatch(afterCommit: true). Then the batch is saved and pushed only after the commit. See Dispatch after the commit.
  • The sync driver runs the jobs at dispatch() and counts them. A job that throws counts as failed, and dispatch() does not throw.
  • The queue events fire for the jobs of a batch like for any job. The batch has its own events too, see Batch events.

docs.title: Prune old batches
docs.text:
dart run bin/queue.dart prune-batches --hours=48
dart run bin/queue.dart prune-batches --hours=48 --unfinished=168

The first line deletes batches that finished, or were cancelled, more than 48 hours ago. The default is 24. --unfinished=168 also deletes batches that never finished and were made more than 168 hours ago. In code, use Queue.pruneBatches(before, unfinishedBefore:).

docs.title: Queue events
docs.text:
Listen to the steps of a job:

Queue.before((QueueEvent event) => print('start ${event.name} ${event.id}'));
Queue.after((QueueEvent event) => print('done ${event.name}'));
Queue.failing((QueueEvent event) => alert(event.name, event.error));
Hook When Queue.queued dispatch() pushed a job Queue.before a worker starts a job Queue.after a worker finished a job and deleted it Queue.released a worker put a job back (release() or a retry) Queue.exceptionOccurred handle() threw and the job will be tried again Queue.failing a job failed for good Queue.looping a worker is about to take the next job Queue.stopping a worker stops

A listener gets a QueueEvent:

Field What it holds type the kind of event job the job. null for looping and stopping, and when the worker can not read the job name the job name of the registry id the job id queue the queue name attempts the try number. 0 for queued, looping and stopping error, stack the error and its stack trace, for exceptionOccurred and failing. batchFailed has error only delay the wait, for queued and released batch the Batch, for the batch events. null for other events
  • Listeners are per isolate. Register them where the app starts, like in a provider. Then the web app and each worker have them.
  • A listener can be async. The queue waits for it.
  • A listener that throws is logged. It never stops the worker or the dispatch.
  • The sync driver, dispatchSync() and dispatchAfterResponse() fire no job events. The sync driver does fire the batch events.
  • Queue.fake() fires no events.
  • Queue.forgetListeners() removes all listeners, for example between tests.

docs.title: Batch events
docs.text:
A batch has its own events. In these events, event.batch is the batch after the step. It holds the id, the name and the counts:

Queue.batchProgress((QueueEvent event) {
  Batch batch = event.batch!;
  print('${batch.name}: ${batch.progress}%');
});
Queue.batchFailed((QueueEvent event) => alert(event.batch!.id, event.error));
Hook When Where it fires Queue.batchDispatched the batch was saved, before its jobs are pushed the process that called dispatch() Queue.batchProgress a job (or a chain) of the batch is done. With allowFailures(), also when one failed the worker that counted it Queue.batchFailed the first job failed for good. event.error is its error the worker that counted it Queue.batchCancelled the batch was cancelled: cancel(), the first failure without allowFailures(), or a push that threw the process that cancelled it Queue.batchFinished every job ran, done or failed the worker that counted the last job
  • Each event fires once per step, also with many workers.
  • When one failure cancels the batch, batchFailed fires first. Then batchCancelled fires.
  • With the sync driver, every event fires in the process that called dispatch().
  • Queue.fake() fires no batch events.

docs.title: Drivers
docs.text: Driver Where jobs are Needs sync nowhere: dispatch() runs the job at once nothing database the jobs and failed_jobs tables dox_queue_database, and Postgres, MySQL 8+, MariaDB 10.6+ or SQLite redis Redis lists and sorted sets Redis

docs.title: Database driver
docs.text:
The database driver is in the dox_queue_database package. Install it and register it in your queue provider (see step 4). Without the registration, QueueConfig(driver: 'database') throws an ArgumentError that names the package.

Jobs are rows in the jobs table. Failed jobs are rows in failed_jobs.

failed_jobs.connection has the name of the queue connection (see Queue connections). It is NULL for the main connection. A failed_jobs table without this column works too. Then the name is not saved. A worker checks for the column once, so restart the workers after you add it. To add the column, write a migration:

await schema.table('failed_jobs', (Table table) {
  table.string('connection').nullable();
});
  • On Postgres, MySQL and MariaDB a worker takes a job with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. Many workers do not wait on each other.
  • On SQLite a worker takes a job with one UPDATE ... RETURNING. SQLite runs one write at a time, so this is safe. It is good for small apps.

Use another connection of config/database.dart with QueueConfig(connection: 'postgres').

docs.title: The failed_at column
docs.text:
failed_jobs.failed_at is the time the job failed. It has one of two types:

  • A big integer: unix time in milliseconds. This is the default.
  • A timestamp in UTC. Turn it on with failedAtTimestamp: true.

FailedJob.failedAt is the same DateTime with both types.

To make a new table with the timestamp column, pass the setting to QueueTables.up in the migration, and set it in the queue config too:

await QueueTables.up(schema, failedAtTimestamp: true);

QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'database',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  failedAtTimestamp: true,
);

The setting counts per connection. Each entry of connections has its own failedAtTimestamp, so two database connections can use tables of different types.

The setting and the column must match. A worker reads the column type once, when it first uses failed_jobs.

What happens when the setting and the column do not match

fail, failed, retry, forget and prune-failed throw a StateError. Nothing is written.

A job that fails all its tries is NOT moved to failed_jobs, and its failed() hook does not run. The job stays in jobs. It comes back after retryAfter and runs again, with an error in the log each time. This goes on until the setting matches the table.

When the type can not be read (for example, the connection dropped), the worker reads it again on the next call. With the setting off, it logs a warning and goes on. With the setting on, the call throws that error, and nothing is written.

The column type on each database:

Database Column How the time is kept SQLite TIMESTAMP ISO text in UTC, with milliseconds Postgres TIMESTAMP (without time zone) the UTC time, with milliseconds MySQL, MariaDB TIMESTAMP whole seconds, in UTC. The queue writes it with FROM_UNIXTIME() and reads it with UNIX_TIMESTAMP(), so the session time zone does not change the time.

A MySQL and MariaDB TIMESTAMP can not hold a time after 2038-01-19.

docs.title: Use the timestamp column on a table with the integer column
docs.text:
Stop all workers first, also on other servers

A worker reads the column type when it first uses failed_jobs, and keeps it. A worker that is still running writes numbers into the timestamp column. On SQLite this works without an error, and then pruning and the order by time are wrong.

  1. Stop all workers, on every server. Stop the app too when it has inProcess: true.
  2. Run the SQL for your database below, in a new migration (await schema.driver.execute('...'); for each line) or in a database client.
  3. Set failedAtTimestamp: true in the queue config.
  4. Start the workers again.

SQLite (3.35 or newer):

ALTER TABLE failed_jobs ADD COLUMN failed_at_utc TIMESTAMP;
UPDATE failed_jobs SET failed_at_utc = strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%fZ', failed_at / 1000.0, 'unixepoch');
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs DROP COLUMN failed_at;
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs RENAME COLUMN failed_at_utc TO failed_at;

Postgres:

ALTER TABLE failed_jobs ALTER COLUMN failed_at TYPE TIMESTAMP USING to_timestamp(failed_at / 1000.0) AT TIME ZONE 'UTC';

MySQL and MariaDB:

ALTER TABLE failed_jobs ADD COLUMN failed_at_utc TIMESTAMP NULL;
UPDATE failed_jobs SET failed_at_utc = FROM_UNIXTIME(failed_at DIV 1000);
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs DROP COLUMN failed_at;
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs CHANGE failed_at_utc failed_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL;

On SQLite the new column allows NULL, because SQLite can not add a NOT NULL column without a default. The queue never writes NULL there.

docs.title: Redis
docs.text:
QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'redis',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  redis: RedisOptions(host: env.redisHost, port: 6379),
);

To read the Redis server from the env, use QueueConfig.redisFromEnv(). It reads REDIS_URL (for example rediss://user:password@host:6380/0, where rediss turns on TLS). When REDIS_URL is not set, it reads REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_USERNAME, REDIS_PASSWORD and REDIS_TLS. A key that is not set keeps the default of RedisOptions.

QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'redis',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  redis: QueueConfig.redisFromEnv(),
);

Each queue has a list of ready jobs, a sorted set of delayed jobs and a sorted set of reserved jobs. A Lua script takes a job, so two workers never get the same one. Failed jobs are in the hash dox_queue:failed.

docs.title: Sync
docs.text:
dispatch() runs the job at once and waits for it. There is no worker, no retry and no delay. When the job throws, failed() runs and dispatch() throws the error. Use it for tests and for local work.

By default the sync driver runs the job object as it is. So a job that is not in jobRegistry, or a field that is not JSON, works here and fails later in the worker. Set serializeSync: true to save the job and read it back before it runs, the way a worker gets it:

Queue.configure(
  QueueConfig(driver: 'sync', jobs: jobRegistry, serializeSync: true),
);

Then dispatch() throws for such a job.

docs.title: Queue connections
docs.text:
One app can use more than one queue store. The config is the main connection. Add more in connections, by name:

QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'redis',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  connections: <String, QueueConfig>{
    'database': QueueConfig(driver: 'database'),
  },
);

Pick a connection when you dispatch:

await SendReport(reportId: 1).dispatch(connection: 'database');

With no connection, the job goes to the main connection. An unknown name throws an ArgumentError.

Run a worker for each connection. Every command of bin/queue.dart takes --connection:

dart run bin/queue.dart work
dart run bin/queue.dart work --connection=database
dart run bin/queue.dart failed --connection=database
  • An entry uses only driver, redis, prefix, connection (the dox_orm one), retryAfter and serializeSync. The jobs of the main config count for all connections.
  • The in-process worker (inProcess) runs the jobs of the main connection only.
  • Two database connections on the same dox_orm connection share the jobs and failed_jobs tables. Give each one its own dox_orm connection. If they share, failed --connection=X lists all failed jobs of the table, not only those of X.
  • Queue.fake() keeps the name in PushedJob.connection.

docs.title: Small apps: a worker in the web server
docs.text:
You can skip the worker process. Set inProcess: true:

QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'database',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  inProcess: true,
);

The first isolate of the web server then runs jobs too. When the server stops, it waits for the running jobs.

Only the web server runs this worker. The scheduler process (bin/schedule.dart) does not.

Heavy jobs slow down your API

The jobs share the isolate with web requests. A long or CPU heavy job makes requests on that isolate slow. Use a worker process when your jobs are heavy or many.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Use the sync driver. dispatch() then runs the job at once, so you can check the result right after.

import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/jobs/send_welcome_email.job.dart';
import 'package:my_app/generated/jobs.g.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  setUp(() {
    Queue.configure(QueueConfig(driver: 'sync', jobs: jobRegistry));
  });

  test('sends the welcome email', () async {
    await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatch();
    // check the email was sent
  });
}

A job that uses Dox() (for example Dox().ioc or Logger) needs the app config. Call Dox().initialize(appConfig) in setUpAll.

To check that your code dispatched a job, without running it, use Queue.fake(). It records every dispatch() in a list. It does not run or save the jobs. It needs no Queue.configure().

late QueueFake queue;

setUp(() {
  queue = Queue.fake();
});

tearDown(Queue.restore);

test('signing up queues the welcome email', () async {
  await signUp(userId: 1);

  queue.assertPushed<SendWelcomeEmail>();
  queue.assertPushed<SendWelcomeEmail>(
    (SendWelcomeEmail job) => job.userId == 1,
  );
  queue.assertPushedTimes<SendWelcomeEmail>(1);
  queue.assertNotPushed<SendInvoice>();
});
Method Checks assertPushed<T>([test]) a T job was pushed. With test, one of them passes it assertPushedTimes<T>(n) exactly n T jobs were pushed assertNotPushed<T>() no T job was pushed assertNothingPushed() no job was pushed at all assertChained(<Type>[A, B]) a chain of exactly these job classes, in this order, was dispatched assertBatched([test]) a batch was dispatched. With test, one of them passes it. test gets a PendingBatch assertBatchedChain(<Type>[A, B]) a batch has a chain of exactly these job classes, in this order assertBatchCount(n) exactly n batches were dispatched

To read the jobs, use queue.pushed. Each item has the job, the queue name and the delay. queue.jobsOf<T>() gives the T jobs. queue.clear() forgets them. Queue.restore() stops the fake.

  • Queue.chain() and Queue.batch() are kept too. Read chains in queue.chains and batches in queue.batches. The chains of a batch are in PendingBatch.chains. Their jobs are not in queue.pushed. Nothing is saved or run, and the batch tables are not needed. In a faked batch, add() adds to the batch, cancel() does nothing and Queue.findBatch() gives null.
  • dispatchSync() runs the job now. dispatchAfterResponse() runs it after the answer, or soon outside a request. The fake does not stop them. It keeps their jobs in queue.dispatchedSync and queue.dispatchedAfterResponse (not in queue.pushed). queue.clear() empties these lists too.
  • The fake does not encode the job. A job that is missing from QueueConfig.jobs, or has data that is not JSON, passes a faked test but fails for real.
  • The fake also catches Mail.queue() on the default queue, but only when Mail.fake() is off. It does not catch a custom queue set with Mail.useQueue(). When both are on, Mail.fake() catches the email first. See Mail.

To test a job alone, call handle():

await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).handle();

To test the queue itself, use the database driver of dox_queue_database with SQLite :memory:, and run a worker that stops when the queue is empty:

await Worker(
  driver: Queue.driver,
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  options: WorkerOptions(stopWhenEmpty: true),
).run();

docs.title: Without Dox
docs.text:
dox_queue also works in a plain Dart app. Add build_runner and dox_builder, so it writes lib/generated/jobs.g.dart:

dart pub add dox_queue dox_core
dart pub add dev:build_runner dev:dox_builder

Write your jobs like in Write a job, and run dart run build_runner build. Then set up the queue and run a worker yourself:

import 'dart:async';
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';
import 'package:my_app/generated/jobs.g.dart';
import 'package:my_app/jobs/resize_image.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  // the worker logs with the Dox logger, so it needs an AppConfig
  Dox().initialize(AppConfig(appKey: 'not-used'));

  Queue.configure(QueueConfig(
    driver: 'redis',
    jobs: jobRegistry,
    redis: RedisOptions(host: '127.0.0.1', port: 6379),
  ));

  await ResizeImage(path: 'photo.png').dispatch();

  Worker worker = Worker(
    driver: Queue.driver,
    jobs: jobRegistry,
    options: WorkerOptions(queues: <String>['default'], concurrency: 4),
  );

  // Ctrl+C: finish the running jobs, then stop
  StreamSubscription<ProcessSignal> signal =
      ProcessSignal.sigint.watch().listen((_) => worker.stop());
  await worker.run();
  await signal.cancel();
  await Queue.close();
}
  • WorkerOptions takes the same settings as the flags of work: queues, concurrency, once, tries, timeout, sleep and stopWhenEmpty.
  • The database driver needs dox_queue_database. There are no providers here, so call QueueDatabase.register() before Queue.configure(). It uses the default dox_orm connection. Set it up first with SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(...).
  • No services are in the Dox container. Make the services of a job in handle().

docs.title: Scheduler
docs.text:
dox_scheduler runs your tasks on a schedule, like cron.

You write the schedule in Dart, in one file. Each task is a plain function. A task runs once per tick, even when many isolates or servers run the schedule.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
dox add scheduler

It adds the package and writes the three files below. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice. A new app already has it.

docs.title: Set it up by hand
docs.text: dart pub add dox_scheduler

docs.title: Set up in a Dox app
docs.text:
A new app from dox create already has these files. In another app, add them:

  • lib/config/schedule.dart: the tasks and the ScheduleConfig. See Define tasks.
  • bin/schedule.dart: the program that runs the schedule. See Run the schedule.
  • lib/providers/schedule_provider.dart (optional): runs the schedule inside the server. See Run inside the server.

Then start it next to your server:

dart run bin/schedule.dart work

docs.title: Without Dox
docs.text:
dox_scheduler also works in a plain Dart app. Leave out app:

import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';

void schedule(Schedule s) {
  s.call('cleanup', cleanup).dailyAt('02:00');
}

Future<void> cleanup() async {
  // delete old files, ...
}

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await SchedulerRunner(schedule: schedule).run(args);
}
  • With no app, no providers start, and the locks use a memory store.
  • For many servers, pass a shared lock store: SchedulerRunner(schedule: schedule, store: myRedisStore). It is a CacheStore from dox_cache.
  • The commands are the same. See Run the schedule.

docs.title: Define tasks
docs.text:
Put the tasks in lib/config/schedule.dart.

import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';

ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig();

void schedule(Schedule s) {
  s.call('cleanup', cleanup).dailyAt('02:00');
  s.call('report', sendReport).hourly();
  s.call('ping', ping).cron('*/5 * * * *').timezone('Asia/Yangon');
}

Future<void> cleanup() async {
  // delete old rows, files, ...
}

s.call(name, function) adds a task. The name must be unique. It shows in the logs and in the lock keys. A task with no frequency runs every minute.

docs.title: Queue jobs
docs.text:
The scheduler does not know about queues. Wrap the job in a function:

s.call('report', () => SendReport().dispatch()).hourly();

The task only puts the job on the queue. A queue worker runs it.

To send the job to a queue connection, pass connection: to dispatch():

void schedule(Schedule s) {
  s.call('send-report', () => SendReport().dispatch()).dailyAt('08:00');
  s.call('prune', () => PruneFiles().dispatch(connection: 'redis')).hourly();
}

The task name must be unique in the schedule. connection: of dispatch() is a queue connection. Without it, the main connection is used.

docs.title: Processes and dox commands
docs.text:
s.exec('pg_dump', args: <String>['-f', 'backup.sql', 'mydb']).daily();
s.command('queue:prune', args: <String>['--hours=48']).hourly();

exec(executable, args: [...]) runs a process. No shell is used, so |, > and * are plain text. Use s.exec('sh', args: <String>['-c', '...']) when you need a shell. A non-zero exit code fails the task. Its stdin is closed, so a program that waits for input ends at once. With timeout(), the process gets SIGTERM when the time is up, and SIGKILL 5 seconds later (Schedule.processGrace). Only the process itself is killed. The children of a shell (sh -c 'a | b') may live on. A stop of work waits for the process to end.

command(command, args: [...]) runs a dox command of your app, as the process dox <command> <args>. When dox is not on PATH, set its full path: Schedule.doxExecutable = '/usr/local/bin/dox';.

The task name is the command line, like dox queue:prune --hours=48. It shows in the logs, the lock keys and list. So do not put a secret (like --token=...) in args without your own name: s.command('sync', args: <String>['--token=$token'], name: 'sync'). A name also lets you add the same command line twice.

The output is dropped. Use the output hooks to keep it.

docs.title: Frequencies
docs.text:
Method Runs everySecond() every second. Also everyTwoSeconds, everyFiveSeconds, everyTenSeconds, everyFifteenSeconds, everyTwentySeconds, everyThirtySeconds everyMinute() every minute (the default) everyTwoMinutes() every 2 minutes everyThreeMinutes() every 3 minutes everyFourMinutes() every 4 minutes everyFiveMinutes() every 5 minutes everyTenMinutes() every 10 minutes everyFifteenMinutes() every 15 minutes everyThirtyMinutes() at minute 0 and 30 hourly() at minute 0 of every hour hourlyAt(17) at minute 17 of every hour everyTwoHours() every 2 hours at minute 0. Also everyThreeHours, everyFourHours, everySixHours. Pass a minute: everyTwoHours(15) everyOddHour() at 01:00, 03:00 ... 23:00. Pass a minute: everyOddHour(30) daily() every day at 00:00 dailyAt('13:00') every day at 13:00 twiceDaily(1, 13) every day at 01:00 and 13:00 twiceDailyAt(1, 13, 15) every day at 01:15 and 13:15 at('13:00') same as dailyAt('13:00') weekly() every Sunday at 00:00 weeklyOn(DateTime.monday, '08:00') every Monday at 08:00 monthly() the 1st of every month at 00:00 monthlyOn(15, '12:00') the 15th of every month at 12:00 twiceMonthly(1, 16, '13:00') the 1st and 16th of every month at 13:00 lastDayOfMonth('15:00') the last day of every month at 15:00 quarterly() January, April, July and October 1st at 00:00 quarterlyOn(4, '14:00') January, April, July and October 4th at 14:00 yearly() January 1st at 00:00 yearlyOn(6, 1, '17:00') June 1st at 17:00. A day the month never has, like yearlyOn(2, 30), throws cron('*/5 9-17 * * 1-5') any 5 field cron expression

A task that runs every few seconds repeats inside each due minute. A frequency, the days, the filters and timezone() still decide if the minute is due: s.call('poll', poll).everyFiveSeconds().between('09:00', '17:00'). Call the seconds method first, then the other frequency. everyFiveSeconds() also sets the task to every minute. If you call it last, it undoes the frequency before it. .everyFiveSeconds().hourly() repeats in minute 0 of each hour. .hourly().everyFiveSeconds() repeats in every minute. when() and skip() are checked before each repeat. A run that takes longer than its step skips the steps it missed. With such a task, run from cron stays until the end of the minute.

You can limit the days. The order does not matter between the day methods (like weekdays() or mondays()) and a time method like dailyAt(). The day methods, weekly(), weeklyOn() and cron() all write the day of the week. The last call wins: .mondays().weekly() runs on Sundays. weekly() and weeklyOn() also set the time, to 00:00 unless you pass one. So call dailyAt() after them, or pass the time to weeklyOn(): .dailyAt('09:00').weekly() runs at 00:00, but .weekly().dailyAt('09:00') runs at 09:00.

Method Runs weekdays() Monday to Friday weekends() Saturday and Sunday mondays() ... sundays() only on that day of the week days(<int>[DateTime.monday, DateTime.friday]) only on these days 
s.call('standup', remind).weekdays().dailyAt('09:00');

A day of the month and a day of the week join with OR, like cron. monthlyOn(15).fridays() runs on the 15th and on every Friday. lastDayOfMonth() is different: it runs only on the last day of the month. lastDayOfMonth().fridays() runs on every last day of the month, on any day of the week. The fridays() part has no effect.

docs.title: Cron expressions
docs.text:
cron() takes the standard 5 fields: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week.

Field Values minute 0-59 hour 0-23 day of month 1-31 month 1-12 or JAN-DEC day of week 0-7 or SUN-SAT (0 and 7 are Sunday)

Each field takes *, a number 5, a range 1-5, a list 1,15, and a step */15 or 0-30/10.

When both day fields are set, a day matches when either field matches. This is the standard cron rule. 0 0 1 * MON runs on the 1st of the month and on every Monday. When one day field starts with *, both must match.

docs.title: Time zones
docs.text:
The schedule uses UTC by default. Use timezone() to read the time in another zone:

s.call('report', sendReport).dailyAt('08:00').timezone('Asia/Yangon');

The name is an IANA name, like Europe/London or America/New_York. The zone data comes from the timezone package.

To use one zone for every task, set it in the config. A task's own timezone() still wins.

ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig(timezone: 'Asia/Yangon');

An unknown name throws an ArgumentError when the schedule starts.

With summer time (DST):

  • A time that does not exist that day (it is skipped when the clock goes forward) does not run that day.
  • A time that happens twice (when the clock goes back) runs once.
  • hourly() and other "every" frequencies keep running every real hour.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
s.call('sync', sync).everyFiveMinutes().between('09:00', '17:00');
s.call('night', night).hourly().between('22:00', '06:00'); // crosses midnight
s.call('quiet', quiet).hourly().unlessBetween('23:00', '04:00');
s.call('emails', sendEmails).daily().environments(<String>['production']);
s.call('promo', promo).daily().when(isPromoOn);
s.call('backup', backup).daily().skip(isHoliday);
Method What it does between('09:00', '17:00') runs only in this time of day, both ends included, in the task zone unlessBetween('23:00', '04:00') does not run in this time of day, both ends included, in the task zone environments(<String>['production']) runs only when APP_ENV is one of these names. Case and spaces around the names do not matter. When APP_ENV is not set or empty, the task does not run. It is read at run time. An empty list or a blank name throws when(function) runs only when the function gives true skip(function) does not run when the function gives true

when and skip take a function that gives a bool or a Future<bool>.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Method What it does withoutOverlapping() does not start while the last run still runs onOneServer() runs once per tick across isolates and servers. On by default onEveryServer() runs on every process that runs the schedule runInBackground() the next task of the same minute does not wait for this one timeout(Duration(minutes: 5)) counts the run as failed when it takes longer. It kills the process of an exec() or command() task

docs.title: withoutOverlapping
docs.text:
A lock is held while the task runs. When the next minute comes and the lock is still held, the task is skipped. The lock expires after 24 hours, in case the process dies. Pass another expiry like this: withoutOverlapping(Duration(hours: 1)).

When the process crashes, the lock stays in the store. The task is then skipped until the lock expires. To run it again at once, remove the lock with clear-cache:

dox schedule:clear-cache

docs.title: Once per tick
docs.text:
Before a task runs, the scheduler takes a lock named after the task and the minute. The first process to take it runs the task. The others skip it. The lock is not released, so a late server can not run the same minute again. It expires after 10 minutes.

The locks use a cache store.

Many servers need Redis

A memory store lives inside one process. A file store lives on one machine. It works for one work process, or for many isolates of one server. When many servers run the schedule, set a Redis store: ScheduleConfig(store: 'redis').

When the store has no locks (null), the scheduler uses a memory store.

At start, the scheduler prints one warning to stderr when a task uses onOneServer() and the lock store is memory or file (or null). These stores are not shared between servers, so the lock works only inside one server. The warning does not print when APP_ENV is development or local, because a dev machine is one server. With one server you can ignore it.

docs.title: Timeout
docs.text: Dart can not stop a running function. After the timeout, the run counts as failed and the hooks run, but the work may go on. The process of an exec() or command() task is killed at the timeout.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
s
    .call('report', sendReport)
    .daily()
    .before(logStart)
    .onSuccess(logDone)
    .onFailure(alertTeam)
    .after(cleanUp);

Future<void> alertTeam(Object error, StackTrace stack) async {
  await notifyTeam('report failed: $error');
}
Hook Runs before before the task. When it throws, the task does not run and counts as failed onSuccess after the task worked onFailure after the task threw or timed out. It gets the error and the stack trace after after the task, always

An error in a task is logged and the next task still runs.

docs.title: Output hooks
docs.text:
These work on exec() and command() tasks. On a function task they do nothing.

Hook What it does sendOutputTo('storage/logs/backup.log') writes the output (stdout and stderr) to the file. It replaces the file each run appendOutputTo('storage/logs/backup.log') adds the output to the end of the file onOutput((String output) {...}) gets the output after the process ends
  • The file gets the output as it comes. onOutput holds the whole output in memory, so do not use it for a very large output.
  • Two runs at the same time write to the same file. Use withoutOverlapping() or appendOutputTo().
  • A file that can not be written fails the task. onOutput still gets the output first.
  • A throwing onOutput hook fails the task.
  • When more than one thing fails, the task fails with the first of: a non-zero exit code, an onOutput error, a file error.
  • After a timeout, the file and onOutput finish a bit later, after the failure hooks ran. An error there is lost.

docs.title: Ping hooks
docs.text:
s
    .call('backup', backup)
    .daily()
    .pingBefore('https://health.example.com/backup/start')
    .pingOnSuccess('https://health.example.com/backup')
    .pingOnFailure('https://health.example.com/backup/fail');
Hook Sends a GET request pingBefore(url) before the task thenPing(url) after the task, always pingOnSuccess(url) after the task worked pingOnFailure(url) after the task failed

Each one also has an If form that takes a bool first, like pingOnFailureIf(isProduction, url).

  • A ping fails after 10 seconds (ScheduledTask.pingTimeout), or on a status of 400 or more.
  • A failed ping is logged. It never fails the task.
  • A url that is not http or https throws an ArgumentError when the schedule is made.
  • In tests, replace the request: ScheduledTask.sendPing = (Uri url) async {...};.

docs.title: Run the schedule
docs.text:
bin/schedule.dart runs the schedule:

import 'dart:io';

import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/schedule.dart';
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await SchedulerRunner(
    schedule: schedule,
    app: appConfig,
    config: scheduleConfig,
  ).run(args);
}

With app, the runner starts your app providers first (like the database). It stops them at the end.

Command What it does dart run bin/schedule.dart work runs due tasks at every minute until you stop it. The default dart run bin/schedule.dart run runs the tasks due this minute once, then exits dart run bin/schedule.dart list shows each task, its schedule and its next run time dart run bin/schedule.dart test cleanup runs one task now dart run bin/schedule.dart clear-cache removes the withoutOverlapping() locks, after a crash

The dox CLI runs the same file: dox schedule:work, dox schedule:run, dox schedule:list, dox schedule:test <name> and dox schedule:clear-cache.

docs.title: work
docs.text:
work is a long running process. Run it next to your server, with the same deploy tool (systemd, Docker, Kubernetes).

It wakes at each full minute and runs the due tasks. With a task that runs every few seconds, it also wakes inside the minute. On Ctrl+C or SIGTERM it starts no new task and waits for the running ones. A second signal stops it at once.

docs.title: run
docs.text:
run is for a system cron. Add one line to the crontab:

* * * * * cd /path/to/app/build/bundle && ./bin/schedule run

It runs the tasks of this minute, waits for them, and exits. The exit code is 1 when a task failed.

./bin/schedule is the binary that dox build makes in build/bundle. It starts fast and needs no Dart SDK. Do not use dart compile exe. It can not build apps with native libraries, like SQLite.

docs.title: list
docs.text:
Task     Schedule                   Next run
cleanup  0 2 * * *                  2026-10-26 02:00 UTC
report   0 * * * *                  2026-10-25 14:00 UTC
ping     */5 * * * * Asia/Yangon    2026-10-25 20:35 Asia/Yangon

The next run time checks the frequency, between() and unlessBetween(). It does not check when(), skip() and environments().

lastDayOfMonth() shows 28-31 in the day field, but it runs only on the last day of the month. The next run time is right.

docs.title: test
docs.text: test <name> runs one task now, with its hooks. It does not check the schedule, the filters or the locks.

docs.title: clear-cache
docs.text:
clear-cache removes the withoutOverlapping() lock of each task in the schedule. Use it after a crash, when a task is skipped because its lock is still there.

$ dox schedule:clear-cache
Removed the overlap lock of report.

When there is no lock, it prints this:

No overlap locks found. Nothing to clear.

The exit code is 0 in both cases.

It removes only the lock key of each task, by its exact name. Other keys in the cache store stay. It does not remove the once-per-tick locks of onOneServer(). Each one is for one minute only, and it expires after 10 minutes.

Only when the task is not running

Do not run it while a task really runs on another process or server. That task could then start a second time.

A memory store lives inside one process, so its locks end with the process. clear-cache is for file and Redis stores.

docs.title: Run inside the server
docs.text:
You can run the schedule inside your Dox server instead of a work process. Add a provider that extends SchedulerProvider:

// lib/providers/schedule_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/schedule.dart';

class ScheduleProvider extends SchedulerProvider {
  ScheduleProvider() : super(schedule: schedule, config: scheduleConfig);
}

Then turn it on in lib/config/schedule.dart:

ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig(inProcess: true);

Run dart run build_runner build. The generated container finds the provider.

How it works:

  • Only the first isolate runs the tasks. The other isolates only serve requests.
  • With many servers, each server runs the loop. The once-per-tick lock makes each task run once. Use a Redis store for this.
  • When the server stops, it waits for the running tasks.

Trade-offs:

  • Tasks use the CPU of the server, so they can slow down requests on the first isolate.
  • A long task makes the server stop slower.
  • With a separate work process, you can deploy, scale and restart the scheduler on its own.

Use work for heavy tasks. Use the in-process provider for small apps.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Scheduler runs the tasks. Give it a fake clock to test a schedule with no waiting:

import 'package:dox_cache/dox_cache.dart';
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/schedule.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

class FakeClock extends ScheduleClock {
  FakeClock(this.time);

  DateTime time;

  @override
  DateTime now() {
    return time;
  }
}

test('cleanup runs at 02:00', () async {
  Schedule s = Schedule(timezone: scheduleConfig.timezone);
  schedule(s);
  Scheduler scheduler = Scheduler(
    tasks: s.tasks,
    store: CacheStore(MemoryDriver()),
    clock: FakeClock(DateTime.utc(2026, 10, 25, 2)),
  );
  Map<String, TaskOutcome> outcomes = await scheduler.runDue();
  expect(outcomes['cleanup'], TaskOutcome.ran);
});

ScheduledTask.isDue(time) and ScheduledTask.nextRun(time) check a schedule with no run at all.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: This page shows how to test a Dox app with the test package: HTTP routes, cache, storage, env and the database.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
A new app from dox create already has the test package. In another app, add it as a dev dependency:

dart pub add dev:test

Put your tests in the test/ folder. Run them with:

dart test

To make a test file, run dox make:test Ping. It writes test/ping_test.dart with a DoxTestClient. Add --unit for a plain test that does not start the app. See dox make:test.

docs.title: Test HTTP routes
docs.text:
DoxTestClient from package:dox_core/testing.dart starts your app inside the test and sends requests to it.

test/http_test.dart
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
  });

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('GET /api/ping', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.get('/api/ping');
    res.expectStatus(200).expectBody('pong');
  });

  test('POST /api/posts', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.post(
      '/api/posts',
      body: <String, dynamic>{'title': 'Hello', 'body': 'My first post.'},
    );
    res.expectStatus(201).expectJson(containsPair('title', 'Hello'));
  });
}
  • DoxTestClient.start(appConfig) runs your providers (like the ORM provider) and adds your routes, the same as a real start.
  • It listens on 127.0.0.1 and a free port that the OS picks. So it does not clash with dox serve, and many test files can run at the same time.
  • It runs on one isolate. serverPort and totalIsolate of the config are not used.
  • client.close() stops the server and runs shutdown() of every provider (for example, it closes the database).
  • With one isolate, you can also add a route inside a test with Route.get(...). It works right away.

docs.title: Send requests
docs.text:
Method What it does get(path) GET. The path can have a query: '/api/users?page=2'. post(path, body: ...) POST. Also put, patch and delete. send('OPTIONS', path) any other method headers: {...} extra headers for one request withHeaders({...}) a copy of the client that sends these headers on every request withToken(token) a copy of the client that sends Authorization: Bearer <token> withSession() a copy of the client that keeps cookies and sends the CSRF token, like a browser. See Keep a session.

A Map or List body is sent as JSON. A String or List<int> body is sent as it is. Redirects are not followed, so you can check a 302 and its Location header.

docs.title: Check the response
docs.text:
Member What it gives res.status the status code, like 200 res.body the body as text res.json the body read as JSON res.header('content-type') one header (any case) res.headers all headers, with lower case names

The expect methods fail the test when the response is not right. They return the response, so you can chain them:

res
    .expectStatus(422)
    .expectHeader('content-type', contains('application/json'))
    .expectJson(<String, dynamic>{'title': 'The title is required'});
Method Fails when expectStatus(200) the status is another one. The message shows the body. expectJson(value or matcher) the JSON body does not match. Use a Map, or a matcher like containsPair('id', 1). expectBody(value or matcher) the text body does not match expectHeader(name, value or matcher) the header does not match. Use isNull for "not there".

docs.title: Keep a session (cookies and CSRF)
docs.text:
client.withSession() gives a client that works like a browser:

  • It keeps the cookies of every response and sends them back.
  • It removes a cookie when the response deletes it (an empty value, Max-Age=0 or an old Expires).
  • On POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE it sends the XSRF-TOKEN cookie in the X-XSRF-TOKEN header, like axios and Inertia. So CsrfMiddleware lets the request in.
  • It does not follow redirects, so you can check a 302 or 303.
test('log in with a form', () async {
  DoxTestClient browser = client.withSession();

  // the first page gives the session and XSRF-TOKEN cookies
  (await browser.get('/login')).expectStatus(200);

  (await browser.post(
    '/login',
    body: <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com', 'password': 'secret123'},
  )).expectStatus(303).expectHeader('location', '/dashboard');

  (await browser.get('/dashboard')).expectStatus(200);
});
  • Each withSession() call gives a new browser with no cookies.
  • browser.cookies has the kept cookies (name to raw value). You can read and change them.
  • A copy made from it (for example with withHeaders) shares its cookies.
  • The normal client keeps no cookies. To send cookies once, use withCookies(res.cookies).

docs.title: Log in as a user
docs.text:
Make a token, then send it with withToken:

TestResponse login = await client.post(
  '/api/auth/login',
  body: <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com', 'password': 'secret123'},
);
DoxTestClient ann = client.withToken(login.json['token'] as String);
(await ann.get('/api/auth/me')).expectStatus(200);

docs.title: Test the cache
docs.text:
Dox().cache is the CacheManager that Cache() uses. Replace it with a memory store, so tests do not write files or need Redis:

setUp(() {
  Dox().cache = CacheManager(CacheConfig(
    defaultStore: 'memory',
    stores: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
      'memory': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'memory'},
    },
  ));
});

test('caches the posts', () async {
  await Cache().put('posts', <String>['a', 'b']);
  expect(await Cache().get('posts'), <dynamic>['a', 'b']);
});

A new CacheManager in setUp gives each test an empty cache. See Cache.

docs.title: Test file storage
docs.text:
Storage.manager.fake(name) (from dox_storage) swaps one disk with an empty memory disk. restore(name) puts the real disk back.

setUpAll(() {
  Dox().initialize(appConfig);
});

test('saves the report', () async {
  Disk fake = Storage.manager.fake('s3');

  String path = await Storage()
      .disk('s3')
      .putFile('reports', <int>[1, 2, 3], extension: 'pdf'); // '/reports/<uuid>.pdf'

  expect(await fake.exists(path.substring(1)), isTrue);
  Storage.manager.restore('s3');
});
  • Call Dox().initialize() first. Without the StorageProvider running, Storage.manager has only the local disk. Start the app, or set the disks yourself: Storage.manager = StorageDiskFactory().create(storageConfig);.
  • Storage() paths start with /. A Disk key does not, so remove the first / when you ask the Disk directly.
  • A disk also has assertExists(key) and assertMissing(key), like await fake.assertExists('reports/a.pdf'). They throw a StateError when the check fails.

See File Storage.

docs.title: Use a test database with .env.testing
docs.text:
Put the values for tests in a .env.testing file, next to .env:

.env.testing
DB_NAME=my_app_test
CACHE_STORE=memory

When the app runs its tests, Dox reads .env first and then .env.testing. A key in .env.testing wins over the same key in .env. Keys that are only in .env stay.

  • "Runs its tests" means dart test, or a real APP_ENV=testing environment variable.
  • A real environment variable still wins over both files. So CI can run DB_NAME=ci_test dart test.
  • It works for Env.get() and for the typed AppEnv.load().
  • Outside tests, .env.testing is never read.

docs.title: Test the env
docs.text:
Pass your own values to AppEnv.load(). Then nothing is read from the shell or the .env file:

AppEnv env = AppEnv.load(
  EnvReader(
    environment: <String, String>{'APP_KEY': 'test'},
    dotEnv: <String, String>{'DB_PORT': '5433'},
  ),
);
expect(env.dbPort, 5433);

A missing or bad key throws an EnvException. So you can also test that your app stops on a bad env. See Environment Variables.

docs.title: Test the database
docs.text:
A test that uses models needs a real database. Run the migrations once in setUpAll. Then empty the tables before each test with refreshDatabase() from package:dox_orm/testing.dart:

test/user_test.dart
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    await Migrator(
      migrations: migrations,
      config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig(),
    ).migrate();
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig); // runs the ORM provider
  });

  // every test starts with empty tables
  setUp(refreshDatabase);

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('register makes a user', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.post(
      '/api/auth/register',
      body: <String, dynamic>{
        'name': 'Ann',
        'email': 'ann@example.com',
        'password': 'secret123',
      },
    );
    res.expectStatus(201);
  });
}
  • refreshDatabase() empties every table and starts the ids at 1 again. The tables stay. It keeps the rows of the migrations table (dox_db_migration).
  • It works on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite. Foreign keys are not checked while it empties the tables.
  • refreshDatabase(keep: <String>['dox_db_migration', 'countries']) keeps the rows of more tables.
  • Use a separate test database. Set its name in .env.testing, or in the env of the test run (DB_NAME=app_test dart test). Never run it on a database with real data.
  • A test without the server can start the ORM with SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig).

See Testing with a database for a full example with SQLite.

Run test files one by one

dart test runs test files at the same time. When two files use the same tables, run them one by one: dart test --concurrency=1.

docs.title: Add a package
docs.text:
dox add adds a Dox package to your app and sets it up.

dox add orm

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
1. Runs dart pub add dox_orm. orm is short for dox_orm. The full name works too.
  2. Runs dart pub get.
  3. Runs the setup command of the package, dox orm:install.

The setup command writes the config files, adds the keys to .env and .env.example, and runs build_runner when the package needs it. At the end it prints what it did and the next steps.

A package with no setup command is only added. dox add then says so.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Words after the name go to the setup command:

dox add orm --driver=postgres

--dev adds the package as a dev dependency.

docs.title: Safe to run twice
docs.text: The setup command never overwrites a file and never changes a .env key that is already there. So you can run dox add again. It only adds what is missing.

docs.title: Packages with a setup command
docs.text:
Command What it sets up dox add orm [--driver=sqlite\|postgres\|mysql] The ORM and migrations. See Database. dox add queue [--driver=database\|redis\|sync] Queued jobs and bin/queue.dart. database is the default and needs dox add orm first. See Queue. dox add scheduler Scheduled tasks and bin/schedule.dart. See Scheduler. dox add mailer [--transport=log\|smtp\|resend\|mailgun\|postmark\|ses] Mail. log is the default. See Mail. dox add cache [--store=file\|redis\|memory\|database] Cache stores. database needs dox add orm first. See Cache. dox add auth Access token auth. Needs dox add orm and a User model first. See Authentication. dox add storage [--disk=local\|s3] File storage. See File storage. dox add socketio [--broadcasting] Socket.IO, and broadcasting with the flag. See Socket.IO. dox add view Views and resources/views/. See Views. dox add inertia The server side of Inertia. It prints the Vite steps. See Inertia. dox add mcp An MCP server with a sample tool. See MCP.

The first dox add orm can download (or build) the Postgres and MySQL drivers once, also the one you do not use. After it, pubspec.yaml skips the unused drivers, so later builds do not get them.

To add a setup command to your own package, see Package commands.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
This page shows how to install the Dox CLI, make a new project and start the server.

Dox needs Dart 3.13 or newer.

docs.title: Install the CLI
docs.text:
dart pub global activate dox

Check that it works:

dox version

dox: command not found

The shell can not find the CLI when the pub bin folder is not in your PATH. Add this line to ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc, then open a new terminal:

export PATH="$PATH":"$HOME/.pub-cache/bin"

docs.title: Create a new project
docs.text:
dox create new_blog

dox create downloads the newest release of dox-sample, the starter project. To get one exact release, add --version with a release tag of dox-sample.

It also makes your .env file from .env.example, with a new random APP_KEY. Then get the packages:

cd new_blog
dart pub get

The starter project uses SQLite, so there is no database to install. The file db/dox.sqlite is created at the first start. To use Postgres or MySQL instead, change DB_CONNECTION and the DB_* values in .env. See Database.

Add Dox to an existing Dart project

Add the packages you need with dart pub add:

dart pub add dox_core dox_orm dox_migration
dart pub add dev:dox_builder dev:build_runner

docs.title: Start the server
docs.text:
dox s

dox s does two things:

  • It runs dart run build_runner watch, so generated files stay up to date.
  • It runs dart run bin/server.dart, and restarts it when a .dart file changes.

To skip the builder, use dox s --ignore-build-runner. To start the server without the CLI, run dart run bin/server.dart.

At each start it also runs the new migrations in db/migration. The server uses the port in APP_PORT in the .env file (3000 by default). Check it:

curl localhost:3000/ping

pong

docs.title: Start the server with Docker
docs.text:
docker compose up -d --build

This starts the app, a queue worker and a Postgres database. The app and the worker always use the Postgres service. They set DB_CONNECTION and DB_NAME themselves. The database port is open on this machine only (127.0.0.1), not on the network. To start only the database and run the app with dox s, use docker compose up -d postgres. Then set DB_CONNECTION=postgres and DB_NAME=dox in .env.

Production

Do not use dox s or dart run in production. Build a native binary with dox build. See Deployment.

docs.title: Run the code generator
docs.text:
Dox makes code for models and DTOs with build_runner. dox s already runs it. To run it alone:

dox build_runner:watch   # runs again on every file change
dox build_runner:build   # runs once

docs.title: AI agents
docs.text:
The Dox packages ship skills for AI coding agents. A skill tells the agent how to use the real API of a package. Install them in your app, after dart pub get:

dart run skills@ get

It finds the skills of your dependencies and installs them for your agent. It works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot and others. Run it again after you add a package or update one. It only reads the packages listed in your own pubspec.yaml. To get the skill of a package that comes in through another one (like ioredis), add it to pubspec.yaml. See skills for the options.

The starter project also has an AGENTS.md file with the rules of the project.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text: Package What it does dox the CLI dox_core HTTP server, routing, requests, responses, validation dox_orm query builder and models dox_migration database migrations dox_auth Login with access tokens, JWT or sessions dox_builder, dox_annotation code generation for models, DTOs and the container dox_validation typed validation schemas dox_openapi OpenAPI docs dox_storage file storage: local, S3 dox_cache cache: memory, file, Redis dox_cache_database cache in a database table dox_socketio Socket.IO server dox_queue background jobs dox_queue_database queue in a database table dox_scheduler scheduled tasks dox_mailer send email dox_view HTML views dox_inertia Inertia.js pages dox_http_native native HTTP server (Rust) dox_postgres_native, dox_mysql_native native drivers for Postgres and MySQL/MariaDB

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
Each guide solves one job from start to end: copy the files, run the commands, and check the result.

The reference pages explain each part in more detail. The guides link to them.

Guide What you get File upload Accept an image, check its size and type, save it, return its URL. Pagination A list route with page and per_page, and the JSON shape it returns. JWT authentication Register, log in, protect routes, read the user, log out. Custom errors Your own exception classes, one JSON shape for every error, logging. Background work Run work after the response, on another thread, in a queue job, or on a schedule. Static files and SPA Serve a folder or a single page app, with cache headers. CORS for a browser front-end The CORS setup that works with a React, Vue or Flutter web app. Environments Dev, staging and production config, .env files, secrets and APP_KEY. Testing with a database Tests on SQLite or a test Postgres, with migrations and cleanup. Share code with Flutter One DTO package that the server and the Flutter app both use to check input. API docs with OpenAPI A docs page for your API, made from your routes, DTOs and models. Docker A small production image, Postgres in Docker Compose, env and a health check. Deploy to a Linux server Your own server with systemd, and Caddy in front for HTTPS. Deploy to Fly.io Fly.io from your Dockerfile, with SQLite on a volume or with Postgres. Deploy to Google Cloud Run Cloud Run from your Dockerfile, with Cloud SQL and Secret Manager.

Most guides use the app that dox create my_app makes. The package name is my_app. Change it to your own package name in the imports. The OpenAPI guide and the deploy guides use the blog API of the tutorial. Its package name is blog.

The code of the app guides is in one app on GitHub: examples/guides. The blog API is in examples/blog-api. CI builds both and runs their tests on every push, so the code on these pages keeps working.

docs.title: API docs with OpenAPI
docs.text: Turn on OpenAPI docs for the blog API, open the docs page, and make the docs better with comments and annotations.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• The blog API from the tutorial, or any Dox app.
  • build_runner and dox_builder. A new app has both. dox_core already has dox_openapi, so you add no package.

docs.title: 1. Write the config
docs.text:
build_runner writes lib/generated/openapi.g.dart. Its openApiRegistry holds what the builder found in your routes, controllers, DTOs and models. Pass it to an OpenApiConfig:

lib/config/openapi.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:blog/generated/openapi.g.dart';

OpenApiConfig openApi = OpenApiConfig(
  info: Info(title: 'Blog API', version: '1.0.0'),
  registry: openApiRegistry,
);

Add it to AppConfig:

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:blog/config/openapi.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  /// OpenAPI docs (config/openapi.dart)
  openApi: openApi,
);

docs.title: 2. Build and start
docs.text:
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
dox serve

.env has APP_ENV=development, so the docs routes are on.

docs.title: 3. Open the docs page
docs.text:
Open http://localhost:3000/docs. It is a Scalar page with every route and "Try it" buttons. It loads Scalar from the jsDelivr CDN.

The app now has three new routes:

Route What it gives GET /docs the Scalar docs page (HTML) GET /openapi.json the OpenAPI 3.1 document as JSON GET /openapi.yaml the same document as YAML

docs.title: 4. Read the JSON
docs.text:
curl http://localhost:3000/openapi.json

This is the real output for the blog API, shortened. The top level:

{
  "openapi": "3.1.0",
  "info": {"title": "Blog API", "version": "1.0.0"},
  "paths": {
    "/api/ping": {},
    "/api/posts": {},
    "/api/posts/{id}": {},
    "/api/auth/register": {},
    "/api/auth/login": {},
    "/api/auth/user": {},
    "/ping": {}
  },
  "components": {
    "schemas": {"Post": {}, "SavePost": {}, "RegisterUser": {}, "LoginUser": {}, "User": {}, "ValidationError": {}},
    "securitySchemes": {
      "bearerAuth": {"type": "http", "scheme": "bearer"}
    }
  }
}

POST /api/posts, as the builder found it. You wrote no docs code for it:

{
  "tags": ["Post"],
  "summary": "POST /api/posts",
  "operationId": "PostController.store",
  "requestBody": {
    "required": true,
    "content": {"application/json": {"schema": {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/SavePost"}}}
  },
  "responses": {
    "200": {"description": "Successful response"},
    "401": {
      "description": "Not logged in",
      "content": {"application/json": {"schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"code": {"type": "string"}, "message": {"type": "string"}}}}}
    },
    "422": {
      "description": "Validation failed",
      "content": {"application/json": {"schema": {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/ValidationError"}}}
    },
    "500": {"description": "Server error"}
  },
  "security": [{"bearerAuth": []}],
  "x-dox-middleware": ["LogMiddleware", "AuthMiddleware"]
}

Where each part comes from:

Part Comes from tags: ["Post"] the class name PostController, without Controller summary the first line of the /// comment: /// POST /api/posts requestBody the argument SavePost body of store 401 and bearerAuth AuthMiddleware on the route 422 the route has a request class 200 with no body store returns DoxResponse, so the builder can not see the body. Step 6 fixes this x-dox-middleware the middleware of the route: the global LogMiddleware and AuthMiddleware

Other routes get more error answers in the same way. The Can middleware or a req.authorize(...) call gives 401 and 403. The GuestMiddleware and ValidateSignature middleware give 403. A req.validateSchema(...) call gives 422.

docs.title: 5. See how a DTO becomes a schema
docs.text:
This is the SavePost DTO of the tutorial:

lib/app/dtos/save_post/save_post.dto.dart
@Dto()
class SavePost {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 3, max: 100)
  final String title;

  @Trim()
  @MinLength(10)
  final String body;

  const SavePost({required this.title, required this.body});

  static const DtoSchema<SavePost> schema = $SavePostDto;
}

And this is its schema in /openapi.json:

"SavePost": {
  "type": "object",
  "title": "SavePost",
  "properties": {
    "title": {"type": "string", "minLength": 3, "maxLength": 100},
    "body": {"type": "string", "minLength": 10}
  },
  "required": ["title", "body"]
}
In the DTO In the schema String title (not nullable) "type": "string" and title in required @Length(min: 3, max: 100) "minLength": 3, "maxLength": 100 @MinLength(10) "minLength": 10 @Email() (in RegisterUser) "format": "email" /// A comment or @Describe('...') "description". @Describe wins over the comment @Trim(), @Lowercase(), @Unique(...) nothing. They change or check the value on the server only

A model becomes a schema too. Post has id, the @Column fields title and body, and created_at and updated_at. Keys in hidden are left out. That is why User has no password.

When you change a rule, run build_runner again, and the docs change with it.

docs.title: 6. Make the docs better
docs.text:
Write a /// comment on a controller method. The first line is the summary. The rest is the description. Add @Tags and @Response (from dox_core) when the automatic result is not what you want.

lib/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart
@Inject()
class PostController {
  /// List all posts
  ///
  /// Newest posts are not first. There is no paging yet.
  Future<List<Post>> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Post().all();
  }

  /// Create a post
  @Tags(<String>['Posts'])
  @Response(201, Post, description: 'The new post')
  Future<DoxResponse> store(SavePost body) async {
    Post post = Post()
      ..title = body.title
      ..body = body.body;
    await post.save();
    return response(post).statusCode(201);
  }

  // ...
}

Run dart run build_runner build again and restart the app. The real result:

"get": {
  "tags": ["Post"],
  "summary": "List all posts",
  "description": "Newest posts are not first. There is no paging yet.",
  "operationId": "PostController.index",
  "responses": {
    "200": {
      "description": "Successful response",
      "content": {"application/json": {"schema": {"type": "array", "items": {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/Post"}}}}
    },
    "500": {}
  }
},
"post": {
  "tags": ["Posts"],
  "summary": "Create a post",
  "operationId": "PostController.store",
  "responses": {
    "201": {
      "description": "The new post",
      "content": {"application/json": {"schema": {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/Post"}}}
    },
    "401": {},
    "422": {},
    "500": {}
  }
}
  • @Response(201, Post) replaces the empty 200. The docs now match the real status code.
  • @Tags(['Posts']) moves the route to the group "Posts" in the docs page.
  • @Summary('...') and @Description('...') set the text without a /// comment.
  • @ApiIgnore() leaves a method (or a whole controller) out of the docs.

See OpenAPI: change the docs for all annotations.

docs.title: 7. Turn it off in production
docs.text:
This is the default. enabled is null, so the docs routes are on only when APP_ENV is development or local. With APP_ENV=production all three routes give 404:

curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost:3000/docs           # 404
curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost:3000/openapi.json   # 404

To show the docs on staging too, but never in production, set enabled yourself:

lib/config/openapi.dart
import 'package:blog/config/env.dart';

OpenApiConfig openApi = OpenApiConfig(
  enabled: env.appEnv != 'production',
  info: Info(title: 'Blog API', version: '1.0.0'),
  registry: openApiRegistry,
);

Warning

enabled: true in production shows every route of your API to anyone. Only do it for a public API.

To give the document to a front-end team without a running server, write it to files with dox openapi:generate. See OpenAPI: write the files.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
curl -s http://localhost:3000/openapi.json | head -n 5

{
  "openapi": "3.1.0",
  "info": {
    "title": "Blog API",
    "version": "1.0.0"

Open http://localhost:3000/docs, find "Create a post" under "Posts", and send a request with "Try it".

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• OpenAPI for all options, the Scalar look, Swagger UI and login schemes
  • Validation rules for the rules and their JSON Schema keys
  • Environments for APP_ENV

docs.title: Background work
docs.text: Answer the request now and do the slow work later: after the response, on another thread, in a queue, or on a timer.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • A Dox app (dox create my_app). A new app has the queue (dox_queue) and the scheduler (dox_scheduler) set up.

docs.title: Pick the right tool
docs.text: You want Use Runs where Lost when the process stops small I/O work after the response (a log line, a cache update) a Future you do not await the same isolate, between requests yes CPU work (resize an image, parse a big file, compute) Isolate.run() a new thread yes work that must not get lost (an email, a payment call), with retries a queue job the queue worker process no work every N minutes (cleanup, sync) a scheduled task the schedule process it runs again at the next tick

docs.title: 1. Work after the response
docs.text:
Start the future and return. unawaited tells the linter you did this on purpose. An error in the future goes to the report method of the ExceptionHandler in AppConfig.

This file has the code of steps 1, 2 and 3:

lib/app/http/controllers/report.controller.dart
import 'dart:async';
import 'dart:isolate';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
