import 'package:my_app/app/jobs/build_report.job.dart';

@Inject()
class ReportController {
  /// POST /api/reports
  /// Answers at once. The work runs after the response, in this isolate.
  Map<String, String> store(DoxRequest req) {
    String id = DateTime.now().microsecondsSinceEpoch.toString();
    unawaited(_build(id));
    return <String, String>{'id': id, 'status': 'queued'};
  }

  /// POST /api/reports/queued
  /// Saves a job in the jobs table and answers at once.
  /// The queue worker (`dox queue:work`) runs it, and tries again when
  /// it fails. The job is not lost when the server stops.
  Future<Map<String, String>> queue(DoxRequest req) async {
    String id = DateTime.now().microsecondsSinceEpoch.toString();
    String jobId = await BuildReport(reportId: id).dispatch();
    return <String, String>{'id': id, 'job': jobId, 'status': 'queued'};
  }

  /// I/O work (database, HTTP calls, email) is fine here. It shares the
  /// event loop with the requests, so it must not block the CPU.
  Future<void> _build(String id) async {
    await Future<void>.delayed(const Duration(seconds: 2));
    print('report $id is ready');
  }

  /// GET /api/primes/{limit}
  /// CPU work runs on another thread with `Isolate.run`.
  /// The request waits for the result, but other requests are not blocked.
  Future<Map<String, int>> primes(int limit) async {
    int count = await Isolate.run(() => countPrimes(limit));
    return <String, int>{'limit': limit, 'primes': count};
  }
}

/// Must be a top level or static function with plain arguments.
/// The new isolate has no Dox, no database and no providers.
int countPrimes(int limit) {
  List<bool> sieve = List<bool>.filled(limit + 1, true);
  int count = 0;
  for (int i = 2; i <= limit; i++) {
    if (!sieve[i]) continue;
    count++;
    for (int j = i * i; j <= limit; j += i) {
      sieve[j] = false;
    }
  }
  return count;
}

Do not block the event loop

_build shares the thread with the requests of this isolate. A long loop makes them all wait. Put a long loop in Isolate.run.

docs.title: 2. CPU work on another thread
docs.text:
Isolate.run runs the function on a new isolate and sends the result back. Pass plain data in (an int, a String, bytes) and get plain data out. Save the result in the request isolate.

primes above waits for the result. To not wait, combine both patterns:

unawaited(Isolate.run(() => countPrimes(limit)).then(saveResult));

docs.title: 3. A job that must not get lost
docs.text:
A future you do not await is gone when the server stops, and it does not retry. For work that must happen, use a queue job. dispatch() saves the job in the database. A worker process takes it and runs handle(). A failed job is tried again.

Make the job:

dox make:job BuildReport
lib/app/jobs/build_report.job.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';

/// Builds a report in the queue worker.
/// Dispatch it: `await BuildReport(reportId: id).dispatch();`
@Job()
class BuildReport extends DoxJob {
  BuildReport({required this.reportId});

  final String reportId;

  /// try 3 times, wait 10 seconds between tries
  @override
  int get tries => 3;

  @override
  List<Duration> get backoff => const <Duration>[Duration(seconds: 10)];

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    Logger.info('report $reportId is ready');
  }
}

The fields of the job (reportId) are saved with it. Use plain values like String, int, bool, DateTime, lists and maps. Save an id, not a model: load the model in handle(). Run dart run build_runner build after you add or change a job. It updates lib/generated/jobs.g.dart.

The queue method of the controller above dispatches it. dispatch() returns the id of the job.

A new app uses the database driver (lib/config/queue.dart). It comes from the dox_queue_database package, which the queue provider registers. Its jobs tables come from the migration db/migration/..._create_queue_tables.dart. The server runs it at start.

Start the worker next to the server, in a second terminal:

dox queue:work

dox queue:failed lists the jobs that failed every try. dox queue:retry all puts them back on the queue. See Queue for Redis, delays and all worker flags.

docs.title: 4. Work on a timer
docs.text:
Put the task in lib/config/schedule.dart. A new app has this file with an empty schedule function.

lib/config/schedule.dart
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

/// `inProcess: false`: run `dox schedule:work` next to the server.
ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig();

/// The tasks. `dox schedule:list` shows them.
void schedule(Schedule s) {
  s.call('cleanup', cleanupUsers).hourly();
}

/// Removes the users that were soft deleted more than 30 days ago.
Future<void> cleanupUsers() async {
  DateTime limit = DateTime.now().subtract(const Duration(days: 30));
  List<User> old = await User()
      .withTrash()
      .where('deleted_at', '<', limit)
      .get();
  int removed = 0;
  for (User user in old) {
    removed += await user.forceDelete();
  }
  print('cleanup: removed $removed users');
}

Start the scheduler next to the server, in a third terminal:

dox schedule:work

dox schedule:list shows each task and its next run. dox schedule:test cleanup runs the task now.

The scheduler runs each task once per tick, also when many processes run the schedule. With many servers, use a Redis cache store for the lock (ScheduleConfig(store: 'redis')). For a small app, you can run the schedule inside the server. See Scheduler: run inside the server.

docs.title: 5. Add the routes
Check it
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/reports

The answer comes at once:

{"id":"1792677668393002","status":"queued"}

Two seconds later, the server prints report 1792677668393002 is ready.

curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/reports/queued

{"id":"1792677670112345","job":"9f2c4e1a7b3d5f60a1c2e3f4a5b6c7d8","status":"queued"}

The terminal of dox queue:work shows a log line with report 1792677670112345 is ready. Stop the worker first, and the job waits in the jobs table until the worker runs again.

curl http://localhost:3000/api/primes/100000

{"limit":100000,"primes":9592}

  • Scheduler for every frequency, time zones and hooks
  • Isolate for what each isolate shares, and what it does not

docs.title: CORS for a browser front-end
docs.text: Let a web app on another origin (http://localhost:5173 in development, https://my.app in production) call your API.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app.
  • A front-end that runs on its own origin, like Vite, Next.js or Flutter web.

docs.title: 1. Write the config
docs.text:
A new app already has lib/config/cors.dart, with enabled: false. Replace the whole file with this one:

lib/config/cors.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

/// `enabled` is true by default, so every route sends the headers.
CORSConfig cors = CORSConfig(
  /// One origin, or a list of origins. Set CORS_ORIGIN to the real
  /// front-end URL in production.
  origin: env.corsOrigin,

  methods: <String>['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'PATCH', 'DELETE'],

  /// the request headers the front-end sends
  headers: <String>['Content-Type', 'Authorization'],

  /// the response headers the front-end may read
  exposeHeaders: <String>['Content-Disposition'],

  /// true only when the front-end sends cookies. Not needed for a
  /// `Authorization: Bearer` token.
  credentials: false,

  /// the browser keeps the preflight answer for 10 minutes
  maxAge: 600,
);

AppConfig in lib/config/app.dart already passes it on with cors: cors.

docs.title: 2. Set the origin per environment
docs.text:
CORS_ORIGIN is a new key. Add a getter for it to the AppEnv class:

lib/config/env.dart
  /// the front-end URL that may call the API
  String get corsOrigin => 'http://localhost:5173';

Run dart run build_runner build to update env.g.dart. Then set the value in .env:

.env
CORS_ORIGIN=http://localhost:5173

In staging and production, set CORS_ORIGIN as a real environment variable: https://my.app. The origin is scheme, host and port. No path, no / at the end.

docs.title: 3. Choose credentials
docs.text:
Your front-end sends origin credentials a token in Authorization: Bearer (see JWT authentication) your front-end URL false cookies (fetch(url, {credentials: 'include'})) your front-end URL, never * true nothing, a public API '*' false

Two or more front-ends

Set origin to a list, like ['https://a.com', 'https://b.com']. Dox compares the Origin header of the request with the list. It sends back only the origin that matches, with Vary: Origin. If none matches, it sends no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, and the browser blocks the call.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
The browser sends a preflight OPTIONS request before a POST with JSON or a custom header. Dox answers it by itself. You do not need an OPTIONS route.

curl -i -X OPTIONS http://localhost:3000/api/users \
  -H 'Origin: http://localhost:5173' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: POST' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: Authorization'

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
access-control-allow-origin: http://localhost:5173
access-control-allow-methods: GET,POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE
access-control-allow-headers: Content-Type,Authorization
access-control-expose-headers: Content-Disposition
access-control-allow-credentials: false
access-control-max-age: 600

A normal request gets the origin header too:

curl -i http://localhost:3000/api/ping -H 'Origin: http://localhost:5173' | grep -i access-control-allow-origin

access-control-allow-origin: http://localhost:5173

In the browser, open the front-end and call the API with fetch. The console shows no CORS error.

docs.title: When it still fails
docs.text: The console says The fix No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header CORS_ORIGIN does not match the page origin exactly. Check http or https, and the port. The value of ... header is 'a.com,b.com' origin is one text with commas. Use a List<String> instead. Request header field x-foo is not allowed Add the header to headers. credentials mode is 'include' with * Set origin to the front-end URL and credentials: true.

docs.title: Webhooks and server-to-server calls
docs.text:
CORS only matters for browsers. A webhook from Stripe or a call from another server ignores these headers. Turn CORS off for such routes to send fewer headers:

Route.disabledCors(() {
  Route.post('/webhooks/stripe', (WebhookController c) => c.handle);
});

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• CORS for every option
  • JWT authentication

docs.title: Custom errors
docs.text: Give your app its own exception classes, send every error in one JSON shape, and log the unexpected ones.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • A Dox app.

docs.title: How Dox handles an error
docs.text:
When a controller or a middleware throws:

Error Status What Dox does an IHttpException, like NotFoundHttpException its code sends {"code": ..., "message": ...}. Does not call report a validation error (bad DTO input) 422 sends the field errors: {"field": "message"}. Does not call report any other Exception or Error 500 sends {"code":"server_error","message":"Server Error"}. When APP_ENV is development or local, it sends the error text. Calls report

report is a method of the exception handler. The response goes through the responseHandler of AppConfig last. This guide sets the shape there.

docs.title: 1. Write your own exceptions
docs.text:
For a quick error, use abort(403) or abort(409, 'The email is taken'). See HTTP exceptions. For errors you throw in many places, write a class.

Extend IHttpException. Set code (the HTTP status), errorCode (a short text for the client) and message.

lib/app/exceptions/app_exception.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// 409. Thrown when the row already exists or was changed by someone else.
class ConflictException extends IHttpException {
  ConflictException({String message = 'Conflict'}) {
    super.code = HttpStatus.conflict;
    super.errorCode = 'conflict';
    super.message = message;
  }
}

Throw them anywhere in a controller, a middleware or a service:

lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/exceptions/app_exception.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class UserController {
  /// GET /api/users/{id}
  Future<User> show(int id) async {
    User? user = await User().find(id);
    if (user == null) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException(message: 'User $id not found');
    }
    return user;
  }

  /// DELETE /api/users/{id}
  Future<Map<String, bool>> destroy(int id) async {
    if (id == 1) {
      throw ForbiddenHttpException(message: 'The first user can not be deleted');
    }
    User user = await show(id);

    /// 0 rows: the user was deleted after show() found it
    if (await user.delete() == 0) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException(message: 'User $id not found');
    }
    return <String, bool>{'deleted': true};
  }
}

docs.title: 2. One JSON shape for every error
docs.text:
The response handler sees every response before it is sent. For an error, the content is the exception object. Turn it into your shape here.

lib/app/http/response_handler.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// Gives every error the same JSON shape:
/// `{"error": {"code": "not_found", "message": "..."}}`.
/// A validation error (422) also has `"errors": {field: message}`.
class ResponseHandler extends ResponseHandlerInterface {
  @override
  DoxResponse handle(DoxResponse res) {
    dynamic content = res.getContent();

    if (content is ValidationException) {
      return res.statusCode(content.code).content(<String, dynamic>{
        'error': <String, dynamic>{
          'code': content.errorCode,
          'message': 'The input is not valid',
        },
        'errors': content.message,
      });
    }

    if (content is IHttpException) {
      return res.statusCode(content.code).content(<String, dynamic>{
        'error': <String, dynamic>{
          'code': content.errorCode,
          'message': content.message.toString(),
        },
      });
    }

    // any other exception: hide the details from the client
    if (content is Exception || content is Error) {
      return res.statusCode(HttpStatus.internalServerError).content(
        <String, dynamic>{
          'error': <String, String>{
            'code': 'server_error',
            'message': 'Something went wrong',
          },
        },
      );
    }

    return res;
  }
}

The last if gives a 500 your shape too, in every environment. Without it, the client gets the default body. When APP_ENV is development or local, that is the error text. It can show a SQL query or a file path.

docs.title: 3. Log unexpected errors
docs.text:
The report method of the exception handler runs for every 500, and for errors outside a request (a future nobody awaited, a timer).

lib/app/error_handler.dart
import 'dart:convert';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// Dox calls [report] for every unexpected error (a `500`, or an error
/// outside a request). It does not run for `IHttpException` errors
/// like `404` or `422`, because those are expected.
/// One JSON line per error. Send it to Sentry or Datadog from here.
class AppExceptionHandler extends ExceptionHandler {
  const AppExceptionHandler();

  @override
  void report(Object error, StackTrace stackTrace) {
    print(
      jsonEncode(<String, String>{
        'timestamp': DateTime.now().toIso8601String(),
        'status': 'error',
        'message': error.toString(),
        'error': <String, String>{'stack': stackTrace.toString()},
      }),
    );
  }
}

docs.title: 4. Register both
Check it
docs.text:
Add a route that throws, only for this check:

Route.get('/boom', (DoxRequest req) => throw StateError('boom'));
Request Status Body GET /api/users/999 404 {"error":{"code":"not_found","message":"User 999 not found"}} GET /api/users/abc 404 {"error":{"code":"not_found","message":"Not Found"}} DELETE /api/users/1 403 {"error":{"code":"forbidden","message":"The first user can not be deleted"}} POST /api/auth/register with {} 422 {"error":{"code":"validation_failed","message":"The input is not valid"},"errors":{"name":"The name is required", ...}} GET /api/boom 500 {"error":{"code":"server_error","message":"Something went wrong"}}

After GET /api/boom, the server prints one line:

{"timestamp":"2026-10-22T14:01:12.000Z","status":"error","message":"Bad state: boom","error":{"stack":"#0  ApiRouter.register.<anonymous closure> (package:my_app/routes/api.dart:41:44) ..."}}

Remove the /boom route when you are done.

A URL with no route

A URL that matches no route is a NotFoundHttpException with the message GET /nothing not found. It goes through the response handler too, so it gets the same JSON shape: {"error":{"code":"not_found","message":"GET /nothing not found"}}.

docs.text:

  • Response: change every response
  • Validation: the error response
  • Isolate: when an isolate crashes

docs.title: Deploy to Google Cloud Run
docs.text:
Run the blog API on Cloud Run from the Dockerfile of your project, with Postgres on Cloud SQL and secrets in Secret Manager.

Note

These steps follow the Cloud Run docs as of 2026-10-22. They were not run on Cloud Run in CI.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Google Cloud project with billing, and the gcloud CLI (gcloud auth login, gcloud config set project PROJECT_ID).
  • The blog API from the tutorial, or any Dox app, with the Dockerfile of a new Dox app. See Docker for how that file works.
  • A Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance with a database and a user. See step 3.

docs.title: The port: PORT and APP_PORT
docs.text:
Cloud Run puts the port it sends requests to in the PORT env variable (default 8080, or the --port value). Dox listens on APP_PORT, or on PORT when APP_PORT is not set. So do not set APP_PORT on Cloud Run.

If you do set APP_PORT, pass the same port with --port.

docs.title: 1. Turn on the APIs
docs.text:
gcloud services enable run.googleapis.com cloudbuild.googleapis.com \
  artifactregistry.googleapis.com secretmanager.googleapis.com sqladmin.googleapis.com

docs.title: 2. Save the secrets in Secret Manager
docs.text:
openssl rand -hex 16 | tr -d '\n' | gcloud secrets create blog-app-key --data-file=-
printf '%s' '<the database password>' | gcloud secrets create blog-db-password --data-file=-

Let the Cloud Run service account read them. By default this is the Compute Engine service account, PROJECT_NUMBER-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com:

for s in blog-app-key blog-db-password; do
  gcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding "$s" \
    --member="serviceAccount:PROJECT_NUMBER-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com" \
    --role="roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor"
done

docs.title: 3. Reach Cloud SQL
docs.text:
Cloud Run reaches Cloud SQL by a Unix socket in /cloudsql/... or by a private IP over a VPC. Dox can use both. This guide uses the socket, because it needs no VPC:

  1. Find the connection name of the instance: gcloud sql instances describe INSTANCE --format='value(connectionName)'. It looks like PROJECT_ID:europe-west1:INSTANCE.
  2. Deploy with --add-cloudsql-instances <connection name> (step 4). Cloud Run then makes the socket in /cloudsql/<connection name>.
  3. Give the service account the roles/cloudsql.client role.
  4. Set DB_HOST=/cloudsql/<connection name>. A host that starts with / is a Unix socket. See Unix socket.

The same with one url: DATABASE_URL=postgres://blog:<password>@/blog?host=/cloudsql/<connection name>.

For Cloud SQL for MySQL, use the same DB_HOST with DB_CONNECTION=mysql. Leave out DB_PORT. Or use one url: DATABASE_URL=mysql://blog:<password>@/blog?socket=/cloudsql/<connection name>.

To use the private IP instead: give the instance a private IP on your VPC network, deploy with Direct VPC egress (--network default --subnet default --vpc-egress private-ranges-only), and use the private IP as DB_HOST.

Do not use SQLite on Cloud Run. The file system of an instance is in memory, and each instance has its own. The data is lost when the instance stops.

docs.title: 4. Deploy from source
docs.text:
--source . uploads the folder. Cloud Build builds the image with your Dockerfile and saves it in Artifact Registry (repository cloud-run-source-deploy).

gcloud run deploy blog \
  --source . \
  --region europe-west1 \
  --port 3000 \
  --allow-unauthenticated \
  --cpu 1 --memory 512Mi \
  --min-instances 1 \
  --add-cloudsql-instances PROJECT_ID:europe-west1:INSTANCE \
  --set-env-vars APP_ENV=production,APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE=1,DB_CONNECTION=postgres,DB_HOST=/cloudsql/PROJECT_ID:europe-west1:INSTANCE,DB_PORT=5432,DB_NAME=blog,DB_USERNAME=blog \
  --set-secrets APP_KEY=blog-app-key:1,DB_PASSWORD=blog-db-password:1
Flag Why --port 3000 the port Cloud Run sends requests to. It also sets PORT=3000, and Dox listens on PORT. See the port --min-instances 1 keeps one instance warm, so the first request does not wait for a cold start. The default is 0. An idle instance still costs money --add-cloudsql-instances makes the Cloud SQL Unix socket in /cloudsql/... --set-env-vars config that is not secret --set-secrets ENV_NAME=SECRET:VERSION. Cloud Run reads the secret when an instance starts. Pin a version number, not latest APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE=1 one isolate per CPU. Set it to the --cpu value

To build the image yourself instead, push it to Artifact Registry and deploy it with --image:

docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT_ID/blog/api:1 .
docker push europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT_ID/blog/api:1
gcloud run deploy blog --image europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT_ID/blog/api:1 --region europe-west1 --port 3000 ...

Use the same other flags as above.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
gcloud run deploy prints the service URL at the end.

curl https://blog-xxxxxxxx-ew.a.run.app/api/ping

pong

gcloud run services logs read blog --region europe-west1 --limit 20
gcloud beta run services logs tail blog --region europe-west1   # live, needs the log-streaming component

The first log lines after the first start:

Migrating: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrated: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrating: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
Migrated: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
{"timestamp":"...","status":"info","message":"Server started at http://[::]:3000 with 1 isolate (native)","logger":{"name":"dox"}}

If the deploy fails with "the container did not listen on the port", the app listens on a different port than --port. Check APP_PORT and --port.

docs.title: HTTPS and the client IP
docs.text:
Cloud Run ends TLS and sends plain HTTP to the container. Only the Cloud Run front end can reach the container port. So ['*'] in trustedProxies is safe, and req.ip() and req.scheme() then show the real client:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  trustedProxies: <String>['*'],
);

See Deployment: HTTPS.

docs.title: Update the app
docs.text:
gcloud run deploy blog --source . --region europe-west1
  • Cloud Run keeps the flags of the last revision. You only pass what changes.
  • A new revision starts, runs new migrations, and takes the traffic when it listens on the port. The old one then stops.
  • When many instances start at the same time, each one runs the migrations. Keep migrations safe to run twice, or run one instance during a deploy with a migration.
  • A new secret version: create it with gcloud secrets versions add, then deploy with the new number in --update-secrets APP_KEY=blog-app-key:2.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Deployment for the bundle and the Dockerfile
  • Environments for all env keys and APP_KEY
  • Docker for a health check binary and Docker Compose
  • Cloud Run docs: container contract, deploy from source, secrets, minimum instances, Cloud SQL

docs.title: Deploy to Fly.io
docs.text:
Run the blog API on Fly.io from the Dockerfile of your project, with SQLite on a volume or with Postgres.

Note

These steps follow the Fly.io docs as of 2026-10-22. They were not run on Fly.io in CI.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Fly.io account and the fly CLI (fly auth login).
  • The blog API from the tutorial, or any Dox app, with the Dockerfile of a new Dox app. See Docker for how that file works.

docs.title: 1. Make the app on Fly.io
docs.text:
In the project folder:

fly launch --no-deploy

fly launch finds the Dockerfile, asks for an app name and a region, and writes fly.toml. --no-deploy stops before the first deploy, so you can set the config first.

docs.title: 2. Write fly.toml
docs.text:
Replace the file with this one. Change app and primary_region to your values.

fly.toml
app = "blog-api"
primary_region = "ams"
# Dox waits up to 8 seconds for open requests on stop. Fly waits 5 by default.
kill_timeout = 10

[build]
  dockerfile = "Dockerfile"

# config that is not secret. Secrets come from `fly secrets set`.
[env]
  APP_ENV = "production"
  APP_PORT = "3000"
  DB_CONNECTION = "sqlite"
  DB_NAME = "/data/blog.sqlite"

[http_service]
  internal_port = 3000
  force_https = true
  # one machine, always on: the SQLite file is on its volume
  auto_stop_machines = "off"
  auto_start_machines = true
  min_machines_running = 1

  [[http_service.checks]]
    grace_period = "10s"
    interval = "30s"
    method = "GET"
    timeout = "5s"
    path = "/api/ping"

# the volume with the SQLite file
[mounts]
  source = "blog_data"
  destination = "/data"

[[vm]]
  memory = "256mb"
  cpu_kind = "shared"
  cpus = 1
  • internal_port is the port the app listens on. Dox reads it from APP_PORT (or PORT when APP_PORT is not set). Keep the two the same.
  • Values in [env] must be strings, so write "3000", not 3000.
  • [[vm]] wins over fly scale vm. Each fly deploy sets the machine to these values.
  • kill_timeout: keep it above shutdownTimeout of AppConfig. See Graceful shutdown.

docs.title: 3. Set the secrets
docs.text:
fly secrets set APP_KEY=<output of dox key:generate>

A secret is an environment variable on every machine of the app. fly secrets list shows the names, not the values. A secret with the same name as an [env] key wins.

docs.title: SQLite on a volume
docs.text:
Make the volume that [mounts] asks for, in the same region:

fly volumes create blog_data --region ams --size 1
  • One volume is attached to one machine only. Fly.io does not copy the data between volumes.
  • So with SQLite, run exactly one machine.

docs.title: Postgres
docs.text:
Create a Managed Postgres cluster with fly mpg create, and attach it to the app:

fly mpg attach <cluster-id> --app blog-api

This sets the secret DATABASE_URL. It wins over the DB_* keys, for the app and the migrations. See DATABASE_URL.

Then delete DB_CONNECTION and DB_NAME from [env], and delete the [mounts] section. If the database asks for TLS, add ?sslmode=require to the url with fly secrets set DATABASE_URL=....

docs.title: 5. Deploy
docs.text:
fly deploy

fly deploy builds the image, makes the machine and starts it. The app runs the migrations at start. Then check that there is one machine:

fly scale show

If the count is more than 1 and you use SQLite, run fly scale count 1.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
curl https://blog-api.fly.dev/api/ping

pong

fly status    # the machines and their state
fly logs      # the app logs, live

The first log lines after the first start:

Migrating: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrated: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrating: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
Migrated: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
{"timestamp":"...","status":"info","message":"Server started at http://[::]:3000 with 1 isolate (native)","logger":{"name":"dox"}}

docs.title: HTTPS and the client IP
docs.text:
Fly.io ends TLS and sends plain HTTP to port 3000. force_https = true sends HTTP visitors to HTTPS. To make req.ip() and req.scheme() show the real client, set trustedProxies in AppConfig. The app port is reachable only through the Fly.io proxy, so ['*'] is safe here:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  trustedProxies: <String>['*'],
);

See Deployment: HTTPS.

docs.title: More CPU, more machines
docs.text:
Dox starts one isolate per CPU core it sees. On cpus = 1 that is one isolate.

You want Do this more speed on one machine raise cpus in [[vm]] (and memory), then fly deploy. Dox uses the new cores by itself more machines use Postgres, then fly scale count 2. With SQLite, stay at one machine a fixed number of isolates set APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE in [env]

Each machine is its own process. Socket.IO rooms and the memory cache are not shared between machines.

docs.title: Update the app
docs.text:
fly deploy
  • Change config in [env] and run fly deploy again.
  • fly secrets set restarts the machines with the new value. With --stage it only saves the value, and the next deploy uses it.
  • The app runs new migrations at start.
  • With one machine there is a short gap while it restarts.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Deployment for the bundle and the Dockerfile
  • Environments for all env keys and APP_KEY
  • Docker for a health check binary and Docker Compose
  • Fly.io docs: fly.toml, secrets, volumes, Managed Postgres

docs.title: Deploy to a Linux server
docs.text:
Run the blog API on your own Linux server (a VPS), with systemd to keep it running and Caddy in front for HTTPS.

Note

These steps follow the systemd and Caddy docs as of 2026-10-22. They were not run on a real VPS in CI.

flowchart LR
  client[Browser or app] -- "HTTPS :443" --> caddy[Caddy]
  caddy -- "HTTP 127.0.0.1:3000" --> dox["/opt/blog/bin/server (systemd)"]

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Linux server (Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.04 or newer) with SSH and sudo.
  • A domain name. Its A (and AAAA) record points to the server.
  • Docker on your machine, to build a Linux binary.
  • The blog API from the tutorial, or any Dox app.

docs.title: 1. Build the bundle for Linux
docs.text:
dox build makes a native binary for the system it runs on. A binary built on macOS does not run on Linux. So build it inside the dart:stable image (it is Debian):

docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/app -w /app dart:stable sh -c \
  'dart pub get && dart pub global activate dox && /root/.pub-cache/bin/dox build'

The result is build/bundle/:

build/bundle/
  bin/server                         the AOT binary
  lib/dox_http_native-linux-*.so     the native HTTP server
  lib/dox_postgres_native-linux-*.so the native Postgres driver
  lib/dox_mysql_native-linux-*.so    the native MySQL driver
  lib/libsqlite3.so                  SQLite
  db/                                the migrations
  .env.example

The container writes Linux paths into your .dart_tool/. So run dart pub get on your machine again before you use dox serve.

Keep bin/ and lib/ together. The binary loads the libraries from ../lib. See Deployment.

Match the CPU of the server

Docker builds for the CPU of your machine. On a Mac with Apple silicon that is arm64. Most VPS plans are x86_64. For them, add --platform linux/amd64 after docker run. Check the server with uname -m.

docs.title: 2. Make a user and the folders
docs.text:
Run this on the server. The app runs as the user dox. This user can not log in.

sudo useradd --system --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin dox
sudo mkdir -p /opt/blog
sudo install -d -o dox -g dox /opt/blog/storage
Path What it holds Owner /opt/blog the bundle (bin/, lib/, db/) root /opt/blog/storage files the app writes (uploads, file cache) dox /var/lib/blog the SQLite file. systemd makes it (see step 5) dox /etc/blog.env config and secrets root, mode 600

docs.title: 3. Copy the bundle to the server
docs.text:
rsync -a --delete --exclude storage/ build/bundle/ you@server:/tmp/blog-bundle/
ssh you@server 'sudo rsync -a --delete --exclude storage/ /tmp/blog-bundle/ /opt/blog/'

docs.title: 4. Write the env file
docs.text:
/etc/blog.env
APP_NAME=blog
APP_ENV=production
APP_PORT=3000
APP_KEY=<output of dox key:generate>

DB_CONNECTION=sqlite
DB_NAME=/var/lib/blog/blog.sqlite

sudo chown root:root /etc/blog.env
sudo chmod 600 /etc/blog.env

systemd reads this file as root, before it starts the app as dox. So dox does not need to read it.

For Postgres, set DB_CONNECTION=postgres and add DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD and DB_NAME. Or set one DATABASE_URL, like postgres://app:secret@localhost:5432/blog. It wins over the DB_* keys. See DATABASE_URL. See Environments for all keys.

Which value wins

systemd passes EnvironmentFile as real environment variables, and those win over a .env file. So /etc/blog.env wins over a /opt/blog/.env. Do not put a .env in /opt/blog, so there is only one place to look.

docs.title: 5. Write the systemd unit
docs.text:
/etc/systemd/system/blog.service
[Unit]
Description=Blog API (Dox)
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=dox
Group=dox
# the binary reads db/ and .env from this folder
WorkingDirectory=/opt/blog
EnvironmentFile=/etc/blog.env
ExecStart=/opt/blog/bin/server
# start again after a crash, and after `kill`
Restart=always
RestartSec=2
# makes /var/lib/blog, owned by the user dox
StateDirectory=blog
# small safety settings
NoNewPrivileges=true
PrivateTmp=true
ProtectSystem=full

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now blog
systemctl status blog
  • Restart=always: when the main isolate dies, the process exits and systemd starts it again. See Deployment: keep it running.
  • The app runs the migrations at start, before it takes requests.
  • Dox starts one isolate per CPU core. Set APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE in /etc/blog.env to change it.

docs.title: 6. Close the app port
docs.text:
Caddy runs on the same machine. So let Dox listen on 127.0.0.1 only. Add this line to /etc/blog.env:

/etc/blog.env
APP_HOST=127.0.0.1

Now only programs on this machine can reach port 3000. Also turn on a firewall, so only SSH, HTTP and HTTPS are open:

sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw allow OpenSSH
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp
sudo ufw enable

docs.title: 7. Put Caddy in front
docs.text:
Install Caddy from its install page. The Debian package runs Caddy with systemd and reads /etc/caddy/Caddyfile.

/etc/caddy/Caddyfile
api.example.com {
    encode zstd gzip

    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:3000 {
        # while the app restarts, wait up to 10s for it instead of failing
        lb_try_duration 10s
        lb_try_interval 250ms
    }
}

sudo caddy validate --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile
sudo systemctl reload caddy
  • Caddy gets a TLS certificate for api.example.com by itself. Ports 80 and 443 must be open.
  • reverse_proxy sets X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto.

docs.title: 8. Trust Caddy in the app
docs.text:
Dox ignores X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto until you list the proxy in trustedProxies. Caddy talks to the app from the same server:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  trustedProxies: <String>['127.0.0.1', '::1'],
);

Now req.ip() is the real client IP and req.scheme() is https. Build and copy again after this change (steps 1 and 3). See Deployment: HTTPS.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
curl https://api.example.com/api/ping

pong

Read the logs. In production the app writes one JSON line per log.

journalctl -u blog -f                     # follow new lines
journalctl -u blog --since "1 hour ago"   # the last hour
journalctl -u blog -b                     # since the last boot

The first lines after the first start look like this:

Migrating: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrated: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrating: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
Migrated: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
{"timestamp":"...","status":"info","message":"Server started at http://127.0.0.1:3000 with 2 isolate (native)","logger":{"name":"dox"}}

(native) means the native HTTP server loaded. When it does not load, the app stops at start and the error says why.

Check that the app port is closed. From your machine:

curl -m 5 http://api.example.com:3000/api/ping   # must time out

docs.title: Update the app
docs.text:
1. Build a new bundle (step 1).

  2. Copy it to the server (step 3). Keep the old one first, so you can go back:

    ssh you@server 'sudo rm -rf /opt/blog.prev && sudo cp -a /opt/blog /opt/blog.prev'
rsync -a --delete --exclude storage/ build/bundle/ you@server:/tmp/blog-bundle/
ssh you@server 'sudo rsync -a --delete --exclude storage/ /tmp/blog-bundle/ /opt/blog/'

  3. Restart the app. It runs new migrations at start.

    ssh you@server 'sudo systemctl restart blog'

  4. Read the logs (journalctl -u blog -n 20) and run the check.

To go back: copy /opt/blog.prev to /opt/blog and restart. A migration that already ran is not undone.

A restart is short, but not zero

A restart takes about one second. New requests do not fail: lb_try_duration makes Caddy wait for the app to come back. For a real zero-downtime update, run two copies on two ports and list both in Caddy. See Deployment: many processes.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Deployment for dox build, Docker, nginx and many processes
  • Environments for config per environment and APP_KEY
  • Docker to run the app and Postgres with Docker Compose
  • Native server

docs.title: Docker
docs.text: Build a small production image with dox build, and run it with Postgres in Docker Compose, with a health check.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app with a database.
  • Docker with Compose.

docs.title: 1. Add a health route
docs.text:
The health check asks this route. It answers 503 when the database does not answer. Put it in register() of WebRouter. QueryBuilder comes from package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart.

lib/routes/web.dart
Route.health(
  '/health',
  checks: <String, HealthCheckFunction>{
    'database': () => QueryBuilder.query('select 1'),
  },
);

See Health check for more checks.

docs.title: 2. Add the health check binary
docs.text:
The final image has no shell and no curl. So the health check is a second small Dart binary.

bin/health.dart
import 'dart:io';

/// Docker health check. The final image has no shell and no curl,
/// so this small binary asks the app itself. Exit 0 = healthy.
Future<void> main() async {
  String port = Platform.environment['APP_PORT'] ?? '3000';
  HttpClient client = HttpClient()
    ..connectionTimeout = const Duration(seconds: 3);
  try {
    HttpClientRequest request = await client.getUrl(
      Uri.parse('http://127.0.0.1:$port/health'),
    );
    HttpClientResponse response = await request.close();
    exit(response.statusCode == 200 ? 0 : 1);
  } catch (_) {
    exit(1);
  }
}

docs.title: 3. Write the Dockerfile
docs.text:
Two stages: the first builds the AOT bundle, the second holds only the Dart runtime and the bundle. For the blog API the final image is about 17 MB.

Dockerfile
# Stage 1: build the AOT bundle with the Dart SDK and the dox CLI.
FROM dart:stable AS build

WORKDIR /app

# Resolve dependencies first, so Docker caches this layer.
COPY pubspec.* ./
RUN dart pub get

COPY . .
RUN dart pub get --offline

# `dox build` runs build_runner, then `dart build cli`.
# The bundle is in build/bundle: bin/server, lib/, db/, .env.example
# (and bin/queue, bin/schedule when the app has them)
RUN dart pub global activate dox \
  && /root/.pub-cache/bin/dox build

# The health check binary. Plain dart:io, so `dart compile exe` is fine.
RUN dart compile exe bin/health.dart -o build/bundle/bin/health

# Lay out the final file tree. /tmp must be writable: uploads bigger
# than 1 MB are streamed to a temp file.
RUN mkdir -p /out/app/storage /out/app/public /out/tmp \
  && chmod 1777 /out/tmp \
  && cp -r build/bundle/. /out/app/ \
  && cp -r public/. /out/app/public/ \
  # the native HTTP server (Rust) needs libgcc_s, which /runtime/ does not have
  && LIBGCC=$(find / -name libgcc_s.so.1 -path '*lib*' | head -n 1) \
  && mkdir -p /out$(dirname $LIBGCC) && cp $LIBGCC /out$LIBGCC

# Stage 2: the Dart AOT runtime and the bundle only. No SDK, no source.
FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /runtime/ /
COPY --from=build /out/ /
WORKDIR /app

# Config comes from env variables. The image has no .env file.
EXPOSE 3000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=15s --timeout=5s --start-period=10s --retries=3 \
  CMD ["/app/bin/health"]
CMD ["/app/bin/server"]

Delete the public lines when your app has no public folder.

Check the start log in the container. It must end with (native):

Server started at http://[::]:3000 with 8 isolate (native)

Without the libgcc_s lines, the native HTTP server does not load. Dox then stops at start with dox_http_native did not load and the reason.

dox build, not dart compile exe

dox_orm bundles SQLite with a build hook. dart compile exe does not run build hooks and stops with an error. dox build runs dart build cli, which does. It puts the native libraries in build/bundle/lib, next to bin/server.

Keep the build context small:

.dockerignore
.dart_tool/
.git/
.github/
.idea/
build/
storage/
.env
.env.*
!.env.example
Dockerfile
docker-compose.yml
pubspec_overrides.yaml

docs.title: 4. Write the compose file
docs.text:
env_file: .env gives the app your .env. The lines under environment win over the file, so the app always talks to the postgres service.

docker-compose.yml
services:
  app:
    build: .
    # secrets and config come from .env, never from the image
    env_file: .env
    environment:
      APP_ENV: production
      APP_PORT: 3000
      DB_CONNECTION: postgres
      DB_HOST: postgres
      DB_PORT: 5432
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    volumes:
      # uploads survive a new image
      - uploads:/app/storage
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
    restart: unless-stopped

  postgres:
    image: postgres:18
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ${DB_USERNAME:-postgres}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:?set DB_PASSWORD in .env}
      POSTGRES_DB: ${DB_NAME:-dox}
    volumes:
      - postgres:/var/lib/postgresql
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "pg_isready", "-q", "-U", "${DB_USERNAME:-postgres}"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  postgres:
  uploads:
  • depends_on with service_healthy: the app starts after Postgres answers. The app runs the migrations at start, so the database must be up.
  • ${DB_PASSWORD:?...}: compose stops with a clear message when .env has no password.
  • restart: unless-stopped: when the main isolate dies, the process exits and Docker starts it again.

docs.title: 5. Write the .env
docs.text:
.env
APP_NAME=my_app
APP_ENV=production
APP_KEY=<output of dox key:generate>
APP_PORT=3000

DB_CONNECTION=postgres
DB_NAME=my_app
DB_USERNAME=postgres
DB_PASSWORD=<a real password>

.env is in .dockerignore and .gitignore. It never goes into the image or into git.

The app now uses Postgres, so the build needs the Postgres driver. A new app skips it in pubspec.yaml. Remove the dox_postgres_native skip lines. See Skip unused drivers.

docs.title: 6. Build and run
docs.text:
docker compose up -d --build
docker compose ps

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
docker compose ps

NAME             STATUS
my_app-app-1       Up 30 seconds (healthy)
my_app-postgres-1  Up 35 seconds (healthy)

curl http://localhost:3000/health

{"status":"ok","checks":{"database":"ok"}}

Stop Postgres with docker compose stop postgres. After about 45 seconds, docker compose ps shows the app as unhealthy.

docs.title: HTTPS
docs.text: Do not add TLS to the app. Put Caddy or nginx in front, and set trustedProxies in AppConfig. See Deployment: HTTPS.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Deployment for dox build, the bundle layout and systemd
  • Environments for dev, staging and production config
  • Migration: run on server start

docs.title: Environments
docs.text: Run the same app in development, staging and production with different config, and keep secrets out of git and out of the image.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app.
  • build_runner for the typed env class (a new app has it).

docs.title: How Dox reads config
docs.text:
1. A real environment variable (shell, Docker, systemd) wins.
  2. Then the .env file in the folder where the app starts.

So: use .env on your machine. Use real environment variables on a server. The .env file is optional there.

docs.title: 1. The typed env class
docs.text:
A new project already has lib/config/env.dart. Its AppEnv class lists every key, its type and its default. In this file of the guides app, corsOrigin and appUrl are added keys. The rest comes with a new project.

lib/config/env.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'env.g.dart';

/// The env of the app, typed. Made by `dox env:generate`.
/// -------------------------------
/// Each getter reads one key: `appName` reads `APP_NAME`.
/// A getter body is the default. A nullable getter is optional.
/// Other getters are required: the app stops at startup when one is missing.
/// Run `dart run build_runner build` after you change this class.
@DoxEnv()
abstract class AppEnv {
  /// reads and checks every key once
  static AppEnv load([EnvReader? reader]) {
    return _$AppEnv.load(reader);
  }

  String get appName => 'dox';

  /// development, staging or production. Not set: production.
  String get appEnv => 'production';

  bool get isDevelopment => appEnv == 'development';

  int get appPort => 3000;

  /// required: used to sign tokens and encrypt cookies
  String get appKey;

  /// isolates (threads) of the HTTP server. Null: one per CPU core.
  int? get appTotalIsolate;

  String get logLevel => 'info';

  /// memory, file or redis
  String get cacheStore => 'file';

  /// local, s3 or memory
  String get storageDisk => 'local';

  /// sqlite, postgres or mysql
  String get dbConnection => 'sqlite';

  /// the database name. For SQLite: the file path.
  String get dbName => 'db/dox.sqlite';

  String get dbHost => 'localhost';

  /// null: 5432 for Postgres, 3306 for MySQL
  int? get dbPort;

  String get dbUsername => 'postgres';

  String get dbPassword => '';

  /// the front-end URL that may call the API
  String get corsOrigin => 'http://localhost:5173';

  /// the public URL of this app, used in file links
  String get appUrl => 'http://localhost:3000';
}

/// The env of the app. Read and checked once, on first use.
final AppEnv env = AppEnv.load();

The key is the getter name in UPPER_SNAKE case: dbPort reads DB_PORT.

  • A getter with a body has a default: int get appPort => 3000;.
  • A nullable getter with no body is optional: int? get dbPort; is null when the key is not set.
  • Any other getter with no body is required: String get appKey;.

A missing required key stops the app at start, with a list of all problems. The part file env.g.dart is made by build_runner.

docs.title: 2. Add a key
docs.text:
Say the app needs a mail host. Add one getter to AppEnv:

  /// the SMTP server for mails
  String get mailHost => 'localhost';

Then run build_runner again:

dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs

Now env.mailHost reads MAIL_HOST. Add MAIL_HOST to .env.example too.

docs.title: 3. Use it in the config files
docs.text:
The config files read the typed getters. A setting that differs per environment becomes one bool.

lib/config/logger.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

LoggerConfig logger = LoggerConfig(
  name: env.appName,
  enabled: true,
  level: env.logLevel,
  // colors on your machine, one JSON line per log in staging and production
  prettyPrint: env.isDevelopment,
);
lib/config/database.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: env.dbConnection,
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.postgres,
      host: env.dbHost,
      port: env.dbPort ?? 5432,
      user: env.dbUsername,
      password: env.dbPassword,
      database: env.dbName,
      // print every query on your machine only
      debug: env.isDevelopment,
    ),
    'sqlite': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.sqlite,
      database: env.dbName,
      debug: env.isDevelopment,
    ),
  },
);

docs.title: 4. Write the env files
docs.text:
Commit .env.example. It lists every key with a safe value. Never commit .env.

.env.example
APP_NAME=my_app
APP_ENV=development
APP_PORT=3000
# run `dox key:generate`
APP_KEY=
APP_URL=http://localhost:3000

DB_CONNECTION=postgres
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432
DB_NAME=my_app
DB_USERNAME=postgres
DB_PASSWORD=postgres

CORS_ORIGIN=http://localhost:5173
LOG_LEVEL=debug

cp .env.example .env
dox key:generate   # writes a new APP_KEY into .env
.gitignore
.env
.env.*
!.env.example
Environment Where the values live APP_ENV your machine .env development staging real env variables (compose environment:, a secrets manager) staging production real env variables production

On a server you can also keep a .env next to the binary, outside git, with chmod 600. systemd reads it with EnvironmentFile=. See Deployment.

docs.title: 5. APP_KEY
docs.text:
APP_KEY encrypts cookies and signs JWT tokens and local signed URLs.

  • Make one per environment with dox key:generate. Never share the production key with staging.
  • APP_KEY must be exactly 32 characters. dox key:generate makes a key of the right length.
  • When APP_ENV is not development, local, test or testing, a bad key stops the app at start: empty, not 32 characters, or a public sample key. An empty APP_ENV counts as production. In development the app only logs a warning.
  • A new key makes every cookie, token and signed URL invalid. Every user is logged out. Plan it.

docs.title: 6. Check the env before a deploy
docs.text:
dox env:check loads AppEnv with the real environment and .env, and prints every missing or bad key. It exits with code 1, so CI stops.

dox env:check

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Start with a key missing:

APP_KEY= dart run bin/server.dart

Unhandled exception:
EnvException: the env is not valid
  - APP_KEY is missing

Start as staging on another port. The real variables win over .env:

APP_ENV=staging APP_PORT=4000 dart run bin/server.dart

The app listens on 4000. env.appEnv is 'staging', and env.isDevelopment is false.

docs.title: Things that differ per environment
docs.text: Setting Development Staging and production prettyPrint of the logger true false (one JSON line per log) debug of the database true false totalIsolate 1 or 2 is enough one per core (the default) CORS_ORIGIN http://localhost:5173 the real front-end URL the server dox serve (JIT) the dox build binary (AOT)

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Environment variables for all types and rules of the typed env class
  • Docker
  • Deployment

docs.title: File upload
docs.text: Accept an image from a form, check its size and type, save it to a disk, and return its URL.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • A Dox app (dox create my_app). A new app has the dox_storage package, lib/config/storage.dart and lib/providers/storage_provider.dart.

docs.title: 1. Set up the disk
docs.text:
The local disk of a new app saves files in the storage folder. Give it a url. Storage().url() uses it to build the public URL of a file.

lib/config/storage.dart
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

StorageConfig storageConfig = StorageConfig(
  defaultDisk: env.storageDisk,
  disks: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    /// uploads go to the `storage` folder.
    /// `url` is the public address of `Storage.route('files', ...)`.
    'local': <String, dynamic>{
      'driver': 'local',
      'root': 'storage',
      'url': '${env.appUrl}/files',
    },
  },
);

APP_URL is a new key. Add a getter for it to the AppEnv class:

lib/config/env.dart
  /// the public URL of this app, used in file links
  String get appUrl => 'http://localhost:3000';

Run dart run build_runner build to update env.g.dart. Then add APP_URL=http://localhost:3000 to your .env.

The provider of a new app sets the disks in every isolate. You do not change it:

lib/providers/storage_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/storage.dart';

class AppStorageProvider extends StorageProvider {
  AppStorageProvider() : super(storageConfig);
}

docs.title: 2. Write the DTO
docs.text:
The DTO checks the file before your controller runs.

lib/app/dtos/upload_image/upload_image.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'upload_image.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class UploadImage {
  /// jpg, jpeg, png, gif, webp or bmp. Dox reads the first bytes of the
  /// file to find the real type. The file name is not trusted.
  @Image()
  @MaxSize('5MB')
  final RequestFile image;

  const UploadImage({required this.image});

  static const DtoSchema<UploadImage> schema = $UploadImageDto;
}

For other file types, use @Mimes(<String>['pdf', 'docx']) in place of @Image().

docs.title: 3. Write the controller
docs.text:
putFile with a RequestFile, on the local disk, moves the upload temp file to a new UUID name (with permissions on, it streams it). It does not read it into memory.

lib/app/http/controllers/upload.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/upload_image/upload_image.dto.dart';

@Inject()
class UploadController {
  /// POST /api/upload (multipart/form-data, field `image`)
  Future<Map<String, String>> store(UploadImage body) async {
    // saves the file as /images/<uuid>.<ext> on the default disk
    String path = await Storage().putFile('images', body.image);
    String url = await Storage().url(path);
    return <String, String>{'path': path, 'url': url};
  }
}

Save the file before you return

A file bigger than 1 MB is written to a temp file while it arrives. Dox deletes that temp file when the response is sent. So call putFile, store or moveTo inside the controller, not later.

docs.title: 4. Add the routes
docs.text:
One route takes the upload. Storage.route serves the saved files at GET /files/{key*}.

lib/routes/api.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/upload.controller.dart';

class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.post('/upload', (UploadController c) => c.store);
  }
}
lib/routes/web.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';

class WebRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    // GET /files/{key*}, any file of the default disk
    Storage.route('files', signed: false);
  }
}

signed: false makes every file public. Leave it out to serve only signed URLs. Then use Storage().signedUrl(path) in place of Storage().url(path).

docs.title: 5. Register the DTOs
docs.text:
Dox finds a DTO in the dtos list of AppConfig. build_runner writes this list to lib/generated/dtos.g.dart. Add it once. Skip this step when your app.dart already has dtos: dtos.

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:my_app/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  dtos: dtos,
  // ...
);

docs.title: 6. Build and run
docs.text:
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
dox serve

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Upload a PNG:

curl -F image=@photo.png http://localhost:3000/api/upload

{"path":"/images/074aa0d0-ce21-11f1-938a-57265e28c4a3.png","url":"http://localhost:3000/files/images/074aa0d0-ce21-11f1-938a-57265e28c4a3.png"}

Open the url in the browser. The image shows.

Upload a text file. You get 422:

curl -F image=@notes.txt http://localhost:3000/api/upload

{"image":"The image must be an image"}

Send no file at all. You get 422 with {"image":"The image is required"}.

docs.title: Bigger files
docs.text: The default limit for a multipart/form-data body is 100 MB. Change it in AppConfig(maxMultipartSize: ...). Set the same limit in your proxy (client_max_body_size in nginx).

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Request: form data for RequestFile
  • Validation: files for @Image, @Mimes, @MimeTypes, @MaxSize, @MinSize, @Dimensions
  • File storage for S3 and signed URLs

docs.title: JWT authentication
docs.text: Let users register and log in, give them a JWT token, protect routes with it, and read the user in a controller.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app (dox create my_app). A new app has a database (SQLite), a User model and a users table with name, email and password columns.
  • The dox_auth package. A new app does not have it. Add it:
dart pub add dox_auth

docs.title: 1. Hide the password in the model
docs.text:
The token holds user.toJson(). Anyone with the token can read it. So the password hash must be in hidden. The model of a new app already does this:

lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel(table: 'users', softDelete: true)
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @override
  List<String> get hidden => <String>['password'];

  @Column()
  String? name;

  @Column()
  String? email;

  @Column()
  String? password;
}

docs.title: 2. Set up the auth provider
3. Write the DTOs
docs.text:
@Unique makes sure the email is not taken. It comes from dox_orm, so hide its Schema class.

lib/app/dtos/register_user/register_user.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart' hide Schema;

part 'register_user.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class RegisterUser {
  @Length(min: 2, max: 50)
  @Trim()
  final String name;

  @Trim()
  @Lowercase()
  @Email()
  @Unique('users', column: 'email')
  final String email;

  @MinLength(8)
  final String password;

  const RegisterUser({
    required this.name,
    required this.email,
    required this.password,
  });

  static const DtoSchema<RegisterUser> schema = $RegisterUserDto;
}
lib/app/dtos/login_user/login_user.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'login_user.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class LoginUser {
  @Trim()
  @Lowercase()
  @Email()
  final String email;

  final String password;

  const LoginUser({required this.email, required this.password});

  static const DtoSchema<LoginUser> schema = $LoginUserDto;
}

docs.title: 4. Write the controller
5. Add the routes
docs.text:
AuthMiddleware reads the Authorization: Bearer <token> header, checks the token and loads the user from the database. A missing or bad token stops the request with 401.

lib/routes/api.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/auth.controller.dart';

class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.post('/auth/register', (AuthController c) => c.register);
    Route.post('/auth/login', (AuthController c) => c.login);

    Route.middleware(<dynamic>[AuthMiddleware()], () {
      Route.get('/auth/me', (AuthController c) => c.me);
      Route.post('/auth/logout', (AuthController c) => c.logout);
      // put every protected route here
    });
  }
}

docs.title: 6. Register the DTOs
docs.text:
Dox finds a DTO in the dtos list of AppConfig. build_runner writes this list to lib/generated/dtos.g.dart. Add it once. Skip this step when your app.dart already has dtos: dtos.

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:my_app/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  dtos: dtos,
  // ...
);

docs.title: 7. Build and run
docs.text:
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
dox serve

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Register:

curl -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Ann","email":"ann@example.com","password":"secret123"}' \
  http://localhost:3000/api/auth/register

{"token":"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...","user":{"id":1,"name":"Ann","email":"ann@example.com","created_at":"...","updated_at":"..."}}

Log in with a wrong password. You get 401:

{"error":{"code":"unauthorized","message":"Wrong email or password"}}

Log in and use the token:

TOKEN=$(curl -s -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"ann@example.com","password":"secret123"}' \
  http://localhost:3000/api/auth/login | jq -r .token)

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://localhost:3000/api/auth/me

{"id":1,"name":"Ann","email":"ann@example.com","created_at":"...","updated_at":"..."}

Without the header, /api/auth/me gives 401 Authentication failed.

The error shape

The {"error": ...} shape comes from the response handler in Custom errors. Without it, the 401 body is {"code":"unauthorized","message":"Wrong email or password"}.

docs.title: Logout and expiry
docs.text:
By default the server checks only the signature, so it can not cancel one JWT. This is what you can do:

You want Do this Log out on this device The client deletes the token. That is all logout does. Limit the damage of a stolen token Keep expiresIn short, for example Duration(hours: 12). Log every user out at once Change APP_KEY. Every old token stops working. Block one user Delete the user. AuthMiddleware loads the user from the database on each request, so a deleted user gets 401.

To cancel one token, or all tokens of a user, turn on revocation. See Revoke tokens. Or use access tokens, which you can revoke at any time.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Authentication for all options of AuthGuard, JwtAuthDriver and AuthProvider
  • Hashing
  • Middleware

docs.title: Pagination
docs.text: Make a list route that takes page and per_page from the query string and returns one page of rows.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • A Dox app (dox create my_app). A new app has a database (SQLite), a User model and a users table.

docs.title: 1. Write the query DTO
docs.text:
A DTO with source: Source.query reads the query string, also for POST. The query key of perPage is per_page, because keys are snake_case by default.

lib/app/dtos/list_users/list_users.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'list_users.dto.g.dart';

/// GET /api/users?page=2&per_page=10
@Dto(source: Source.query)
class ListUsers {
  @Min(1)
  final int page;

  @Range(1, 100)
  final int perPage; // query key: per_page

  const ListUsers({this.page = 1, this.perPage = 20});

  static const DtoSchema<ListUsers> schema = $ListUsersDto;
}

Both fields have a default, so both are optional. @Range(1, 100) stops a client from asking for 10000 rows.

docs.title: 2. Write the controller
docs.text:
paginate() runs one count query and one select query. It returns a Pagination. A controller can return it as it is. Dox sends toJson().

lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/list_users/list_users.dto.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class UserController {
  /// GET /api/users?page=1&per_page=20
  Future<Pagination<User>> index(ListUsers query) async {
    return User()
        .orderBy('id', 'desc')
        .paginate(currentPage: query.page, perPage: query.perPage);
  }
}

Always add an orderBy. Without it, the database may return the rows in a different order on each page.

Add a where before paginate to filter: User().where('role', 'admin').orderBy('id').paginate(...).

docs.title: 3. Add the route
docs.text:
lib/routes/api.dart
Route.get('/users', (UserController c) => c.index);

docs.title: 4. Register the DTOs
docs.text:
Dox finds a DTO in the dtos list of AppConfig. build_runner writes this list to lib/generated/dtos.g.dart. Add it once. Skip this step when your app.dart already has dtos: dtos.

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:my_app/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  dtos: dtos,
  // ...
);

docs.title: 5. Build and run
docs.text:
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
dox serve

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
With 3 users in the table:

curl 'http://localhost:3000/api/users?page=2&per_page=2'

{
  "total": 3,
  "per_page": 2,
  "last_page": 2,
  "current_page": 2,
  "data": [
    {"id": 1, "name": "User 1", "email": "user1@example.com", "created_at": "2026-10-22T14:01:07.843207Z", "updated_at": "2026-10-22T14:01:07.843207Z"}
  ]
}
Key Meaning total rows that match the query, on all pages per_page rows per page last_page the number of the last page current_page the page you asked for data the rows of this page, from toJson() of the model

A page after the last one gives an empty data list.

Bad input gets 422 before the controller runs:

curl 'http://localhost:3000/api/users?page=0&per_page=500'

{"page":"The page must be greater than or equal 1","per_page":"The per_page must be between 1 and 100"}

docs.title: Change the shape of a row
docs.text:
Return a serializer for each row, when the model has fields you do not want to send. dox make:serializer User makes lib/app/serializers/user.serializer.dart. page.data gives the typed rows (List<User>):

Future<Map<String, dynamic>> index(ListUsers query) async {
  Pagination<User> page = await User()
      .orderBy('id', 'desc')
      .paginate(currentPage: query.page, perPage: query.perPage);
  return <String, dynamic>{
    ...page.toJson(),
    'data': UserSerializer(page.data).toJson(),
  };
}

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Query builder: paginate
  • Validation: where the data comes from
  • Serializer

docs.title: Share code with Flutter
docs.text:
Put a @Dto class in a shared Dart package, so the Dox server and the Flutter app check input with the same rules and error messages.

The generated DTO code imports only dox_validation, which is pure Dart (no dart:io, no dart:mirrors). So it runs in Flutter and on the web.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app (dox create server). Here it is in the server folder.
  • A Flutter app (flutter create app). Here it is in the app folder.

docs.title: The layout
docs.text:
my_blog/
  packages/
    blog_shared/     # the DTOs. Pure Dart.
  server/            # the Dox app
  app/               # the Flutter app

flowchart LR
    S[packages/blog_shared<br>SaveBlog + SaveBlog.schema] --> A[app: Flutter<br>checks the form]
    S --> B[server: Dox<br>checks the request]
    A -- "POST /api/blogs (JSON)" --> B

docs.title: 1. The shared package
2. The Dox server
docs.text:
Add the shared package to the dependencies of the server:

server/pubspec.yaml
dependencies:
  # ... the packages of the new app stay
  blog_shared:
    path: ../packages/blog_shared

Run dart pub get.

Dox finds a DTO in the dtos list of AppConfig. The server's own lib/generated/dtos.g.dart lists only the DTOs in the server. So add the list of the shared package too:

server/lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:blog_shared/generated/dtos.g.dart' as shared;
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:server/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  dtos: <DtoSchema<Object>>[...dtos, ...shared.dtos],
);

When the server has no DTOs of its own, its dtos list is empty. The line above still works.

The controller asks for SaveBlog like any other DTO. Dox checks the body before the method runs. Bad input gets 422.

server/lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart
import 'package:blog_shared/blog_shared.dart' show SaveBlog;
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

@Inject()
class BlogController {
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> store(SaveBlog body) async {
    // body.title is already trimmed and checked.
    return <String, dynamic>{'title': body.title, 'saved': true};
  }
}
server/lib/routes/api.dart
Route.post('/blogs', (BlogController c) => c.store);

Why show SaveBlog

dox_core has its own ValidationException (it answers 422). blog_shared exports the one from dox_validation. show keeps only the DTO from blog_shared, so the two names do not clash in server code.

A bad request gets the errors as {"key": "message"}:

POST /api/blogs  {"title": "ab", "description": "short"}
422 {"title":"The title must be between 3 and 255 characters","description":"The description must be at least 10 characters"}

docs.title: 3. The Flutter app
Static files and SPA
docs.text: Serve a folder of files, or a single page app (React, Vue, Flutter web), from the Dox app, with the right cache headers.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app.
  • A public folder with the built front-end (index.html, assets/...).
  • For the storage way and the controller below: the dox_storage package, with its provider. See File storage.

docs.title: Serve a folder: one line
docs.text:
Route.staticFiles serves the files of a folder. Add it in register() of WebRouter.

lib/routes/web.dart
Route.staticFiles('/', 'public');

GET /app.js sends public/app.js with the right Content-Type. A route always wins over a file. A missing file goes to Route.fallback if you added one, else to 404. It sends ETag and Last-Modified, and the browser gets 304 when it already has the file. Add maxAge: to send a Cache-Control header. See Routing: serve static files for all the rules.

For a single page app, add Route.fallback to send index.html for every URL that has no route and no file. See Routing: fallback route.

docs.title: Or serve a storage disk
docs.text:
Storage.route serves every file of a storage disk. Add a public disk for the folder in lib/config/storage.dart:

lib/config/storage.dart
StorageConfig storageConfig = StorageConfig(
  defaultDisk: env.storageDisk,
  disks: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    'local': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'local', 'root': 'storage'},

    /// the front-end files
    'public': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'local', 'root': 'public'},
  },
);

Then add the route in register() of WebRouter. Storage comes from package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart.

lib/routes/web.dart
Storage.route('static', disk: 'public', signed: false); // GET /static/{key*}

GET /static/app.js sends public/app.js, streamed, with the right Content-Type. A missing file answers 404. The disk rejects .. in the path, so a client can not read files outside public.

This is enough for a few files. It sends no Cache-Control header. For an SPA, go on.

docs.title: Serve an SPA
docs.text:
An SPA needs two things:

  • index.html for every URL the SPA router handles, with no cache.
  • The built assets with a long cache. Build tools put a hash in the file name (app.3f9c2b.js), so a new build has new names.

docs.title: 1. Write the controller
2. Add the routes
docs.text:
The catch-all route must come last. Put the API router before the web router in AppConfig.

lib/routes/web.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/static.controller.dart';

class WebRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    // the SPA: assets with a long cache, every other URL gets index.html
    Route.get('/assets/{path*}', (StaticController c) => c.asset);
    Route.get('/', (StaticController c) => c.index);
    Route.get('/{path*}', (StaticController c) => c.index);
  }
}
lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  /// the SPA catch-all route is in WebRouter, so it must come last.
  /// Listed routers come first, in this order.
  routers: <Router>[ApiRouter(), WebRouter()],
  // ...
);

Keep the route for / as well, so the start page is always served.

docs.title: 3. Put the build in public
docs.text:
# React (Vite)
npm run build && cp -r dist/. public/

# Flutter web
flutter build web && cp -r build/web/. public/

Vite puts the files in assets/. Flutter web puts them next to index.html. For Flutter, change the asset route to match, or serve everything with Storage.route and give index.html the catch-all.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
curl -i http://localhost:3000/

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
cache-control: max-age=0
content-type: text/html

curl -i http://localhost:3000/settings/profile   # same answer: index.html
curl -i http://localhost:3000/assets/app.js

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
cache-control: max-age=31536000
content-type: text/javascript

GET /assets/nope.js answers 404. GET /assets/..%2Fpubspec.yaml answers 404 too. GET /api/nothing answers 404, not the page.

docs.title: In production
docs.text: Put the proxy in front of Dox, and let it do gzip. See Deployment. For a big site, serve public from the proxy or a CDN, and keep Dox for the API only.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Routing: serve storage files
  • Response: files and big responses
  • File storage

docs.title: Testing with a database
docs.text:
Run model tests against a real database: SQLite for fast local tests, or a test Postgres for the real thing.

Migrations run once, and every test starts with empty tables.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • A Dox app (dox create my_app). A new app has the User model, a users migration in db/migration and the test package.

docs.title: 1. Check the migration
docs.text:
A new app has this migration. Its file name starts with another date. For a new table, run dox make:migration create_posts_table.

db/migration/2026_10_22_000000_create_users_table.dart
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

class CreateUsersTable extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.create('users', (Table table) {
      table.id();
      table.string('name');
      table.string('email').unique();
      table.string('password');
      table.timestamps();
      table.softDeletes();
    });
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.dropIfExists('users');
  }
}

db/migration/migrations.dart is the list of all migrations. dox make:migration updates it. The test imports that list. A Dart migration works on Postgres, MySQL and SQLite, so the same test runs on all of them.

docs.title: 2. Write the test (SQLite)
docs.text:
SQLite needs no server. The test makes its own config, so your .env does not matter.

test/user_test.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

/// One SQLite file for this test file. No server, no Postgres.
const String dbFile = 'storage/test.sqlite';

DatabaseConfig testDatabase = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: 'sqlite',
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'sqlite': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.sqlite,
      database: dbFile,
      debug: false,
    ),
  },
);

Future<void> deleteDbFile() async {
  for (String suffix in <String>['', '-wal', '-shm']) {
    File file = File('$dbFile$suffix');
    if (await file.exists()) await file.delete();
  }
}

void main() {
  setUpAll(() async {
    await deleteDbFile();
    await Migrator(
      migrations: migrations,
      config: testDatabase.getConnectionConfig(),
    ).migrate();
    SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(testDatabase);
  });

  // every test starts with empty tables
  setUp(refreshDatabase);

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await deleteDbFile();
  });

  test('saves and finds a user', () async {
    User user = User()
      ..name = 'Ann'
      ..email = 'ann@example.com'
      ..password = Hash.make('secret123');
    await user.save();

    User? found = await User().where('email', 'ann@example.com').getFirst();
    expect(found?.id, user.id);
    expect(found?.name, 'Ann');
    expect(Hash.verify('secret123', found!.password!), isTrue);
  });

  test('the tables are empty again', () async {
    expect(await User().count(), 0);
  });
}

What happens:

  1. setUpAll deletes an old database file, runs the migrations, and starts the ORM on the same file.
  2. setUp runs refreshDatabase() before each test. It empties every table (not the migrations table) and starts the ids at 1 again.
  3. tearDownAll deletes the file.

A file, not :memory:

The migrator and the ORM each open their own connection. Two connections to :memory: are two different databases. A file is shared. Put storage/test.sqlite in .gitignore.

docs.title: 3. Run it
docs.text: dart test test/user_test.dart

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
The migration names start with the dates of your files. A new app also has the tables of the queue.

00:00 +0: (setUpAll)
Migrating: 2026_10_22_000000_create_users_table
Migrated: 2026_10_22_000000_create_users_table
Migrating: 2026_10_23_000000_create_queue_tables
Migrated: 2026_10_23_000000_create_queue_tables
00:00 +1: saves and finds a user
00:00 +2: the tables are empty again
00:00 +2: All tests passed!

docs.title: The same test on Postgres
docs.text:
Use a separate database for tests. Never the one you develop on.

Start one with Docker:

docker run -d --name my_app_test -p 5433:5432 \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres -e POSTGRES_DB=my_app_test postgres:18

Change the config at the top of the test:

DatabaseConfig testDatabase = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: 'postgres',
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.postgres,
      host: 'localhost',
      port: 5433,
      user: 'postgres',
      password: 'postgres',
      database: 'my_app_test',
      debug: false,
    ),
  },
);

Delete deleteDbFile() and its two calls. The rest is the same. Or read the values from the env, and run DB_PORT=5433 DB_NAME=my_app_test dart test.

docs.title: Many test files
docs.text:
Each test file runs in its own process. Two files that use the same table at the same time break each other. Either give each file its own SQLite file (storage/test_users.sqlite, storage/test_posts.sqlite), or run them one by one:

dart test --concurrency=1

docs.title: Test a route with the database
docs.text:
This test uses the GET /api/users route of the Pagination guide. DoxTestClient starts the app inside the test. It runs the providers, so the ORM is set up by ORMProvider from lib/config/database.dart. Set the database with env variables, so the app picks the test database:

test/api_test.dart
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    await Migrator(
      migrations: migrations,
      config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig(),
    ).migrate();
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
  });

  setUp(refreshDatabase);

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('GET /api/users has no rows', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.get('/api/users');
    res.expectStatus(200);
    expect(res.json['data'], isEmpty);
  });
}

DB_CONNECTION=sqlite DB_NAME=storage/test.sqlite dart test test/api_test.dart

See Testing: test HTTP routes for all client methods.

docs.title: Cache
docs.text:
This page shows the full API of dox_cache, the cache behind Cache() in Dox.

It has remember, tags, atomic locks and four drivers.

docs.title: In a Dox app
docs.text:
