docs.text: Member Returns What it gives On IDoxRequest method String The HTTP method in upper case. yes uri Uri The request URI. yes route RouteData The matched route. no getRouteData() RouteData Same as route. yes path() String The request path, like /admin/users/5. no fullUrl() String The full URL with the query string. no pathIs(String pattern) bool true when the path matches. * matches any text. no routeIs(String pattern) bool true when the route name matches. It is false for a route with no name. no getRouteIdentifier() String base64 of <method>|<domain><path>. Useful as a cache or rate limit key. yes httpRequest HttpRequest The dart:io request. Use it for raw access. yes

docs.title: DoxResponse
docs.text:
Source: packages/dox-core/lib/http/response/dox_response.dart. Every setter returns the same DoxResponse, so calls chain.

Member Returns What it does DoxResponse(dynamic content) DoxResponse The constructor. content can be a String, number, Map, List, a JSON serializable object, a Stream<List<int>>, a File, a StreamFile or a DownloadableFile. statusCode(int code) DoxResponse Sets the status. Default 200. status int? The status set with statusCode(), or null (which means 200). content(dynamic content) DoxResponse Replaces the content. getContent() dynamic The content as it was given. stream(Stream<List<int>> stream) DoxResponse Sets a byte stream as content. contentType(ContentType type) DoxResponse Sets Content-Type. A File without it gets the type from its extension. header(String key, dynamic value) DoxResponse Sets one header. A second call with the same key replaces the value. cache-control and Cache-Control are one header. headers Map<String, dynamic> The headers set so far, by name. withHeaders(Map<String, dynamic> values) DoxResponse Adds these headers. A key replaces the header with the same name, in any case. Other headers stay. cookie(DoxCookie cookie, {bool setExpire = false}) DoxResponse Adds a Set-Cookie header. setExpire: true sends the cookie as expired, which removes it. cache(Duration duration) DoxResponse Sets Cache-Control: max-age=<seconds>. process(HttpRequest request) dynamic Internal. Writes headers, status, cookies and the body.

docs.title: Response helpers
docs.text:
Top level functions in the same file. They give a DoxResponse.

Function What it does response([dynamic content]) Same as DoxResponse(content). redirect(String url, {int status = 302}) A redirect to url. It sets the Location header. back(DoxRequest req, {String fallback = '/'}) A 302 redirect to the Referer header, or to fallback when there is none.

How the content is sent (responseDataHandler in packages/dox-core/lib/http/http_response_handler.dart):

Content Sent as null an empty body String text, as it is Map, List, number, bool, object with toJson() JSON, Content-Type: application/json DateTime its ISO 8601 text File streamed, with Content-Length, Accept-Ranges and one Range supported StreamFile streamed with its content type. An HTML, XML or JavaScript type is sent as a download, in a sandbox. DownloadableFile streamed with Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="<name>" Stream<List<int>> streamed chunk by chunk IHttpException its status and toResponse(), see HTTP exceptions other Exception or Error 500 with {"code": "server_error", "message": "Server Error"}. When APP_ENV is development or local, the body is toString() as text.

A plain value returned from a controller (not a DoxResponse) is sent the same way. It only goes through a DoxResponse when AppConfig.responseHandler is set, or when it is a File, StreamFile or DownloadableFile.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
This page lists known problems, with the text you see, the cause and the fix.

The texts come from the source code.

docs.title: The native HTTP library did not load
docs.text:
Symptom. The app stops at start with this error:

Unsupported operation: dox_http_native did not load: <reason>.
Fix: install Rust (cargo, see https://rustup.rs), then run the app again ...

At build time (dart pub get, dox serve or dox build) you may also see one of these:

dox_http_native: no native library for <os>-<arch>. Install Rust (cargo) to build it from source.
dox_http_native: download dox_http_native-<os>-<arch>.<ext>: 404
dox_http_native: download dox_http_native-<os>-<arch>.<ext> failed: <error>
dox_http_native: sha256 of dox_http_native-<os>-<arch>.<ext> does not match
dox_http_native: cargo build failed

Cause. The build hook of dox_http_native (hook/build.dart in its repo) tries, in this order: the lib_path user define, a local native/target/release build, the GitHub release download, and cargo build. None of them worked. Common reasons:

  • No internet during dart pub get, or the release has no build for your OS and CPU (there are builds for macOS arm64 and x64, Linux x64 and arm64, Windows x64).
  • Rust is not installed, so the fallback cargo build can not run.
  • You compiled with dart compile exe. It does not run build hooks, so no native library is in the binary.
  • The <reason> is native library ABI <x>, expected <y>: the library on disk is from another version of the package.

Fix. Pick one:

  1. Install Rust with rustup and run dart pub get again. The hook builds the library with cargo.
  2. When the reason is an ABI mismatch and you set lib_path, rebuild that library: cargo build --release in the native folder of the dox-http-native repo.

  3. Download the library from the GitHub release v<version> of dartondox/dox-http-native yourself and point to it in the root pubspec.yaml:

    hooks:
  user_defines:
    dox_http_native:
      lib_path: /path/to/libdox_http_native.so

  4. Build with dox build (it runs dart build cli), not with dart compile exe.

The native database drivers find their library the same way. When it does not load, the app stops too, with:

dox_postgres_native did not load: <reason>.
dox_mysql_native did not load: <reason>.

The fix is the same as above, with the dox-postgres-native or dox-mysql-native repo.

See Native server, Postgres native and MySQL native.

docs.title: Port already in use
docs.text:
Symptom. At start:

SocketException: dox_http_native: bind failed (<code>) (OS Error: errno = <errno>), port = 3000

<errno> is the OS error: 48 on macOS, 98 on Linux. <code> is -1000 minus it: -1048 on macOS, -1098 on Linux.

Cause. Another process listens on the port. Often it is an old bin/server.dart that dox serve did not stop, or a second copy of the app.

Fix. Find and stop the process, or use another port.

lsof -i :3000          # macOS and Linux: who has the port
kill <pid>

Or set APP_PORT=3001 in .env (a new project reads it into serverPort).

docs.title: build_runner: conflicting outputs
docs.text:
Symptom. dox build_runner:build, dox serve or dox build stops with a build_runner message that starts with Conflicting outputs were detected, and names files like lib/generated/dtos.g.dart or lib/app/models/user/user.model.g.dart.

Cause. The generated .g.dart files are on disk, but .dart_tool/build does not know them. This happens after a git clone with committed .g.dart files, after deleting .dart_tool, or after a Dart SDK update.

Fix. Delete the build cache and build again:

rm -rf .dart_tool/build
dart run build_runner build

If that is not enough, delete the named .g.dart files and build again. New build_runner versions have no --delete-conflicting-outputs flag, so the Dox CLI does not pass it.

docs.title: Ambiguous import: Uuid, Name or Schema
docs.text:
Symptom. The analyzer or the build says a name like Uuid, Name, Range, Image or Schema is an "ambiguous import".

Cause. dox_core exports the validation names of dox_validation: the rule annotations (Uuid, Name, Range, Image, ...) and the Schema class. Another import has a class with the same name, like package:uuid. dox_orm also has a Schema class.

Fix. Hide the name you do not use in that file:

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart' hide Uuid;
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart' hide Schema;

docs.title: A .env value with #
docs.text:
A # after a space starts a comment. The comment is not part of the value.

APP_PORT=3000 # dev port   -> 3000
DB_PASSWORD=abc#123        -> abc#123 (no space before the #)
DB_PASSWORD="abc # 123"    -> abc # 123 (quotes keep the #)

When a value must have # in it (a space, then #), put the value in quotes. The quotes are removed.

docs.title: Hash.make throws on a long password
docs.text:
Symptom. Saving a user, or registering, gives a 500. The log shows:

Invalid argument(s) (password): The password is too long. bcrypt takes at most 72 bytes.

Cause. Hash.make() and Hash.makeAsync() use bcrypt. bcrypt takes at most 72 bytes, so Dox throws an ArgumentError for a longer password. The text does not hold the password, so it is safe in logs.

Fix. Refuse long passwords in your DTO, before you hash them:

@MaxLength(72)
final String password;

@MaxLength counts characters, not bytes. A password with non-ASCII characters can still be over 72 bytes.

Hash.verify(password, hash) does not throw. It gives false when hash is not a valid bcrypt hash, for example a plain password or an empty string in the column. Make sure every stored password went through Hash.make().

For normal login use Auth().attempt() from dox_auth. See Hashing.

docs.title: MySQL 8 login fails
docs.text:
Symptom. The connection to MySQL 8 is refused at login, while the same user works from the mysql client. Often the user was made with the default caching_sha2_password plugin.

Cause. caching_sha2_password needs either TLS or the server RSA public key to send the password. A client that has neither can not log in.

Fix. The Dox MySQL driver (dox_mysql_native) supports caching_sha2_password (MySQL 8.4) and MariaDB 11. Check these settings on the connection in lib/config/database.dart:

Setting What to do Remote host without TLS Turn on useSSL: true. useSSL: true The server must have TLS on. host, port, user, password A wrong value gives the same login error. DB_PORT is 3306 by default for MySQL.

As a last resort, change the user on the server:

ALTER USER 'app'@'%' IDENTIFIED WITH mysql_native_password BY 'secret';

docs.title: SQLite: the database file
docs.text:
Symptom. An SqliteException with unable to open database file, or an empty database after dox build.

Cause. database is a file path. A relative path is relative to the folder you start the app from. dox build tells you to run cd build/bundle && ./bin/server. So the default DB_NAME=db/dox.sqlite is then build/bundle/db/dox.sqlite. dox build does not copy your SQLite files into the bundle, so that database starts empty. SQLite makes a missing file, but not a missing folder.

Fix.

  • Use an absolute path, or make the folder first.
  • Set it with DB_NAME (a new project reads it): DB_NAME=/var/lib/my_app/dox.sqlite.
  • Migrations use DB_DATABASE or DB_NAME as the path too. Use the same value for both.

:memory: and isolates

:memory: opens a new empty database in each isolate. With totalIsolate above 1, every isolate sees different data. Use a file, or totalIsolate: 1.

Dox opens a file database with journal_mode = WAL, synchronous = NORMAL, foreign_keys = ON and busy_timeout = 5000 (change it with extra: {'busyTimeout': ...}).

docs.title: dox: command not found after dart pub global activate
docs.text:
Symptom.

zsh: command not found: dox

right after dart pub global activate dox.

Cause. dart pub global activate puts the dox script in $HOME/.pub-cache/bin. That folder is not in your PATH.

Fix. Add it to your shell profile and open a new terminal:

export PATH="$PATH":"$HOME/.pub-cache/bin"

On Windows the folder is %LOCALAPPDATA%\Pub\Cache\bin.

docs.title: Other startup errors
docs.text: Short errors, like a bad route, a missing DTO or a bad env key, are in the Error index.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
This page shows how to let users register, log in and log out, and how to protect routes. Follow it from the top. At the end of each way, your app has working auth.

dox_auth gives you:

  • a password login against your user table (bcrypt hashes)
  • three ways to keep a user logged in: access tokens, JWT tokens and sessions
  • AuthMiddleware, which protects a route and loads the user
  • req.auth, the logged-in user in your controller
  • a login throttle, and tools to revoke and renew tokens

dox_auth has no password reset, no email check, no "remember me" and no two-step login (2FA). Your app builds these. The tools on this page help, for example the two-step login recipe. Who may do what (roles, "may this user edit this post") is on the Authorization page.

docs.title: Which one do I need?
docs.text:
Your app Use Why An API for a mobile app, a front end on another domain, or scripts Access tokens You can revoke each token at any time, give it abilities, and renew it. The token is checked in a database table. An API where other services must check the token with a key JWT The token is signed. There is no token table. It works until it expires, unless you turn on revocation. Web pages served by this app (forms, Inertia) Session The browser sends the session cookie. The client does nothing. Web pages and an API in one app More than one guard A session guard for the pages, a token guard for the API.

Not sure? For an API, use access tokens.

Two words used on this page:

  • A guard is a named way to log in, like api or web. It says how the login is kept (access token, JWT or session) and which model holds the users.
  • An ability is a name like posts:read on an access token. It says what the token may do.

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text: These steps start from a new app made with dox create my_app. It has a SQLite database, a User model and a users table with name, email and password columns. Do these steps once, then follow one of the ways below.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
dox add auth

It needs the ORM (dox add orm) and a User model in lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart (dox make:model User -m) first. A new app has both. It does steps 1, 4 and 5 below. It also writes the token table migration of Access tokens, so you do not need dox auth:tokens-table there. Run dox migrate. Then do steps 2, 3 and 6 yourself. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice.

docs.title: Set it up by hand
docs.text: Do all the steps below when you do not use dox add auth.

docs.title: 1. Add the package
docs.text:
A new app does not have dox_auth. Add it:

dart pub add dox_auth

docs.title: 2. Check the user model
docs.text:
The password hash must never leave the server. Put it in hidden, so toJson() leaves it out. The model of a new app already does this:

lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel(table: 'users', softDelete: true)
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @override
  List<String> get fillable => <String>['name', 'email', 'password'];

  @override
  List<String> get hidden => <String>['password'];

  @Column()
  String? name;

  @Column()
  String? email;

  @Column()
  String? password;
}

docs.title: 3. Add the input checks
docs.text:
These DTOs check the body of the register and login requests. Bad input gets 422, and the controller does not run. See Validation.

lib/app/dtos/auth/auth.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart' hide Schema;

part 'auth.dto.g.dart';

/// The body of a register request.
@Dto()
class RegisterUser {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 1, max: 255)
  final String name;

  @Trim()
  @Lowercase()
  @Email()
  @Unique('users', column: 'email')
  final String email;

  /// bcrypt reads at most 72 bytes
  @Length(min: 8, max: 72)
  final String password;

  const RegisterUser({
    required this.name,
    required this.email,
    required this.password,
  });

  static const DtoSchema<RegisterUser> schema = $RegisterUserDto;
}

/// The body of a login request.
@Dto()
class LoginUser {
  @Trim()
  @Lowercase()
  @Email()
  final String email;

  final String password;

  const LoginUser({required this.email, required this.password});

  static const DtoSchema<LoginUser> schema = $LoginUserDto;
}

docs.title: 4. Add the auth config
docs.text:
The config lists the guards. Each guard has a driver (how the login is kept) and an AuthProvider (which model holds the users). This config has one guard, api, with access tokens. The JWT and session ways give their own version of this file.

lib/config/auth.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

AuthConfig authConfig = AuthConfig(
  defaultGuard: 'api',
  guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
    'api': AuthGuard(
      driver: AccessTokenAuthDriver(expiresIn: const Duration(days: 30)),
      provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
    ),
  },
);

Auth() and AuthMiddleware() use defaultGuard. All options are in the reference.

docs.title: 5. Load the config when the app starts
docs.text:
This class gives the config to dox_auth when the app starts. It is a DoxProvider (a class that Dox runs at startup). It is not the AuthProvider of step 4.

lib/providers/auth_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/auth.dart';

class AppAuthProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Auth.initialize(authConfig);
  }
}

You do not register it by hand. Dox finds every DoxProvider.

docs.title: 6. Run the code generator
docs.text:
It writes the DTO code and adds AppAuthProvider to lib/generated/container.g.dart.

dart run build_runner build
dart analyze

Do not start dox s yet. The first way below makes a migration first.

docs.title: Access tokens
docs.text:
An access token is an API token that you can revoke at any time. It is like an AdonisJS access token.

  • A token looks like oat_12.<secret>. 12 is the row id in the token table.
  • The table keeps only a SHA-256 hash of the secret. You see the plain token once, when you make it.
  • A token works until it expires or you revoke it.
  • Each token has abilities. The default is * (all abilities).

The setup above already added the api guard with AccessTokenAuthDriver.

docs.title: 1. Add the token table
docs.text:
dox auth:tokens-table --users-table=users
dox migrate

dox auth:tokens-table writes a migration in db/migration. dox migrate adds it to db/migration/migrations.dart, runs it, and makes the auth_access_tokens table.

The migration it writes looks like this:

// ignore_for_file: file_names
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

/// The auth_access_tokens table of dox_auth.
class CreateAccessTokensTable extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await AccessTokenTables.up(schema, usersTable: 'users');
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await AccessTokenTables.down(schema);
  }
}

--users-table=users adds a foreign key with cascade delete. So when you delete a user, the tokens of the user are deleted too. The command does not overwrite: when a create_access_tokens_table migration is already there, it prints so and stops. For users with uuid or text ids, see Users with uuid or text ids. All flags are in the reference.

docs.title: 2. Write the auth controller
3. Add the routes
docs.text:
AuthMiddleware() protects a route. A request with no good token stops with 401. A rate limit on register and login slows down password guessing.

lib/routes/api.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/api.controller.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/auth.controller.dart';

class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.get('/ping', (ApiController c) => c.pong);

    // for guests
    Route.post('/auth/register', <dynamic>[
      RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'register'),
      (AuthController c) => c.register,
    ]);
    Route.post('/auth/login', <dynamic>[
      RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'login'),
      (AuthController c) => c.login,
    ]);

    // for logged-in users
    Route.get('/auth/me', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), (AuthController c) => c.me]);
    Route.post('/auth/logout', <dynamic>[
      AuthMiddleware(),
      (AuthController c) => c.logout,
    ]);
  }
}

Run the generator again, then start the app:

dart run build_runner build
dox s

docs.title: 4. Try it
docs.text:
The client sends the token in the Authorization header: Authorization: Bearer oat_12.<secret>. The word Bearer can be in any case. Run these in a second terminal. Where a step says "keep it in", copy the token from the answer into a shell variable.

# make an account
curl -X POST localhost:3000/api/auth/register -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Ada","email":"ada@example.com","password":"secret-pass"}'
# 201 {"token":"oat_1.c79C...","user":{"id":1,"name":"Ada","email":"ada@example.com",...}}

# a wrong password
curl -X POST localhost:3000/api/auth/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"ada@example.com","password":"wrong-pass"}'
# 401 {"code":"unauthorized","message":"Wrong email or password"}

# log in, and keep the token in TOKEN
curl -X POST localhost:3000/api/auth/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"ada@example.com","password":"secret-pass"}'
# 200 {"token":"oat_2.OTAG...","user":{"id":1,...}}
TOKEN='oat_2.OTAG...'

curl localhost:3000/api/auth/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# 200 {"id":1,"name":"Ada","email":"ada@example.com",...}

curl localhost:3000/api/auth/me
# 401 {"code":"unauthorized","message":"Authentication failed"}

# log out
curl -X POST localhost:3000/api/auth/logout -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# 200 {"logged_out":true}
curl localhost:3000/api/auth/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# 401 {"code":"unauthorized","message":"Authentication failed"}

The password is never in an answer, because it is in hidden. The ids (oat_1, oat_2, ...) count up in your table, so yours may differ.

Your app has a working login. The next part adds script tokens, abilities and token renewal. You can skip it until you need it.

docs.title: Abilities
docs.text:
createAccessToken(user, abilities: <String>['posts:read']) gives a token that can do only these things. The default is <String>['*']: all abilities. attempt always gives *.

Check an ability in the controller, after AuthMiddleware:

Auth auth = req.auth as Auth;
if (!auth.tokenCan('posts:write')) {
  throw ForbiddenHttpException();
}
auth.currentAccessToken; // the AccessToken of this request
  • tokenCan is true when the token has the ability, or *.
  • tokenCan is false when there is no access token. So a session or JWT login never passes it.
  • A route with no tokenCan check takes every good token, whatever its abilities. Check an ability on each route that needs one.
  • A token without the ability gets 403. A request with no good token gets 401 from AuthMiddleware.

docs.title: Script tokens
docs.text:
Users can make extra tokens, for example for a script that only reads posts. This controller lists, makes and revokes them. Each action needs the tokens:manage ability. A login token has *, so it passes. A script token does not, so a leaked script token can not make new tokens.

lib/app/http/controllers/token.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class TokenController {
  /// GET /api/tokens: all tokens of the user, newest first.
  Future<List<AccessToken>> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    Auth auth = _manager(req);
    return auth.accessTokens(auth.user<User>()!);
  }

  /// POST /api/tokens: a token for a script. It can only read posts.
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> store(DoxRequest req) async {
    Auth auth = _manager(req);
    AccessToken token = await auth.createAccessToken(
      auth.user<User>()!,
      name: 'script',
      abilities: <String>['posts:read'],
      expiresIn: const Duration(days: 90),
    );
    return <String, dynamic>{'token': token.value};
  }

  /// DELETE /api/tokens/{id}: revoke one token of the user.
  Future<Map<String, bool>> destroy(DoxRequest req, int id) async {
    Auth auth = _manager(req);
    if (!await auth.revokeAccessToken(auth.user<User>()!, id)) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException();
    }
    return <String, bool>{'revoked': true};
  }

  /// The Auth of the request, when its token may manage tokens.
  Auth _manager(DoxRequest req) {
    Auth auth = req.auth as Auth;
    if (!auth.tokenCan('tokens:manage')) {
      throw ForbiddenHttpException();
    }
    return auth;
  }
}

A route that needs the posts:read ability:

lib/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

@Inject()
class PostController {
  /// GET /api/posts: needs a token with the posts:read ability.
  List<String> index(DoxRequest req) {
    if (!(req.auth as Auth).tokenCan('posts:read')) {
      throw ForbiddenHttpException();
    }
    return <String>['Hello'];
  }
}

In lib/routes/api.dart, add the imports at the top:

import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/token.controller.dart';

And add the routes at the end of register():

Route.get('/tokens', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), (TokenController c) => c.index]);
Route.post('/tokens', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), (TokenController c) => c.store]);
Route.delete('/tokens/{id}', <dynamic>[
  AuthMiddleware(),
  (TokenController c) => c.destroy,
]);
Route.get('/posts', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), (PostController c) => c.index]);

Run dart run build_runner build. dox s restarts by itself.

/auth/me and /auth/logout have no ability check, so a script token can call them too. That is fine: it sees its own user, and its logout revokes only itself.

Try it. Log in first and keep the token in TOKEN, like above.

# make a script token, and keep it in SCRIPT_TOKEN
curl -X POST localhost:3000/api/tokens -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# 200 {"token":"oat_4.pwwK..."}
SCRIPT_TOKEN='oat_4.pwwK...'

curl localhost:3000/api/posts -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCRIPT_TOKEN"
# 200 ["Hello"]

# the script token may not manage tokens
curl -X POST localhost:3000/api/tokens -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCRIPT_TOKEN"
# 403 {"code":"forbidden","message":"Forbidden"}

# list the tokens, then revoke the script token (id 4)
curl localhost:3000/api/tokens -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# 200 [{"id":4,"name":"script","type":"api","abilities":["posts:read"],...},...]
curl -X DELETE localhost:3000/api/tokens/4 -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# 200 {"revoked":true}
curl localhost:3000/api/posts -H "Authorization: Bearer $SCRIPT_TOKEN"
# 401 {"code":"unauthorized","message":"Authentication failed"}

docs.title: List and revoke tokens
docs.text:
await Auth().accessTokens(user);           // all tokens of the user, newest first, expired ones too
await Auth().revokeAccessToken(user, id);  // false when the user has no token with this id
await Auth().revokeAllAccessTokens(user);  // all tokens of the user, eg. after a password change
await Auth().revokeToken(req);             // the token of this request (a logout)
await Auth().pruneExpiredAccessTokens();   // delete expired tokens, eg. from a scheduled job
  • A revoked token is deleted from the table, so it stops working at once.
  • token.toJson() has no hash and no plain token, so you can send it to the client. GET /api/tokens above does this.
  • On the Auth of AuthMiddleware, (req.auth as Auth).revokeToken(req) uses the token that was already checked. It does not check it again.
  • Expired tokens stay in the table until you call pruneExpiredAccessTokens(). Run it from a scheduled task.

docs.title: Rotate a token
docs.text:
Rotate a token to renew it before it expires. rotateAccessToken makes a new token in place of an old one. The new token has the same user, name and abilities as the old one.

Add this method to AuthController:

/// POST /api/auth/refresh: a new token in place of the token of this
/// request. The old token stops working at once.
Future<Map<String, dynamic>> refresh(DoxRequest req) async {
  Auth auth = req.auth as Auth;
  if (!auth.tokenCan('tokens:manage')) {
    throw ForbiddenHttpException();
  }
  AccessToken next = await auth.rotateAccessToken(auth.currentAccessToken!);
  return <String, dynamic>{
    'token': next.value,
    'expires_at': next.expiresAt?.toIso8601String(),
  };
}

And this route at the end of register() in lib/routes/api.dart:

Route.post('/auth/refresh', <dynamic>[
  AuthMiddleware(),
  (AuthController c) => c.refresh,
]);

Run dart run build_runner build. The tokens:manage check keeps a script token from renewing itself.

Try it. Log in first and keep the token in TOKEN.

curl -X POST localhost:3000/api/auth/refresh -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# 200 {"token":"oat_6.-qAk...","expires_at":"2026-12-11T04:43:15.701944Z"}
NEW_TOKEN='oat_6.-qAk...'

curl localhost:3000/api/auth/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# 401 {"code":"unauthorized","message":"Authentication failed"}
curl localhost:3000/api/auth/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $NEW_TOKEN"
# 200 {"id":1,"name":"Ada",...}

grace is how long the old token still works. The default is zero: the old token ends at once, like above. You need a grace only when one client sends requests in parallel. Then a request that is on the way with the old token does not fail. Keep it short, a few seconds: rotateAccessToken(token, grace: const Duration(seconds: 10)). If the old token ends sooner than grace, it keeps its own end.

The rules:

  • A token can be rotated only once. A second rotate of the same token throws an UnAuthorizedException (401, The access token was already rotated.). This is also true in the grace time. Nothing is made.
  • A revoked or expired token is refused the same way: 401 with The access token is revoked or does not exist. or The access token is expired.
  • When two rotates of one token run at the same time, only one works.
  • It runs in one transaction. When it fails, nothing is changed.
  • expiresIn: sets how long the new token works. null (the default) gives the expiresIn of the driver. When that is null too, the new token has no end.
  • name: gives the new token another name. null keeps the old name.
  • A token of another guard, or a negative grace, throws an ArgumentError.

Safety notes:

  • A longer grace gives a stolen old token more time. In that time it works on every route, also the token routes, so it can make new tokens. Only rotate refuses it. Keep grace short, or zero.
  • Each rotate gives a full new life. So a client that rotates again and again stays logged in forever. A rotated token has a new createdAt and no link to the first token. To set a limit, keep the first login time yourself. For example, save it in a column, or in the token name with rotateAccessToken(token, name: ...). Or ask for the password again after some time.

Rotate needs the rotated_at column. A table made by dox auth:tokens-table has it.

docs.title: A token table without rotated_at
docs.text:
A token table without the rotated_at column works for everything except rotate. rotateAccessToken then throws a StateError that names the column:

Bad state: The table 'auth_access_tokens' has no rotated_at column. rotate() needs it. Add it in a new migration: ...

To add the column:

  1. Stop dox s if it runs. It runs new migrations when it restarts. It would run the new, still empty file, and then the column is never added.

  2. Make a migration:

    dox make:migration add_rotated_at_to_auth_access_tokens

  3. Paste this into the new file in db/migration (its name starts with the date and time):

    // ignore_for_file: file_names
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

class AddRotatedAtToAuthAccessTokens extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.table('auth_access_tokens', (Table t) {
      t.dateTimeTz('rotated_at').nullable();
    });
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.table('auth_access_tokens', (Table t) {
      t.dropColumn('rotated_at');
    });
  }
}

  4. Run dox migrate, then start dox s again.

docs.title: JWT tokens
docs.text:
A JWT is a signed token. The server keeps no list of tokens. The token works until it expires, unless you turn on revocation. The user is still loaded from the database on each request, by the id in the token.

Do the setup first. This way needs no token table.

docs.title: 1. Change the guard
2. Write the auth controller
3. Add the routes
4. Try it
docs.text:
curl -X POST localhost:3000/api/auth/register -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Ada","email":"ada@example.com","password":"secret-pass"}'
# 201 {"token":"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...","user":{"id":1,"name":"Ada",...}}

# log in, and keep the token in TOKEN
curl -X POST localhost:3000/api/auth/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"ada@example.com","password":"secret-pass"}'
# 200 {"token":"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...","user":{"id":1,"name":"Ada",...}}
TOKEN='eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...'

curl localhost:3000/api/auth/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# 200 {"id":1,"name":"Ada","email":"ada@example.com",...}

curl -X POST localhost:3000/api/auth/logout -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# 200 {"logged_out":true}

curl localhost:3000/api/auth/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# 401 {"code":"unauthorized","message":"Authentication failed"}

If Ada already has an account from another way, register answers 422. Then just log in. For a longer JWT walkthrough, see the JWT auth guide.

docs.title: Small tokens
docs.text: By default, a token holds the user (toJson(), hidden fields left out), plus the iat, exp and jti claims. Anyone can read a JWT payload. It is signed, not secret. minimalPayload: true is the safer choice. The token then holds only the user id (the sub claim). Load the user with req.auth?.user<User>(), not from the token. A front end that reads user fields from the token must then get the user from the API.

docs.title: Revoke tokens
docs.text:
By default, a token works until it expires. There is no server list of tokens. Turn on revocation to stop a token before it expires:

JwtAuthDriver(
  secret: SecretKey(env.appKey),
  revocation: true,
  revocationStore: 'auth',
)

Each token has a random id (the jti claim). With revocation on, the driver keeps revoked tokens in the app cache (Cache() of dox_core). A revoked token stops working at once:

await Auth().revokeToken(req);     // revoke the bearer token of this request (a logout)
await Auth().revokeAllTokens(id);  // revoke all tokens of a user, eg. after a password change or a ban
await Auth().forgetUser(id);       // drop the user from `userCacheTtl`, eg. after a ban
  • With revocation off, these three methods throw a StateError. So no one thinks a token is revoked when it is not.
  • With revocation off, a token check never reads the cache.
  • A revoked token stays on the deny-list only until it expires.
  • revokeAllTokens keeps tokens made after the call. A token made in the same second as the call also still works, because iat is in whole seconds.
  • A token with no jti claim can not go on the deny-list, so revokeToken does nothing for it. revokeAllTokens still stops it when it has an iat claim. Tokens from JwtAuthDriver have one.
  • The revokeAllTokens time comes from the server clock. Keep server clocks in sync (NTP).
  • Give auth its own cache store, and never flush it. For example, a redis store with its own prefix. Pick it with revocationStore. With no revocationStore, the default app store is used. A flush of this store (Cache().flush()), or a memory store with max_size that drops old keys, brings revoked tokens back until they expire.
  • Cost: a token check reads this store on every request, also with userCacheTtl. It is one many() call: one round trip on redis and memory. On the file store (the default) it is 2 or 3 file reads per request. Use memory for one isolate, or redis for many isolates or servers. A memory store is seen by one isolate only.
  • When the store can not be read, the token is checked with only the signature and exp, and a warning is printed once. So a cache outage does not log everyone out. But revoked tokens work until the store is back.

docs.title: Change the JWT secret
docs.text:
New tokens are always signed with secret. A token is checked with secret first, then with each old secret. Only a wrong signature moves on to the next secret. An expired token fails at once.

  • The secret is APP_KEY (SecretKey(env.appKey)): follow Change the key. The old keys in AppConfig.previousKeys are used. You need nothing more.

  • A separate JWT secret: give the old one to the driver.

    JwtAuthDriver(
  secret: SecretKey(env.jwtSecret),
  previousSecrets: <JWTKey>[SecretKey(env.jwtOldSecret)],
)

Remove the old secret once expiresIn has passed. Then every old token has expired anyway. Do not keep a leaked secret: anyone who has it can make tokens. To log out everyone at once, change the secret and keep no old secrets.

docs.title: Session login for web pages
docs.text:
For web pages, keep the login in the session instead of a token. The browser sends the session cookie, so the client does nothing. It needs SessionMiddleware and CsrfMiddleware. See Session and CSRF protection.

Do the setup first. This way needs no token table.

docs.title: 1. Change the guard
2. Write the controller
docs.text:
This controller answers JSON, for a front end with axios or Inertia. axios sends the CSRF token by itself. For HTML forms, see CSRF protection.

lib/app/http/controllers/session.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/auth/auth.dto.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class SessionController {
  /// POST /register: make an account and log in.
  Future<DoxResponse> register(DoxRequest req, RegisterUser body) async {
    User user = User()
      ..name = body.name
      ..email = body.email
      ..password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
    await user.save();

    Auth().loginSession(req, user);
    return response(user).statusCode(201);
  }

  /// POST /login: check the email and password, keep the login in the session.
  Future<User?> login(DoxRequest req, LoginUser body) async {
    Auth auth = Auth();
    bool ok = await auth.attemptSession(req, <String, dynamic>{
      'email': body.email,
      'password': body.password,
    });
    if (!ok) {
      throw UnAuthorizedException(message: 'Wrong email or password');
    }
    return auth.user<User>();
  }

  /// GET /me: the logged-in user.
  User? me(DoxRequest req) {
    return req.auth?.user<User>();
  }

  /// POST /logout: remove the login and all session data.
  Map<String, bool> logout(DoxRequest req) {
    Auth().logout(req);
    return <String, bool>{'logged_out': true};
  }
}

For a form post, answer with a redirect instead. The method then returns Future<DoxResponse>:

if (!ok) {
  req.session.flashErrors(<String, dynamic>{'email': 'Wrong email or password'});
  return back(req);
}
return redirect('/dashboard');

docs.title: 3. Add the routes
docs.text:
The session and CSRF middleware go on the web router only. The API routes stay without a session.

lib/routes/web.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/session.controller.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/web.controller.dart';

class WebRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[
    const SessionMiddleware(),
    const CsrfMiddleware(),
  ];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.get('/ping', (WebController c) => c.pong);

    Route.post('/register', <dynamic>[
      RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'register'),
      (SessionController c) => c.register,
    ]);
    Route.post('/login', <dynamic>[
      RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'login'),
      (SessionController c) => c.login,
    ]);
    Route.get('/me', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), (SessionController c) => c.me]);
    Route.post('/logout', <dynamic>[
      AuthMiddleware(),
      (SessionController c) => c.logout,
    ]);
  }
}

To send a guest to the login page instead of a 401, use AuthMiddleware(redirectTo: '/login'). With the jsonNoRedirect flag on, a JSON or XHR client gets a 401 and no redirect.

Run dart run build_runner build, then dox s.

docs.title: 4. Try it
docs.text:
A browser keeps the cookies by itself. With curl, keep them in a file, and send the XSRF-TOKEN cookie back in the X-XSRF-TOKEN header. Ada must have an account. Make one with POST /register (same body as below, plus name), or use the one from another way.

# the first request gives the session and XSRF-TOKEN cookies
curl -c jar.txt localhost:3000/ping
XSRF=$(grep XSRF-TOKEN jar.txt | cut -f7)

curl -b jar.txt -c jar.txt -X POST localhost:3000/login -H "X-XSRF-TOKEN: $XSRF" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"email":"ada@example.com","password":"secret-pass"}'
# 200 {"id":1,"name":"Ada","email":"ada@example.com",...}

XSRF=$(grep XSRF-TOKEN jar.txt | cut -f7)   # login gives a new CSRF token
curl -b jar.txt localhost:3000/me
# 200 {"id":1,"name":"Ada",...}

curl -b jar.txt -c jar.txt -X POST localhost:3000/logout -H "X-XSRF-TOKEN: $XSRF"
# 200 {"logged_out":true}

curl -b jar.txt localhost:3000/me
# 401 {"code":"unauthorized","message":"Authentication failed"}

A POST with no CSRF token gets 419 (csrf_token_mismatch).

docs.title: End other sessions when the password changes
docs.text:
By default, a session stays logged in after the user changes the password. So a stolen session still works. Turn on the endSessionsOnPasswordChange flag to fix this. The session then keeps a fingerprint of the password hash. When the hash changes, the session ends on its next request that checks the login. That is a request through AuthMiddleware. For a socket, it is a call of Auth().userFromSession(session). A route with no login check does not end it. The flag is off by default.

lib/config/auth.dart
AuthConfig authConfig = AuthConfig(
  defaultGuard: 'web',
  guards: guards,
  flags: const AuthFlags(endSessionsOnPasswordChange: true),
);

A password change now ends all sessions of the user, also the current one. When your app changes the password itself, keep the current session with updateSessionPasswordHash. Call it after save():

user.password = await Hash.makeAsync(newPassword);
await user.save();
Auth().updateSessionPasswordHash(req, user);

A rehash on login changes the hash too. Call updateSessionPasswordHash after that save() as well.

Pass a fully loaded user to updateSessionPasswordHash and loginSession. A model from a select() with no password column looks like a user with no password. The session then ends on its next request that checks the login. The user must be the user of the session. Another user throws an ArgumentError. The password column must give the same value on every read. A hook or cast that makes a new value each time ends every session.

docs.title: Log out other devices
docs.text:
logoutOtherDevices ends all other sessions of the user and keeps this one. It checks the password, hashes it again and saves the user. It needs a session guard and the flag.

/// POST /logout-others: end the sessions on other devices.
Future<Map<String, bool>> logoutOthers(DoxRequest req, ConfirmPassword body) async {
  await (req.auth as Auth).logoutOtherDevices(req, body.password);
  return <String, bool>{'done': true};
}

ConfirmPassword is a DTO like LoginUser. A missing field gets 422 before the controller runs. Add it to the same file as LoginUser, then run dart run build_runner build:

lib/app/dtos/auth/auth.dto.dart
@Dto()
class ConfirmPassword {
  final String password;

  const ConfirmPassword({required this.password});

  static const DtoSchema<ConfirmPassword> schema = $ConfirmPasswordDto;
}
  • A wrong password throws an UnAuthorizedException with status 401 and code wrong_password. Catch it to show an error on your form.
  • Without the flag, it throws a StateError and changes nothing.
  • When a model hook stops save(), it throws a StateError. The sessions do not change.
  • When save() throws, the old hash is put back on the model and the error is thrown again.
  • It checks a password, so put a limit on the route, like on a login. See Login throttle and Rate limiting.

docs.title: Sessions made before the flag
docs.text:
A session made while the flag was off has no fingerprint. It is not logged out. Its first request that checks the login, with the flag on, stores the fingerprint. Until then, a password change does not end it. So a session stolen before you turned the flag on can stay.

To end all old sessions once, change APP_KEY and do not put the old key in previousKeys. This also breaks other data made with the old key, like encrypted values and JWTs. With the cache session driver, you can clear the session store instead.

A fingerprint made with a key in previousKeys still works. When you remove that key from previousKeys, sessions that still hold such a fingerprint are logged out.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
DoxTestClient runs your app in the test. withToken sends Authorization: Bearer <token>. This test is for the access token way. It also works for JWT. The test uses the database of .env, so it runs the migrations first.

test/auth_test.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    Dox().initialize(appConfig);
    await Migrator(
      migrations: migrations,
      config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig(),
    ).migrate();
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
  });

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('register, then use the token', () async {
    String email = 'test-${DateTime.now().microsecondsSinceEpoch}@example.com';
    TestResponse register = await client.post(
      '/api/auth/register',
      body: <String, dynamic>{
        'name': 'Test',
        'email': email,
        'password': 'secret-pass',
      },
    );
    register.expectStatus(201);
    String token = register.json['token'] as String;

    TestResponse me = await client.withToken(token).get('/api/auth/me');
    me.expectStatus(200);
    expect(me.json['email'], email);
    expect(me.json.containsKey('password'), isFalse);
  });

  test('no token gives 401', () async {
    (await client.get('/api/auth/me')).expectStatus(401);
  });
}

Run it with dart test.

To act as a user with no HTTP login, make a token in the test: await Auth().createAccessToken(user), then client.withToken(token.value!). For a session app, use client.withSession(). It keeps cookies and sends the CSRF token, like a browser. See Testing.

docs.title: More than one guard
docs.text:
Each guard has its own driver and its own user model. For example, a session for web pages, access tokens for the API, and admins in their own table. Admin is a model of your own, like User:

lib/config/auth.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/admin/admin.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

AuthConfig authConfig = AuthConfig(
  defaultGuard: 'web',
  guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
    'web': AuthGuard(
      driver: SessionAuthDriver(),
      provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
    ),
    'api': AuthGuard(
      driver: AccessTokenAuthDriver(),
      provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
    ),
    'admin': AuthGuard(
      driver: AccessTokenAuthDriver(table: 'admin_access_tokens'),
      provider: AuthProvider(model: () => Admin()),
    ),
  },
);

Pick the guard by name:

String? token = await Auth(guard: 'admin').attempt(credentials);

Route.get('/admin', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(guard: 'admin'), (AdminController c) => c.index]);

// try the guards in order
Route.get('/me', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(guards: <String>['web', 'api']), (UserController c) => c.me]);
  • With guards:, the first guard with a good login sets req.auth.
  • Set guard: or guards:, not both. Both, or an empty list, throws an ArgumentError.
  • A JWT keeps the guard name in its aud claim, and an access token keeps its type. So a token of one guard does not work on another guard.
  • Give each user model its own token table, with table: on the driver and in the migration (AccessTokenTables.up(schema, table: 'admin_access_tokens')). With one shared table and usersTable, the foreign key fails for admin tokens, and deleting a user also deletes the tokens of the admin with the same id.
  • Pass a user of the guard's model: Auth(guard: 'admin').createAccessToken(admin). A user of another model throws an ArgumentError.

docs.title: Pages for everyone and pages for guests
docs.text:
A public page can still know the user. AuthMiddleware(optional: true) sets req.auth when the login is good, and lets guests through too. Login and register pages are for guests only. GuestMiddleware lets only guests through.

Route.get('/posts', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(optional: true), (PostController c) => c.index]);
Route.get('/login', <dynamic>[GuestMiddleware(redirectTo: '/dashboard'), (PageController c) => c.login]);
  • With optional: true, a guest, or a bad, expired or revoked token, goes on with req.auth as null.
  • With the JWT and access token drivers, a database error also goes on as a guest, and it is reported. With AccessTokenAuthDriver(throwOnError: true) it is thrown instead (see When the database fails).
  • With the session driver, a database error is not caught, so the answer is 500.
  • redirectTo is not used when optional: true.
  • GuestMiddleware sends a logged-in user to redirectTo. With no redirectTo, the answer is 403 with the code already_logged_in.
  • Both take guard:, like AuthMiddleware(guard: 'admin').
  • req.can() of Authorization also works on a page with optional: true.

docs.title: Two-step login (2FA)
docs.text:
A two-step login asks for a password, then for a code (from a mail or an app). dox_auth does not make or check the code: your app does that. setAccessTokenAbilities helps: it replaces the abilities of a token. The plain token stays the same.

This flow replaces the normal attempt() login of the access token way. An app has one login flow.

How it works:

  1. Step one checks the password with once(). It gives a token with only 2fa:pending. The token works 10 minutes.
  2. Step two checks the code. Then it rotates the token, and gives the new token the abilities of a full login (*, like attempt() gives). The client gets the new token with a full life. The step-one token ends at once.
  3. Each route that needs the second step uses the requireTwoFactor middleware. A * token passes it, a 2fa:pending token does not.

Add the DTO for the code:

lib/app/dtos/two_factor_code/two_factor_code.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'two_factor_code.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class TwoFactorCode {
  @Length(min: 6, max: 6)
  final String code;

  const TwoFactorCode({required this.code});

  static const DtoSchema<TwoFactorCode> schema = $TwoFactorCodeDto;
}

Add the controller with both steps:

lib/app/http/controllers/two_factor.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/auth/auth.dto.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/two_factor_code/two_factor_code.dto.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class TwoFactorController {
  /// POST /api/auth/login, step one: check the password. The token
  /// works 10 minutes, and only for step two.
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> login(DoxRequest req, LoginUser body) async {
    Auth auth = Auth(ip: req.ip());
    bool ok = await auth.once(<String, dynamic>{
      'email': body.email,
      'password': body.password,
    });
    if (!ok) {
      throw UnAuthorizedException(message: 'Wrong email or password');
    }
    AccessToken token = await auth.createAccessToken(
      auth.user<User>()!,
      name: 'login',
      abilities: <String>['2fa:pending'],
      expiresIn: const Duration(minutes: 10),
    );
    // send the code to the user here, for example by mail
    return <String, dynamic>{'token': token.value, 'two_factor': true};
  }

  /// POST /api/auth/two-factor, step two: check the code. Give a new
  /// token for a full login. The step-one token ends.
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> verify(DoxRequest req, TwoFactorCode body) async {
    Auth auth = req.auth as Auth;
    AccessToken token = auth.currentAccessToken!;
    if (!token.abilities.contains('2fa:pending')) {
      throw ForbiddenHttpException();
    }
    if (!_codeIsGood(auth.user<User>()!, body.code)) {
      throw UnAuthorizedException(message: 'Wrong code');
    }
    // a new token with the expiresIn of the driver. It still has 2fa:pending.
    AccessToken full = await auth.rotateAccessToken(token);
    // all abilities, like a normal login
    await auth.setAccessTokenAbilities(full, <String>['*']);
    return <String, dynamic>{'token': full.value};
  }

  /// Check the code with your own two-step code. Make each code expire,
  /// and limit the wrong tries per user.
  bool _codeIsGood(User user, String code) {
    throw UnimplementedError('check the two-step code');
  }
}
  • verify checks abilities.contains('2fa:pending'), not tokenCan, because tokenCan is also true for *. So only a step-one token can do step two.
  • The order matters: rotateAccessToken first, then setAccessTokenAbilities on the new token. Rotate copies 2fa:pending to the new token. When a step fails, no token has *: the user logs in again.
  • After step two, the step-one token stops working. A copy of it, taken before step two, is of no use.
  • Rotate needs the rotated_at column. A table made by dox auth:tokens-table has it. Without it, step two fails and the step-one token stays 2fa:pending. See A token table without rotated_at.

Add a middleware that needs the second step:

lib/app/http/middleware/two_factor.middleware.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// Lets a request through only when its token did the second step.
/// Put it after AuthMiddleware.
dynamic requireTwoFactor(DoxRequest req) {
  Auth? auth = req.auth as Auth?;
  if (auth == null || auth.currentAccessToken == null) {
    throw UnAuthorizedException();
  }
  if (auth.currentAccessToken!.abilities.contains('2fa:pending')) {
    throw ForbiddenHttpException();
  }
  return req;
}

Then change the app in these steps:

  1. In AuthController.register, give no token: the user logs in with the two steps after register. Replace the method with:

    /// POST /api/auth/register: make an account. Log in after it.
Future<DoxResponse> register(RegisterUser body) async {
  User user = User()
    ..name = body.name
    ..email = body.email
    ..password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
  await user.save();
  return response(<String, dynamic>{'user': user}).statusCode(201);
}

  2. In lib/routes/api.dart, add the imports at the top:

    import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/two_factor.controller.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/middleware/two_factor.middleware.dart';

  3. In register() of lib/routes/api.dart, change the login route to the new controller, and add the step-two route under it. This removes the normal login. You can delete AuthController.login.

    Route.post('/auth/login', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'login'),
  (TwoFactorController c) => c.login,
]);
Route.post('/auth/two-factor', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'two-factor'),
  AuthMiddleware(),
  (TwoFactorController c) => c.verify,
]);

    The rate limit slows down guessing of the code from one ip. It is not enough alone: your code check must also make each code expire, and limit the wrong tries per user.

  4. Add requireTwoFactor after AuthMiddleware() on each route of a logged-in user:

    Route.get('/auth/me', <dynamic>[
  AuthMiddleware(),
  requireTwoFactor,
  (AuthController c) => c.me,
]);

    For many routes, use a group: Route.middleware(<dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), requireTwoFactor], () { ... });.

  5. Run dart run build_runner build.

Things to know:

  • A route without requireTwoFactor still takes a step-one token. AuthMiddleware only checks that the token is good. The routes with a tokenCan check (like /tokens and /auth/refresh) refuse it too, because it has no *.
  • A script token has no 2fa:pending, so it passes requireTwoFactor. Its own abilities still limit it. Only a full login token can make one, because /tokens needs tokens:manage.
  • Any other place in your app that gives a token must also give a step-one token, or check the code first.
  • tokenCan on the same Auth sees new abilities at once. The next requests read them from the table.
  • setAccessTokenAbilities throws an UnAuthorizedException (401) when the token is gone (revoked). It does not check the expiry. A token of another guard throws an ArgumentError. It works on a token table without the rotated_at column too.

Try it, with the code check of your app in place:

# step one, and keep the token in PENDING
curl -X POST localhost:3000/api/auth/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"ada@example.com","password":"secret-pass"}'
# 200 {"token":"oat_7.Ab1x...","two_factor":true}
PENDING='oat_7.Ab1x...'

curl localhost:3000/api/auth/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $PENDING"
# 403 {"code":"forbidden","message":"Forbidden"}

# step two, and keep the new token in TOKEN
curl -X POST localhost:3000/api/auth/two-factor -H "Authorization: Bearer $PENDING" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"code":"123456"}'
# 200 {"token":"oat_8.Zq9p..."}
TOKEN='oat_8.Zq9p...'

curl localhost:3000/api/auth/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# 200 {"id":1,"name":"Ada",...}
curl localhost:3000/api/auth/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $PENDING"
# 401 {"code":"unauthorized","message":"Authentication failed"}

docs.title: When the database fails
docs.text:
The access token check reads the database. When the database fails, the default is to fail closed: the check gives no user, the request gets 401, and the error goes to the report of your exception handler.

But a 401 tells many clients "you are logged out". A short database problem then logs users out. Turn on throwOnError to stop this:

lib/config/auth.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

AuthConfig authConfig = AuthConfig(
  defaultGuard: 'api',
  guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
    'api': AuthGuard(
      driver: AccessTokenAuthDriver(
        expiresIn: const Duration(days: 30),
        throwOnError: true,
      ),
      provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
    ),
  },
);

With throwOnError: true, an error in a token check is thrown. This is a database error, a token row that can not be read, or a guard that is not set up. It goes to your exception handler. The default answer is 500. In production the 500 body is only {"code":"server_error","message":"Server Error"}. When APP_ENV is development or local, the error text is sent instead.

To answer 503, so the client tries again, catch the database error in render. Each database has its own error class. On SQLite (the default database of a new app), the class is in the sqlite3 package. Add it:

dart pub add sqlite3

Make a new file for the handler:

lib/app/exception_handler.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:sqlite3/sqlite3.dart' show SqliteException;

class AppExceptionHandler extends ExceptionHandler {
  const AppExceptionHandler();

  @override
  dynamic render(Object error, HttpRequest req) {
    // a database error: ask the client to try again
    if (error is SqliteException ||
        error is PgException ||
        error is MysqlException) {
      return HttpStatusException(503, headers: <String, String>{'retry-after': '5'});
    }
    return super.render(error, req);
  }
}

On Postgres or MySQL only, drop the sqlite3 package, its import and error is SqliteException. Then set the handler in lib/config/app.dart. Add the import at the top, and exceptionHandler in AppConfig:

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:my_app/app/exception_handler.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  exceptionHandler: const AppExceptionHandler(),
  // ... the other settings stay
);

The answer is then 503 with a Retry-After: 5 header and {"code":"service_unavailable","message":"Service Unavailable"}.

  • throwOnError also counts for AuthMiddleware(optional: true): a database error is thrown, not turned into a guest.
  • A failed last_used_at write is never thrown. It is reported, and the request goes on.

docs.title: Check a login with no request
docs.text:
Code that has no request, like a Socket.IO login, can check a token or a session itself:

User? user = await Auth(guard: 'api').userFromToken(token);
User? user = await Auth(guard: 'web').userFromSession(session);
  • userFromToken runs the same checks as a request with a Bearer header. For a JWT: signature, algorithm, guard, exp and revocation. For an access token: the hash, the type, the user table, expires_at and revocation. Give the token with no Bearer prefix. A missing, bad, expired, revoked or changed token gives null. It needs a guard with JwtAuthDriver or AccessTokenAuthDriver.
  • With an access token, currentAccessToken and tokenCan work on the same Auth after userFromToken. The driver method behind it is check(token, guard), an instance method of AccessTokenAuthDriver.
  • userCacheTtl is a cache, not a check. With it on, a deleted or banned user can still connect until the cache time ends, unless forgetUser runs.
  • userFromSession gives the user of a session, or null. Load the session with SessionMiddleware().fromCookie(value). See Session. It needs a guard with SessionAuthDriver.

docs.title: Your own guard (API key)
docs.text:
You can check the user in your own way, like an API key in the header. Write a driver: extend AuthDriver and return the user from verifyToken. AuthMiddleware and req.auth then work as with the other drivers.

The table stores a SHA-256 hash of each key in an api_key_hash column, not the key itself. So a leak of the table does not leak the keys. The example uses the crypto package (dart pub add crypto).

lib/app/auth/api_key_auth_driver.dart
import 'dart:convert';

import 'package:crypto/crypto.dart';
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

/// `Authorization: Bearer <api key>` gives the user with this key.
class ApiKeyAuthDriver extends AuthDriver {
  @override
  Future<Model<dynamic>?> verifyToken(IDoxRequest req, String guard) async {
    String header = req.header('Authorization') ?? '';
    if (!header.startsWith('Bearer ')) return null;
    String key = header.substring(7).trim();
    String hash = sha256.convert(utf8.encode(key)).toString();
    Model<dynamic> model = AuthEngine().guard(guard).provider.model();
    return await model.where('api_key_hash', hash).getFirst();
  }

  /// no password login for this guard
  @override
  Future<Model<dynamic>?> attempt(Map<String, dynamic> credentials, String guard) async => null;

  /// no token to make: the key is the token
  @override
  String? createToken(Map<String, dynamic>? userPayload, String guard) => null;
}

Add it as a guard, and use the guard in the route:

'key': AuthGuard(
  driver: ApiKeyAuthDriver(),
  provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
),

Route.get('/me', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(guard: 'key'), (DoxRequest req) => req.auth?.user<User>()]);

Make each key long and random, like openssl rand -hex 32. Then a fast hash like SHA-256 is safe. Do not use bcrypt here: you can not search by a bcrypt hash.

If you already have your own middleware, set the user with Auth().setUser(req, user). It needs no token and no password check. req.auth then gives this user:

User? user = await keys.userForKey(key);
if (user == null) throw UnAuthorizedException();
Auth(guard: 'api').setUser(req, user);
return req;

docs.title: Log in with another field
docs.text:
attempt searches by the fields in identifierFields of the AuthProvider, and checks the column in passwordField:

AuthProvider(
  model: () => User(),
  identifierFields: <String>['username'],
  passwordField: 'password_hash',
)

attempt runs bcrypt also when no user is found, or when the user has no password. So the answer time does not tell whether an email has an account. It returns null when the password is not a String, when no identifier is given, when an identifier is not a string or a number (a map or a list from the body), or when the password does not match.

docs.title: Users with uuid or text ids
docs.text:
Access tokens keep the user id in the tokenable_id column. By default it is an unsigned big int, like Sanctum and AdonisJS.

  • uuid ids: dox auth:tokens-table --uuid and AccessTokenAuthDriver(uuidIds: true). tokenable_id is then a uuid column (UUID on Postgres), so --users-table works with a uuid id. A uuid is kept and compared in lower case, like Postgres does. On other databases, keep uuids in lower case in the users table.
  • text ids: dox auth:tokens-table --string-ids and AccessTokenAuthDriver(stringIds: true). Text ids are compared exactly.

Use the same choice in the migration and on the driver. Session and JWT guards need nothing for this.

docs.title: Login throttle
docs.text:
The login throttle limits failed logins per account and ip. It is off by default. Turn it on where the config is loaded:

lib/providers/auth_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/auth.dart';

class AppAuthProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Auth.initialize(authConfig);
    // 5 failed logins a minute. Change it with maxAttempts: and decay:
    Auth.throttle = LoginThrottle();
  }
}
  • After maxAttempts failed logins for the same login field (eg. the email) and ip, the next try throws LoginThrottledException (429) until decay has passed. Its retryAfter says how long to wait.
  • A good login clears the count. The login field is trimmed and lower case, so A@x.com and a@x.com share one count.
  • The counts live in the app cache. Pick a store with LoginThrottle(store: 'redis'). Use a shared store like redis for many isolates or servers.
  • Auth.throttle is static, so each isolate has its own copy. Set it in setup() or boot() of a provider. If you set it in main() before the server starts, only the first isolate throttles.
  • Without an ip, attempt counts per account only. Then anyone can lock an account for decay. So pass the ip: Auth(ip: req.ip()). attemptSession takes the ip from the request.
  • attemptSession sends a Retry-After header with the 429. attempt has no request, so catch LoginThrottledException and set the header from retryAfter if you need it.
  • once counts like attempt.
  • Parallel tries are not stopped. The limit is checked before a failed try is counted, so tries that run at the same time all pass the check. A burst of parallel wrong logins can all run, far past maxAttempts. In a test, 50 parallel wrong logins with maxAttempts: 5 all ran. The throttle works for tries that come one after another. To stop fast parallel guessing, also put RateLimit on the login route, like the routes on this page do.

docs.title: Password hash cost
docs.text:
Passwords use bcrypt with cost 10 by default. Each step up doubles the time of a login. To raise it, set the cost for new hashes and tell the driver. Then a login for an unknown email takes as long as a wrong password:

Hash.rounds = 12;
JwtAuthDriver(secret: SecretKey(env.appKey), hashRounds: 12);
SessionAuthDriver(hashRounds: 12);
AccessTokenAuthDriver(hashRounds: 12);

Old hashes keep their own cost, so they still work. Hash them again on the next good login:

if (Auth.needsRehash(user.password!)) {
  user.password = await Hash.makeAsync(password);
  await user.save();
  // with a session login and the endSessionsOnPasswordChange flag:
  // Auth().updateSessionPasswordHash(req, user);
}

With the endSessionsOnPasswordChange flag, a new hash ends the other sessions of the user. Call updateSessionPasswordHash to keep the current one.

Auth.needsRehash(hash, rounds: 12) checks against another cost. Auth.hashCost(hash) gives the cost of a hash. bcrypt reads at most 72 bytes. A longer password throws an ArgumentError, so limit the length in the DTO.

docs.title: 401 or 403?
docs.text:
• 401 (unauthorized): the user is not logged in. There is no token, or it is bad, expired or revoked. AuthMiddleware gives it. The client should log in again.
  • 403 (forbidden): the user is logged in, but may not do this. A missing ability, a failed gate or policy, or GuestMiddleware for a logged-in user. Logging in again does not help.
  • 419 (csrf_token_mismatch): a session request with no CSRF token. See CSRF protection.
  • 429: too many failed logins. See Login throttle.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text: Error Cause Fix LateInitializationError: Field 'config' has not been initialized. Auth.initialize did not run. AppAuthProvider is missing, or the generator did not run. Add AppAuthProvider, then run dart run build_runner build. 401 Authentication failed No Authorization header, a bad, expired or revoked token, a deleted user, or a token of another guard. Send Authorization: Bearer <token>. Log in again. 401 Wrong email or password Your login controller: attempt gave null. Check the email and password. 403 Forbidden Your controller: the token does not have the ability. Use a token with the ability. See Abilities. Invalid argument (guard): no auth guard with this name: "admin" Auth(guard: ...) or AuthMiddleware(guard: ...) with a name that is not in guards. Fix the name, or add the guard. Bad state: The auth guard 'api' does not use SessionAuthDriver. Use attempt() and login() for a token, and revokeToken() to log out. logout, attemptSession or loginSession on a token guard. Use revokeToken(req) to log out a token. Bad state: The auth guard 'api' does not use AccessTokenAuthDriver. An access token method on a JWT or session guard. Use Auth(guard: ...) of a guard with AccessTokenAuthDriver. Turn the flag on. See End other sessions.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
Access tokens:

  • A token fails (401) when its format is bad, the secret is wrong, it is expired, it was revoked, its user is gone, it has another type, or it was made for a guard with another user table.
  • tokenable_type is the table name of the user model. If you rename the users table, the old tokens stop working.
  • Each token has a type. By default it is the guard name. So two access token guards do not take each other's tokens. If you rename a guard, set AccessTokenAuthDriver(type: 'old-name') to keep its tokens working.
  • A token name over 255 characters throws an ArgumentError. Nothing is written.
  • When you delete a user, call revokeAllAccessTokens(user) too, or use --users-table (usersTable:) in the migration. Then old tokens can never match a new user with the same id.
  • The migration makes the table on the default connection. If the driver uses another connection, like AccessTokenAuthDriver(connection: 'other'), make the table on that connection.
  • last_used_at is written at most once a minute per token. So a busy token does not write on every request. If this write fails, the error is reported and the request goes on.
  • On MySQL, expires_at is kept to the second: MySQL rounds the time. So a token can stop working up to half a second before or after its exact time.

JWT:

  • The token is not secret. By default, anyone with the token can read user.toJson(). Keep private columns in hidden, or use small tokens.
  • The user is loaded on each request, by the id in the token. A deleted user can not log in, even with a valid token.
  • userCacheTtl skips that query. With Duration(seconds: 30), a deleted or changed user is seen only after 30 seconds, unless forgetUser runs. Each isolate has its own cache. Requests in that time share one user object, so do not change it per request.
  • Dox does not sign with the secret text as it is. The HMAC key is made from it with HKDF-SHA256 and the label dox:jwt. Another service that checks the tokens needs that key: driver.signingKey.
  • JwtAuthDriver.bearerToken(req) gives the token of a request.

Sessions:

  • Login and logout give the session a new id and a new CSRF token. So an id that someone saw before the login is of no use.
  • With the default cookie session driver, all session data sits in the cookie. So an old copy of the cookie still works after logout, until the session lifetime ends. If logout must really end old cookies, use the cache session driver, like SessionConfig(driver: 'cache', store: 'redis').
  • The session keeps only the user id. AuthMiddleware loads the user from the database on each request, so a deleted user is logged out.

After AuthMiddleware, req.auth holds the login.

Code What it gives req.auth an IAuth?. null for a guest, and on a route with no AuthMiddleware. A query or body field can not set it req.auth as Auth the Auth, for tokenCan, currentAccessToken and revokeToken req.auth?.isLoggedIn() true when a user is loaded req.auth?.id() the primary key of the user, or null req.auth?.user<User>() the user model req.auth?.toJson() the user as a map, without hidden fields

docs.title: AccessTokenTables.up and dox auth:tokens-table

Option Flag Default What it does table none (edit the migration) 'auth_access_tokens' the table name. Use the same name as the driver table uuidIds --uuid false tokenable_id is a uuid column (UUID on Postgres) stringIds --string-ids false tokenable_id is text. Do not use it with --uuid usersTable --users-table=users none adds a foreign key from tokenable_id to usersKey of this table, with cascade delete. The two id columns must have the same type usersKey --users-key=uid 'id' the key column of usersTable. Alone, the flag prints a warning and does nothing

AccessTokenTables.down(schema, table: 'auth_access_tokens') drops the table. Pass the same table as in up.

The table has these columns: id, tokenable_type, tokenable_id, type, name, hash, abilities, last_used_at, expires_at, rotated_at, created_at, updated_at. There is an index on expires_at. The time columns are DATETIME on MySQL, so a token can expire after 2038. auth:tokens-table is a package command of dox_auth. The same flag twice is an error: it writes nothing and exits with code 1.

When set, the check also reads it hashRounds 10 the bcrypt cost of your stored hashes.
