docs.title: Authorization
docs.text:
This page shows how to say what a user may do, with gates and policies from dox_auth.

Authentication says who the user is. Authorization says what this user may do. For example, a user may edit their own post, but not the post of another user.

There are two ways to write the rules:

  • A gate is one rule, written as a function.
  • A policy is a class with all the rules of one model, like Post.

docs.title: Register the rules
docs.text:
Gates and policies are kept per isolate. Dox runs many isolates, so add them in a provider. The setup() of a provider runs in every isolate.

lib/providers/gate_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/policies/post_policy.dart';

class GateProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Gate.define('update-post', (User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id);
    Gate.policy<Post>(PostPolicy());
  }
}

Dox finds the provider by itself. Run dart run build_runner build and it is in lib/generated/container.g.dart.

docs.title: Gates
docs.text:
A gate gets the user and a subject. It gives true when the user may do it. The user and subject types come from the function. A check with another type is denied.

Gate.define('update-post', (User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id);

A gate with no subject uses _ for the second parameter:

Gate.define('create-post', (User user, _) => user.verified == true);

A gate can be async:

Gate.define('publish-post', (User user, Post post) async {
  return await user.canPublishIn(post.categoryId);
});

docs.title: Check a gate
docs.text:
if (await Gate.allows(user, 'update-post', post)) {
  // the user may update the post
}

if (await Gate.denies(user, 'create-post')) {
  // the user may not create a post
}

// stop the request with 403 when denied
await Gate.authorize(user, 'update-post', post);

// true when the user may do at least one, or all of them
await Gate.any(user, <String>['update-post', 'delete-post'], post);
await Gate.all(user, <String>['update-post', 'delete-post'], post);

An ability with no gate and no policy is denied.

docs.title: Give a reason
docs.text:
A check can give a GateResponse instead of a bool. The reason of GateResponse.deny is the message of the 403 answer.

Gate.define('delete-post', (User user, Post post) {
  if (post.published == true) {
    return GateResponse.deny('You can not delete a published post.');
  }
  return post.userId == user.id;
});

GateResponse response = await Gate.inspect(user, 'delete-post', post);
print(response.allowed);
print(response.message);

docs.title: Policies
docs.text:
A policy holds the rules of one model. Write one method per ability. A method takes the user, and the model when the ability needs one. List the methods in abilities.

lib/app/policies/post_policy.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

class PostPolicy extends Policy<User, Post> {
  bool create(User user) => user.verified == true;

  bool update(User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id;

  bool delete(User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id;

  @override
  Map<String, Function> get abilities => <String, Function>{
    'create': create,
    'update': update,
    'delete': delete,
  };
}

Add the policy for its model:

Gate.policy<Post>(PostPolicy());

A check with a Post as the subject now uses the policy. For an ability with no model, like create, pass the type Post:

await Gate.allows(user, 'update', post);
await Gate.allows(user, 'create', Post);
await Gate.authorize(user, 'delete', post);

Each method must take (User user) or (User user, Post post). A method with another signature fails at Gate.policy, so you see the mistake when the app starts.

When the policy has no method with the ability name, the gate with that name is used.

Why a map of methods

Dart has no runtime reflection in compiled apps. So Dox can not find a method by its name. The abilities map links each name to its method. The methods stay normal typed Dart methods, so you can also call them directly in a test.

docs.title: In a controller
docs.text:
req.can, req.cannot and req.authorize use the logged-in user of req.auth. Use them after AuthMiddleware.

Future<Post> update(DoxRequest req, Post post) async {
  await req.authorize('update', post);
  post.title = req.input('title');
  await post.save();
  return post;
}

Future<Map<String, dynamic>> show(DoxRequest req, Post post) async {
  return <String, dynamic>{
    'post': post,
    'can_edit': await req.can('update', post),
  };
}

req.authorize answers 401 for a guest and 403 for a user who may not do it. With the forbidGuest flag, a guest gets 403 too.

docs.title: On a route
docs.text:
The Can middleware checks an ability before the controller runs. Put it after AuthMiddleware.

// a gate with no subject
Route.get('/admin', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), Can('view-admin'), adminController.index]);

// a policy method with no model
Route.post('/posts', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), Can('create', subject: Post), postController.store]);

// a policy method with the model of the route param
Route.bind<Post>('post', (String id) => Post().find(id));
Route.put('/posts/{post}', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), Can('update', param: 'post'), postController.update]);

With param, the subject is the value of Route.bind for that route param. When Route.bind finds nothing, the answer is 404.

The answers:

  • A guest who may not do it gets 401. With the forbidGuest flag, it is 403.
  • A logged-in user who may not do it gets 403.

docs.title: Guests
docs.text:
A guest has no user. The user is null. A gate or a policy is denied for a guest, unless its user type is nullable:

Gate.define('view-post', (User? user, Post post) {
  return post.published == true || post.userId == user?.id;
});

class CommentPolicy extends Policy<User?, Comment> {
  bool view(User? user, Comment comment) => comment.visible == true;

  @override
  Map<String, Function> get abilities => <String, Function>{'view': view};
}

Can('view-post', param: 'post') without AuthMiddleware then works for guests too. But then a logged-in user is a guest too, because nothing loads the user. Use AuthMiddleware(optional: true) on a public route. It loads the user when the login is good, and lets guests through:

Route.get('/posts/{post}', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(optional: true), Can('view-post', param: 'post'), postController.show]);

req.can() then also sees the user on a public route.

docs.title: Before and after hooks
docs.text:
Gate.before runs before every check. It gives true or false to decide at once, or null to go on with the normal check. For example, an admin may do anything:

Gate.before((User user, String ability) => user.isAdmin == true ? true : null);

A hook runs only for users of its type. A User hook does not run for guests.

Gate.after sees the answer of every check, for example to log it. It can not change the answer.

Gate.after((User user, String ability, GateResponse response) {
  print('${user.id} $ability ${response.allowed}');
});

A policy can have its own before. It runs before the methods of that policy:

class PostPolicy extends Policy<User, Post> {
  @override
  bool? before(User user, String ability) => user.isAdmin == true ? true : null;

  // ...
}

docs.title: Auth flags
docs.text:
Some answers are opt-in. Turn them on with flags: in AuthConfig. All flags are off by default.

AuthConfig authConfig = AuthConfig(
  defaultGuard: 'web',
  guards: guards,
  flags: const AuthFlags(forbidGuest: true, jsonNoRedirect: true),
);

The flags:

  • forbidGuest: req.authorize and Can give a guest 403, not 401. The 403 has the message of the gate. AuthMiddleware runs first on most routes, and it still gives a guest 401.
  • jsonNoRedirect: AuthMiddleware(redirectTo: '/login') gives a JSON or XHR client a 401, not a redirect. A JSON client sends an Accept header with json, a JSON body, or X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest. An Inertia request still gets the redirect.
  • endSessionsOnPasswordChange: a session login ends when the password of the user changes. It also turns on logoutOtherDevices. See End other sessions when the password changes.

AuthFlags.all() turns on every flag:

AuthConfig(defaultGuard: 'web', guards: guards, flags: const AuthFlags.all());

The flags are part of AuthConfig. Auth.initialize(authConfig) runs in the setup() of your auth provider, so every isolate gets the same flags.

docs.title: In tests
docs.text: Gate.flush() removes all gates, policies and hooks. Call it in setUp when each test adds its own rules.

docs.title: CORS
docs.text:
This page shows how to let a web page on another domain call your API.

A browser blocks a request from https://my.app to https://api.my.app by default. The API must send CORS headers to allow it. Dox adds these headers from CORSConfig.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
The config is in lib/config/cors.dart. Pass it to AppConfig(cors: cors). A new app has this file with enabled: false, so it sends no CORS headers. Set origin to the URL of your front end, and set enabled: true.

lib/config/cors.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

CORSConfig cors = CORSConfig(
  enabled: true,
  origin: 'https://my.app',
  methods: <String>['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'PATCH', 'DELETE'],
  headers: <String>['Content-Type', 'Authorization'],
  exposeHeaders: <String>['Content-Disposition'],
  credentials: true,
  maxAge: 600,
);
lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  cors: cors,
  // ...
);

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Each option sets one response header. An option that is null sends no header. All options except enabled are null by default. So with no origin, Dox sends no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, and the browser blocks pages on other domains.

Option Header Value enabled - true adds the headers to every route. Default: true origin Access-Control-Allow-Origin one origin, a List<String> of origins, or '*' for all. A text is sent as it is, so do not put many origins in one text methods Access-Control-Allow-Methods a List<String> or a text like 'GET,POST'. '*' allows all headers Access-Control-Allow-Headers a List<String> or a text. '*' allows all exposeHeaders Access-Control-Expose-Headers the response headers the page may read credentials Access-Control-Allow-Credentials true lets the browser send cookies maxAge Access-Control-Max-Age how many seconds the browser keeps the preflight answer

For methods, headers and exposeHeaders, a list is joined with commas.

docs.title: More than one origin
docs.text:
Access-Control-Allow-Origin accepts only one origin or *. So when origin is a list, Dox checks the Origin header of the request:

  • The origin is in the list: Dox sends back that one origin.
  • The origin is not in the list: Dox sends no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header. The browser blocks the call.
  • The list has '*': Dox sends *.

With a list, Dox also sends Vary: Origin. This tells caches that the answer depends on the origin.

CORSConfig cors = CORSConfig(
  origin: <String>['https://my.app', 'https://admin.my.app'],
);

credentials with *

Do not use origin: '*' with credentials: true. Dox then sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, and the browser blocks every call that has cookies. When you need cookies, set origin to your real front-end URL, or to a list of URLs. A page on an allowed origin can send requests with the cookies of your users, so list only sites you trust.

docs.title: Preflight requests
docs.text: Before some requests, the browser sends an OPTIONS request. You do not need an OPTIONS route for this. Dox answers it with 204 No Content and the CORS headers. It uses the CORS setting of the route that the browser asks about.

docs.title: Turn CORS on or off for some routes
docs.text:
enabled is the default for all routes. Change it for a group of routes:

lib/routes/api.dart
// CORS headers only on these routes (use with enabled: false)
Route.enabledCors(() {
  Route.get('/public/posts', (PostController c) => c.index);
});

// no CORS headers on these routes
Route.disabledCors(() {
  Route.post('/webhooks/stripe', (WebhookController c) => c.handle);
});

docs.title: CSRF protection
docs.text:
Cross site request forgery (CSRF) is an attack.

Another site makes the browser of your user send a form to your app. The browser sends your session cookie with it, so the request looks real.

CsrfMiddleware stops it. Each session has a secret token. A request that changes data must send it back. Another site can not read the token, so it can not send it.

docs.title: Turn it on
docs.text:
It needs a session, so put it after SessionMiddleware:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    const SessionMiddleware(),
    const CsrfMiddleware(except: <String>['/api/*', '/webhooks/stripe']),
  ],
  // ...
);

Now every POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE request must send the token. A request with no token, or a wrong one, gets 419 with {"code": "csrf_token_mismatch", "message": "CSRF token mismatch"}.

GET, HEAD and OPTIONS requests are not checked. Do not change data in a GET route.

docs.title: Send the token
docs.text:
Dox reads the token from one of these places:

  • the _token field of the body (not the query string: a url ends up in logs and in the Referer header)
  • the X-CSRF-TOKEN header
  • the X-XSRF-TOKEN header

The token is req.session.token. Do not put it in a URL. URLs are kept in logs and in the browser history.

docs.title: HTML forms
docs.text:
Put the token in a hidden field. With views, @csrf writes this field for you:

<form method="POST" action="/posts">
  @csrf
  ...
</form>

@csrf must be alone on its line. In the middle of a line, use {{ csrfField() }}. It prints the same field.

csrfToken() gives only the token, for example for a <meta> tag.

docs.title: axios and Inertia
docs.text:
Dox also sets an XSRF-TOKEN cookie with the token. It is not HttpOnly, so page scripts can read it. axios reads this cookie and sends it in the X-XSRF-TOKEN header by itself. Inertia uses axios, so it works with no code.

With fetch, read the cookie and send the header yourself:

const token = document.cookie
  .split('; ')
  .find((c) => c.startsWith('XSRF-TOKEN='))
  ?.split('=')[1];

fetch('/posts', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'X-XSRF-TOKEN': token, 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ title: 'Hi' }),
});

docs.title: Skip some paths
docs.text:
Routes that other servers call (webhooks) or token based APIs can not send the token. List them in except:

const CsrfMiddleware(except: <String>['/api/*', '/webhooks/stripe']);
  • A path that ends with * matches everything that starts with it: /api/* matches /api/posts and /api/users/5.
  • Any other path must match exactly.

An excluded path is not checked and gets no XSRF-TOKEN cookie. Only skip paths that do not use the session login. A webhook should check its own signature instead.

docs.title: After login
docs.text: req.session.regenerate() also makes a new token. Dox sends the new XSRF-TOKEN cookie with the same response. regenerate(keepToken: true) keeps the token, so forms open in other tabs keep working. Do not use it at login. A token from before the login would stay valid after the login.

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
This page shows how to encrypt and decrypt text with Crypt and AESEncryptor.

Dox uses AESEncryptor to encrypt cookies with your APP_KEY. You can also call it yourself.

docs.title: Encrypt with the app key
docs.text:
Crypt uses the APP_KEY of the app. You do not pass the key.

String secret = Crypt.encryptString('card-1234');
String card = Crypt.decryptString(secret); // 'card-1234'

String data = Crypt.encrypt(<String, dynamic>{'id': 5}); // any JSON value
Map<String, dynamic> map = Crypt.decrypt(data);
  • decryptString and decrypt also try the old keys in AppConfig.previousKeys.
  • They throw DecryptException when the text was changed or made with another key.
  • Crypt.encryptString(v) gives the same as AESEncryptor.encode(v, appKey).

docs.title: Encrypt and decrypt with your own key
docs.text:
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

String secret = env.appKey;

String encoded = AESEncryptor.encode('Hello world', secret);
String decoded = AESEncryptor.decode(encoded, secret); // 'Hello world'
  • encode returns base64 text.
  • The same text gives a different output each time.
  • decode throws DecryptException when the text was changed, or the key is wrong. It is a 400 Bad Request error. The flag decryptServerError makes it a reported 500. See Core flags.
  • The AES key is not the secret itself. Dox makes a 32-byte key (AES-256) from the secret with HKDF-SHA256 (RFC 5869) and a label. The default label is dox:encrypt. Pick another one with purpose:, like AESEncryptor.encode(text, secret, purpose: 'app:invoice'). decode needs the same purpose.

Make a new 32-character APP_KEY with the CLI:

dox key:generate

It writes a random key of letters and digits to APP_KEY in .env.

docs.title: One key per purpose
docs.text:
Dox does not use APP_KEY as it is. It makes one key per purpose from it, with HKDF-SHA256 and a label:

Label Used for dox:cookie encrypted cookies, and the cookie session driver dox:jwt the HMAC key of JwtAuthDriver (with a SecretKey) dox:encrypt AESEncryptor when you give no purpose dox:signed-url for signed URLs

So a value made for one purpose can not be used for another one. KeyDerivation.forAppKey(label) gives the 32-byte key of a label. Each isolate makes it once.

At startup Dox checks APP_KEY. When it is empty, not exactly 32 bytes, or an old public sample key, the app stops. In development, local, test and testing it only prints a warning.

  • Keep APP_KEY in .env or in the secrets of your host. Never put it in code or in git.
  • If you change APP_KEY with no previousKeys, old encrypted cookies and sessions can not be read any more, so every user is logged out. JWT tokens signed with it stop working too. See Change the key.

docs.title: Change the key (key rotation)
docs.text: Change APP_KEY from time to time, or when someone who knew it leaves the team. With previousKeys, users stay logged in while you change it.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Copy the current APP_KEY to APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS.

  2. Run dox key:generate. It writes a new APP_KEY. Now .env has both:

    .env
    APP_KEY=the-new-32-character-app-key....
APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS=the-old-32-character-app-key....

  3. Read it in the env class, and give it to AppConfig:

    lib/config/env.dart
    List<String> get appPreviousKeys => <String>[]; // APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS=a,b
    lib/config/app.dart
    AppConfig(
  appKey: env.appKey,
  previousKeys: env.appPreviousKeys,
)

  4. Deploy. Every instance must get the new env at the same time.

  5. Wait until the old cookies have expired: the session lifetime, and the maxAge of your own cookies.
  6. Remove the old key from APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS and deploy again.

APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS can hold more than one key, comma separated. Dox tries them in order.

docs.title: What reads the old keys
docs.text:
Value With an old key encrypted cookies (req.cookie) read cookie session driver read CSRF token read (it is in the session) JWT tokens of JwtAuthDriver(secret: SecretKey(env.appKey)) checked. A JWT secret that is not APP_KEY needs its own previousSecrets option, see Authentication. Crypt.decryptString and Crypt.decrypt read AESEncryptor.decode in your code read only when you pass previousSecrets: Dox().config.previousKeys anything new made with APP_KEY only

Dox writes a cookie with the new key the next time it sends that cookie. So a user who comes back during step 5 moves to the new key without noticing.

docs.title: When the key leaked
docs.text: Do not put a leaked key in previousKeys. Anyone who has it can still make cookies and JWT tokens that Dox accepts. Change APP_KEY with no previousKeys. Every user is logged out, and that is what you want.

docs.title: Cookies
docs.text:
DoxCookie encrypts its value with APP_KEY by default. req.cookie(key) decrypts it. To decrypt a raw cookie value yourself, call DoxCookie.decrypt(name, value). It returns null when the value was changed, was made with another key, or was made for another cookie name.

return response().cookie(DoxCookie('theme', 'dark'));  // encrypted
DoxCookie('theme', 'dark', encrypt: false);             // plain text

String? theme = req.cookie('theme');                    // decrypted
String? raw = req.cookie('theme', decrypt: false);      // as sent

req.cookie(key) returns null when the cookie was changed, was made with another APP_KEY, or was made for another cookie name. The cookie name is bound to the encrypted value, so a value can not be copied from one cookie to another.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
AESEncryptor uses AES-256-GCM. The work runs in Rust (in dox_http_native), with the AES instructions of the CPU. One cookie takes about 1–2 µs.

  • Each message gets a new random 12-byte nonce.
  • The output is base64 of nonce + encrypted text + tag.
  • The 16-byte tag checks the message. If someone changes one byte, decode throws.
  • encode and decode also take associatedData, a text like a cookie name. It is not in the output, but decode needs the same value. Cookies use the cookie name here.

To store passwords, do not encrypt them. Hash them. See Hashing.

docs.title: Hashing
docs.text:
This page shows how to hash passwords with Hash and check them later.

A hash is one-way. You can not turn it back into the password. Hash uses bcrypt with a new random salt each time. It is in package:dox_core/dox_core.dart.

docs.title: Hash a password
docs.text:
Hash the password before you save it.

user.password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
await user.save();

makeAsync runs bcrypt in another isolate. See Without blocking the server.

The result looks like $2a$10$.... It holds the salt, so you only store this one string. The same password gives a different hash each time.

docs.title: Check a password
docs.text:
bool ok = Hash.verify('secret', user.password!);

Hash.verify(password, hashedPassword) returns true when the password matches. Hash.check does the same. It returns false when the password does not match, or when hashedPassword is not a valid bcrypt hash (for example an empty string).

docs.title: Without blocking the server
docs.text:
Hash.make and Hash.verify block the request isolate while bcrypt runs. In a request handler, use the async versions. They run bcrypt in another isolate.

user.password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
bool ok = await Hash.verifyAsync('secret', user.password!);

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
Hash.rounds is the bcrypt cost for new hashes. The default is 10. Each step up doubles the time. The cost must be from 4 to 31. Do not go below 10.

Hash.rounds = 12;
String hash = Hash.make('secret', rounds: 12); // or per call

Old hashes keep their own cost, so they still verify. If you change it, also set hashRounds on JwtAuthDriver or SessionAuthDriver to the same value. Then a login with an unknown email takes as long as a wrong password. See Authentication.

docs.title: Long passwords
docs.text:
bcrypt reads at most 72 bytes. Hash.make and Hash.makeAsync throw an ArgumentError when the password is longer than 72 bytes (UTF-8). The error text does not hold the password, so it is safe in logs. Hash.verify returns false for such a password.

So limit the length in your DTO, like @Length(min: 8, max: 72). @Length counts characters, and a letter outside ASCII can use up to 4 bytes. So a password with such letters can still be too long. Catch the error and answer 422, or use a smaller max.

docs.title: Compare secrets
docs.text:
To check an API key or a token, use Hash.equals(given, expected), not ==. == stops at the first wrong character, so the time can tell how much of the key was right. Hash.equals takes the same time for every value of the same length.

bool ok = Hash.equals(req.header('X-Api-Key') ?? '', Env.get<String>('API_KEY'));

docs.title: Store tokens
docs.text:
For a long random secret that you keep in the database (an API key, an access token), store only Hash.sha256(token). Find the row by the hash of what the client sends. SHA-256 is fast and gives the same hash for the same input, so a unique index works on it.

String stored = Hash.sha256(token);          // save this, never the token
Token? row = await Token().where('hash', Hash.sha256(given)).getFirst();

Never use Hash.sha256 for passwords. A password is short and can be guessed, so use Hash.make (bcrypt).

docs.title: With login
docs.text: You do not need Hash.verify for normal login. Auth().attempt() from dox_auth finds the user and checks the password with bcrypt. See Authentication.

docs.title: Things to know
docs.text:
• Never store or encrypt a plain password. Hash it.
  • Never send the hash to the client. Put the column in the model hidden list.
  • bcrypt is slow on purpose, so guessing is slow too. Do not hash in a loop on hot paths.

docs.title: Rate limiting
docs.text:
RateLimit is a middleware that stops a client that sends too many requests.

Use it on login, sign up and other routes that bots like to hammer.

docs.title: Limit a route
Limit every route
docs.text:
Put it in globalMiddleware:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    RateLimit(max: 120),
  ],
  // ...
);

docs.title: Count by user, not by ip
docs.text:
key picks who is counted. The default is req.ip(). The key is any String. For example, count by user id after AuthMiddleware:

Route.get('/reports', <dynamic>[
  AuthMiddleware(),
  RateLimit(
    max: 100,
    key: (DoxRequest req) => '${req.auth?.user<User>()?.id ?? req.ip()}',
  ),
  (ReportController c) => c.index,
]);

Use a key the client can not choose

Do not count by a raw header, like req.header('X-Api-Key'). A client can send a new value with each request and get a new count each time. Count by a value that you checked first, like the id of the logged in user.

Behind a proxy

Behind Caddy, nginx or a load balancer, every request comes from the proxy ip. Then all clients share one count. Add the proxy to AppConfig.trustedProxies, so req.ip() is the real client ip. See App config.

docs.title: Two limits on the same key
docs.text:
Two RateLimit with the same max and per share one counter for the same key. Give each one a name to keep them apart:

Route.post('/auth/login', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'login'),
  (AuthController c) => c.login,
]);
Route.post('/auth/register', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'register'),
  (AuthController c) => c.register,
]);

docs.title: Where the counts live
docs.text:
Where the counts are kept depends on the default cache store:

  • When the default cache store is Redis, the counts are in Redis. All isolates and all servers share them. Use this when you run more than one server.
  • Else the counts are in the main isolate. All isolates of the server share them, so max holds for the whole server. The other isolates send each count to the main isolate and wait for the answer. This is one small message per limited request. Each server has its own counts, so with 3 servers a client can send up to 3 x max requests. This is also true for the default file store of a new app.

To use one store by name, pass store:

RateLimit(max: 10, store: 'redis')

A memory store named in store counts in the main isolate too. A store passed in cacheStore is used as it is.

docs.title: How it counts
docs.text:
By default it is a fixed window. With per: Duration(minutes: 1) the count starts at 0 at the start of each minute. So a client can send max requests at the end of one minute and max more at the start of the next. That is fine for most apps.

A blocked request still counts. A client that keeps sending while it is blocked stays blocked.

docs.title: Sliding window
docs.text:
Set sliding: true to stop the burst at the edge of a window:

RateLimit(max: 5, per: Duration(minutes: 1), sliding: true)

The count is then a guess of the requests in the last minute. It is the count of this minute, plus a part of the count of the minute before. That part gets smaller as the minute goes on.

For example, the client sent 4 requests last minute and 1 this minute. We are 15 seconds into this minute. The count is 4 x 45/60 + 1 = 4.

  • X-RateLimit-Remaining is max minus this count, rounded up.
  • Retry-After is the time until one more request fits, if the client sends nothing in between.
  • It costs one more read per request. Each count is kept for 2 windows.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Middleware
  • Security headers
  • Production checklist

docs.title: Security headers
docs.text:
SecurityHeaders is a middleware that adds safe HTTP headers to every answer.

The browser reads them and blocks some common attacks, like showing your page in a frame on another site.

docs.title: Turn it on
docs.text:
Put it in globalMiddleware:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    const SecurityHeaders(),
  ],
  // ...
);

Every answer now has these headers:

Header Default value What it does X-Content-Type-Options nosniff The browser does not guess the file type. X-Frame-Options DENY No site can show your page in a frame. Referrer-Policy strict-origin-when-cross-origin Other sites only see your domain, not the full url. Permissions-Policy camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=() The page can not use the camera, the microphone or the location. Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy same-origin A page of another site that opens yours can not reach it. Strict-Transport-Security max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains The browser uses only https for one year. Sent only on https requests.

Content-Security-Policy is off by default. A good policy depends on your pages.

Without this middleware, the server already sends three headers on every answer, also on a 404: X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and X-XSS-Protection: 0. SecurityHeaders replaces them with its own values. X-XSS-Protection: 0 turns the old XSS filter of browsers off, like OWASP says. The filter is gone from new browsers, and in old ones it can make holes. Use Content-Security-Policy instead.

docs.title: Change or turn off a header
docs.text:
Each header has an option. Give a new value to change it, or null to turn it off. null removes the header, also one the server sends by default (like frameOptions: null for X-Frame-Options). The option for X-XSS-Protection is xssProtection (default '0'). In extra, a null value removes that header too.

const SecurityHeaders(
  frameOptions: 'SAMEORIGIN', // allow frames from your own site
  permissionsPolicy: null, // do not send this header
  contentSecurityPolicy: "frame-ancestors 'none'",
  extra: <String, String>{'Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy': 'same-origin'},
)
Option Header contentTypeOptions X-Content-Type-Options frameOptions X-Frame-Options referrerPolicy Referrer-Policy permissionsPolicy Permissions-Policy crossOriginOpenerPolicy Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy strictTransportSecurity Strict-Transport-Security contentSecurityPolicy Content-Security-Policy extra any other headers, name to value

docs.title: HSTS behind a proxy
docs.text:
Dox serves plain http. The https part is done by a proxy (Caddy, nginx, a load balancer). Dox sends Strict-Transport-Security only when the request came in over https. It knows that from the X-Forwarded-Proto: https header, and it only believes this header from a trusted proxy. So add your proxy to AppConfig.trustedProxies:

AppConfig(trustedProxies: <String>['127.0.0.1', '::1']);

Without it, Dox never sends HSTS. See App config.

Note

Middleware runs only for routes that exist. A 404 for an unknown url gets only the three server headers. A preflight OPTIONS answer gets only them too. Put SecurityHeaders first in globalMiddleware. Then an error from a later middleware, like a 419 or a 429, also gets the headers.

docs.text:

docs.title: Signed URLs
docs.text:
A signed url has a signature in its query.

Nobody can change the url without the APP_KEY. Use it for links in emails, like "unsubscribe" or "download your file", where the user is not logged in.

docs.title: Make a signed url
docs.text:
Give the route a name and add the ValidateSignature middleware:

lib/routes/web.dart
Route.get('/unsubscribe/{user}', <dynamic>[
  const ValidateSignature(),
  (UserController c) => c.unsubscribe,
]).name('unsubscribe');

Then make the url with Route.signedUrl:

String url = Route.signedUrl(
  'unsubscribe',
  params: <String, Object>{'user': 5},
);
// https://example.com/unsubscribe/5?signature=3f9a...

A url with no signature, a wrong one, or a changed path or query gets 403 Forbidden.

docs.title: A url that expires
docs.text:
Give expires. The url gets an expires query param (unix seconds), and it is signed too. After that time the url gets 403.

String url = Route.signedUrl(
  'download',
  params: <String, Object>{'file': 12},
  expires: Duration(hours: 1),
);

docs.title: Absolute and relative urls
docs.text:
By default the url is absolute. Dox puts APP_URL from the env in front, like https://example.com. The scheme and host are signed too. Give baseUrl: to use another one.

  • The Host of the request must be the host of APP_URL, with the same port.
  • The scheme must match too. Behind a proxy that ends TLS, add the proxy to AppConfig.trustedProxies, so Dox reads X-Forwarded-Proto: https.

With absolute: false, only the path and the query are signed. Check it with ValidateSignature(absolute: false):

Route.get('/files/{id}', <dynamic>[
  const ValidateSignature(absolute: false),
  (FileController c) => c.show,
]).name('files.show');

String url = Route.signedUrl(
  'files.show',
  params: <String, Object>{'id': 3},
  absolute: false,
);
// /files/3?signature=...

docs.title: Check in a controller
docs.text:
ValidateSignature.hasValidSignature(req) gives true or false, so you can answer in your own way:

if (!ValidateSignature.hasValidSignature(req)) {
  return redirect('/link-expired');
}

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• The signature is HMAC-SHA256 of the url, with a key made from APP_KEY (KeyDerivation.signedUrl).
  • Dox compares it in constant time.
  • After you change APP_KEY, urls made with an old key still work when the old key is in AppConfig.previousKeys.
  • signature is a reserved query param. Any other param added to a signed url makes it invalid.

docs.title: Controller
docs.text:
A controller holds the code that answers a route.

It can be a class method, a static method or a plain function.

docs.title: Class based controller
docs.text:
Make one with the CLI:

dox make:controller Blog

It writes lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart with an empty index method. Fill it in:

lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

@Inject()
class BlogController {
  String index(DoxRequest req) {
    return 'all blogs';
  }
}
lib/routes/api.dart
Route.get('/blogs', (BlogController c) => c.index);

@Inject() puts the controller in the container. Run dart run build_runner build after you add one. The constructor can ask for services and repositories. See Dependency injection.

docs.title: Static method
docs.text:
class AppController {
  static String ping(DoxRequest req) {
    return 'pong';
  }
}

Route.get('/ping', AppController.ping);

docs.title: Function based controller
docs.text:
String listBlog(DoxRequest req) {
  return 'all blogs';
}

Route.get('/blogs', listBlog);

docs.title: Resource controller
docs.text:
A resource controller has the 7 methods that Route.resource uses.

Make one with the CLI:

dox make:controller Blog -r
lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// Route: Route.resource('path', BlogController);
@Inject()
class BlogController {
  /// GET /resource
  Future<dynamic> index(DoxRequest req) async {}

  /// GET /resource/create
  Future<dynamic> create(DoxRequest req) async {}

  /// POST /resource
  Future<dynamic> store(DoxRequest req) async {}

  /// GET /resource/{id}
  Future<dynamic> show(DoxRequest req, int id) async {}

  /// GET /resource/{id}/edit
  Future<dynamic> edit(DoxRequest req, int id) async {}

  /// PUT|PATCH /resource/{id}
  Future<dynamic> update(DoxRequest req, int id) async {}

  /// DELETE /resource/{id}
  /// delete() gives the number of rows it deleted, so 0 is a 404:
  /// `if (await Blog().where('id', id).delete() == 0) throw NotFoundHttpException();`
  Future<dynamic> destroy(DoxRequest req, int id) async {}
}
lib/routes/api.dart
Route.resource('blogs', BlogController);

You can delete methods you do not need. Route.resource skips them. See Routing: resource routes.

docs.title: API resource controller
docs.text:
An API has no form pages. --api makes the resource controller without create and edit:

dox make:controller Blog --api

docs.title: Resource controller for a model
docs.text:
--model makes a resource controller that uses a model:

dox make:controller Blog --model=Blog
lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/blog/blog.model.dart';

/// Route: Route.resource('path', BlogController);
@Inject()
class BlogController {
  /// GET /resource
  Future<dynamic> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Blog().all();
  }

  /// GET /resource/create
  Future<dynamic> create(DoxRequest req) async {}

  /// POST /resource
  /// create() takes only the fillable columns of Blog.
  /// Set fillable in the Blog model first. While it is empty, this throws.
  Future<dynamic> store(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Blog().create(req.body);
  }

  /// GET /resource/{id}
  /// Dox loads blog by the {id}. No row answers 404.
  Future<dynamic> show(DoxRequest req, Blog blog) async {
    return blog;
  }

  /// GET /resource/{id}/edit
  Future<dynamic> edit(DoxRequest req, Blog blog) async {
    return blog;
  }

  /// PUT|PATCH /resource/{id}
  /// update() takes only the fillable columns of Blog.
  /// Set fillable in the Blog model first. While it is empty, this throws.
  Future<dynamic> update(DoxRequest req, Blog blog) async {
    await blog.update(req.body);
    return blog;
  }

  /// DELETE /resource/{id}
  Future<dynamic> destroy(DoxRequest req, Blog blog) async {
    await blog.delete();
  }
}
  • show, edit, update and destroy take the model. Route model binding loads it by the {id}.
  • create() and update() take only the columns in the model's fillable list. Add your columns there.
  • Use --api and --model together for an API controller with a model.
  • dox make:model Blog -r makes the model and this controller in one step.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
A controller asks for what it needs by type. Dox fills each parameter.

Route.put('/teams/{teamId}/users/{id}', (UserController c) => c.update);

@Inject()
class UserController {
  Future<User> update(int teamId, int id, UpdateUser body) async { ... }
}
Parameter type Dox gives DoxRequest the request a @Dto class the checked body or query. See Validation. String, int, double, num, bool the path params, in the order of the route the same types with ? an optional path param ({id?}). null when it is not in the URL. a @DoxModel class the model, loaded by the route param. See route model binding. an @Inject() class the instance from the container

Rules:

  • The order of parameters is free. Path params are matched by position: the first path-param parameter gets the first {...} in the route.
  • DoxRequest is not needed. Add it only when you use it.
  • At most one @Dto parameter.
  • Only positional parameters. Named and [optional] parameters are not supported.
  • A catch-all {path*} param is a String.
  • The same rules work for static methods and plain functions.
  • Dox reads the parameter types once, at start. It does not use dart:mirrors.

Path param types. Dox converts the text from the URL:

  • int: "42" is 42. "abc" or "4.5" answers 404 Not Found.
  • double, num: "4.5" is 4.5.
  • bool: true or 1 is true. false or 0 is false.
  • Any other text answers 404 too.
  • Path params are checked first. When one is wrong, the DTO is not checked.

Checked at start. The server does not start when:

  • a parameter type is not in the list above (did you run dart run build_runner build?),
  • the method has more path-param parameters than the route has {...} params.

docs.title: What to return
docs.text: Return a String, a Map, a model, a File and more. See Response.

docs.title: Dependency injection
docs.text:
Dox has a container.

It makes your classes and gives each constructor what it needs. You do not register classes by hand. Put @Inject() above a class, and dox_builder adds it to the container. Dox does not use dart:mirrors. All the wiring is generated code.

docs.title: A full example
docs.text:
A repository reads the database. A service holds the business logic. A controller answers the route.

lib/app/repositories/user.repository.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class UserRepository {
  Future<User?> find(int id) => User().find(id);
}
lib/app/services/user.service.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/repositories/user.repository.dart';

@Inject()
class UserService {
  UserService(this.users);

  final UserRepository users;

  Future<User> show(int id) async {
    User? user = await users.find(id);
    if (user == null) throw NotFoundHttpException();
    return user;
  }
}
lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/services/user.service.dart';

@Inject()
class UserController {
  UserController(this.service);

  final UserService service;

  Future<User> show(int id) => service.show(id);
}
lib/routes/api.dart
class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.get('/users/{id}', (UserController c) => c.show);
  }
}

Run the builder:

dart run build_runner build

It writes lib/generated/container.g.dart. Give it to the app once:

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:my_app/generated/container.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  container: registerContainer,
  // ...
);

That is all. GET /api/users/5 makes the repository, the service and the controller, and calls show(5).

docs.title: The generated file
docs.text:
lib/generated/container.g.dart has one function. Each class gets a factory that calls its constructor.

lib/generated/container.g.dart
// GENERATED CODE - DO NOT MODIFY BY HAND
// Made by dox_builder. Run `dart run build_runner build`.
// ignore_for_file: type=lint

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart' as i1;
import 'package:my_app/app/repositories/user.repository.dart' as i2;
import 'package:my_app/app/services/user.service.dart' as i3;
import 'package:my_app/providers/orm_provider.dart' as i4;
import 'package:my_app/routes/api.dart' as i5;
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart' as i6;

/// Puts every class of the app into the container: the
/// `@Inject()` classes, routers, providers and model binders.
/// Use it in `AppConfig(container: registerContainer)`.
void registerContainer(IocContainer c) {
  c.singleton<i1.UserController>(
    (IocContainer c) => i1.UserController(c.get<i3.UserService>()),
  );
  c.singleton<i2.UserRepository>((IocContainer c) => i2.UserRepository());
  c.singleton<i3.UserService>(
    (IocContainer c) => i3.UserService(c.get<i2.UserRepository>()),
  );
  c.provider<i4.ORMProvider>((IocContainer c) => i4.ORMProvider());
  c.router<i5.ApiRouter>((IocContainer c) => i5.ApiRouter());
  c.bindModel<i6.User>((String id) {
    int? key = int.tryParse(id);
    if (key == null) return null;
    return i6.User().find(key);
  });
}

Do not edit it. Run the builder again after you add a class.

docs.title: Lifetime
docs.text:
• @Inject(): one instance per isolate. It is made on first use.
  • @Inject(singleton: false): a new instance each time it is asked for.

Dox runs one server per isolate. Isolates do not share objects. So each isolate runs registerContainer and has its own instances. Do not keep state in a singleton that all isolates must see. Use the cache or the database for that.

docs.title: Constructor parameters
docs.text:
Each constructor parameter is found by its type.

  • Positional and named parameters both work.
  • An optional parameter whose type is not in the container keeps its default value.
  • A nullable parameter whose type is not in the container gets null.
  • Any other parameter whose type is not in the container stops the build.

docs.title: Routes to controller methods
docs.text:
Pass a function that picks the method. Dox finds the controller by the parameter type:

Route.get('/posts', (PostController c) => c.index);
Route.post('/posts', (PostController c) => c.store);
Route.put('/posts/{id}', (PostController c) => c.update);
Route.delete('/posts/{id}', (PostController c) => c.destroy);

The controller comes from the container. Dox gets it once per isolate, at start. A request does no extra work. .name(), groups and middleware lists work the same:

Route.get('/posts/{id}', (PostController c) => c.show).name('posts.show');
Route.get('/me', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), (AuthController c) => c.me]);

For resource routes, pass the class:

Route.resource('posts', PostController);

The method still gets its parameters as usual: DoxRequest, a @Dto, path params and bound models. See Controller: parameters.

docs.title: Handler parameters
docs.text:
A controller method (or a plain route function) can ask for any class of the container:

Route.get('/stats', (StatsService stats) => stats.today());

A singleton is read once, at start. A singleton: false class is made on each request.

docs.title: Route model binding
docs.text:
Every @DoxModel class gets a binder in lib/generated/container.g.dart. When a handler has a parameter of a model type, Dox loads the model by its primary key.

Route.get('/posts/{post}', (PostController c) => c.show);

@Inject()
class PostController {
  Post show(Post post) => post;
}
  • The route param with the name of the model is used: {post} for Post, {blogPost} for BlogPost.
  • When there is no such param, the next route param in order is used, like {id}.
  • A missing row answers 404.
  • An int key that is not a number answers 404, with no database call.
  • A route without a parameter of the model type does not load the model.
  • A binder from Route.bind wins over this one. See Routing: route model binding.

docs.title: Routers and providers
docs.text:
You do not need @Inject() on them.

  • Every class that extends Router is found. Its routes are registered at start.
  • Every class that extends DoxProvider is found. Its setup() runs at start, in every isolate.

Their constructors get parameters from the container too.

They run in the order of their file path, then the order in the file. To pick the order, list them in AppConfig:

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  container: registerContainer,
  providers: <DoxProvider>[ORMProvider()], // runs first
  routers: <Router>[ApiRouter()],       // registered first
);

A listed class comes first. The others follow. No class runs twice. A listed provider is also the instance that the container gives.

A provider can add global middleware with Dox().addGlobalMiddleware(...) in setup(). They run before the app's globalMiddleware. See Middleware.

docs.title: Use the container in code
docs.text:
Dox().ioc is the container of the current isolate.

UserService users = Dox().ioc.get<UserService>();
Method What it does get<T>() the instance of T. Throws when T is not registered. has<T>() true when T is registered singleton<T>(factory) one instance per isolate, made on first use factory<T>(factory) a new instance on each get instance<T>(value) value is the instance, eg. a config object override<T>(value) replace T, eg. with a fake in a test clearOverrides() remove every override

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Replace a class with a fake before the app starts:

setUpAll(() async {
  Dox().ioc.override<UserRepository>(FakeUserRepository());
  client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
});

tearDownAll(() async {
  await client.close();
  Dox().ioc.clearOverrides();
});

An override stays when the app registers its classes again. Call it before DoxTestClient.start. Controllers get their objects once, at start.

docs.title: Build errors
docs.text:
The build stops with a clear message when:

  • a required parameter has a type that is not in the container,
  • a parameter has an abstract type, and two or more classes in the container implement it,
  • classes need each other in a circle. The message shows the chain, like A -> B -> C -> A,
  • @Inject() is on an abstract class or a generic class,
  • a class has no unnamed constructor.

The message shows the file and line of the problem.

A private class (like _AdminRouter) is not put in the container. The build shows a warning for it. Remove the _ to add it.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Dox finds classes in lib/ only.

  • The container is keyed by the class. A constructor parameter of an abstract type gets the one container class that implements it:

    abstract class Mailer {}

@Inject()
class SmtpMailer implements Mailer {}

@Inject()
class SignupService {
  SignupService(this.mailer); // gets the SmtpMailer

  final Mailer mailer;
}

    This works for constructor parameters only. c.get<Mailer>() and handler parameters still need the class itself. - Two classes with the same name in two files both work. But use the typed route style (Route.get<C>(...)) for them. They can not be handler parameters, because Dox can not tell them apart by name.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
Every error that a route throws goes to one place: the exception handler. It does two things:

  • report(error, stackTrace) logs the error.
  • render(error, req) decides what the client gets.

docs.title: The default answer
docs.text:
You do not need to set anything. With the default handler:

Error Status Body an IHttpException, like NotFoundHttpException its code {"code": "not_found", "message": "Not Found"} a ValidationException (bad input) 422 the field errors, like {"name": "The name is required"} a ValidationException on a request with a session that does not want JSON, like a form post 302 a redirect back. The errors and the old input are in the session. a URL with no route 404 {"code": "not_found", "message": "GET /x not found"} any other error 500 {"code": "server_error", "message": "Server Error"}

For a 500, the error text is sent only when APP_ENV is development or local. In production the client never sees it, because it can hold SQL, file paths or hosts.

report is called for every error, except an IHttpException with a 4xx code. A 4xx exception is a normal answer (like 404), so it is not logged. A 5xx exception, like InternalErrorException, is reported. The default report prints the error and the stack with the logger.

See HTTP exceptions for the built-in exception classes.

docs.title: An HTML error page
docs.text:
By default an error is sent as JSON. In development or local, a 500 is plain text with the error text. A browser that opens a bad URL sees JSON or text, not a page. To send an HTML page to browsers, turn on htmlErrors:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  htmlErrors: true,
  // ...
);

The page has the status and its title, like 404 Not Found. It loads no files from outside.

  • Only a request that does not want JSON gets the page. A request wants JSON (DoxRequest.expectsJson()) when it has an Accept header with json, a JSON body, or X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest. An Inertia request does not want JSON, so it gets the page.
  • Only when APP_ENV is development or local, the page also shows the error text and the stack trace.
  • A JSON client gets the same answer as without htmlErrors.
  • A validation error does not change. It keeps its 422 JSON or its redirect.
  • An answer from your own ExceptionHandler.render does not change.

To make your own page, set errorPage. It gets the status, the error, the stack trace and a debug flag. debug is true when APP_ENV is development or local. Escape every value you put in the page.

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  htmlErrors: true,
  errorPage: (int status, Object error, StackTrace stack, bool debug) =>
      '<h1>Sorry, error $status</h1>',
  // ...
);

defaultErrorPage is the default. You can call it from your own function, for example for the statuses you do not handle.

docs.title: Your own handler
docs.text:
Extend ExceptionHandler. Override one method or both.

lib/app/exception_handler.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class PaymentRequiredException implements Exception {}

class AppExceptionHandler extends ExceptionHandler {
  const AppExceptionHandler();

  @override
  void report(Object error, StackTrace stackTrace) {
    // send it to your error tracker
    print('ERROR $error\n$stackTrace');
  }

  @override
  dynamic render(Object error, HttpRequest req) {
    if (error is PaymentRequiredException) {
      return response(<String, String>{'message': 'Please pay'})
          .statusCode(402);
    }
    // everything else: the default answer
    return super.render(error, req);
  }
}

Set it in AppConfig:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  exceptionHandler: const AppExceptionHandler(),
  // ...
);

docs.title: What render can return
docs.text:
render returns anything a controller can return: a DoxResponse, a map, a string. Return the error itself (this is what super.render does) to get the default answer.

req is the raw HttpRequest. It is there even when the error came before Dox read the body. Use it to read headers, like req.headers.value('accept').

If render itself throws, Dox logs that error and sends the default answer. The client always gets a response.

docs.title: Errors outside a request
docs.text: Some errors do not belong to a request. For example a future that nobody awaits, or an error in the shutdown() of a provider. Dox passes them to report too. The server keeps running.

docs.title: The response handler
docs.text:
The responseHandler of AppConfig still runs after render. It sees every response, also error responses. Use render to change errors, and responseHandler to change all responses (for example, to add a header).

See Custom errors for a full example with your own exception classes.

docs.title: Inertia
docs.text:
Inertia lets you build a single page app with React, Vue or Svelte, and keep routes and controllers in Dox.

You do not write an API. A controller gives a page name and its props. Inertia shows the page in the browser. The first visit gets a full HTML page. After that, links and forms get only JSON, and the page changes without a reload.

The dox_inertia package is the server side of Inertia. Use it with the Inertia 3 client for your front-end (@inertiajs/react, @inertiajs/vue3 or @inertiajs/svelte, version 3) and Vite.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
dox add inertia

It adds the package and does steps 1 to 3 of Set it up by hand (root view, config, provider). Then do steps 4 to 6 (Vite, the built files and the middleware) yourself. It prints a short list of them. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice.

docs.title: Set it up by hand
docs.text: dart pub add dox_inertia

docs.title: 1. Root view
docs.text:
The root view is the HTML page of the first visit. Dox puts the script and style tags in place of @vite, and the page in place of @inertia. It is plain HTML, with no template engine. It can hold {{ key }} marks for values like the title, see Root view data.

resources/views/app.html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>My app</title>
    @vite
  </head>
  <body>
    @inertia
  </body>
</html>

@inertia becomes the page data and the element the app renders into:

<script data-page="app" type="application/json">{"component":"Home",...}</script><div id="app"></div>

This is the format of the Inertia 3 client. In the JSON, <, > and & are written as \u003c, \u003e and \u0026, so a prop can not end the script tag.

docs.title: 2. Config
3. Provider
docs.text:
The provider sets up Inertia in every isolate. Put it in lib/ so the generated container finds it.

lib/providers/inertia_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_inertia/dox_inertia.dart';

import '../config/inertia.dart';

class AppInertiaProvider extends InertiaProvider {
  AppInertiaProvider() : super(inertiaConfig);
}

With no provider, Dox uses the defaults of InertiaConfig.

docs.title: 4. Vite
5. Serve the built files
docs.text:
In production the browser loads /build/assets/.... Add a route for them, or let your proxy (nginx, Caddy) serve public/build.

lib/routes/web.dart
Route.get('/build/{path*}', (String path) {
  if (path.contains('..')) throw NotFoundHttpException();
  // the file names have a hash, so the browser can keep them for a year
  return response(File('public/build/$path')).cache(const Duration(days: 365));
});

docs.title: 6. Middleware
docs.text:
Add three middleware to globalMiddleware, in this order:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    const SessionMiddleware(),
    const CsrfMiddleware(),
    HandleInertiaRequests(),
  ],
  // ...
);
  • SessionMiddleware gives each request a session. Inertia uses it for validation errors and flash data.
  • CsrfMiddleware stops cross site form posts. It sets the XSRF-TOKEN cookie. The Inertia client reads it and sends it back in the X-XSRF-TOKEN header. You do not write any code for this.
  • HandleInertiaRequests is your InertiaMiddleware, see Shared props. With no props to share, use const InertiaMiddleware().

You can also add them to a router, in the same order, if only some routes are Inertia pages.

docs.title: Render a page
docs.text:
Give the request, the page name and the props. The page name is the file in resources/js/Pages, without the extension.

lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_inertia/dox_inertia.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class UserController {
  Future<DoxResponse> index(DoxRequest req) {
    return inertia(req, 'Users/Index', <String, dynamic>{
      'title': 'Users',
      'users': () => User().query().all(),
    });
  }
}
  • A normal request gets the root view as HTML.
  • An Inertia request (X-Inertia: true) gets the page as JSON, with X-Inertia: true and Vary: X-Inertia.

A prop can be a function, like users above. It runs only when the prop is sent. It can give a Future. Props become JSON. A model or any object with toJson() works. A DateTime becomes ISO text. A Dart int above 2^53 in a prop loses precision. JavaScript reads the page JSON, in the browser and on the SSR server. Send such a number as a string.

Inertia.render(req, 'Users/Index', {...}) does the same as inertia(...).

docs.title: Shared props
docs.text:
Shared props go to every page, like the signed in user or the app name. Extend InertiaMiddleware and add it to globalMiddleware (see Middleware).

lib/app/http/middleware/handle_inertia_requests.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_inertia/dox_inertia.dart';

class HandleInertiaRequests extends InertiaMiddleware {
  @override
  Map<String, dynamic> share(DoxRequest req) {
    return <String, dynamic>{
      'appName': 'My app',
      'auth': () => req.auth?.toJson(),
    };
  }
}

A page prop with the same name wins over a shared prop. share can be async. The page lists the names of the shared props in sharedProps. The client keeps them on an instant visit. You can also share from any middleware or controller with Inertia.share(req, {...}).

For a value that is the same for the whole app, use Inertia.shareGlobal(key, value). Call it once in the setup() of your InertiaProvider, so it runs in every isolate:

class AppInertiaProvider extends InertiaProvider {
  AppInertiaProvider() : super(inertiaConfig);

  @override
  void setup() {
    super.setup();
    Inertia.shareGlobal('appName', 'Dox');
  }
}

A global value is kept for all users and all requests. Use it only for a constant, or a function that does not read a request. Data of one user, like the signed in user, must go in InertiaMiddleware.share. A prop shared for the request wins over a global one.

docs.title: Partial reloads
docs.text:
The client can ask for some props only: router.reload({ only: ['users'] }). Dox reads the headers and sends only those props. Function props that are not sent do not run.

Four helpers change when a prop is sent:

return inertia(req, 'Users/Index', <String, dynamic>{
  /// only when a partial reload asks for it
  'stats': Inertia.optional(() => Stats.load()),

  /// on every request, also on a partial reload that does not ask for it
  'notices': Inertia.always(notices),

  /// not on the first visit: the page loads it right after
  'comments': Inertia.defer(() => Comment().query().all()),
  'likes': Inertia.defer(() => Like().query().count(), group: 'side'),

  /// deferred, and the page adds the new items to the old ones
  'feed': Inertia.defer(() => Post().query().all()).merge(),

  /// the page adds the new items to the old ones (infinite scroll)
  'posts': Inertia.merge(posts),
});
Helper First visit Partial reload plain value or function sent sent when asked Inertia.optional not sent sent when asked Inertia.always sent always sent Inertia.defer not sent, listed in deferredProps sent when asked Inertia.merge sent, listed in mergeProps sent when asked

Deferred props of the same group load in one request. The default group is default. Inertia.lazy is the same as Inertia.optional. A deferred prop with .merge() (or merge: true) is also listed in mergeProps when it is sent.

docs.title: Forms and validation errors
docs.text:
A form post needs no extra code for errors. The flow is:

  1. The page posts the form: router.post('/users', data) or useForm.
  2. The controller validates. The validation fails.
  3. Dox flashes the errors and the old input to the session, and redirects back.
  4. The page loads again. It gets the errors in the errors prop.
Future<DoxResponse> store(DoxRequest req) async {
  await req.validateSchema(
    v.object(<String, Schema<Object?>>{
      'name': v.string().min(2),
      'email': v.string().email(),
    }),
  );
  // ... save the user
  return redirect('/users');
}

const { data, setData, post, errors } = useForm({ name: '', email: '' })
// errors.email holds the message, or is undefined

Every page gets errors. It is {} when there are no errors. It is sent on every request, also on a partial reload. The old input is in req.session.old('email'). Password fields are not kept.

With router.post(url, data, { errorBag: 'login' }) or form.post(url, { errorBag: 'login' }), the client sends the X-Inertia-Error-Bag header. Then the errors are under the bag name: errors.login.email. Use it when one page has two forms.

You do not need to pass errors yourself. A page prop named errors still wins.

docs.title: Redirects
docs.text:
After a form, redirect with redirect(url) or back(req) from Dox.

After PUT, PATCH or DELETE, the browser must follow the redirect with GET, not with the same method. So InertiaMiddleware turns a 302 into 303 for these Inertia requests. You do not need to do anything.

When a controller gives an empty 200 answer to an Inertia request (eg. it returns nothing), InertiaMiddleware sends the browser back to the page it came from, like back(req). Only a Referer of the same site is used. Any other Referer goes to /. A request without X-Inertia gets the empty answer as it is.

Future<DoxResponse> update(DoxRequest req, int id) async {
  // ... save the user
  return redirect('/users'); // 303 for an Inertia PUT
}

To go to an outside site, or any page that is not an Inertia page, use Inertia.location. An Inertia request gets 409 with X-Inertia-Location, and the client loads the url with a full page load. Other requests get 302.

return Inertia.location(req, 'https://checkout.example.com/pay/1');

docs.title: Flash data
docs.text:
Flash data is a short message for the next page, like "User saved". Use Inertia.flash. The next page gets it in page.flash, once.

Future<DoxResponse> store(DoxRequest req) async {
  // ... save the user
  Inertia.flash(req, 'message', 'User saved');
  return redirect('/users');
}

import { usePage } from '@inertiajs/react'

const { flash } = usePage()
// flash.message is 'User saved'

The client also fires a flash event, and calls the onFlash callback of the visit. Inertia.flash needs SessionMiddleware.

docs.title: Vite
docs.text:
In dev mode, @vite loads @vite/client and the entry files from the Vite dev server. With reactRefresh: true it adds the React Fast Refresh code first.

Dox is in dev mode when:

  • devServerUrl is set, or
  • the file public/hot exists. Its text is the dev server url. Some Vite plugins write this file while vite runs. Dox ignores this file only when APP_ENV is production (in any case, like Production), and prints a warning. Other values, like staging or an empty value, still use it.

In production (no dev server), Dox reads public/build/.vite/manifest.json. @vite gives a <link> tag for the css of each entry and of the chunks it imports, and a <script type="module"> tag for each entry.

Set devServerUrl from the env, so production does not use it:

lib/config/inertia.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_inertia/dox_inertia.dart';

InertiaConfig inertiaConfig = InertiaConfig(
  entryPoints: <String>['resources/js/app.jsx'],
  devServerUrl: Env.get<String>('APP_ENV') == 'development'
      ? 'http://localhost:5173'
      : null,
  reactRefresh: true,
);

docs.title: Asset version
docs.text:
Each page has a version. When you deploy new assets, the version changes. A browser with the old version that makes an Inertia GET request gets 409 with X-Inertia-Location. The client then loads the whole page again, with the new assets.

The default version is a hash of the Vite manifest. Dox reads it once per isolate, so restart the server after vite build (a deploy does this). To set your own, use version in the config, eg. the git commit.

docs.title: Root view data
docs.text:
Page props go to the JavaScript page. Sometimes the root view itself needs a value, like the <title> or a CSRF meta tag. Use Inertia.withViewData for that.

Write {{ key }} in the root view:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <meta name="csrf-token" content="{{ csrfToken }}">
    <title>{{ title }}</title>
    @vite
  </head>
  <body>
    @inertia
  </body>
</html>

Set the values in the controller:

Future<DoxResponse> index(DoxRequest req) {
  Inertia.withViewData(req, <String, Object?>{'title': 'Users'});
  return inertia(req, 'Users/Index', <String, dynamic>{
    'users': () => User().query().all(),
  });
}
  • The values are for the root view only. They are not page props. They are never sent as JSON, so an Inertia request (a link or a form) does not get them.
  • Each value is HTML escaped (&, <, >, " and '). A null value gives empty text.
  • Put a value in text or in a quoted attribute only. It is not safe inside a <script> block, an unquoted attribute or a link address.
  • You can call withViewData many times, also in a middleware. The data is merged. For the same key, the last call wins.
  • A key has letters, digits and _. The spaces are optional: {{title}} works too.
  • {{ key }} with a key that you did not set stays as it is. So set every key that the root view uses.
  • {{ csrfToken }} is filled for you with the CSRF token of the session. It needs SessionMiddleware. With no session it stays as it is. Your own csrfToken value wins.
  • Only {{ key }} in the root view file is replaced. The same text in a prop, or in the HTML from the SSR server, is not touched.

A title set this way is for the first page load only. On later visits the browser does not load the root view again. There, the <Head> component of the Inertia client changes the title. So set the title in <Head> too. With SSR, the <Head> title is also added to the first page, so use only one of the two for the title.

docs.title: Another root view for some pages
docs.text:
Inertia.setRootView uses another HTML file for one request, eg. for an admin area:

Future<DoxResponse> dashboard(DoxRequest req) {
  Inertia.setRootView(req, 'resources/views/admin.html');
  return inertia(req, 'Admin/Dashboard');
}

RootViewMiddleware does the same for every page of a router:

class AdminRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[
    const RootViewMiddleware('resources/views/admin.html'),
  ];

  // ...
}

The path is from the project root, like rootView in the config. Use a fixed path. Never pass a value from the request: it could show any file of the server as the page. The file works like the default root view, with @vite, @inertia and {{ key }}.

docs.title: History encryption
docs.text:
The browser keeps the props of each page in its history, so the back button is fast. After a logout, the back button can still show a page with private data. History encryption stops this.

With it, the browser encrypts the page data before it goes into the history. The key stays in the browser, in session storage. When you clear the history, the browser makes a new key, and the old pages can not be read any more. The back button then asks the server for the page again.

The browser can only encrypt on HTTPS, and on localhost.

Turn it on for all pages in the config:

lib/config/inertia.dart
InertiaConfig inertiaConfig = InertiaConfig(
  encryptHistory: true,
);

Or for one page, in the controller. false turns it off for one page when the config turns it on.

Future<DoxResponse> show(DoxRequest req) {
  Inertia.encryptHistory(req);
  // Inertia.encryptHistory(req, false);
  return inertia(req, 'Account/Show', props);
}

Or for all pages of a router, with EncryptHistoryMiddleware:

class AccountRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[const EncryptHistoryMiddleware()];

  // ...
}

Call Inertia.clearHistory(req) to clear the history, for example on logout:

Future<DoxResponse> logout(DoxRequest req) async {
  // ... sign the user out
  Inertia.clearHistory(req);
  return redirect('/login');
}

The next Inertia page tells the browser to clear its history, once. The mark is kept in the session, so it works with a redirect. It needs SessionMiddleware. With no session, it only works when the same request renders a page with inertia(...).

docs.title: Server side rendering (SSR)
docs.text:
By default, the first visit gets an empty page, and the browser renders it. With SSR, the first visit gets the full HTML of the page. Search engines can read it, and the visitor sees the page sooner.

The page is rendered by the Inertia SSR server. It is a Node process that you build with Vite and run next to your Dox app. On a first visit, Dox sends the page to it and puts the answer in the root view. Inertia requests (links and forms) never use it.

docs.title: 1. The SSR entry file
2. Hydrate in the browser
docs.text:
The browser must reuse the HTML from the server, and not render the page again. Change setup in your app file:

resources/js/app.jsx
import { createInertiaApp } from '@inertiajs/react'
import { createRoot, hydrateRoot } from 'react-dom/client'

createInertiaApp({
  resolve: (name) => {
    const pages = import.meta.glob('./Pages/**/*.jsx', { eager: true })
    return pages[`./Pages/${name}.jsx`]
  },
  setup({ el, App, props }) {
    if (el.hasAttribute('data-server-rendered')) {
      hydrateRoot(el, <App {...props} />)
    } else {
      createRoot(el).render(<App {...props} />)
    }
  },
})

The else part is for a page that was sent without SSR.

docs.title: 3. Build and run
docs.text:
Build the browser files, then the SSR file. Then start the SSR server with Node.

vite build
vite build --ssr resources/js/ssr.jsx --outDir bootstrap/ssr
node bootstrap/ssr/ssr.js

The file is ssr.js when your package.json has "type": "module". Else it is ssr.mjs. The SSR file loads your packages from node_modules, so keep that folder on the server. Keep the Node process running with your process manager, like the Dox app. Build and start it again on each deploy.

docs.title: 4. Turn it on
The root view with SSR
docs.text:
The root view needs no change. It must have @inertia. Head tags also need a </head> tag.

  • The HTML from the SSR server goes in place of @inertia. It holds the page data and the rendered <div id="app">.
  • The head tags of the page (from the <Head> component, like <title>) go right before the first </head>. </HEAD> works too. A root view with no </head> gets no head tags.

When your pages set a title with <Head>, remove the <title> from the root view, so the page does not have two.

docs.title: When the SSR server fails
docs.text: When the SSR server is down, is too slow, or gives a bad answer, the visitor gets the normal page and the browser renders it. No error is shown. Dox prints one warning to stderr for the first failure, and no more until the SSR server works again.

docs.title: Not included
docs.text:
• The Inertia 1 and 2 clients. They read the page from <div id="app" data-page="...">. Use the Inertia 3 client.
  • Once props, scroll props (infinite scroll), prependProps, deepMergeProps and matchPropsOn.
  • Partial reloads of nested props with dots, like only: ['auth.user']. Ask for the top level prop (auth).
  • Starting the SSR server from Dox. You run the Node process yourself.

Inertia needs sessions for the errors, flash data and redirects. The client sends the CSRF token by itself, see CSRF.

docs.title: Middleware
docs.text:
Middleware is code that runs before the controller, and if you want, after it too.

Use it for checks like login, logging or rate limits, or to change the response.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
A middleware gets the request. It then does one of these:

  • Return the request. Dox goes on to the next middleware, then to the controller.
  • Return something else (a String, a Map, a response(...)). Dox sends it as the response. The controller does not run.
  • Throw an exception, like NotFoundHttpException(). Dox sends the error response. See Response: errors.

A middleware can be async. Dox waits for it.

docs.title: Class based middleware
docs.text:
Create one with the CLI. It writes lib/app/http/middleware/logger.middleware.dart.

dox make:middleware Logger

Write your code in handle. For example:

lib/app/http/middleware/logger.middleware.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class LoggerMiddleware implements IDoxMiddleware {
  @override
  dynamic handle(IDoxRequest req) {
    print('${req.method} ${req.uri.path}');
    return req; // go on to the next middleware
  }
}

Then put it on a route:

lib/routes/api.dart
Route.get('/ping', <dynamic>[LoggerMiddleware(), (WebController c) => c.pong]);

Note

handle takes an IDoxRequest, not a DoxRequest.

Warning

Do not forget return req. A middleware that returns null ends the request with an empty 200, and the controller does not run. When APP_ENV is development or local, Dox prints a warning to stderr the first time a middleware does this.

docs.title: Function based middleware
docs.text:
A function that takes a DoxRequest also works as middleware.

lib/app/http/middleware/api_key.middleware.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

dynamic apiKeyMiddleware(DoxRequest req) {
  String apiKey = Env.get<String>('API_KEY');
  String given = req.header('X-Api-Key') ?? '';
  if (apiKey.isEmpty || !Hash.equals(given, apiKey)) {
    return response(<String, String>{'message': 'Unauthorized'}).statusCode(401);
  }
  return req;
}

The key comes from the API_KEY env variable, not from the code. Hash.equals takes the same time for every wrong key, so the time does not tell how much of the key was right. A normal == stops at the first wrong character.

lib/routes/api.dart
Route.get('/ping', <dynamic>[apiKeyMiddleware, (WebController c) => c.pong]);

docs.title: Run code after the controller
docs.text:
A middleware can also get a next function. await next() runs the rest of the middleware and the controller, and gives the response. Code after that line runs after the controller. Change the response, then return it.

lib/app/http/middleware/see_other.middleware.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// a redirect after a form post becomes 303, so the browser does a GET
class SeeOtherMiddleware implements IDoxNextMiddleware {
  @override
  Future<DoxResponse> handle(DoxRequest req, Next next) async {
    // before the controller
    DoxResponse res = await next();
    // after the controller
    if (res.status == 302 && req.httpRequest.method != 'GET') {
      res.statusCode(303);
    }
    return res;
  }
}

The response from next() is always a DoxResponse, so you can use all its methods: statusCode(...), header(...), cookie(...), content(...). Read the status with res.status (null means 200) and the headers with res.headers.

When the controller (or a later middleware) throws an error, next() does not throw. It gives the error response from the ExceptionHandler, like a 404 or a 422. So the code after next() always runs.

A function works too. It takes the request and next:

Future<DoxResponse> timerMiddleware(DoxRequest req, Next next) async {
  Stopwatch watch = Stopwatch()..start();
  DoxResponse res = await next();
  return res.header('X-Time', '${watch.elapsedMilliseconds}ms');
}

To stop early, return a response and do not call next().

Speed

A route with no next middleware runs exactly as before. Only routes that have one pay for the extra step.

docs.title: Run code after the answer is sent
docs.text:
A middleware can run code after the answer has gone to the client, in its terminate method. Use it for work the client should not wait for: logs, metrics, cleanup. Implement IDoxTerminableMiddleware:

lib/app/http/middleware/metrics.middleware.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class MetricsMiddleware implements IDoxMiddleware, IDoxTerminableMiddleware {
  @override
  dynamic handle(IDoxRequest req) => req; // before the controller

  @override
  void terminate(DoxRequest req, DoxResponse res) {
    // the answer is already sent
    print('${req.method} ${req.uri.path} ${res.status}');
  }
}
  • res.status is the status that was sent, also for an error answer.
  • terminate can be async.
  • An error in terminate goes to ExceptionHandler.report. It never changes the answer.
  • The handle part is not needed. A class can implement only IDoxTerminableMiddleware.

Speed

Dox checks each route once for such a middleware. Other routes do not pay for it.

docs.title: From any code, with AfterResponse
docs.text:
